The Mind-Dharmadhātu comprises two gates: first, the gate of the true suchness of mind; second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind.
Although these two gates each comprehensively encompass all phenomena, these two gates are neither separate from one another nor are they confused.

This is because the waves that comprise water are not still, and the water that comprises the waves is not moving. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states in the "Chapter on the Inquiry of Vimalakīrti":

"The realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings are ultimately without distinction; to know them all completely is the domain of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the verse from the "Forest of Awakening" says:
"One should know that the Buddha and the mind are both, in their essential nature, inexhaustible. And the Deity of the Forest Lord says: "Able, within one..."
Within all differentiated objects, one enters the samādhi of equality and non-differentiation;
within this undifferentiated and equal Dharma, one manifests the wisdom of mastery that possesses differentiation, and so forth. Regarding the "gate of mutual sublation where there is no locus":

this means that because there is no objective reality, it is not irrational; thus, the objective reality is [simultaneously] non-reality. As the Sūtra says: "Form is itself emptiness. Because there is no rationality, it is not a thing; thus, rationality is [simultaneously] non-rationality.
This is the principle. The Sūtra says: "Emptiness is itself form. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:

"The conditioned and the unconditioned are two dharmas that are neither conjoined nor dispersed. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "All dharmas are briefly of two kinds, namely the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Among these, the conditioned is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; the unconditioned is neither unconditioned nor conditioned," and so forth. Thus we know.
It cannot be said to be conditioned or unconditioned; it cannot be said to be identical to form or not identical to form, identical to emptiness or not identical to emptiness, and so forth.
Therefore, while cultivation is naturally without a basis, phenomena do not lose their reality. For anything that has a point of reliance fails to accord with the Dharma.
The tenth dedication states: "Dedicating like the dharma-realm’s aspect of being without dependence," and so forth. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in the "Appearance" chapter, states:
"The nature of phenomena does not reside in verbal discourse; it is beyond speech, free from speech, and eternally quiescent.

Regarding the gate of the total integration of the three pairs, wherein both nature and characteristics are transcended, there are ten sub-sections: first, because characteristics are transcended, phenomena vanish and are identical with principle; second, because...

1. Because of the departure from nature (*svabhāva*), principle (*li*) is extinguished while remaining identical to phenomena (*shi*). 2. Because of the departure from nature without extinguishing nature, principle is identical to phenomena yet principle persists;

this is because that which is not principle is taken as principle. 3. Because of the departure from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) without destroying characteristics, phenomena are identical to principle yet phenomena persist.
This is because one takes that which is not a phenomenon to be a phenomenon. For this reason, phenomena and principle are made to coincide, being without obstruction and without attainment.

Fifth, because it is free from the non-differentiation of nature and free from the non-differentiation of characteristics, there is the simultaneous negation of both phenomena and principle, transcending words and thought.

Sixth, because they are neither destroyed, nor different, nor extinguished, the two realms of initial phenomena and principle both exist together, manifesting before one in a brilliant and visible manner. Seventh...

Because it is neither obliterated nor destroyed, neither different nor devoid of characteristics or intrinsic nature, it constitutes the single reality of the dharma-dhātu, which is free from attainment.
Thus, this wondrous Dharma that transcends sight and hearing is not without constant penetration through seeing and hearing;

and this profound meaning that defies thought and deliberation has never been subject to verbalization or conceptualization. Eighth, by means of the principle that integrates phenomena, it causes phenomena to be without limitation, such that they are as pervasive as the principle itself.
Thus, one enters all; as the principle encompasses all, so all enters one equally. Therefore, each and every phenomenon of dependent origination individually subsumes the inexhaustible *dharmadhātu*.

Ninth, because the *dharmadhātu* of cause and effect each fully subsumes the other, the body of Samantabhadra is infinitely present in every Buddha, and within every pore of every Buddha, Samantabhadra appears in infinite layers. Tenth, the *dharmadhātu* of cause and effect...
There is no differentiated phenomenon that is not encompassed, for there is nothing left out within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

This is because each individual phenomenon, each practice, each stage, and each virtue individually encompasses a layer upon layer of phenomena. Thus, vast lands, great bodies, minute motes of dust, and even the pores of the skin are all entirely inexhaustible.
For this reason, when Sudhana encountered the Rishi, they held hands for many kalpas, traveling through boundless realms.
A single hair-pore of Samantabhadra is equal to all Buddhas. Among the ten [aspects], the final three constitute the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (shishi wu'ai).

Taking these to encompass the preceding ones, there is no longer any separate practice of phenomena and principle; for since the one and the many are not identical, they simply return to the unobstructed Dharma-realm of the One.

Yet, by taking up one, all are fully encompassed; they differ only according to the specific gate through which they are explained. Thus, in their totality, they are the *dharmadhātu*; in their particularity, they are phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth.

When identical, they are the non-contradictory *dharmadhātu*; when differentiated, phenomena and principle are opposed. When established, they are equally expounded as the *dharmadhātu*; when disintegrated, each abides in its own phenomena and so forth.

Therefore, there is no attainment, for it is a layering of the inexhaustible within the inexhaustible. The rest is as explained in the section on the "Gate of the Meaning of What is Expounded. Already [concluded].

The object of entry has been explained. Second, the subject who enters is clarified. In general, this refers to the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, which encompass everything without exception. Specifically, there are two aspects:
first, entry by means of the body; second, entry by means of the mind. Since the body is realized through the mind, the mind is extensively analyzed. This is entry by means of the mind.
There are three: first, right faith; second, right understanding; and third, right practice. These three are each fully present within each of the three aforementioned stages of entry.
That is to say, when entering the aforementioned principle-dharmadhātu, one must first have right faith—profoundly accepting, desiring, and delighting [in it] so as to purify the mind.
Next, there is right understanding—decisively comprehending with clarity such that one cannot be led astray. Finally, one must...

Right Practice (*samyak-pratipatti*) means that the mind reaches this principle; through understanding, practice arises, and as practice arises, understanding is transcended. Although the characteristics of understanding are transcended, one does not lose that understanding.
Therefore, these three matters must also be perfectly integrated. If one were to correlate each of the various practices with what precedes them, they can be understood through reflection;
a brief explanation is provided below.
The third section, concerning the perfect accord between subject and object, clearly elucidates the meaning of "entry. "Entry" is a term for thorough comprehension and realization.

In general, there are two stages: first, the stage of fruition (*phala*); second, the stage of cause (*hetu*). Regarding the stage of fruition, there are two types: first, the ultimate and perfected fruition.
This refers to the ocean of fruition realized by the Tathāgata himself, which transcends words and is beyond the reach of mind and intellect; it can only be accessed through samādhi.
The manifestation of signs and the accomplishment of benefit are expressed through words; this is precisely the fundamental portion [of the teaching].
It is as when the Tathāgata himself entered the *siṃhaviśpandita-samādhi* (the Lion’s Stretch Samādhi), transmitting mind-to-mind and causing the great assembly to suddenly realize the *dharmadhātu*.

Second, when that which is capable of realization accords with suchness and merges with the Buddha-wisdom, it is called the "ocean of fruition. This too cannot be described; hence it is said to be like the tracks of a bird in the sky.
The wisdom of the Muni is like the characteristic of wind in space; it is extremely difficult to discern through conceptual differentiation.

It is only by following its characteristics and through practice that one speaks of its accordant realization, which is termed the "realized wisdom of the ten stages. [Section on] the Second: The Stage of Causality.

As for Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, they are designated as "causality" because they can be expressed through conventional language. In explaining the characteristics of this causality, there are briefly two gates. First, the specific...

The Realization of Clear Wisdom. This consists of a comparative analysis of the two bodies and wisdom. Regarding the first [of these], there are five gates: (1) the distinctness of subject and object; (2) the non-duality of subject and object;
(3) the simultaneous submergence of subject and object; (4) the non-attainment of existence and non-existence; and (5) the inclusion of the whole by the mention of one.

These five gates apply universally to both phenomena and principle (*dharma* and *tattva*). Since the realization of the principle is subtle and hidden, I shall explain it first. First, the distinctness of subject and object...
"Clearly manifest" means that by means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one accords with the principle of non-differentiation. Mind and object merge; wisdom and the spirit unite.
Thus, the realizing wisdom and the realized principle become one in their single, equal characteristic. Therefore, the aforementioned sutra says:

"Entering the treasury of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-garbha*), wisdom is without differentiation. Because the treasury of the dharma-realm is inherently without difference, the realizing wisdom now becomes identical to it.
The Dharma-realm is without discrimination; it is free from the marks of subject and object, and is entirely ungraspable. Thus it is said: "How distant is the Way?
It is true in every encounter. How distant is the Sage? Embodying it, one becomes divine. Because one unites with the Way through this divinity, one is free from the grasping of subject and object.
Although there is no dualistic grasping, it is not that characteristics are entirely absent. It is like the sun joined with space:

though they occupy the same place and are difficult to distinguish, one cannot say that light and space are one. This is because sunlight is not space; light possesses the function of illumination, as its essence is form (*rūpa*). Space is not sunlight;
it lacks the function of illumination, existing only as the absence of obstruction (*anupalabdhi*). The realization of principle by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise...

Thus, although they share the same characteristic, are equal, and are of one flavor, they cannot be said to be identical. Wisdom is not that which is realized; it possesses the function of illumination because it is dependently originated.
Principle is not the realizer; it lacks the function of illumination because it is merely quiescent. Therefore, while they are equal, wisdom and principle remain distinct.
Regarding the second point, the non-duality of subject and object: this is because one knows that all phenomena are precisely the mind.

Regarding self-nature (*svabhāva*): by means of the wisdom that is identical to its own substance, one illuminates the substance of the mind. To raise up one [aspect] is to encompass the whole. Raising up the principle (*tattva*) encompasses wisdom;
wisdom is not external to the principle. Raising up wisdom encompasses the principle; the substance of wisdom is itself quiescent. Therefore, the aforementioned sutra says:

"There is no suchness (*tathatā*) outside of wisdom that could be entered by wisdom, nor is there wisdom outside of suchness that could realize suchness. It is like a single bright pearl; the pearl itself possesses [its radiance]."
The light returns to illuminate the substance of the pearl; it is not that there is a separate light coming to illuminate the pearl. A good spiritual friend said:

"That which is the function of the substance is called 'knowing' (jñāna); that which is the substance of the function is called 'quiescence' (śānti). Since substance and function are not two, knowing and quiescence cannot be divided into two.
It is not only the single character 'knowing' that is the gate to all wonders. Whether pure or defiled, whether Buddha or mind, [there is no distinction]."
Not all are so. This is the single-character Dharma-gate, the one-taste true Way. Regarding the third point, where both subject and object are extinguished:
because wisdom is identical to principle, wisdom is not wisdom, for it is entirely identical to principle and lacks independent substance.

Because principle is identical to wisdom, principle is not principle, for it is entirely identical to wisdom and lacks self-establishment. Thus, the two mutually negate one another, such that both principle and wisdom are extinguished.
Quiescence. Just as waves are water, the aspect of movement is empty; since water is the waves, the aspect of stillness is likewise hidden.
Once both movement and stillness have vanished, then essence and appearance are equally transcended. As the Sūtra says: "In the equal and true Dharma-realm, there is no Buddha and no sentient beings.
And again: "The profound realm of the Tathāgata is equal in measure to space; all sentient beings enter it, yet in reality there is nothing [to be entered]."
Entering [this state], one realizes that there is not only no Buddha and no sentient beings, but also no realm and no non-realm, no entry and no non-entry.
One should know it thus; through such faith and understanding, the characteristics of dharmas do not arise. With no mind directed toward principle, principle vanishes;

with no mind directed toward wisdom, wisdom is forgotten. Serene and without dependence, principle spontaneously merges in the profound mystery. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "There is no wisdom, nor is there..."
There is attainment; there is that which is attained and that which is realized. Within the Buddha-dharma, this constitutes *adhimāna* (arrogance).

While the preceding gate forcefully asserts "mind itself is Buddha," this present gate likewise asserts "neither mind nor Buddha. This is the Dharma-gate of non-characterization (*amala-dharmaparyāya*).

Since even "non-existence" does not persist, how much less could "existence" remain? Regarding the fourth [gate], the non-grasping of both persistence and cessation: it is because the previous three gates have explained the sequence of existence and the essence of the body.
Because there is no duality: if one considers it in terms of being free from characteristics and free from intrinsic nature, then both subject and object vanish together;

if one considers it in terms of not destroying nature and characteristics, then subject and object remain distinct. Since it is precisely by being free from nature and characteristics that they are not destroyed, there is no grasping at existence or non-existence.

This does not mean that one must first sweep away all things and block sight and hearing before one can accord with the Truth. Rather, because both are simultaneously negated and eternally quiescent, they are said to "vanish together. Quiescence...
To illuminate the mind and its objects simultaneously is called "dual persistence. Because it illuminates while negating, it is said to be "without attainment.

This is termed "stillness that neither discards nor illuminates"; movement does not depart from stillness. When both are absent, one correctly enters the state where stillness and illumination flow as one.
Fifth, regarding "raising one to encompass all": the four gates listed above are intended, first, to provide a sequential path of stages, and second, to synthesize the various scriptures.

Although there are differing explanations, since the ultimate principle is already harmonized and accords with the Way without duality, the four gates are of one intent; by citing one, all are fully encompassed.

Just as a single drop of the great ocean contains the full flavor of the sea and also possesses the essence of the hundred rivers, it is only through a mind that is humble, open, and harmonious that one can perceive its profound mystery.

Thus far, the Dharma-realm of the realization of principle has been briefly explained. If we consider the realization of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomenon, as well as the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena...

Regarding the realization of the *dharmadhātu*: it is simply as previously described regarding the *dharmadhātu*. When one’s faith and understanding are clear and lucid, the mental activities will spontaneously manifest, and one will suddenly realize and enter [it].

If one were to describe its characteristics, they would become even more vast and extensive. Just as by recognizing the conventional and the ultimate, one realizes the wisdom of the conventional and the ultimate;

and by recognizing the Middle Way, one realizes the wisdom of the Middle Way—when wisdom is spoken of apart from its objects, that wisdom cannot be known. Therefore, through subtle and careful analysis, one will naturally understand it for oneself.
One enters into realization. Furthermore, by means of the distinct clarity of subject and object, one realizes the *dharmadhātu* of phenomena;

by means of the single characteristic of subject and object, one realizes the *dharmadhātu* of principle, as well as the gate of the non-obtaining (*anupalabdhi*) of the mutual identity of phenomenon and principle. When both subject and object are extinguished, one realizes the gate of the non-obtaining of form and substance within the non-duality of phenomenon and principle.
With neither existence nor non-existence obtained, one fully realizes the gate of the unobstructed non-obtaining of phenomenon and principle; thus, quiescence and illumination are without—

Second, the single mind accords with the Middle Way in which emptiness and existence are mutually fused; by raising one, all are fully encompassed, thereby realizing the gate of the non-obstruction of phenomena (shishi wuai).
Since the Dharma-realm that is realized is mutually interpenetrating, the realizing subject must likewise accord with it through a single principle, for by realizing one, all are realized.
Only those who have extinguished words can harmonize with the Dao; only those whose [conceptual] attachments have dissolved can accord with the Principle.
Penetration. Those who have darkened their minds may be granted the True One; those who have cast aside wisdom may be made equal to the Sage.

"Matching Meanings" (gēyì) is a narrow and dogmatic approach, making it difficult to discuss the Way with such people. Second, regarding the mutual correspondence between body and wisdom, there are also five stages:

first, realization through the body, which is like entering a multi-storied pavilion and then closing the door behind one; second, realization through wisdom, which is the discernment of boundless phenomena and principles; third...

First is simultaneous realization: entering the body of Samantabhadra and comprehending it universally. Second is simultaneous merging: the illumination of wisdom is non-dual, such that both [subject and object] vanish.
Third is simultaneous perfection: attaining the sovereign mastery of Samantabhadra. Furthermore, since body and wisdom are non-dual, the mention of one fully encompasses both.
Fourth is simultaneous fusion through the six aspects (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*): transcending words and cutting off discursive thought. This concludes the definitive determination of the fundamental principle.
Commentary on the Newly Translated Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Zhenyuan Era, Scroll One.
Engraved by imperial decree at Daexingwang Temple in the Kingdom of Goryeo during the year of Yihai, the first year of the Shouchang era.
*Commentary on the Newly Translated Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Zhenyuan Era*, Scroll Two (covering the first five scrolls and five lines of the first fascicle).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Dachongfu Monastery in Taiyuan Prefecture, by Imperial Decree.

[The commentary] consists of five gates and two divisions of the sūtra. Regarding the five gates: first, the fifth gate, the Gate of the Profundity and Shallowness of Cultivation and Realization; second, the sixth gate, the Gate of Manifesting the Nature and Substance of the Teaching; third, the seventh gate, the Gate of the Categories, Chapters, and Assemblies; fourth, the eighth gate, the Gate of the Transmission... [text continues].

The Gate of Transmitting the Penetration of Response (Gantongmen). Fifth, the Gate of Explaining the Title of the Sutra. The sutra has two divisions: first, the Introductory Division (Nidāna); second, the Division of the Request (Yingfen).

Fifth, regarding the discernment of the shallowness and depth of cultivation and realization: throughout this single scripture, the various sections from beginning to end all clarify cultivation and realization.

Fearing that the text may be overly voluminous, I have again extracted its essentials. Since the Great Master’s Dharma-eye vanished at the Twin Trees, the transmission of the lamp by successive sages has shone on without interruption.
Taking the holy teachings as a mirror and taking mental resonance as a secret tally, it is therefore said:
It is said that the mind is transmitted by means of the mind and does not reside in words and letters. If one can grasp what lies beyond the written text, why worry about the text itself?
One cannot mistake the trap for the fish, nor can one discard the mirror while seeking the image.

Since the single flavor became turbid and chaotic, dividing into Northern and Southern schools, the teachings of the expressive and the expressed were established as the two studies of Samādhi and Prajñā. Furthermore, within the study of Prajñā, the categories of Nature (Svabhāva) and Characteristics (Lakṣaṇa) were distinguished; and within Samādhi...
Among scholars, there are differences between the gradual and the sudden approaches. The two schools of *Xing* (nature) and *xiang* (phenomena) have been explained as before.

The distinctions between the gradual and the sudden shall now be briefly discussed. Regarding those who speak of the gradual: they examine the mind, cultivate pure expedient means, and penetrate the sutras;

this may involve sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation, or gradual cultivation followed by gradual awakening. Regarding those who speak of the sudden: they point directly to the essence of the mind, or suddenly discard all language, or suddenly...

There are those who awaken suddenly and then cultivate, and there are those for whom there is neither cultivation nor awakening. Although these differ, both seek to recognize the mind and together hope to perceive the principle.

If one grasps the meaning, both paths are excellent; though the routes diverge, they reach the same destination. If one loses the essential intent, both are harmed; the loss of the sheep is no different in either case.
Now, I employ words as a trap to convey the principle, so that you may catch the moon at the tip of the finger. As for what is awakened to, some say it is the essence of the mind free from thought.

The nature of reality is intrinsically pure, neither arising nor ceasing; this primarily pertains to the gradual approach. Alternatively, it is described as non-abiding emptiness and quiescence, true suchness beyond all marks;
or as false emptiness and true existence; or as false existence and true emptiness; or as the mind itself being the Buddha, or neither mind nor Buddha;

or as the Buddha-dharma being inherently present. These mostly belong to the sudden approach. Nevertheless, none of these deviate from the nature and characteristics of the mind, and thus they are all mutually compatible.
Application. If one is clear enough to awaken to and enter the Dharma, the thousand gates do not depart from concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, the two gates of concentration and wisdom are like the sun and moon in the sky, or like heaven and earth in the *I Ching*. Why is this? For the mind is like water and fire: when it is clarified and gathered, its function is complete;
when it is grasped and dispersed, its function is diminished. Thus, when waves stir, reflections shatter; when water is turbid, reflections are obscured. [Only when] clear...

When clarity brings stillness to transparency, both the great and the small are reflected therein. Without concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one is either mad or foolish. To cultivate only a single gate is gradual and remote;
if both are applied together in dual quiescence, only then does it constitute the true gate. To become a Dvipada-sarvajña (the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings) is impossible without this.
If one says that not giving rise to the mind constitutes the path of cultivation, then concentration (samādhi) is the gate.

If one says to look at the mind, contemplate the mind, realize the essence of the mind, awaken to the mind, seek the mind, or harmonize the mind, then wisdom (prajñā) is the gate. If one says there is no-thought and no-cultivation, then concentration is the gate.
If one says to know the emptiness and stillness of the mind, to know that seeing is non-thought, and to have a clear penetration that illuminates stillness, then wisdom is the gate. If...
To say that "tranquil illumination" or "knowing non-thought" constitutes the dual clarification of the gates of samādhi and prajñā;

whereas to say that "raising an eyebrow or staring with wide eyes" is all called the Way—that is what is meant by "cultivation. This encompasses two meanings: first, it causes one to know that whatever meets the eye is the Way.

This is the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*). Second, causing the mind to have nothing to which it clings; this is the gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The rest may be understood by analogy; they do not transcend concentration and wisdom.

As for the characteristics of clear awakening, they do not exceed two types: first, awakening through understanding (*adhigama*), which refers to clearly comprehending the nature and characteristics [of phenomena];

second, awakening through realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), which refers to the mind reaching the profound ultimate. Regarding the clarification of gradual and sudden [awakening], there are many approaches. If one speaks of the "sudden,"...

"Awakening through gradual cultivation" refers here to awakening through understanding. This means that after one has suddenly realized the nature of the mind, one subsequently engages in gradual cultivation and study to bring about its perfect realization.
Thus, awakening is like the moonlight shining, which instantly illuminates all phenomena; cultivation is like wiping a mirror, which becomes increasingly polished and bright.

If one speaks of "gradual cultivation and sudden awakening," it means that first one gathers all objects into the mind-only; next, one perceives that the mind is fundamentally pure; and finally, both mind and objects are simultaneously stilled. In a flash...
Arising is non-arising; the boundaries of past and future are severed. It is as tranquil as a still ocean, as vast as empty space. This is called "awakening" (wu) by way of its realization (zheng).
Thus, cultivation is like polishing a mirror, while awakening is like the clarity of the mirror. If one speaks of gradual cultivation and gradual awakening, this too is a form of realized awakening;
in this case, cultivation and awakening are both like ascending a tower: as the feet step higher, that which is reflected becomes increasingly distant. If one speaks of sudden awakening...

"Sudden cultivation" (dunxiū) encompasses three meanings. If one first attains awakening and subsequently practices, it is called "awakening" (wù) when one suddenly realizes the state of vast openness.

It is called "cultivation" (xiū) when, without viewing, without realizing, without gathering, and without encompassing, one is expansively in accord with the Way. This refers to awakening through understanding.
This concentration serves as the gateway. It is like a mirror that becomes clear of its own accord without being wiped or polished.

If one says that realization comes after cultivation—meaning that by relying on prior practice, one suddenly perceives the nature of the mind and this is termed "realization"—then cultivation is like taking medicine and realization is like the curing of the illness.
If one says that cultivation and realization are simultaneous—meaning that there is no deliberate mind and one forgets even illumination, remaining in spontaneous stillness—[this is another aspect].

When one knows this, concentration and wisdom are practiced in tandem. Like a clear mirror that reflects myriad forms instantaneously without intention, one awakens to the Way and attains realization.
If it is said that all Buddha-dharmas are inherently possessed, this is called "sudden. In a single thought-moment, the ten perfections and myriad practices are fully complete.
To call this "cultivation" is like drinking the water of the great ocean; awakening is like obtaining the flavor of the hundred rivers.
This applies equally to both understanding and realization. If one says "neither mind nor Buddha," it is called "sudden. To have no-thought and no-cultivation is called "cultivation";

this refers to the sudden [teaching] in terms of sweeping away traces to reveal the principle. Cultivating by way of the gate of concentration (samādhi) takes this as awakening; this also applies equally to both understanding and realization. If...
To speak of neither gradual nor sudden is what is called "sudden"; to speak of neither awakening nor non-awakening is what is called "awakening.

This, too, is termed "sudden" by erasing traces and focusing on principle. It applies to the cultivation of the gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and it also encompasses both understanding and realization. If one truly grasps the meaning, all becomes concentration and wisdom;
if one loses the essential point, it becomes deluded thought, which then falls into the state of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If one says that what is called "sudden" clarifies...

Principle cannot be divided; when awakening reaches its ultimate, it illuminates through sudden clarity. This meaning admits no duality. Awakening that is non-dual accords with a principle that is indivisible.
Thus, when both principle and wisdom are explained together, it is called "sudden awakening"; yet, in terms of realization alone, it is designated as "awakening."

Faith and understanding are termed "cultivation. If one speaks of establishing sequential stages, it is called "gradual" (zhan) rather than "sudden" (dun); yet this also encompasses both understanding and realization.

This refers to the meaning of "sudden" within the Sudden Teaching that extends back to the preceding [gradual] sense. According to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, four types of gradual and four types of sudden are taught.

Regarding the "four gradual [processes]": first, like the mango fruit, which ripens gradually and not instantaneously; second, like the works of a potter, which are completed gradually and not instantaneously;
third, like the great earth, which grows [its vegetation] gradually and not instantaneously; and fourth, like the mastery of an art, which is achieved gradually and not instantaneously.

These four refer to the ten levels of faith and the three stages of worthiness prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*). Regarding the "four instantaneous [processes]": first, like a bright mirror, which reflects all things instantaneously.
First, like the sun and moon suddenly illuminating all forms and images; second, like the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) suddenly cognizing all objects;

third, like the light of a Buddha suddenly capable of radiating illumination; and fourth, [the nature of reality]. These four refer to the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) attained from the first bhūmi upward.

They are divided into four based on the *sambhogakāya* and *dharmakāya* of the first and eighth bhūmis respectively. Thus, while the practice and cultivation are gradual, the realization of the principle is termed "sudden. If...
To designate the *Avataṃsaka* as "sudden and perfect" (*yuántùn*) while characterizing all others as "gradual" (*jiàn*) is based on the meaning of the principles they expound.

That is to say, the fact that the initial mind is suddenly endowed [with all qualities] is termed "sudden"; the adornment of these complete virtues is termed "perfect. There is also the realization of profound contemplation, the meaning of which has been explained previously.

If one were to claim that the initial teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* is termed "sudden," while the subsequent teachings of the Hīnayāna and even the Mahāyāna are [termed gradual], [this would be incorrect].

This constitutes the gradual [approach]. This is based on both the ritual of transformation (*vyavahāra*) and the method of transformation (*dharmopāya*); for it first employs the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in a sudden manner, and subsequently teaches the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) gradually.
If one were to say that teaching impermanence first and permanence later is called "gradual," yet [the Buddha] taught them all at once, [this would be the case].
It is termed "sudden" solely with respect to the ritual of conversion. As for the Dharma taught, there is no difference between the gradual and the sudden.

If one says that entering the Great Vehicle from the Small is called "gradual," while entering directly into the Great Vehicle is called "sudden," this distinction is based on the difference in how the capacities of the practitioners are matched to the Dharma;
yet the Dharma taught does not transcend the Three Vehicles. These three preceding meanings do not pertain to the practice of contemplative cultivation.

Regarding the gradual and the sudden: depending on which one of these—gradual or sudden—one follows, these many approaches are condensed here. How could one dare to dogmatically cling to a single word, claiming it encompasses the entirety of the Buddha-dharma?

Whether it be out of attachment to one’s own views or out of disparagement of the true means [of expression], I pray that all future students will not be overly eager for mere knowledge and will not be attached to names.
Do not disparage the sages; do not be obstructed by words; do not deceive yourself; do not compete in speech or silence. These points are as extensive as the scriptural text.

Sixth, regarding the manifestation of the nature and essence of the teaching: the inexhaustible ocean of teachings has an inconceivable essence and nature. Fundamentally quiescent and solitary, how could it be deep or shallow?
Words are forgotten and conceptual proliferation ceases; it is neither one nor many. Now, by means of the wordless word, its non-existence is manifested.

Regarding the essence of essence, from the shallow to the profound, ten essences are briefly elucidated: first, the essence of vocal sounds and language; second, the essence of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*);

third, the essence that comprehensively encompasses these four factors; fourth, the essence that universally subsumes the signified meaning; fifth, the essence in which all phenomena manifest their meaning;

sixth, the essence in which the apprehended object is subsumed within mind-only; seventh, the essence of entering reality by reconciling conditions; eighth, the essence of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena; ninth...

The essence of all phenomena is non-obtainable; the essence of the ten ocean-seals manifests with brilliant clarity. Among these ten, the first five are solely essence (*tī*), while the latter five are both essence and nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, the first four are common to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), while the latter six pertain exclusively to the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). The first seven are common to the three vehicles (*triyāna*), while the last three pertain solely to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The first eight are categorized under the "teaching of sameness" (*paryāya-śāsana*), while the final two pertain solely to the "distinctive teaching" (*viśeṣa-śāsana*). The essence of the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra] resides precisely in these final two.
Synthesizing the preceding eight [points], there is no obstacle to attainment.

Regarding the essence of the first [category], sound, speech, and language: the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 126) states, "What constitutes the essence of the Buddha’s teaching? One response says:
"It should be stated that its essence is vocal action (*vāk-karman*). Vocal action is that which expresses and signifies; this is what is meant."
Regarding the Buddhist teachings (*buddhadharma*): their names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) are merely functional activities;

they are not the essence of the teaching itself. Second, regarding the "essence consisting of names, phrases, and phonemes": this refers to the claim of certain masters that names and so forth constitute the essence.

A name (*nāma*) expresses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); a phrase (*pada*) expresses a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*); and a phoneme (*vyañjana*) is identical to a syllable (*akṣara*), serving as the basis for the former two. When combined in successive order, they are able to express meaning.
Therefore, it is called the essence of the teaching (*śāstratattva*).

Since sound is merely the basis for names and so forth, the third [position]—which universally includes the essences of all four factors—is that the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu had no fixed attachment; whichever [of the four] he takes, they are all equally valid.
Therefore, it may be applied universally. Thus, that verse says: "The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma;

their essence is either speech or names, and these are subsumed within the aggregates of form and formations. The above is based on the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva vehicles; the internal meaning is likewise largely the same.
This means that when subsuming the provisional under the real, sound constitutes the essence, because sound is the real entity.

When following the essence from its function, name and so forth constitute the essence, because the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes possess the function of being able to express and indicate meaning. When discussing both the provisional and the real together, one generally employs these four dharmas.
These two are mutually dependent, for neither can exist independently on its own.
Regarding the fourth point, which subsumes the essence of the referent (*abhidheya*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (81) states: "The essence of all sūtras is, in brief, of two kinds:
first, the letter (*vyañjana*); second, the meaning (*artha*). If it did not express meaning, it would not be the holy teaching (*āgama*)."
Fifth, regarding the essence of the manifestation of meaning through all phenomena (*dharmas*): this refers to the manifestation of the principles of the teachings.

All phenomena serve as the substance of the teaching (*deśanā*). As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, fascicle three, states: "There are those who perform the Buddha-work by means of light," and so forth. Furthermore, the fourth fascicle of the ten-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"Mahāmati, it is not the case that in all Buddha-fields the Dharma is taught through speech; there are Buddha-fields where [the Dharma is taught] by direct gazing."
The absence of speech is called the preaching of the Dharma, and so forth. Thus, in the world of Gandhavatī, the samādhi is manifested by partaking of fragrant food;

in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, right mindfulness is perfected by listening to the wind through the branches of the trees. Stringed and wind instruments can transmit the mind, and the binding of the eyes serves to preserve the Way.

Since both speech and silence, as well as looking and blinking, are all preaching, then seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are entirely listening. If one can thus attain the Dharma and reach accord with it—
O Divinities, why need there be reliance on verbal discourse? Moreover, in the ocean of the nature of the *Avataṃsaka*, the jeweled nets of the cloud-platforms all proclaim wondrous sounds;
the light from every pore is capable of preaching the Dharma; flowers, fragrances, clouds, and trees are themselves the Dharma-gates of the Dharma-realm;
and lands and sentient beings are fundamentally the true embodiment of the ten bodies. How could any of these not be the teaching? Thus, the Sūtra says: "Lands preach, and sentient beings..."

It is said that all teachings of the three periods of time are taught [here]. Furthermore, it says: "All the various objects of the entire world can all cause the turning of the wheel of Dharma," and so forth.

Regarding the sixth [point], the subsumption of objects as being solely the essence of mind: this generally encompasses the preceding five, as none of them are separate from the mind. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts state:

Because all that exists is a manifestation of mind alone, there are two gates: first, the correspondence between the original and its reflection; second, the complete inclusion of both speaker and listener.

Within the former, based on the various teachings, four propositions are established: 1. There is only the original, no reflection. This refers to the Hīnayāna teachings, because they do not realize that [all is] mind-only.
2. There is both the original and the reflection. This refers to the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna, namely, the Buddha himself...
It is taught that whether in terms of words or meaning, all are manifestations of the pure consciousness associated with the Tathāgata’s wondrous discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*);

this is termed the "essential teaching" (*mauladharma*). Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "According to one interpretation, through the power of the listeners' roots of goodness, fundamental vows, and superior conditions, the aspects of word and meaning arise within the consciousness of the Tathāgata. These aspects of word and meaning are the Buddha's roots of goodness for benefiting others."
That which arises is called "the Buddha's teaching. If the words and meanings manifested upon the consciousness of the listener are called the "image," the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"By the power of the Tathāgata’s compassion, original vows, and superior conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the aspects of words and meanings arise within the consciousness of the listener.

Although these aspects of words and meanings arise directly dependent on the power of one's own roots of goodness, they are designated as 'the Buddha' in reference to their dominant condition (*balavat-pratyaya*)."
It is taught that the third [category] consists solely of reflections without an original; this refers to the Mahāyāna’s ultimate teaching (*siddhānta*).

Apart from the minds of sentient beings, the Buddha-fruit possesses no physical form or vocal qualities; there exists only the persistence of suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*).

These manifest as the Buddha’s physical form and voice preaching the Dharma within the minds of those to be converted whose faculties have matured. Therefore, the holy teachings are merely reflections within the minds of sentient beings.
The *Yamaka-gāthā* states: "The Buddhas have no dharma; what dharma, then, could the Buddha preach? It is only in accordance with their own minds that they speak of such dharmas.
This fourth [point] is neither the original nor the reflection, as explained in the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*). It is not merely that there are no forms or sounds of the Buddha outside the mind;
the images within the minds of sentient beings are likewise empty, for their nature is fundamentally detached from them. To transcend words and cut off deliberation is to be a Buddha.

This is the teaching regarding the ear. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* states: "The one who preaches the Dharma has neither speech nor demonstration; the one who hears the Dharma has neither hearing nor attainment.
These four phrases converge into one, being perfectly interfused and without obstruction, serving as the Tathāgata’s skillful means for gathering in sentient beings.

Regarding the second point, the total inclusion of both speaker and listener: this relies solely upon the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Here, the Buddha is the speaker and sentient beings are the listeners; these two aspects—
This forms four propositions. First, outside the Buddha’s true mind there are no separate sentient beings, because the true mind of sentient beings is identical to the true mind of the Buddha.

Thus, there is only the speaker and no listener; consequently, the teachings spoken are manifested solely by the Buddha. Therefore, within the gateway of the fruit (*phala-dvāra*), all phenomena are subsumed without exception.
How much more so, then, could the teachings spoken not be the Buddha’s own teaching? Thus, the subsequent scripture states: "The wisdom of the Buddha is vast..."

The Great Sameness of empty space pervades the minds of all sentient beings. When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives within his own body all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment and so forth.

Apart from the true mind of sentient beings, there is no separate Buddha, because the true mind of the Buddha is identical to the true mind of sentient beings. Thus, there is only listening and no speaking; therefore, the teachings that are spoken...
That is, sentient beings manifest of themselves. As the Sūtra says: "Know that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind. It further states:

"To contemplate the profound true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of sentient beings is to encompass all phenomena through the gate of causes without exception; how much more so the teachings one hears—could these not be the existence of sentient beings?
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* chapter says: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that their own minds are always possessed of the Buddha in every thought-moment."
Regarding the attainment of perfect enlightenment and so forth: when the true mind of the three Buddhas manifests, it does not prevent the true mind of sentient beings from manifesting;

thus, both speaker and listener coexist, and the two teachings stand together. Sentient beings and Buddhas exist within one another; each is real and not false. Cause and effect interpenetrate, manifesting simultaneously and in their entirety.
Accordingly, according to any single sacred teaching, the whole resides within these two minds. Therefore, the Buddha within the mind of a sentient being is the [Buddha] within the mind of a Buddha.

Sentient beings preach the Dharma; the Buddha within the mind of sentient beings listens to the Buddha preaching the Dharma within the minds of sentient beings. Since the four Buddhas are identical to sentient beings, they are not Buddhas;
since sentient beings are identical to the Buddhas, they are not sentient beings. As they mutually negate one another, both vanish. Preaching and listening are thus quiescent.

According to this single sacred teaching, neither of the two minds exists; thus, there is no listener among the sentient beings within the Buddha’s mind, nor is there a preacher among the sentient beings within their own minds.

The Buddha of the Middle Way has nothing to say. As the Sūtra states: "In the equal and true Dharma-realm, there is neither Buddha nor sentient being. Since even the concepts of "sentient being" and "Buddha" do not exist, who could speak and who could listen?
Nevertheless, because these four lines encompass the whole by mentioning any single part, any given sacred teaching is perfectly integrated and without deficiency;
only thus does it constitute the profound principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
The seventh assembly: entering the true substance by means of conditions. The preceding six gates all enter into the single reality;
there are also two further gates. First, subsuming the derivative within the fundamental: this means that all sacred teachings flow from True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Since the fundamental is suchness, the derivative is also suchness. Second, returning characteristics to their nature: this means that all those various differentiated teachings are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) due to their dependence on conditions. When...

The essence is suchness (*tathatā*). The *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states: "O Great King, the Dharma is fundamentally suchness; the *geya* is suchness; and even the *upadeśa* is suchness.

Eighth is the essence of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu'ai ti*). This means that although the entirety of all teachings is suchness, it does not obstruct the ten [categories].

The two divisions of the teaching’s phenomena remain distinct and clear. Although True Suchness (tathatā) takes its entire substance as all phenomena, it does not lose its single flavor of profound, serene equality.
Because True Suchness is without differentiation, the Buddha’s voice also accords with Suchness without differentiation, for it is always in correspondence with the wisdom of Suchness.
The ninth is the essence of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai ti*). Both its words and meaning are perfect. The words are the Perfect Sound (*yuan yin*).

Within this, it also possesses ten profound gateways (*xuanyuan*). First, as stated in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs": "The Buddha, with a single wondrous voice, causes it to be heard throughout the lands of the ten directions;

all various sounds are fully contained therein, and the rain of Dharma pervades everywhere. This is the teaching-body of simultaneous, complete, and corresponding manifestation (*tongshi juzu xiangying jiaoti*). Second is the "Ten Abodes" (*ershizhu*).
The Chapter says: "If one were to fully expound a single phrase of the Dharma, it would not be exhausted for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, yet the words and meanings would each remain distinct.

By this, the Bodhisattva first generates the aspiration for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*). Thus, the essence of the teaching is neither broad nor narrow; it is also called the "essence of the pure and the mixed.
A single phrase is not destroyed—this is narrowness and purity. That the words and meanings are not the same—this is breadth and mixture. (30)
The "Chapter on Tolerance" (Kṣānti-paṭala) states: "Within a single dharma, one understands many; within many dharmas, one understands one.

Such instances all refer to the teaching-body (śāsana-deha) wherein the one and the many are mutually inclusive. The "Chapter on Manifestation" (Prādurbhāva-paṭala) states: "The Tathāgata’s voice universally enters into all things, just as, for example, written characters [interpenetrate].
This, too, is the essence of mutual inclusion. The "Chapter on the Forty Abodes" (Catvāriṃśad-vihāra-paṭala) states: "One is precisely many; many are precisely one."

The phrasing follows the meaning, and the meaning follows the phrasing; this mutual correspondence constitutes the essence of the teaching (*śāsana*). In the fifth chapter, "The Manifestation," it says:

"In the place of enlightenment, all hear [the teaching] without leaving the assembly, each according to their own understanding. This refers to the essence of the teaching as both hidden and manifest. It further states:

"The vocal sounds of the Tathāgata are of but a single flavor, yet they appear in infinite distinctions according to the differences in the mental capacities of sentient beings. This, too, concerns the hidden and manifest aspects of the teaching.

Regarding the essence of the teaching (*śāsanakāya*), there is also the pure and mixed essence of the teaching. Sixth, it says: "Within a single utterance, the Tathāgata expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras.
This refers to the subtle essence of the teaching, such as that of the goddess Suvaktrā. Seventh, the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* states:
"Within each and every sūtra, the distinct dharma-gates are unspeakable; within each and every dharma-gate," [the distinctions are likewise unspeakable].
Furthermore, it is said that all phenomena are ineffable, and so forth. Since this is true for one phenomenon, it is likewise true for all others;
they interreflect one another in infinite layers, which is the teaching-body (*śāstra-tattva*) of the Indra’s Net. Eighth, all eight sensory objects are phenomena;

this is the teaching-body that manifests the Dharma by relying upon phenomena to generate understanding. Ninth, the instantaneous unfolding in a single thought-moment is the teaching-body of the ten periods of time. Tenth, as in various assemblies, this...
As it is said regarding this direction, so it is in all other directions; this constitutes the essence of the primary and attendant teachings.

If one follows and explains even a single dharma-gate, there are immeasurable sūtras that serve as its retinue. Although these may not constitute the primary [teaching], they are nonetheless of the nature of attendants.

However, the ten meanings mentioned above are for the time being based on verbal expression. If one extends this analogy to all phenomena, it refers to the signified meaning (*artha*). This meaning is itself the Universal Dharma (*samantabhadra-dharma*).
It possesses the ten gates of mystery (*daśa-guhya-mukha*).

According to the delimitation of their meanings, the tenth is the essence in which the ocean-seal (*sāgara-mudrā*) vividly manifests. Such infinite, differentiated teachings all manifest simultaneously within the Tathāgata’s ocean-seal samādhi;
they are also manifested through the lion’s stretch (*siṃha-vijṛmbhita*). Furthermore, for those beings to be converted, they also...
They share the same conditions for arising and manifest vividly within meditative concentration. Therefore, samādhi alone constitutes the essence of this teaching.
By means of these ten gates, all things are encompassed and subsumed; there is not a single dharma that is not the essence of the teaching.
Furthermore, the final two gates constitute the very core of the sutra’s doctrine, which fully integrates the preceding eight gates without leaving anything out.

Section Seven: On the Categories and Assemblies. Having already understood that the substantial reality is profound and vast, one has yet to discern the extent—whether broad or narrow—of the linguistic expressions that convey it.
This section consists of two parts: first, clarifying the categories; second, clarifying the assemblies.
● First: The exposition of the Ocean of Nature is constantly and universally proclaimed; its words exhaust the Dharma-realm and are difficult to measure.

Now, proceeding from the narrow to the broad, I shall briefly categorize it into ten types. First, the *Prakīrṇaka-sūtras* (Separate Practice Sūtras), such as the *Daśabhūmika* and *Daśabhūmi-vibhāṣā*, as well as the present commentary itself, because they circulate individually according to the capacity and suitability of beings.
Second, the *Laghu-sūtras* (Abridged Texts), which consist of one hundred thousand verses and forty [fascicles].

The eight-fascicle version is now eighty fascicles; this is a brief abridgment of that [original]. Among these three versions, the *Middle-length Sūtra* (*Madhyama-sūtra*) consists of 498,800 verses and 1,200 chapters.

The *Longer Sūtra* (*Dīrgha-sūtra*) consists of as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms and as many chapters as there are atoms in a four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*). These three aforementioned sūtras were [expounded by] Nāgārjuna.
The Bodhisattva saw what was in the Dragon Palace, as described below. This *Pañcacakṣus-sūtra* (Five Universal Eye Sūtra) is that which the Ocean-Cloud holds.

Even if one were to use ink equal in volume to the great ocean and pens as numerous as the Mount Sumerus, one could not write even a small fraction of a single gate within a single chapter of this *Pañcacakṣus-dharmaparyāya*, nor a single meaning within a single dharma, nor a single phrase within a single meaning. What [other] incantation [could there be]?
It can be exhausted; however, it is sustained solely by the power of the dhāraṇī of the bodhisattvas who have entered the Dharma-realm. Sixth, the simultaneous preaching of the sūtras:

this refers to, for example, in a single class of world-system such as Sahā, speaking with vocal sound throughout every place in space even as small as the tip of a hair, without end, such that each and every phrase and sentence fills the entire Dharma-realm.
Seventh, the diverse preaching of the sūtras: this refers to the tree-shaped [form].
Since worlds differ and the classes of beings vary, their conventional designations are not uniform; thus, it is impossible to definitively determine whether their words are "not words" and so forth.

Consequently, the categories [of these teachings] are difficult to measure. Regarding the eight sūtras of the primary and attendant [teachings]: this means that in each assembly of every chapter and in each dharma-gate, they all form a comprehensive connection.
For example, when the Dharma of the Ten Abodes is taught here in this region, it forms a comprehensive connection with the infinite worlds as numerous as the dust motes throughout the ten directions.
Because it is stated identically in all locations such as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, this direction serves as the primary [locus], while the others serve as its attendants;
the other directions serve as the primary, while this one serves as the attendant. Because these primary and attendant elements are layered infinitely upon one another, there is no end to them.

As for the *Navaparivāra-sūtra*, it refers to those who possess the capacity but are unable to hear this complete dharma-gate; for their sake, the teaching is expounded according to their specific faculties and needs, and thus it cannot be considered an attendant.
All are termed "retinues. The *Daśaparipūrṇa-sūtra* refers to the aforementioned [sections], the fundamental [text], and their total integration as a single inexhaustible Dharma-gate;
because each and every word and phrase encompasses the inexhaustible. In the subsequent text, it is named the *Prajñācakṣu-paripūrṇa-sūtra*.
● Regarding the distinctions between the assemblies in the second fascicle, there are again two sections: first, a general clarification of the assemblies;
second, correlating the present with the past. △ Now, for the first: we shall first explain the nine assemblies. As for the "nine assemblies":

the first is the Assembly at the Bodhimaṇḍa, which explains the causes and effects of the Buddha’s *pariṇāmanā* (dependent retribution). The second is the Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance, which explains the Buddha’s *mūla-āśraya* (primary retribution) and the ten...
The Dharma Gate of Faith. Third, the Assembly in the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which expounds the first stage of the Ten Abodes of the Worthy.

Fourth, the Assembly in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven, which expounds the middle stage of the Ten Practices of the Worthy. Fifth, the Assembly in the Palace of the Tuṣita Heaven, which expounds the superior stage of the Ten Transferences of the Worthy.
Sixth, the Assembly in the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, which expounds the Ten Grounds of the Sages. Seventh, the Reassembled Assembly in the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall.

The Hall Assembly. It explains the two types of awakening—causal perfection and resultant fulfillment. The eighth is the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall Assembly, which explains the Great Conduct of Samantabhadra.
The ninth is the Jetavana Grove Assembly, which explains the realization and entry resulting from the completion of practice.
Now, these nine assemblies are consolidated into four sections because there are extensive inquiries in four locations. The first section consists of the first assembly.

This is the section on "Exalting the Fruit to Encourage Joyful Faith," which means exalting the Tathāgata’s pervasive cloud-like body throughout the Flower Treasury Sea of Lands to cause sentient beings to rejoice;

by knowing that all possess this potential, they give rise to faith. The second part, from the second assembly through the seventh assembly, is named the "Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding.
This means cultivating the perfect causes of the five stages to accord with wondrous enlightenment.
The fulfillment of the fruit, because it causes sentient beings to correctly understand the characteristics of cause and effect.

The third [section] uses the eighth assembly and is titled "The Section on Entrusting Oneself to Dharmas to Advance in Practice and Accomplish Conduct. This means that by entrusting oneself to all the dharma-gates of the six stages, one advances in cultivation so that all become accomplished conduct;
for understanding resides within conduct. The fourth [section] uses the ninth assembly and is titled "The Section on Relying on Persons to Realize Entry and Accomplish Virtue."
This refers to individuals who, relying upon the causes and fruits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, realize and enter the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), embodying all virtues within their own bodies;

for through such practice, there will inevitably be realization and entry into the fruit. Although the teachings of the Buddha are numerous, they do not exceed these four: faith-understanding, practice, and realization.
Although these four stages all contain elements of one another, each is given its own name according to its predominant quality.

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, clarifying the two assemblies; second, manifesting the five phases. Now, for the first part, the scripture is divided into two.

The first, from the beginning through the third sutra, is called the Root Assembly (*mūla-parivarta*). The second, from the fourth sutra through the fortieth, is all called the Branch Assemblies (*anta-parivarta*).

It is called the "Root Assembly" because it is the primary realization of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in its various root assemblies. It is called the "Branch Assembly" because it relies upon persons to progress in cultivation. From...
Because it flows forth from the assembly of the Tathāgata, it is like the great river originating from Mount Min; it is not something trivial.

Its initial title is "The Assembly for the Sudden Realization of the Dharma-realm," because the Tathāgata himself enters the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi, causing all bodhisattvas to suddenly realize and enter it.
Its subsequent title is "The Assembly for the Gradual Realization of the Dharma-realm," because Sudhana realizes it gradually through the successive stages.

Furthermore, it is initially called the "Buddha Assembly" because the Buddha is the presiding host of the assembly; subsequently, it is called the "Bodhisattva Assembly" because the bodhisattvas are the presiding hosts.
Likewise, it is initially called the "Fruitional Dharma-realm" because the Buddha himself enters it; subsequently, it is called the "Causal Dharma-realm" because the bodhisattvas enter it.

Yet, it is not without the fundamental that the derivative can be transmitted; nor is it without the derivative that the fundamental can be revealed. Although the fundamental and the derivative differ, they are one in their inconceivability.

It is like this: when there is a bright moon in the sky, its reflections flow through the hundred rivers; only when all the hundred rivers simultaneously reflect it does one come to know the wondrousness of the moon.
Although the moon and its reflections differ, they are one in their inconceivability. It is not without the sudden that the perfect can be revealed; nor is it without the gradual that one can ascend.

Advancing: Without the fruit, there would be no means to cultivate the cause; without the cause, one could not approach the fruit. Therefore, it is necessary that the fundamental and the derivative interilluminate, and the gradual and the sudden encompass one another, so that cause and fruit may be perfectly integrated to manifest this realization and entry.
As for the subsequent manifestation of the five phases (*pañca-lakṣaṇa*), this refers to the fifty-five individuals of the final assembly who are subsumed into these five phases.
First, there are forty-one individuals, termed the "phase of practicing by correlating with stages. [End of section on] persons.

The first is designated as "Entrusting to One," because it causes beings to practice the teachings. Second, below Māyādevī, there are eleven persons named "Assembling Conditions to Enter the True Aspect" (*yuan-jiao-ru-shi-xiang*);
this means that by assembling diverse conditions, they cause them to accord with illusory wisdom and enter into the single reality.

Third is Maitreya Bodhisattva, named "Gathering Virtues to Form the Cause Aspect" (*she-de-cheng-yin-xiang*); this means that he gathers the two preceding aspects to bring about the perfect cause for the stage of the Future Buddha (*upapadya-bhūmi*).
Therefore, the liberation thus attained is called "unforgetting mindfulness throughout the three periods of time," which encompasses all virtues without exception.
Fourth is the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, named "Wisdom Illuminating the Non-dual Aspect. True wisdom reflects back upon itself; it is not different from the original mind.
It is a single, perfect wisdom, with no further distinctions such as before or after, clarity or obscurity. Fifth is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, named "Manifestation..."

Because the causal characteristics are vast, there is no duality between beginning and end; they are darkly identical with the *dharmadhātu*. Since the *dharmadhātu* is all-inclusive, it causes the causes one cultivates to all accord with the *dharmatā*.
This is because entering a single pore is identical to the boundless *dharmadhātu*. Second, regarding the clarification of mutual inclusion:
the fundamental assembly includes the first section, "Exalting the Fruit and Encouraging Joyful Faith," for the Tathāgata himself...

Entering the *bimbi-samādhi*, the body and lands of the *dharmadhātu* are suddenly manifested in their full extent; this is the manifestation of the fruit-phase (*phala-lakṣaṇa*). It causes the great assembly to suddenly realize the *dharmadhātu*;

this is the encouragement toward the benefit of joy (*prāmodya-anuśaṃsā*). Within the final assembly, the preceding four phases subsume the fifth phase of the second section, "The Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding" (*hetu-bhāvanā-phala-anukūla-vijñapti-utpatti-bhāga*), and the sixth phase of the third section, "The Section on Entrusting Oneself to the Dharma to Advance in Practice and Accomplish Conduct" (*dharma-āśraya-pratipatti-sādhana-bhāga*). Regarding the former...
Among the four phases, the first—consisting of Mañjuśrī alone—is assigned to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), encompassing the second assembly;
for the second assembly is titled "The Assembly on Accomplishing Virtue through Faith.

The second [phase], from the bhikṣu Śrīmegha to the ten individuals including the maiden Maitrīcaryā, is assigned to the stage of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), encompassing the third assembly; for the third [assembly] begins with the bhikṣu Sudarśana and continues through to Samantagata.
The ten non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are associated with the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*) and comprise the fourth assembly.

The ten individuals from the elder Blue Lotus (*Nīlotpala*) to the earth goddess Self-Nature Immovable (*Svabhāva-acalā*) are associated with the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) and comprise the fifth assembly.
The ten individuals from the night goddess Spring Harmony (*Vasanta-samaya*) to the Śākya maiden Gopā are associated with the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) and comprise the sixth [assembly].

This concludes the first section on the characteristics of practice through the provisional stages, which encompasses the first five assemblies. Next, the three characteristics [of the subsequent sections] encompass the seventh assembly;

for in the seventh assembly, the causes are perfected and the fruit is fulfilled, thereby elucidating the stage of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). In the present assembly, conditions are brought together to enter the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

The section on "Gathering Virtues to Form the Cause" (攝德成因相) reveals that wisdom illuminates the non-dual aspect; because both the beginning and the source are equally non-dual, this fifth part manifests the aspect of the vastness of the cause.
It comprises the eighth assembly’s section on "Entrusting the Dharma and Progressing in Practice to Accomplish Conduct.

This is because [the Master] responded to two hundred questions with the flow of a river, pouring forth two thousand answers—asking one and answering ten—to suddenly manifest the myriad practices, thereby revealing [the truth].
Because Samantabhadra’s causes are vast and great, as soon as Sudhana sees Samantabhadra, each of his causal practices accords with the *dharmadhātu*;

thus, he is able to encompass them. One should understand from the text that this encompasses the characteristics mentioned previously. Therefore, although this is but a single assembly and a single portion [of the narrative], its meaning leaves nothing out.
It is like the space beneath a bird's feet being no different from the great void, or a single drop of water in the great ocean.
It is no different from [the case of] abundant water. Within a single phrase, even the boundless is encompassed; how could the forty-fascicle text not be fully contained therein?
○ Eighth, the transmission and spiritual resonance. This section has three parts: first, tracing the origin; second, the translation and transmission; third, the accounts of spiritual resonance.

First: The circulation of this sutra depends generally upon the previously explained causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; to cite its essentials specifically, there are briefly two conditions:

first, the protection and sustenance of all Buddhas; second, the responsive resonance of the faculties of sentient beings. Therefore, it was stated above: "In accordance with the resonance of their faculties."
For the sake of benefiting future generations, the Great Master [Mañjuśrī] concealed his traces for six hundred years before appearing in the Five Regions (India).

After twelve hundred years, he began to transmit [the teachings] to the Eastern Land (China). When the capacity of sentient beings has not yet fully awakened, it was difficult even while the Buddha was present; how much more so after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa?
With the times approaching the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the first Mahāyāna Piṭaka was [transmitted] by Mañjuśrī and Ānanda.
The ocean. This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was compiled among the Cakravāḍa Mountains; as soon as the compilation was finished, it was taken into the Dragon Palace.

Six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna dwelt on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and was prophesied to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nourishment (*Sukhāvatī*).
Originally, he dwelt among those of heterodox learning; having abandoned the false to return to the true, he relied on his own cleverness until he had recited all the scriptures of Jambudvīpa.

Intending to assist in the transformation of beings, he sought to propagate and expound them. The Great Dragon Bodhisattva, fearing that he would give rise to false views, led him into the dragon palace and commanded him to seek out the scriptures expounded by Śākyamuni.
Although he examined their titles for ninety days, he could not finish them; only then did he come to know the Buddha.
The teachings are profound and vast, difficult to fathom. Thus, one encounters the three versions of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: first, the Upper Version; second, the Middle Version;
and third, the Lower Version, as clarified in the preceding section on textual categories. Of these, the first two versions were beyond the mental capacity of the people of Jambudvīpa.
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, however, recited the Lower Version, which was subsequently transmitted to the kingdom of Śākala.

Since there exists the fundamental basis for its realization, we know that the flow of the Dharma depends upon the timing and the resonance of conditions. During the era of the True Dharma, liberation was firm and stable;

yet, even then, there were none whose capacities were truly suited to the ultimate perfection. Once submerged in obscurity for over six hundred years, the holy multitudes of the Three Vehicles did not even sip from its waves, let alone ordinary beings who could hear or behold it.
Thus we know that those who have cultivated firm seeds in past lives [are now able to encounter it], even amidst the three miserable realms.

Having heard the teaching, those who lack the vessel of faith find themselves at odds with both the ordinary and the holy. Even śrāvakas of superior virtue block their own sight and hearing, and bodhisattvas who have accumulated practices still bear only provisional names.
That we are now able to hear it is a joy resulting from our past vows.

Regarding the second transmission and translation: since its arrival in the Eastern Land (China), there have been three major translations. The first was by the Śramaṇa Zhi Falin of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Devoted to the Mahāyāna, he sacrificed his life to seek the Dharma. Upon reaching the kingdom of Cakravāḍa, he obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka* in thirty-six thousand verses.
He then invited the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra from Northern India, whose name in the language of Tang is...
Bodhiruci returned together with them to undertake the translation work. Bodhiruci was a descendant of King Amṛtarāśi. From his youth, he possessed keen intelligence;

as he grew older, he became profoundly learned and erudite. He attained the third fruit of the Mahāyāna and frequently sought guidance from Maitreya, receiving many miraculous responses, which are recorded in detail in separate biographies.
At the request of Xi Sīkōng in Yangzhou, he translated thirty-six thousand verses from the Sanskrit original, completing the work.
The Jin edition consisted of sixty fascicles. The śramaṇas Fayè and others transcribed it by hand, while Huìyán, Huìguān, and others polished the text.
This marked the beginning of the great transformation. In the fourteenth year of Yìxī, one thousand two hundred years had passed since the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
In the first year of Zhèngshèng of the second [dynasty], the Great Táng, the cyclical year being Yǐwèi, nearly four hundred years had elapsed once again.

The Sanskrit manuscript was welcomed. The Khotanese monk Śikṣānanda (translated into Chinese as *Xixue*, "Delighting in Learning") was summoned by imperial decree to the Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital to retranslate the existing text and supplement its various omissions.

This added nine thousand stanzas, bringing the total to forty-five thousand stanzas, compiled into eighty fascicles of the Tang edition. [This was accomplished by] the śramaṇa Yijing and the Chan Master Hongjing Yuan.
Translated by the Dharma Masters Cè, Shényīng, Fǎbǎo, and Xiánshǒu, and refined by the Dharma Master Fùlǐ.

Thirdly, in the current year of Zhēnyuán twelve, the cyclical year Bǐzǐ, an imperial edict was issued for the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kapiśa to translate [the work] at Dàchóngfú Temple in the capital, resulting in forty fascicles; this is the "Entering the Dharma Realm" from the old translation.
Chapter. From the first year of the Zhengsheng era to the twelfth year of the Zhenyuan era, a total of one hundred and two years have passed since this [scripture] was transmitted to this land.

It is now the fifth century of its circulation. Although it has undergone several translations—whether as the great root text of nine assemblies, or as individual chapters circulated separately, or brought by the Tripitaka masters, or invited by dispatched envoys—never before has there been a time like the present holy age in the South.

The King of India personally presented this Sanskrit manuscript. Having crossed a hundred thousand miles of misty waves and traversed a thousand days of perilous obstacles, he brought his imperial decree to offer to our Sage Ruler.

Were it not for one whose virtue harmonizes with heaven and earth, whose light illuminates the three antiquities, whose majesty presides over the eight directions, and whose transformation permeates the myriad regions—who else could achieve such magnificent and glorious deeds, so inconceivable and perfect, now once again proclaiming the ultimate truth?

The Divine Land (China). Now, the transmission of the Teaching does not depend on a single condition; its essential requirement is that the times be peaceful and the Way prosperous, so that the True Transformation may be implemented.

In this great nation, the Central Kingdom, with its imperial city and phoenix-gate palaces, enlightened kings and sagely emperors revere and honor the Dharma-gate. Their ministers and assistants are virtuous and capable, supporting and promoting the profound transformation.
