The people are for the most part intelligent and quick-witted, possessing the capacity to uphold the Way. Only then do the holy spirits move secretly and provide hidden protection.

Undaunted by toil and hardship, he transmitted and translated [the teachings] into the Middle Kingdom. His mastery of phonology served both regions, and his understanding of meaning encompassed both the provisional and the ultimate. Wise sages of lofty insight have praised and extolled him;
those within and without have dedicated their whole hearts to protect him, both in secret and in public. Thus, the Perfect Teaching has been made to circulate for those who had not yet heard it.

Reflecting upon the accounts transmitted from antiquity, they are for the most part incomplete and deficient. Such magnificent events as these have never been more prevalent than in the present dynasty.

Regarding the third [section], "Manifestations of Spiritual Resonance": Now, the profound words and ultimate truths encompass a virtue of vast brilliance; yet the wondrous purport beyond speech must rely upon words for its proclamation.
Therefore, those who cultivate mindfulness and refine their minds will invariably receive responsive signs. Thus, the subtle words translated during the Jin dynasty were doubled...

A child manifested auspicious omens; the nectar of the Ultimate Teaching (the *Zhìjiào Gānlù*) presented its portents. Divine protection was clearly manifest as the Emperor personally applied his imperial brush.

When the treatise was completed in the Western Regions, the earth shook and light flowed forth. His resolve reached the Qingliang Mountains, where he attained profound realization through spiritual resonance.

As for the transcription of the text, the fragrance of the paper spread in all directions, the radiance of the sutra shone in five colors, winter chrysanthemums burst into bloom, and auspicious birds carried flowers in their beaks. Upon recitation, [the obstacles] were vanquished...

Yet, as he stepped upon the void, it was as clear as gazing into a mirror; every time he held the *śarīra*, he would encounter a divine monk who would leap from the ground, manifesting a golden body, or ascend to heaven to halt the battle of the Asuras.
This Great Sūtra is the work of a Great Being; it is not something those of limited capacity can fathom.
As for its contemplative practice, one enters realization through the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Verses of praise fill the sky, and when the Sea God hears them, timely rain falls.

As the water flowed forth, Tiantong went to meet it, and the great waters spread out. In his lectures, he harmonized the sounds of both Chinese and Sanskrit, which all beings—humans and devas alike—followed.
When the floodwaters were cut off and divine light entered the hall, it was truly because the subtlety of a single phrase encompasses all meaning without omission;

thus, the merit of a single verse can shatter hell, while even the water used for washing one’s hands can bring supreme benefit to living beings. One should therefore engage in reading, reciting, contemplating, and practicing.

His merit is equal to that of the All-Knowing One (Sarvajñā). What good fortune it was for me in past lives to encounter such a sublime teaching! His deeds are clearly manifest and fully recorded in various biographies.

Regarding the ninth section, the explanation of the title of the scripture: first, the explanation of the title of the sutra; second, the explanation of the chapter name. Within the former, there is the general explanation.
The title is encompassed within a distinct meaning, subsuming inconceivable Dharma-gates. Within that which is nameless, I have provisionally distinguished ten sections:

first, a general explanation of how the name is obtained; second, a comparative analysis of the opening and closing [of the gates]; third, a full manifestation of the categories of meaning; fourth, a specific explanation of how the name is obtained;

fifth, an infinite unfolding; sixth, the complete inclusion of all characteristics; seventh, the non-obstruction between unfolding and inclusion; eighth, the perfection of meaning through these principles.
9. Gathering [all things] into the single mind; 10. Dissolving them into the equality [of suchness]. △ Now, first:

There are many ways in which various sūtras are titled. Some are named after persons, while others are named after dharmas. Regarding persons, there are distinctions such as those who requested the teaching;

regarding dharmas, there are differences such as the actual teaching (dharma) versus the metaphorical teaching (upamā). Furthermore, there are titles based on essence or function, or based on cause or fruit.

As for the causes [of these titles], they alternate between being compound and simple, their varieties being numerous and extensive. Currently, the titles bestowed upon the sutras also differ in many ways.

First, names are designated according to their numerical count, such as when the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty refers to the "Hundred Thousand Sutras," which refers to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* consisting of one hundred thousand verses.
Second, names are received based on metaphors, such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*, which designate this sutra [by such means].

First, it is named from its subject matter (*dharmoddeśa*): because the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is compiled through the convergence of the myriad practices and dependent origination. Second, it is named from its title:
as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains in its commentary on the "Entrusting" chapter, this sūtra is designated as the *Acintyavimokṣa Sūtra*. Third, it is named from its functional meaning:
such as the ten distinct titles given to each of the "Leaving the World" chapter and the "Manifestation" chapter. Fourth, it is based on... [text truncated]
Taken as a whole, it is designated by its title. In the Sanskrit original, it is fully called *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*.
This translates here as the *Great Vaipulya Buddha’s Garland-Adornment Sūtra*. For the present, the two characters "garland" (*avaṃta*) and "adornment" (*bhūṣaṇa*) have been omitted.
Regarding the three preceding alternative names, their meanings are mostly general and abbreviated; for the ten causes across the two chapters, they mostly follow the specific names. Furthermore...

Because it corresponds to this specific category, the present translator has provided the title in its entirety using six characters. Thus, both the person and the dharma are mentioned together; the dharma and the metaphor are presented in tandem.
It encompasses both the essence and the function, as well as the fruit and the cause. Since it exhausts the principles and perfects the meaning, it is placed at the beginning of the sutra.
△ Second, the comparative analysis of the opening and closing [of the title]. Regarding the seven characters in the title, there are ten items arranged in five pairs.

First, the pair of Teaching and Meaning: the character *jing* (sūtra) refers to the teaching as the means of expression (*abhidhāna*), while the six characters *da fangguang fo* refer to the meaning as that which is expressed (*abhidheya*).
Second, within the meaning, the pair of Dharma and Metaphor: *Da Fang Guang Fo* is the Dharma; *Hua Yan* is the metaphor. Third, within the Dharma...
First is the pair of person and dharma: "Mahā" (Great) refers to the dharma that is realized, and "Buddha" refers to the person who realizes it.

This is also called the pair of object and wisdom, because the Buddha is wisdom. Fourth, within the dharma, there is the pair of essence and function: "Mahā" is the essence, and "Vaipulya" (Extensive) is the function.
Fifth, regarding persons, the character "hua" (flower) from below is borrowed to metaphorize the cause; thus, it refers to cause and effect.
A pair. Because the Buddha is the fruit [of practice].
△ Third, regarding the full manifestation of the categories of meaning: this means that the meanings of the seven characters, beginning with "Great" (mahā), are all immeasurable.

They are each explained through ten meanings to manifest their inexhaustibility. In the Vaipulya [section], these are further combined and explained: there are twenty for the Buddha and thirty for the Adornments. For...

110. Furthermore, if one explains "Great" (大), all seven characters are "Great. If one explains "Buddha" (佛) and so forth, all seven are "Buddha" and so forth. This is particularly distinct from the ancients. First, regarding the ten meanings of "Great":
first is the Greatness of Essence (體大), which means that whether it be its characteristics (相) or its functions (用), they are all identical to the true nature (真性) and are eternal.
Because it is all-pervasive, it is the "Great Letter. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is called 'great' is named 'permanent. This clarifies that its essence is immutable;
it is like that which is formed from chaos and arises before heaven and earth, such that no thing precedes it in being established. Therefore, it is called "great. Furthermore, it says:
"That which is called 'great' has a nature as vast and expansive as empty space. This clarifies that its essence is pervasive. These are the two aspects.

"Great" (*mahat*) means that there are no inherent qualities (*dharmas*), as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, that are not fully possessed. Because they mutually interpenetrate into subtle, layered profundity and possess the ten gates of mystery (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*), all of these are its characteristics;
this corresponds to the character "fang" (方) in the sutra. "Fang" means "dharma. Third is "greatness of function" (*kārya-mahattva*);

it means that its karmic activity is universal, just as its essence is pervasive; this corresponds to the character "guang" (廣) in the sutra. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, that which is called 'great' is able to..."

To establish the Great Meaning (mahārtha) is precisely to define it by its function. This is because *nirvāṇa* has no "extensiveness" (*vaipulya*); since extensiveness and the Great are identical, the Great is explained by means of extensiveness.

Furthermore, "Extensive Vaipulya" (*vaipulya*) has no "Greatness" (*mahat*); since the Great and the Extensive are conjoined, the Extensive is explained by means of the Great. Since this sutra possesses both, [it is called the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra].

The greatnesses are fivefold. First is the greatness of the cause, which refers to the six perfections. Second is the greatness of the practice, which refers to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Third is the greatness of the scope, which refers to the fact that these practices are not limited to a single realm but extend to all realms.

Fourth is the greatness of the fruit, which refers to the fact that wisdom, abandonment, the support (the body), and the supported (the environment) all pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*; this corresponds to the character "Buddha" (*buddha*) in the title. Fifth is the greatness of the cause, which refers to generating the bodhicitta, giving rise to understanding and practice, making vows and attaining realization, and accomplishing the various stages through diligent and tireless effort; this corresponds to the character "Flower" (*puṣpa*) in the title. Sixth is the greatness of wisdom, which refers to great wisdom acting as the sovereign, directing...
Regarding the myriad practices, they universally adorn all things without exception; this is precisely the character *yan* (adornment) in the title of the sutra.

Seventh is the greatness of the teaching (*jiao-da*), meaning that not a single word or phrase fails to connect throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, unfolding in infinite layers; this is the character *jing* (sutra) in the title.
Eighth is the greatness of the meaning (*yi-da*), meaning that the dharmas explained exhaustively penetrate the entire dharma-realm, even to the extent of Indra’s net, without anything left out.
Therefore, these are collectively the six characters explained in the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka*. Ninth is the greatness of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-mahattva*):

because the aforementioned seven characters—the dharmas of both the signifier and the signified—universally take the inexhaustible realms of all sentient beings as their field of conversion. Tenth is the greatness of activity (*karma-mahattva*):
meaning that throughout the three periods of time and across the entire extent of the dharma-realm, one constantly employs this Dharma to benefit sentient beings without ceasing.
Because it is a rest, it also encompasses seven characters. The seven kinds of greatness in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts are not separate from this.

Regarding the "ten meanings in two directions," "direction" (*fang*) means "dharma. That is to say, the aforementioned ten greats are all termed dharmas; namely, the dharma of essence, the dharma of characteristics, and the dharma of application, and so forth.

Regarding the "three extensive [aspects] of the ten meanings": "extensive" (*vaipulya*) means "many. Because many functions arise profusely and they encompass everything without exception, all ten are "many.
Furthermore, because one penetrates all, it is called "great" (*mahā*); because one subsumes all, it is called "extensive" (*vaipulya*). These have already been explained individually above;
if explained collectively, the Vaipulya [Pitaka] also possesses ten meanings. The first is the meaning of being "vast and transcendent," which is not within the scope of mind or consciousness.

1. Because it is that which can be known by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is the letter *Dha*. Its essence is free from all characteristics and is inconceivable. 2. The meaning of "vast" as transcending:
because there are no phenomena capable of being compared to it, it is the letter *Pa*. 3. The meaning of "vast" as encompassing:

because it universally encompasses infinite and diverse categories of phenomena, it is the letter *Va*. 4. The meaning of "vast" as knowing: because it is fully endowed with various types of knowledge and destroys false views.

1. The meaning of "obstruction": because there is nothing that is not known, it is the character for Buddha (*buddha*). 2. The meaning of "extensive destruction": because it destroys all obstructions without exception, it is the character for *padma* (lotus). 3. The meaning of "extensive remedy":
because it fully encompasses the boundless dharmas of antidotes as the means of remediation, it is the character for *vimala* (stainless).

4. The meaning of "extensive production": because it can produce immeasurable and vast fruits, it is the character for *kusuma* (flower). The three meanings above are all the character for "flower" (*kusuma*), for the flower is the cause.
Therefore: (8) the meaning of the extensive virtues, because it is fully endowed with the merits of the two adornments; this is the character *yan* (adornment).

(9) The meaning of the extensive basis, because the verbal teachings are vast and extensive, serving as the primary basis; (10) the meaning of the extensive exposition, because it proclaims the vast and profound Dharma.
The former two meanings both constitute the character *jing* (sūtra). These ten types of "extensive" (*shifang guang*) arise from the *Za* (Miscellaneous) [Āgama].

The remaining six [categories] are derived from the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*. Taken together with the sūtras and so forth, they are fully encompassed by the seven characters in their sequential order.

Regarding the fourfold interpretation of the ten meanings of the Buddha: these are the ten Buddhas; the ten Buddhas are the ten bodies (*daśakāya*); and "Great" (*mahat*) is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Buddha" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "square" refers to the Buddha of Original Nature, which is the Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).

"Broad" refers to the Buddha of Majestic Power and the Buddha of Accordance with Desire, which are the Body of Majestic Power and the Mind-made Body (*manomayakāya*). "Buddha" refers to the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment, named the Bodhi-body (*bodhikāya*).
"Flower" refers to the Buddha of Vows and the Buddha of Samādhi; these are the Body of Vows and the Merit-body (*puṇyakāya*). Samādhi constitutes merit.
Because of this excellence, "Adornment" (*vyūha*) refers to the Buddha of karmic retribution; this is the body adorned with the marks and signs. "Sūtra" (*sūtra*) refers to the Buddha of maintenance;

this is the body sustained by power. In total, none of these depart from the mind. All seven characters are the Buddha of the mind, which is the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body), for it manifests in accordance with the mind.

The meaning of the ten bodies has already been seen in the preceding text. Furthermore, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, there are ten meanings of the Buddha, namely: being endowed with... [the text continues].
With omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), being free from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
he is able to awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects for himself, and is also able to awaken all sentient beings.
Because he is like one waking from sleep or a lotus flower opening, he is called a Buddha.

The five flowers have ten meanings. First, the meaning of containing the fruit (*phala*): this signifies that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) contains the virtues of its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*).

This corresponds to the character "great" (*mahat*) in the sūtra. Second, the meaning of radiant purity: this signifies that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is clearly manifest. This corresponds to the character "square" (*caturaśra*) in the sūtra. Third, the meaning of subtle and wondrous:

this signifies that each and every practice is identical with the dharma-realm. Fourth, the meaning of appropriateness and joy: this signifies that [the teachings] accord with the capacities of sentient beings. The preceding two [meanings] correspond to the character "vast" (*vipula*) in the sūtra.

5. The meaning of inducing the fruit: because practice acts as the cause for the arising of perfect enlightenment; this corresponds to the character "Buddha" (buddha) in the sūtra. 6. The meaning of physical excellence:
because practice is conjoined with vows and lacks nothing; 7. The meaning of non-defilement: because each and every door of practice is accompanied by samādhi.
The first two correspond to the character "flower" (*puṣpa*) in the sūtra: (8) the sense of skillful accomplishment, because the virtuous deeds practiced are skillfully perfected;
this corresponds to the character "adornment" (*vyūha*) in the sūtra. (9) The sense of fragrance, because the various virtues abide and maintain their excellence, spreading their scent far and wide;

this corresponds to the character "perfume" (*gandha*) in the sūtra. (10) The sense of blossoming, because the various practices flourish and cause the mind to open; this corresponds generally to the seven characters [of the title]. Now, there are two kinds of flowers.
First, the metaphor of flowers from grasses and trees represents the causes of the myriad practices (*sādhana*). Yet, some [flowers] coexist with their fruits;

how much more so for the perfectly integrated (*yuanrong*) cause, since cause and fruit are fused therein? Or, some do not coexist with their fruits; how much more so for the sequentially distributed (*xingbu*) cause, since cause and fruit are distinct therein?

Second, the flowers adorning the body—comprising gold, jade, and so forth—represent the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and various marks (*lakṣaṇa*); these exist only simultaneously with their fruits. Among the ten preceding meanings, [the numbers] one, five, and nine [apply].
The ten [types of adornment] are restricted to grasses and trees; the remainder apply to both types of flowers.

Regarding the six explanations of "adornment" (*vyūha*): that is, the aforementioned ten flowers collectively adorn a single Buddha. Because the modes of adornment differ, these also constitute ten meanings.
Furthermore, the ten flowers above adorn the ten Buddhas mentioned previously in their respective order; these are the ten meanings.

Thus, when the flowers were explained earlier, the ten meanings were already applied to the ten preceding Buddhas. However, since there is no contradiction between the general and the specific, there are yet another ten meanings:

First, because the cause is employed to adorn the fruit so as to constitute a person, this is a Buddha adorned by flowers; for the Buddha’s wondrous fruit is attained through causes. Second, by means of the fruit...
The causes are made solemn so as to manifest their excellence; once the fruit is realized, each and every cause is shown to be boundless. This is the *Avataṃsaka* of the Buddha.

Third, the person is used to solemnify the Dharma so as to manifest its function: that is to say, it is only after the Buddha has cultivated causes through vast eons that the Dharmakāya is manifested.
Because essence and function are fundamentally complete, this is the "Great Vaipulya" (Dafangguang) of the Buddha’s *Avataṃsaka*. Fourth, one uses the Dharma to adorn persons to manifest perfection;
for if one does not attain the essence and function of the Dharma, cause and effect cannot be perfectly wondrous—this is the "Buddha-avataṃsaka" (Fohuayan) of the Great Vaipulya.
Fifth, one uses the essence to adorn the function so that it may be pervasive; for if the function does not attain the essence, it will not be all-encompassing.

Therefore, it is the greatness of the vastness. Sixth, by using the function to adorn the essence, one knows the source; for if there were no great function, the vastness of the source would not be manifested—this is the vastness of the greatness.
Seventh, by using the essence to adorn the marks, one knows the wondrousness; that is to say, if the marks were without essence...
It cannot be immediately entered because it is layered upon layers; this is the "Great" aspect of the "Vast" (大方). Eighth, the body [of the Dharma] is adorned with marks to clarify its mystery;
for without marks, the profound mystery of the body would not be manifest; this is the "Vast" aspect of the "Great" (方之大方). Ninth, the teaching is adorned with meaning to transcend words and thought;
for that which is expressed is inconceivable, and the expressing words are detached from it; this is the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* of the Buddha’s Great Vastness (大方廣佛華嚴之經). Tenth, all...
They are mutually integrated through their mutual adornment. For example, without wisdom, meditation cannot exhaust its stillness;

without meditation, wisdom cannot deepen its illumination, and so forth—all of which are contained within the two characters "Huayan" (Flower Adornment). Furthermore, each of the ten aforementioned adornments possesses four propositions regarding mutual support and mutual identity.
To explain this first by means of the mutual adornment of principle and practice, we shall clarify the four propositions concerning their mutual support.

First, because practice manifests the principle; by practicing the principle of the Avataṃsaka, one adorns practice with the principle. Second, because practice issues forth from the principle; thus, one adorns the principle with practice.
Third, because principle and practice are mutually fused; though non-dual, they appear as two. Without conduct that flows from the Truth, there is no way to accord with the Truth.

It is not the truth that arises from practice, nor is it manifested through practice. This is because the essence is harmonized with practice so that the cause is perfected, and practice encompasses the truth so that the fruit is fulfilled.
For this reason, it is designated as the *Buddhāvatamsaka*. Fourth, both principle and practice are extinguished; they are two yet non-dual.

Because it is the practice of principle, it is not practice; because it is the principle of practice, it is not principle. Thus, both subject and object vanish, transcending emotion and severing conceptualization.
It is neither adorned nor unadorned; this is called the fourfold negation of the *Avataṃsaka* regarding the mutual identity of principle and practice, wherein all is fully encompassed.
This can be understood through reflection. Thus, the Dharma and its metaphors illuminate one another, their significance clearly manifest.

Regarding the seven explanations of the ten meanings of the Sūtra: first is "gushing spring," because it flows forth without exhaustion; second is "production," because it increases progressively and becomes abundant;
third is "manifestation," because it reveals both phenomena and principles; fourth is "plumb line," because it measures and determines the correct from the deviant.
Therefore: fifth is "pervasive penetration," because it penetrates all that is taught; sixth is "sustaining," because it sustains those to be converted;
seventh is "eternal," because it is the constant norm throughout the ten thousand ages; eighth is "Dharma," because it is the true track for a thousand autumns;
ninth is "scripture," because its correct principle is free from error; tenth is "path," because it is the route for transcending birth and death. Thus far...
The detailed explanation of the categories of meaning is complete.
△ Fourth, the specific explanation of the derivation of the name: "Mahā" (Great) receives its name according to its essential nature, with "eternal" and "pervasive" as its meanings.

"Eternal" means that vertically there is no beginning; "pervasive" means that horizontally it encompasses all without exception. "Dharma" receives its name in relation to phenomena, with "guidance" and "sustenance" as its meanings.
The term "Buddha" (Fo) is derived from its function; it signifies "encompassing" and "vast. To encompass means to contain extensively;
to be vast means to pervade extensively. The Buddha is named according to the person [who embodies this quality]; its meaning is "awakening-illumination.

Illumination clarifies the profound depths of the myriad dharmas, while awakening realizes the heavy darkness of the great night. The term "Flower" (Hua) is derived from a metaphor; it signifies "inspiration."
The meaning of "fruit" (*phala*) is the adornment of the body. When the fruit is realized, the myriad practices are perfected; when the body is adorned, all virtues are embodied.

It is named after its function of "adornment," with the sense of providing resources for embellishment—meaning it provides the resources for the vast essence and function, and adorns the Buddha-bodies of the True and the Responsive.
The term "sūtra" (*sūtra*) is derived from its capacity to express; its meaning is "to uphold"—meaning it upholds the inexhaustible nature and characteristics, and gathers in the multitude.
The birth [of this teaching] is boundless.
△ Fifth, the infinite unfolding: This refers to how, initially, within the most pure *dharmadhātu*, it is opened into two gates—principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*)—namely, *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*.
Furthermore, principle is opened into essence and function, namely *Mahā* and *Vaipulya*; wisdom is divided into cause and fruit.
This is precisely the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*. Taken collectively as a whole, it constitutes the seven characters of the title.

Furthermore, expanding upon this title, it forms nine assemblies (*parivarta*), each of which fully possesses the seven meanings beginning with "Great" (*mahā*). As in the current assembly, the thirty questions are followed by ten "oceans," which constitute the *Mahāvaipulya*.
Although these are spoken from the perspective of the Buddha, they apply universally to all things; for the essence and function of the Tathāgata are that which [is expressed].

Because it is realized through direct testimony (*sākṣātkāra*). The first twenty phrases constitute the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*; the initial "Buddha-ground" (*buddhabhūmi*) and so forth represent the meaning of "Buddha.

The subsequent ten [phrases] concerning the cultivation of causal practices represent the "Avataṃsaka. Furthermore, when the Tathāgata himself enters the *Viśvabhujā* (or *Pratibhāna*) samādhi and merges with the essence of the Dharma, this is "Mahā" (Great).
The pure and adorned characteristics and functions of the oceans of lands within a single pore represent "Vaipulya" (Extensive). Moreover, it causes bodhi...
All [beings] are able to realize this instantaneously; it is also the Vaipulya [genre]. Seeing the Buddha everywhere is the fruit of Buddhahood.
The Bodhisattva enters all at once; Sudhana traverses the stages, beginning with Mañjuśrī and ending with Samantabhadra—this is the Avataṃsaka. You shall surely see me.
One shall attain the ten bodies, all of which are the fruition of adornment. Furthermore, these nine assemblies extend throughout the ten directions, reaching even to the lands within atoms.
As the verse of Samantabhadra says: "All Buddhas residing upon a single hair-tip, as numerous as the atoms within a single Buddha-field."
Within all these assemblies of bodhisattvas, they universally proclaim the practices of Samantabhadra and so forth;
even unto the infinitely layered and inexhaustible, none of it transcends the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya Buddha.

△ Regarding the "comprehensive inclusion of characteristics" (*saṃgraha-lakṣaṇa*) in the sixth fascicle: this refers to the gradual winding back from the end until one does not depart from the nine assemblies (*navasaṃnipāta*).

The nine assemblies do not depart from the general title; the general title does not go beyond principle and wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, because it is not the case that there is no wisdom apart from principle, there is no wisdom outside of principle;

and because it is not the case that there is no principle apart from wisdom, there is no principle outside of wisdom. Thus, principle and wisdom are non-dual (*advaya*), and wisdom is also subsumed within principle.
Apart from its essence, there is no function; function is subsumed within the essence because the nature of the essence is itself detached.
Thus, the essence is non-essence, primordially pure, neither having a basis nor being pure. It is only through conventional designation that it is termed the "Pure Dharma-realm.
Therefore, from the ultimate infinite down to a single character or no character, all are subsumed within the ocean of the nature of the *Avataṃsaka* without exception.
△ Seventh, the non-obtaining of unrolling and rolling up. This means that at the very moment one is unrolling [the scroll], it is simultaneously and constantly rolled up;

and at the very moment one is rolling it up, it is simultaneously and constantly unrolled. Because it rolls up while unrolling, the ocean of Dharma-gates as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field is fully expounded by a single word without remainder.
Because it unrolls while rolling up, the Tathāgata expounds infinite seals within a single utterance.
The Ocean of Sūtras.

△ Eighth, the comprehensive inclusion by means of meaning: The Dharma-gates discussed above are either fully subsumed within seven characters, or fully subsumed within teaching and meaning, or fully subsumed within principle and wisdom, or fully subsumed within person and dharma, or within understanding, practice, and realization.
All are subsumed [within these]. Alternatively, they are subsumed solely within the three holy ones: Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and Vairocana.

Some say that *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Extensiveness) is Samantabhadra, because Samantabhadra represents the *dharmadhātu* which is realized. *Avataṃsaka* (Flower Ornament) is Mañjuśrī, because Mañjuśrī represents the means of realization.
The Buddha is Vairocana, because he possesses both the means and the object of realization. Furthermore, "Great" (*mahā*) is Samantabhadra, for the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra...
Because its self-substance is all-pervasive, Fangguang (Vast and Broad) is Mañjuśrī; for Mañjuśrī is the wisdom of the substance itself.
Hua (Flower) is Samantabhadra; for he is the practice. Yan (Adornment) is Mañjuśrī; for Mañjuśrī gives rise to practice through understanding.

Fo (Buddha) is the Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī of perfected understanding and practice, the Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī who realize the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*, who have accomplished Vairocana.
That radiance shines everywhere.
△ Ninth, the summary into the one mind: All the preceding gates, up to the inexhaustible, do not depart from the one mind. The one mind is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The essence of the mind is great, for the essence of the mind is free from thought and is equal to empty space. As for the characteristics of the mind...

Function is itself the Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings). Contemplating the mind to give rise to practice is itself the Avataṃsaka (Flower Ornament). Awakening to the nature and characteristics of the mind is what is called the Buddha.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "What else could the Buddha-mind be? It is right awakening that awakens the world. This awakening does not come from without, for it is entirely identical to that which is awakened.
Thus, principle and wisdom are not distinct; there is only one perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). If form and negation both vanish, then one is far removed from [the notion of] awakening.

That which is awakened to is a state where the mind is absent yet there is no loss of illumination; it is a spontaneous, tranquil knowing. Thus, every thought-moment is constantly the profound ocean of nature of the Great Vaipulya Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddhas.

△ Tenth, "Merging into Equality": This is for the sake of those who have not yet realized [the truth], so as to lead them to understand that all is but mind. If one knows that whatever is encountered...
All are mind. Only when one fully realizes the nature of the mind does the *Brahmacarya-parivarta* state: "To know all phenomena is to realize that their self-nature is mind.

Yet, contemporary practitioners either abandon the internal while seeking externally, or lose the external conditions while illuminating within; both are instances of partiality and stagnation, failing to understand the true source.

Once one realizes that the mind and its objects are *tathatā* (suchness), they are equal and without attainment. This is like holding two polished mirrors facing each other, reflecting a single object.
A single lamp is placed before a single image, yet their lights intermingle in successive layers, and the Buddhas appear endlessly.
Behold how mind and object mutually illuminate fundamental wisdom, both entering into the heart. One awakens to the inexhaustible realm; within that realm, the inconceivable mind is realized.

Thus, the successive layers of mind and object exist as the illumination of wisdom. Furthermore, by means of the mind, one realizes the Buddha of the objective realm; by means of the realm, one perceives that it is but mind-only.

In the Tathāgata, the Buddhas of the mind are layered upon one another; yet, when the nature of original enlightenment is grasped as a single whole, it cannot be apprehended, and thus both mind and object vanish.
When its illumination is inexhaustible, then principle and wisdom penetrate each other. Since this is so for the mind and its objects, so it is for every object in relation to every other object.

Mind and mind investigate one another; the myriad transformations, though profuse and intricate, are all of one essence. Only when realization and response correspond is it called the *Buddhāvatamsaka*.

Second, regarding the explanation of the title of this chapter, there are two parts: first, a general explanation; second, a specific explanation. △ Now, the first [the general explanation]. It is said:
Regarding the title *The Chapter on Entering the Realm of Inconceivable Liberation through the Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra*, these twelve characters are divided into three sections.
"Entering the realm of inconceivable liberation" refers to that which is entered; "the practices and vows of Samantabhadra" refers to that by which one enters.

The single character "entering" (*ru*) applies to both the subject and the object. When the mind and wisdom are in perfect accord, awakening, understanding, and realization are attained; this is collectively termed [the entry].
Entering [this state] is beyond the reach of mind and speech, and is thus called "inconceivable. Its activity being free from obstructions is termed "liberation.

The domain created by wisdom is called the "sphere of experience" (*viṣaya*). Virtue being all-pervasive, wholesome, and compliant is designated as "Samantabhadra. The cultivation and aspiration for this is termed "vow and conduct" (*caryāpraṇidhāna*).
△ Second, the detailed explanation. This section has three parts: first, the explanation of that which is entered; second, the explanation of that which enters;
and third, the explanation of the character "enter" (入). ▲ Now, the first part. What dharma is inconceivable? It refers to the sphere of liberation (*vimukti*). There are two kinds of liberation:
first, liberation through function (*kāritra-vimukti*), meaning mastery over function because one is freed from bondage, as attained by Vimalakīrti. Regarding that:
The Sūtra says: "There is a liberation called 'inconceivable. A Bodhisattva who dwells in this liberation can place the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed.
This refers to the liberation attained by the aforementioned virtuous friend. Thus, Maitreya said:
"Do you understand the inconceivable liberation of the Bodhisattva? Its textual exposition is very extensive. Second is liberation through the removal of hindrances (*āvaraṇa-vinirmukta-vimukti*).
Because one is liberated from the two hindrances through the internal illumination of wisdom, this present function includes the removal of hindrances;
for it is essential that there be no hindrance within and no fetter without. What are the objects? There are also two kinds: first, the object of scope (*pramāṇa-viṣaya*), such as a kingdom...
Each realm has its own distinct boundaries. However, because the scope of the virtues and functions of all Buddhas and Samantabhadra is boundless, there are two kinds of objects of knowledge:
first, the objects of phenomena and principles, both of which are boundless, as they are the objects of knowledge known only to the Buddhas and Samantabhadra;
second, the present text contains both, because the agent and object of the karmic actions are completely integrated. Why are these inconceivable? Briefly, there are three reasons.
First, the phenomena of things are boundless, for they can be known only by Buddha and Buddha; thus, they are inconceivable in their vastness.

Second, the ultimate principle is profound, remote, subtle, and transcends all marks; thus, it is inconceivable in its depth. Third, phenomena and principle are non-dual, such that the one and the many are mutually inclusive.
It is both profound and vast, and is thus inconceivable. These three non-attainments (*anupalambha*) are especially difficult to conceive. In what sense are they inconceivable?

Because the three types of wisdom belonging to the lower stages cannot contemplate them. For what purpose are they inconceivable? To reveal that the Dharma transcends the realm of the emotions and causes speech to cease.
All that precedes constitutes the sphere of entry; if one contrasts the sphere of Samantabhadra’s scope with the principle realized therein, it is likewise called [the inconceivable].
One is able to enter. ▲ Second, the explanation of "able to enter" refers to the practices and vows of Samantabhadra. Why are the practices and vows of Samantabhadra necessary?
It is like a dragon spreading a honeyed cloud, which will inevitably pour down a great rain; so too, when a Bodhisattva gives rise to the great vow, they will certainly cultivate all practices.
These two support one another, like the two wheels of a chariot or the two wings of a bird; soaring through the sky and traveling to distant realms, there is nothing that does not depend upon them.

What is meant by "the conduct of Samantabhadra"? It refers to the comprehensive inclusion of all practices, wherein their sequential arrangement and their perfect fusion are unified. Why is it called the conduct of Samantabhadra?
Briefly, there are two meanings. First, taking the person to understand the dharma: because it is the practice of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Second, speaking directly of the dharma:

because each and every practice accords with the *dharmadhātu* and is universally harmonized and perfected. Furthermore, to explain the meaning of "universal" (*samanta*) in detail, there are briefly ten aspects that reveal its inexhaustibility.
The first is the universality of what is sought: this refers to the diligent seeking of all Tathāgatas and so forth.

First, the universality of what is realized; second, the universality of those to be transformed. Regarding the first: within the space of a single hair-tip there are many sentient beings, pervading the entire dharma-realm without limit or end, all of whom are fully transformed.
Regarding the third, the universality of severing hindrances: a single thought of anger constitutes a million gates of obstruction;
likewise, the eighty thousand afflictions are as numerous as dust motes and grains of sand, yet they are all completely severed—once severed, all are eliminated.
Fourth is the universality of practice through non-interruption; for there is no practice among the boundless ocean of eighty thousand gates of liberation that is not performed.

Fifth is the universality of practice through principle; for according to whatever one practices, one penetrates deeply into the infinite and reaches the very source of principle. Sixth is the universality of practice through non-attainment.
7. The universality of the integrated practice, because the two modes of practice—phenomenal and noumenal—interpenetrate one another; 8.
The universality of the great function that transcends all, because there is not a single function that does not pervade everywhere; 9. The universality of the spheres of practice.
The eight gates above are so called because they practice throughout the Indra-net worlds;

the ten times of practice are universal because they exhaust the three periods of time, with every thought-moment being perfectly interfused without end. The ten universals above are interpenetrating yet unmixed, entering into one another in layers of depth;
thus, when Sudhana enters a single pore of Samantabhadra, the merit of that single hair is inexhaustible. Furthermore, this...

Universal practice is able to enter the supreme realm. If we speak in terms of this practice, that which was previously unattained and is now being cultivated and realized is called "that which is entered.

Third, regarding the explanation of "entering": when the subject and object are in perfect accord, such that all distinctions are extinguished and there is no place for reliance, only then is it true entry.

As explained in detail within our school’s tradition, not every chapter or sutra explicitly marks its sequential structure; this is similar to the "Buddha-Word Essence Chapter" (*Buddhaghoṣa-citta-parivarta*) of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Tenth: Exegesis according to the Text. Following the sublime judgment of Master Dao’an of Miti, regardless of whether a sutra is Mahayana or Hinayana, it is customarily divided into three parts.

Preface, Main Body, and Circulation. Since the sages established their teachings, there must necessarily be a gradual progression. As they were about to transmit the subtle words, they first manifested the underlying principles;
therefore, this is followed by the "Section on the Preface. Once the principles have been manifested, the Dharma is bestowed according to the capacities of the roots;

therefore, this is followed by the "Section on the True Doctrine. Once the True Doctrine has been set forth, the focus is on opening and saving: to strengthen those present at the assembly in the near term, and to benefit those of the future in the distant term, so that for a thousand ages...

The transmission of the great principles has continued without interruption; therefore, it is received and circulated. Regarding the three parts of the present scripture: first, the entire assembly is enumerated as the introductory section (*nidāna*);
second, from the passage "At that time, the bodhisattvas, the virtuous śrāvakas, and the various kings of the world" onwards, the true doctrine (*samyak-siddhānta*) is elucidated;
third, at the end of the fortieth fascicle, it says: "At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, expounded..."
When this supreme dharma-gate of the inconceivable realm of liberation was thus expounded, the following section distinguishes its circulation.

If we follow the sequence of questions and answers, this is now the fourth part: the Section on the Accomplishment of Virtues through Human Realization, also known as the Section on Entering the Cause and Effect of Realization.
Therefore, it is said that cause and effect are extinguished, for there is only the correspondence of realization, which is ineffable. If one follows...
The entirety of the beginning and the end is comprehensively included, with the divisions being even more numerous. Specifically, the primary assembly constitutes one division;
Mañjuśrī’s transformation of six thousand bhikṣus constitutes the second division; his transformation of those of various vehicles in the eastern part of Puṇyavatī constitutes the third division;

and Sudhana’s journey through fifty-four assemblies constitutes fifty-four divisions. Together with the preceding ones, these form fifty-seven divisions. If the three thousand [divisions] are added...

Taking one virtuous friend as a unit, there are fifty-eight parts. If one takes fifty-four virtuous friends as one hundred and ten, and three thousand as one, then there are one hundred and fourteen parts.
If the preceding eight assemblies are added, there are one hundred and twenty-two parts.
In the Western Regions and this land [of China], it is commonly said that there are fifty-five people; thus, they represent the positions of the individuals.
Regarding the dual enumeration: because one person’s own advancement (*sva-viśeṣa*) is intended to equal two people, fifty-five is stated to correspond to one hundred and ten.
However, speaking in terms of actual reality, there are only fifty-four, as Mañjuśrī appears twice.

If one were to combine the general assembly with the specific ones, and since Guṇākara and Guṇavatī appear together in a single assembly, if one were to count by way of *dharmamukha* (dharma-gates), there would be only five.
Thirteen. Because the single person Samantabhadra did not attain the Dharma, while Guṇākara and Guṇavanta shared the same Dharma; based on the individuals, there are thus fifty-four.

Including the stages of self-perfection (*svabhāga*) and superior progress (*viśeṣa*), they total one hundred and eight. These represent the one hundred and eight phrases that remedy the one hundred and eight afflictions.

Regarding the mention of "one hundred and ten," this is merely citing a rounded number. If there were three thousand virtuous friends, each would constitute a separate assembly, and the assemblies would be even more numerous.

◎ Next is the formal explanation of the text. Within the first section, the Introduction, there are two parts: first, the *Saddharmapratyaya-nidāna* (The Preface of Certification and Faith); second, the *Nidāna* (The Prologue).

The Prologue. Now there is testimony of faith, complete with the six accomplishments (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-sampad*). Since the first assembly has already been explained at length, the introduction is here abbreviated.
If one were to include them in full, among the six accomplishments, the first two consist solely of testimony of faith, while the latter four possess both aspects. Ānanda introduced them.

This serves as the "evidence of faith" (*saddhā-deśanā*). Since [the teaching] already exists at the time of its proclamation, it serves as the "origin" (*nidāna*). If there were no master, who would speak?
For when the Dharma is being correctly taught, there must necessarily be a time, a place, and an audience; therefore, the latter four meanings include the origin and are further divided into three.
First, a general manifestation of what was heard; second, the designation of the teacher, time, and place; third, the perfection of the retinue. Regarding the first:
it is "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). This means that the meaning of this entire sūtra was personally heard by me from the Buddha in the past.
As the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The transmitters of the Buddha’s teaching say: 'Such matters as these were heard by me in the past.'"
"Clearly" (*ming*) refers to the preceding title. "I have heard" (*wu wen*) is Ānanda’s own self-designation;

it demonstrates that this was neither spoken by me nor heard from others, so as to inspire faith in sentient beings. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, these constitute the six perfections of authenticity (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-sampad*), whereas here two of them are present.
These two characters, "Thus" (evam), signify the accomplishment of faith. The *Śāstra* says: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma:
faith is that by which one enters; wisdom is that by which one crosses over. This is because one who has faith says, "This matter is thus," while one who lacks faith says, "This matter is not thus.
Master Zhao said: "'Thus' is a term for faithful compliance. When there is faith, the principle of what is spoken is compliant; when there is compliance, [the teacher...]"

The Way of the Provisions is perfected. The scriptures are neither elaborate nor concise; yet without faith, one cannot ascend to them. Therefore, it is said: "Thus" (evam). The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said:
"When the ultimate truth does not contradict the conventional, it is called 'thus' (ru); when the conventional accords with the ultimate, it is called 'so' (shi).

Since the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual, they are called 'thus-so' (evam). This is based on the Two Truths. It serves as an opponent to the two characters *ā* and *u* used by the non-Buddhists, and possesses profound significance.
This means that at the beginning of non-Buddhist (tīrthika) scriptures, the term *a-yu* is always placed first. "A" signifies non-existence (*abhāva*), and "yu" signifies existence (*bhāva*).

Although the myriad phenomena are numerous, they do not transcend existence and non-existence; this is precisely the heterodox view of annihilationism and eternalism. Now, it is said that "suchness" (*tathatā*) is identical to true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

This is precisely the "wondrous existence" (*miao-you*). Because the ultimate is not external to existence, emptiness is not nihilism; because the conventional is not external to emptiness, existence is not permanence.
This serves to refute heterodox schools and manifest the Middle Way. Thus, at the beginning of their sutras, all Buddhas of the three periods of time establish this principle.

Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Buddhas rely upon the two truths to teach the Dharma to sentient beings. There are many further explanations, the meaning of which is as previously discussed.

Regarding the phrase "I have heard": this refers to the accomplishment of hearing. It indicates that what was previously unheard is now being transmitted, thereby clarifying that one has personally heard it.

Because the aggregates (*skandhas*) are merely provisional designations, they are referred to as "I. Since consciousness arises from the interaction of the sense faculties and their objects, it is called "hearing. Although hearing belongs to the ear, because it governs the specific [sensory data], it is provisionally designated as "I have heard.
One hears by means of conditions, yet in hearing there is no hearing. Only when one does not hear while hearing can it be called true hearing.
According to this sutra, the Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma, by means of the true self that is neither "self" nor "non-self"— a non-dual self—
and through the wondrous ear which is neither identical to nor different from the sense organs and their objects, hears the suchness of the unobstructed dharma-realm.
● Second, "At one time" and below indicates the master, the time, and the place. There are three accomplishments [of these].
First, "at one time" refers to the accomplishment of time. Time is of two kinds: first, general time; second, specific time.

In this sutra, "specific time" refers to the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, or the specific time of the *Nirvāṇa* on the fifteenth day of the second month, and so forth. This is either in reference to what is symbolized, or for the sake of clarification.

Therefore, it must be mentioned separately. Regarding the term "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*): it simply says "at one time. Since there are many occasions for preaching the Dharma, it is impossible to mention them individually;

thus, by using this single phrase, the matter is briefly encompassed, and so it is called "at one time. This refers to the time when the Dharma King inaugurates his reign, a period of auspicious assembly.

Alternatively, it is called "at one time" because the capacity of the disciples and the teaching correspond to one another. *Buddha* means the master of accomplishment. In Sanskrit it is called *buddha*, which is translated here as "Awakened."
Regarding this term: the Sanskrit original for "Bhagavān" (The Blessed One) should encompass six meanings; therefore, the older translations rendered it as "World-Honored One" (Shizun).
As for these six meanings, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: first, the meaning of sovereignty, because he is forever unbound by any afflictions (*kleśa*);
second, the meaning of blazing intensity, because he is refined and tempered by the fiercely burning fire of wisdom; third, the meaning of majesty, [referring to] the thirty-two...

1. The sense of being adorned by marks (*lakṣaṇa*), because he is embellished by them. 2. The sense of renown (*yaśas*), because all supreme qualities are perfected and there is nothing he does not know.
3. The sense of auspiciousness (*śrī*), because all those in the world approach him, make offerings, and praise him. 4.
The sense of nobility (*āryatva*), because he possesses all virtues, constantly employs skillful means, benefits the world, brings peace and happiness to all, and never grows weary or negligent.
Therefore, the term "Buddha" used here merely follows the conventions of various sūtras, as the sixfold perfection (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-sampad*) frequently mentions the Buddha;
it possesses ten meanings, as explained in the title. From "in Śrāvastī" up to "the majestic multi-storied pavilion," this clarifies the perfection of place (*sthāna-sampad*).
There are three types of such places: first, the city-state. Its full name is Śrāvastī, which means "The Hearer. (See *Xiyuji* [Records of the Western Regions]).
It is said: In ancient times, there was an elder seer who dwelt in this place. Later, a junior seer named Śravaṇa came here to study under him.
After the elder seer passed away, the junior seer established a city wall here; thus it took its name from him.
It is also called "Śravastī" (The Place of Renown), because many people of noble wisdom, broad learning, and great fame have emerged from within this city. Thus it is.
Within the borders of Central India, there are two sites: the Jeta Grove and the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden. "Bright Monastery" (Ming Jing-she) is its designation.

It is located three or four *li* to the south of the city wall. "Jeta" is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "Victorious in Battle," which was the title of the Prince. "Anāthapiṇḍada" is the Sanskrit name;
a literal translation is "One Who Relieves the Helpless," while its meaning is rendered as "Provider for the Orphaned and Solitary. That is...

Regarding the title "Elder" (*śreṣṭhin*): An elder is benevolent, wise, and compassionate; one who accumulates wealth yet is able to disperse it, providing relief to those in extreme want and poverty, and showing pity for the orphaned and succoring the aged.
Because people of the time praised his virtue, this title was established for him. The Elder used gold to purchase land, and the Crown Prince donated a tree.
Together they accomplished their karmic endeavors; the two men venerated [the Buddha] in this manner. They jointly established the name of the *gālaya* (monastery).

Regarding the "three great majestic multi-storied pavilions," these specifically clarify the locations where the Dharma was preached. They are called "great" because their measure pervades the *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, their manifest adornments are as described below.
If considered in terms of what they symbolize, the essence of the realized *dharmadhātu* is nowhere not pervasive; therefore, it is termed "great. This is the virtue.
Nothing is not complete; this is called "Adornment" (*vyūha*). Based on the essence, the function arises, and the two wisdoms are doubly perfected; therefore, it is named a "Pavilion.

● Third, from "Together with the Bodhisattvas" downward, the support and wings are perfected, which constitutes the accomplishment of the assembly. First, the meaning is analyzed; second, the text is explained.
△ Now, for the first [section], five gates are briefly opened: first, the intent of the collection; second, the causes for the collection; third, the classification of types.
The fourth section concerns the number; the fifth concerns the provisional and the real. Now, for the first: what is the purpose of their coming to the Buddha’s presence? There are ten reasons:
first, to serve as manifestations (echoes and shadows) acting as principal and attendants; second, to act as assistants who constantly follow him; third, to protect the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
fourth, to adorn the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); fifth, to make offerings to the Buddha and his enlightenment...

1. Because of their resolve (saṃkalpa). 2. Because they wish to honor the Tathāgata. 3. Because they wish to pay homage to the Dharma. 4. Because they wish to pay homage to the Saṃgha. 5. Because they wish to manifest the majesty of the Tathāgata. 6. Because they wish to initiate this dharma-gate. 7.

Because they wish to obtain supreme benefit from hearing the Dharma. 8. Because they wish to manifest the Dharma and reveal its profound principles. 9. Because they wish to accord with realization and demonstrate that their teaching is not in vain.

10. Because they wish to contrast and reveal the uniqueness of the Dharma. It is for these many reasons that they have come to the presence of the Buddha; it is not merely for the sake of attaining faith, for attaining faith is merely a means of transmitting the Dharma.

Because of the mind. What are the causes and conditions by which one reaches the presence of the Buddha? There are also ten causes: first, because one has previously accumulated merit together with the Tathāgata;
second, because one was once received by the Buddha through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); third, because in the past, while within *saṃsāra*, one heard the perfect Dharma;
fourth, because one previously gave rise to the great resolve (*mahācitta*) to protect all beings; fifth, because of former great vows...
1. Because of serving the Buddha; 2. because of following the Tathāgata without weariness; 3. because of delighting in hearing the True Dharma with a tireless mind; 4.
because of being well able to dispel and extinguish the mind of *māna* (self-conceit); 5. because the body is fully pervaded by the already purified merit and wisdom; 6.

because the roots of goodness arise from the single ocean of the same nature (*ekadharmatā-samudra*). Among these ten causes, the first four and the last two are exclusively causes of accumulation (*saṃbhāra-hetu*).
The fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth [sections] clarify the meaning of the assembly. Because one makes vows to make offerings to the Buddhas, one attains a place within the Buddha’s assembly;

this is the cause for the assembly. Because one comes by virtue of those vows, this is the intent of the assembly. The remaining points may be inferred accordingly. Third, the classification of types:

based on the aforementioned intent of the assembly, ten categories of assemblies are established: first, the assembly of reflections and echoes; second, the constantly accompanying assembly; third, the protective assembly; fourth, the assembly that adorns the gathering.

The fivefold assembly of offerings; the sixth, the assembly that initiates [the teaching]; the seventh, the assembly of those who are the primary audience; the eighth, the assembly representing the Dharma; the ninth, the assembly realizing the Dharma;

and the tenth, the assembly manifesting the Dharma—these may be understood according to the preceding [explanation]. As for the fourth, the fixed number of the assembly that accords with the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), how could it ever be known by counting?

Speaking according to the text: within this single sutra, there are two assemblies. The assembly of the final session consists of an immeasurable number of categories, differing according to the varying degrees of their spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Within the primary assembly, there are only four groups in total: first, the assembly of bodhisattvas.

Second, the assembly of śrāvakas; third, the assembly of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). These three constitute the ancient assemblies. Fourth is the newly assembled assembly, the text for which appears in the "Correct Teaching" (*samyak-artha*) section.
However, these world-protectors are identical to the thirty-ninth assembly of the first convocation; their names are not listed in full here, as both the words and the meaning are already implied.
The text states: "Furthermore, he was together with immeasurable world-rulers. This clearly shows that [the assembly] was complete, because the first assembly pervades all eight assemblies.
Since they all do not arise from the King of Bodhi Trees yet are omnipresent, the subsequent text says:
"Within every single atom, there are great bodhisattvas sitting upon lotus thrones and attaining perfect enlightenment; this is precisely seeing the first assembly," thereby clarifying its nature.

The various assemblies are interconnected throughout the preceding and succeeding sections; thus, their numbers are the same as in the first assembly. The rest is clarified elsewhere. Regarding the fifth point, the provisional and the real:

among the ten preceding categories of assemblies, those who are "echoes and reflections" (influences) are exclusively provisional, while those who are "responsive to the occasion" are real. The others are common to both the provisional and the real, and they include those both before and on the stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, within the category of echoes and reflections, there are two types: the first is the fruition virtue, referring to the echoes and reflections of the Buddha.
Thus, it is also termed neither provisional nor real. The bodhisattvas of the two highest stages act as the "echoes and shadows," which means they are entirely provisional;

yet they may also all be provisional, because they manifest through the Ocean Seal Samādhi. Alternatively, they may both be real, because they are subsumed within real virtues and remain unmoved from this assembly while pervading the entire Dharma-realm—this is inconceivable.
△ Second, the explanation of the text. The three assemblies are divided into three distinct sections: first, the assembly of Bodhisattvas; second, the assembly of Śrāvakas;
third, the assembly of World Rulers (*Lokendra*). ▲ Now, for the first [section]: the text on the Bodhisattvas is divided into five parts: 1. Indicating the categories and numbers;
2. Indicating the leaders; 3. Listing the individual names; 4. Concluding with the number and praising their excellence; 5. Praising their sublime virtues.
First, regarding the initial point: first, we shall define the categories. The full term is *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*. *Bodhi* means "enlightenment" (*jue*).
*Sattva* means "sentient being" (*zhòngshēng*), and it is also translated as "valiant" (*yǒngměng*). This name is established collectively for three reasons:
first, *bodhi* refers to the fruit of Buddhahood sought; second, *sattva* refers to the sentient beings to be transformed, which are the objects of both compassion and wisdom.

The name "Bodhisattva" is established based on its object; thus, it is called a Bodhisattva. Second, "bodhi" (enlightenment) is the fruit sought, and "sattva" is the person who seeks it. By combining the subject and the object, it is named Bodhisattva.

Third, since "sattva" signifies "valiant," one who valiantly seeks great bodhi is called a Bodhisattva; this is likewise a designation that combines the subject and the object. "Mahā" means "great. Briefly stated: *Note:
This passage provides a threefold etymological and conceptual analysis of the term "Bodhisattva" (覺有情), explaining it as the union of the goal (bodhi) and the being (sattva).*
There are four meanings: first, greatness of aspiration, because one seeks great bodhi; second, greatness of practice, because the two benefits are accomplished;
third, greatness of time, because it passes through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; fourth, greatness of merit, because one is fully endowed with all the virtues of the One Vehicle.

The former two apply to the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*), while the latter two pertain exclusively to the grounds themselves. Some say that only from the grounds onward can they be so designated.
"Great" refers to the fact that it possesses four meanings. "Five thousand people" is the enumeration; while the old translation says "five hundred," the current version says "five thousand.
Compared to the other eight assemblies, both numbers are small because those who practice and understand are many, whereas those who have realized and entered [the path] are rare.

It is essential to say "five" to signify that all five stages are equally realized and entered. Each of the five stages has ten, which corresponds to the ten pāramitās; each pāramitā encompasses [all others].
Ten. Thus, for five thousand [beings], one cultivates the causes in this manner to realize entry into the ocean of fruition.
Second, the section on Samantabhadra marks the primary leader, because these two great sages assist the Lord of Transformation; it is also to symbolize the Dharma.
This shall be clarified below. Regarding the term "Samantabhadra": in Sanskrit, *samanta* means "universal" (*pu*) and *bhadra* means "virtuous" (*xian*).
It possesses many meanings: first, its essence is all-pervasive, hence it is called "Universal"; second, it accomplishes virtues in accordance with conditions, hence it is called "Virtuous.
This refers to its own nature. Thus, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* states: "All sentient beings are the Tathāgatagarbha; Samantabhadra Bodhisattva himself..."

Because its essence is all-pervasive; furthermore, because it saves all beings without exception, it is called "Universal" (Pú). Because it approaches the Ultimate and ranks alongside the Sages, it is called "Worthy" (Xián).

This refers to the Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) across all stages, for both the Three Worthies and the Ten Sages have all given rise to the mind of Samantabhadra. Furthermore, because its virtues encompass the entire Dharma-realm, it is called "Universal";

because its supreme compliance is harmonious and excellent, it is called "Worthy. This refers to the Universal Worthy within his own specific stage; Samantabhadra is precisely [the embodiment of] equality.

Because it pertains to the state of awakening (*bodhi*). Furthermore, that the fruit is inexhaustible is called "Universal" (*Samantabhadra*); that it does not abandon the gateway of the cause is called "Worthy" (*Bhadra*).

This refers to Samantabhadra after Buddhahood; even after attaining Buddhahood, he is still called Samantabhadra. Within this stage, Samantabhadra operates with the simultaneous movement of compassion and wisdom.

After becoming a Buddha, Samantabhadra’s ocean of wisdom is already full, yet he employs compassion that is identical to wisdom. Quiescent yet constantly active, he extends through the limits of the future.
He transforms and guides sentient beings. Furthermore, "one is all" is called *pu* (universal); "all is one" is called *xian* (worthy).
These terms refer to the principle of harmonious integration. As for Mañjuśrī, he is also called Mañjuśrī. "Mañju" means "wondrous," and "śrī" means "auspicious.

In ancient translations, it was rendered as "virtue" (*de*); thus, combined, it is "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*). He is also called *Pǔshǒu* (Universal Head) and *Rúshǒu* (Gentle Head). He is also called...
"O Wondrous Head! Because the word 'Śrī' contains manifold meanings, he manifests his dwelling in this land. His birth is marked by ten signs;

he comes from another direction, his essence encompasses ten thousand virtues, he subdues Māra and restrains outsiders, and his penetrating eloquence is inconceivable. He is called 'Wondrous Auspiciousness' (Mañjuśrī) and also called 'Wondrous Virtue' (Mañjughoṣa).
Furthermore, because he presides over Prajñā and clearly perceives the nature [of reality], he is called 'Wondrous Virtue. Moreover, he knows the realm of the Buddhas."
Because of this realm, all actions performed therein are nothing but auspicious. Furthermore, all Buddhas have awakened their bodhicitta by following it;
it is eternally the mother of all Buddhas and the universal teacher of all Bodhisattvas. Its body pervades all lands throughout the ten directions;
having long ago attained perfect enlightenment, it is already titled the Honored King of the Dragon Lineage (Nāgavarṇarāja), and has manifested the realization of Bodhi.

This is called Maṇiratnasañcaya (Jewel-Treasury). He shall attain perfect enlightenment and again be titled the Tathāgata Samantadarśin (Universally Seeing). His transformations shall fill the dust-like directions, and his virtue shall pervade the entire Dharma-realm;

therefore, he is called Wondrous Virtue (Guṇaratna), which is to say Auspiciousness (Śrī). Regarding the Three Vehicles, they are honored for being fully endowed with both meditative concentration and wisdom.

Among the disciples of all Buddhas, there are often two great disciples: one of wisdom and one of supernatural powers. Regarding the One Vehicle, they are honored for the fusion of principle and wisdom.
Therefore, they are designated as the foremost among the two sages.
Third, their individual names are listed below. Now, sages have no names; names are applied to them by force for the sake of sentient beings.

Although there are a thousand variations in these names, they mostly rely upon their virtuous conduct. Since they possess every virtue, it is impossible to enumerate them all; thus, they are individually designated according to what is appropriate.
All of these possess profound meanings; fearing prolixity, I shall not explain them individually, but will cite their general categories to manifest the underlying principles.
Within this, there are fifteen stages, totaling one hundred and fifty-two persons. These are divided into two parts:

the first fifty-one persons generally represent the five stages beginning with "dwelling" (*vihāra*), while the latter one hundred and one bodhisattvas specifically represent the ten grounds (*bhūmi*). Within the former group, there are five sections; the first consists of ten [persons].
The "Victorious Wisdom" (Jñānavijaya) represents the ten stages (*bhūmi*), for the stage is defined as "understanding. This was not present in the old translations.

The twenty "Banners" (*dhvaja*) represent the ten directions of application (*mukha*), for their virtuous practice rises high above others. The thirty "Lights" (*prabhā*) represent the practices (*caryā*), for the light of wisdom illuminates the practice.

As for the phrase "the practice moves forward and yet retreats," it means that the practice and the vow support one another without priority or sequence. The forty "Treasuries" (*kośa*) represent the stages (*bhūmi*), for they generate, sustain, and maintain [the path]. Fifty-one...

The eye and other faculties represent awakening; because they directly illuminate quiescence, the ten positions beneath the celestial crown of the second heaven represent, in sequence, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
Regarding the ten crowns: the first stage’s crown of the perfection of giving (*dāna*) stands at the head of all the myriad practices of the various stages.
Regarding each position having ten: it is because a single stage is fully endowed with the virtues of all stages, and a single perfection is endowed with the ten.
Because of his adornment: the twenty topknots represent the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), signifying that his observance of the precepts and self-restraint is most sublime.

The thirty flames of light represent the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), signifying the generation of the light of learning and retention to illuminate the patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*).

The forty clusters represent the accumulation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and the mass of wisdom. The fifty voices refer to entering the mundane world to transform sentient beings, whereby he uniquely attains renown; thus it is said in the sutra.
It is called "Thunder" because it proclaims samādhi like the sound of thunder. It is the "Sixty Arisings" because prajñā manifests before one, giving birth to all virtues.
It is "Auspiciousness" because skillful means in the realm of emptiness and the sublime conduct within existence constitute auspiciousness.
It is the "Sovereign King" because immovable great vows are endowed with the ten masteries. It is "Sound" because of excellent wisdom.

According to the power of the Dharma Master’s exposition, there are eleven types of awakening: first, because those in the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā) receive their office and enter the number of Buddhas;

second, because through the *Prajñāpāramitā* they awaken to the dharmas without omission. This correlation is made to manifest their specific distinctions; it is not to be taken as a rigid or exclusive tenet.
The fourth [section] concludes the enumeration of the principal figures and praises their excellence. Regarding the praise of their excellence:
because they are all principal figures, the first two were the foremost among five thousand, while these present ones are the foremost among the remaining five thousand.
As for the enumeration, the Sanskrit original states in full that "five thousand people were together."
Fifth, all [the following] extol his supreme virtues from below; there are eleven phrases. The first is general, while the others are specific.

Within the general section, the "Universal Worthy’s Practices and Vows" refers to the ten subsequent phrases as well as his inexhaustible virtues, which are briefly explained in the commentary on the title and extensively in the sutra itself.

However, while names are established according to specific distinctions, his virtues are fully possessed without exception; thus it is said that they are "all produced from him," because the vast activities of all bodhisattvas [originate therein].

This is because their reverence for virtue is coextensive with the Dharma-realm and equal to that of all Buddhas. Second, regarding the ten phrases within the section on "Non-attainment" (*anupalambha*) in the specific practice, each phrase has two parts:
the first indicates the heading and the second provides the explanation. These form five pairs, which are thus divided into five sections.

First is the pair of "Exhausting the Basis" and "Approaching the Correct": one knows there is no attainment only by pervading all lands; one knows the multiplicity of bodies only by approaching all Buddhas. Second...
Free from all inferior manifestations, supernatural powers, views, and functions, as well as hindrances and coverings, one is only then able to manifest supernatural powers.

Just as the light and shadow of a pure lunar orb pervade everywhere, when one realizes all dharmas through direct awakening and the ten eyes become perfectly clear and bright, one first beholds the Tathāgata’s great, non-localized activity.

3. Regarding "Attaining Immeasurable Radiance": This corresponds to internal illumination and external manifestation. Only by illuminating the ocean of the Buddha-dharma does one obtain great radiance; only when endowed with the four kinds of non-obstruction can one long manifest it.

4. Regarding "Abiding in the Most Supreme": This corresponds to the purity of wisdom and the conformity of form. When one's conduct is free from attachment, the purity of wisdom first becomes manifest;
when one can manifest [forms] according to the mind, the state of being without dependence is revealed. 5. Regarding "Detached from All...": This refers to profound compassion and wisdom.

Extensive Confrontation: Only by realizing the emptiness of sentient beings does one leave behind the obstacle of compassion; only when the net of light shines everywhere does one first awaken to the omnipresence of wisdom.
The former emptiness takes purity as its object; this emptiness takes vastness as its object.
▲ Second, "Furthermore, with five hundred... and below lists the assembly of Śrāvakas. Now, this single assembly of Śrāvakas is absent from all eight assemblies;

that it appears here alone is to manifest that the realization of the Dharma is not common [to them]. That they were seated yet did not hear [the teaching] serves to manifest that in the previous eight [assemblies], it was not their portion;

therefore, they were not listed previously. Furthermore, according to the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), they are present in all nine assemblies; thus, they are established at the very beginning.
Revealed all at once without before or after. As for those who are śrāvakas, the nine periods of time are mutually integrated; this is spoken of in terms of the Dharma.
If one does not destroy their distinct characteristics, the sutra has three sections. In the first five assemblies, immediately upon attaining perfect enlightenment, he speaks of it all at once.

This is because the initial [assembly] says "just now attained," while the [subsequent] three heavens all say "not departing from bodhi," as they arise based on what preceded them. The sixth, seventh, and eighth...
The teaching was given over seven days. This is because there are two periods of fourteen days in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (*Bie xing shi di*).
