Appearing in myriad different forms—whether as sixteen feet or a thousand cubits—when one speaks of its true essence, its magnitude encompasses the entire Dharma-realm. Those whose faculties are not yet mature are not permitted to hear of it; they know it only according to the Dharma.

It is only when the Buddha has fully investigated and exhausted all things that he truly knows it; therefore, it is not of unlimited measure. The second half of the verse provides a double conclusion, which consists of two parts.
The meaning is as follows: First, the negation of both the finite (*pramāṇa*) and the infinite (*apramāṇa*) is itself transcendence. Second, it is a "sweeping away" (*vibhava*).

By employing the provisional infinite to dispel the finite, one realizes that even the infinite is not [ultimately] infinite. By employing the provisional finite to dispel the infinite, one realizes that even the finite is not [ultimately] finite.

Therefore, both are swept away; for both the finite and the infinite are merely conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "I speak of the measure of the mind that is no-mind."
Because it is for the sake of the mind-only (cittamātra), one eliminates it and then eliminates that elimination, until there is no further elimination;

only then does it constitute the meaning of transcendent silence. Among the seven subsequent metaphors: the first metaphor corresponds to the preceding "vastness," also fundamentally eliminating delusion;

the second metaphor corresponds to the preceding "perfection," also subsequently producing benefit; the third metaphor corresponds to the preceding "manifesting supernormal powers," while also expounding the inexhaustibility of the Dharma; the fourth metaphor corresponds to the preceding "crushing."

One sees that the mind is like space and cannot be grasped; it is only through the power of seeing otherwise that [delusion] can be destroyed. The fifth simile corresponds to the preceding [section on] following the minds of sentient beings;

the sixth simile illustrates transformation without defilement; the seventh simile generally relies upon Buddha-wisdom. These latter two verses illustrate the preceding [section on] transcending measure.
Because it moves through space like the wind, it is not finite; because it does not destroy its support, it is not infinite.

The fourth section, the northern direction, consists of ten verses and nine similes, praising the profound and vast qualities of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*). This section has two parts: the first three verses designate the three virtues—first, grace (*anugraha*);
second, abandonment (*prahāṇa*); and third, wisdom (*jñāna*)—while the subsequent seven verses provide an explanation, which is further divided into three. The first three of these explain wisdom.
Regarding virtue (*guṇa*): among these, the first is that which can produce wisdom—namely, that based on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) arises;

and based on subsequently attained wisdom, the wisdom of bodhisattvas, the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and so forth, can arise. The latter two verses clarify profound and vast wisdom, for its arising of function from its essence is difficult to measure. The text contains only one simile.
Next, the following two [verses] establish the quality of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*), because they fulfill vows and illuminate sentient beings. The final two [verses] establish...
The virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Because it accords with reality and purifies the faculties.
Fifth, the ten verses on the northeast praise the virtue of universally benefiting sentient beings. This section is divided into five parts:

first, one verse causes the wisdom of beings to become identical [to his]; second, one verse universally causes their obstructions to be purified; third, one verse clarifies the profundity of its benefit. Regarding Bodhi...

Because the [Buddha] has just now attained full realization, there are four verses on the four modes of existence (*catur-yoni*) which clarify the universality of his benefit: first, the universality of entering the Dharma; second, the universality of attaining enlightenment;

third, the universality of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and fourth, the universality of manifesting conduct. Following this, there are three verses that conclude by exhorting practice and study; first, one verse provides the formal exhortation.
The latter two verses provide an exhortation: first, because their activity is universally purifying; second, because they can provide salvation according to the minds [of beings].

The sixth section, consisting of ten verses on the southeastern direction, praises the virtue of inconceivable great activity. This section has three parts: first, three verses clarify the inconceivable person;

Even the two vehicles, whose afflictions are exhausted, cannot know this final [state], let alone an ordinary person bound by all fetters; how then could such a person conceive of the Buddha?
Thus, there are four verses that bring forth the inconceivable Dharma. First, because it transcends language, the principle where speech ceases is lost when words arise;
since the principle is perfect while words are partial, it cannot be expressed. Vimalakīrti remained silent, intending thereby to cause words to vanish. Next, one [verse] clarifies...

Because the cause is profound, there are three meanings when comparing the Dharma to this metaphor: first, the perfection of its marks is like the full moon; second, the fruit of patience constitutes its majesty;
and third, its manifestation through transformation is like its radiance. If this moon metaphor were not placed at the beginning, it would instead occupy the end;

however, as it stands now, it occupies the second position, serving merely to illustrate the adornment of its marks. The subsequent verse clarifies its vast extent, while the final verse possesses [all these qualities].
Because it is profound and vast; that is to say, its boundless virtues are each individually infinite, as they are the domain of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) alone.

Three verses clarify the person who possesses this knowledge: first, because they are endowed with aspiration and joy; second, because they have accumulated merit and wisdom; and third, because they rely upon the Buddha-wisdom.
If one possesses these three qualities, even if they do not distinguish between the ordinary and the noble, they shall yet attain Buddhahood—how much more so for those who are unable to know [it]?

The seventh section, consisting of ten verses in the southwest, praises the inconceivable virtues of the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*). This is divided into four parts. The first verse generally demonstrates its inconceivability:
even the noble ones do not know it, let alone ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle, because the conceptualizing mind is agitated and thus deviates from the Buddha’s wisdom.

The second section consists of one verse, which cites the cause to manifest the fruit: how could the accomplishment of inconceivable karma be an object of thought? The third section consists of six verses, which demonstrate the characteristics of the inconceivable.
Because it gives birth to the Buddha-wisdom, this verse has three meanings: first, pervasiveness; second, permanence; and third, supremacy. Supremacy refers to opening the gate of Bodhi.
From the gate of Bodhi, one enters the primordial nature of Nirvana. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "By means of one..."
Bodhi is the knowledge that the entire dharma-realm is the very nature of nirvāṇa. The "Chapter on Manifestation" states:

"The Tathāgata possesses immeasurable gateways to the attainment of perfect enlightenment; they are pervasive, eternal, and supreme—how could they be conceived by thought? Second, because it universally purifies hindrances; third, because it universally fulfills vows;
fourth, because it manifests in profound and vast ways. It manifests forms according to the capacities of beings, like a mani jewel reflecting various colors, yet its essence is not color itself.

Just as the myriad phenomena rely upon space, yet space itself has nothing upon which it can rely, form has no support or abode. It manifests various distinctions according to conditions; because it is vast, it is inconceivable.
Since form that lacks support is in fact "no-form," it is likewise inconceivable. Thus, the aforementioned sutra says: "The Buddhas are also like this:
they universally manifest immeasurable forms, yet these are not within the sphere of the mind, such that none at all can behold them. (5.6)

Regarding the two verses, they are because of the fusion of mindfulness and wisdom (*smṛti-jñāna*). However, the fifth [verse] concerns horizontal manifestation, while the sixth concerns vertical manifestation.
Yet, in the older version of the sutra, both verses refer to wisdom; that is, the Buddha-wisdom. Thus, that sutra says: "In a single thought-moment, one can awaken to all phenomena.
How could one wish to measure the limits of the Tathāgata’s wisdom? In a single thought-moment, one fully and clearly penetrates all things throughout the three periods of time."
The Dharma. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha’s wisdom is inexhaustible and indestructible. The general meaning of the Sanskrit original is the same as the old translation.

There are two verses in the fourth section, which conclude by exhorting one to practice and study. Among them, the former verse provides the direct exhortation, while the latter verse explains the reason for the exhortation.

Within the former, the first phrase causes [the mind] to be wholesome; the second phrase causes it to be constant; the third phrase shows that the object of contemplation is solely the attainment of the wisdom of contemplation; and the final phrase [is] one...
The mind advances. Regarding the term "well-considered" (*suvicintita*): because it is a state of non-thought (*acintya*), what was previously called "not thinking" is now referred to as "thinking";
this merely indicates that it is difficult to conceive, not that there is no thought at all. Thus, the old sūtra says: "One should think in this way.
The *Tathatālakṣaṇapariṇāmanā* states: "The Bodhisattva dwells in this inconceivable; within it, thought cannot be exhausted. Entering this is 'inconceivable'."
[This] is the deliberation. Since both thought and non-thought are quiescent, it is difficult to conceive. The subsequent verse explains the exhortation:

because all Buddhas arise from this inconceivable realm, one should emulate them and sever all conceptualization. The first line indicates [the subject]; the next two lines explain; the final line concludes by showing how [it] gives rise [to the Buddhas].
Its nature is beyond words; only by transcending words does one accord with it. Fundamentally, it is not an object of mind; it is beyond thought.
How can one know it? It is the thought of non-thought; the essence of wisdom is limpid and serene, giving birth to all Buddhas.
The eighth section, consisting of ten verses on the northwest, praises the Buddha’s profound, vast, and unknowable virtues, for only by possessing the bodhisattva practices can one truly know them.
This is divided into two parts: the first five verses specifically detail the various practices, and the latter five detail the practice of non-abiding. Now, the first part:

This constitutes the Five Practices: first, the simultaneous functioning of quiescence and illumination. "Pure" means that because one is quiescent, there are no delusions or afflictions; thus, one can leave behind distracted thoughts.

"Illumination" means the power of clear mindfulness; thus, one can leave behind ignorance. When these two are constant and eternal, they constitute true vigor. One then upholds the true Dharma-nature, pure Bodhi.
The wisdom of contemplation becomes perfect, merging with the nature of Bodhi. It is profound such that no marks are perceived, and vast such that it has no limits.

The boundaries are profound, serene, eternal, and constant, forming an inexhaustible ocean. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "To realize that the self-nature of phenomena is free from all conceptual discrimination is identical to bodhi.
Second is the practice of decisively severing doubt; third is the practice of uninterrupted aspiration; fourth is the practice of accumulating merit while remaining detached from signs;
fifth is the practice of long-term cultivation and realization. The latter five constitute the practice of non-abiding. This section is further divided into two parts.

The first two [verses] provide the formal exposition; the latter three explain and establish it. Now, for the first [section]: the initial verse concerns conduct that dwells neither in saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.

Because the first line contains great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one acts within saṃsāra yet does not dwell in nirvāṇa. Because the second line contains great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), one does not dwell in saṃsāra yet does not abandon nirvāṇa.
Non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*) is the exclusive domain of the Buddhas. Since there is non-dwelling in both, why...

This is indeed a point of doubt. The final verse concerns non-abiding in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The first three lines do not abide in the conditioned; the fourth line does not abide in the unconditioned.
Furthermore, the first three lines do not exhaust the conditioned, because they possess wisdom that realizes the emptiness of the world.
The fourth line does not abide in the conditioned, because the merits of the Buddhas are not conditioned. This concludes the latter three verses.
Regarding the explanation of the accomplishment: one interpretation states that because one gives rise to inverted delusions, one constantly dwells in birth and death;

only by dwelling therein without being defiled can one universally save others. This explains the first verse. The next verse says: "Only by universally manifesting without movement can one abandon the conditioned and yet be able to cultivate everywhere.
This explains the second [verse]. The final [verse] provides a general explanation for the reason why one does not dwell [in extremes]: it is because one possesses both compassion and wisdom.

● Section Seven: From "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... onwards is the section on the Manifestation of the Pure Land by Samantabhadra.

The pure land manifests its signs to reveal the Dharma-realm; since Samantabhadra presides over this, his manifestation of the ocean of fruition—which transcends words—is revealed through the gateway of causes.

The Expedient Means. III. The Correct Clarification of the Manifestation. △ Now, for the first [section]: "Observing the assembly. Above, the Buddha entered samādhi and manifested signs to show the assembly, causing them to witness and realize it directly.

here, it is placed third, because it is intended to form a single class with the middle eight phrases. The first phrase begins with the character "by" (yi), which runs through all the subsequent phrases; each of these phrases is...

Among these, three types of space correctly clarify that its vastness has no boundaries; the next eight demonstrate its multiplicity without limit. [The category of] light and shadow is one...

The meaning of "kind" (*jāti*) encompasses both the profound and the vast. Because reflected images manifest according to the capacities of beings, this [text] reveals that there are many moon-reflections in water, which are neither existent nor non-existent;
this is to reveal its profound meaning. The aforementioned Sūtra says: "All phenomena are like light and shadows because they are pure.
The Jin translation says: "The light-shadow of phenomena. △ Third, from "He addressed the Bodhisattvas... onwards, it correctly clarifies the opening [of the teaching].

The text is divided into four distinct sections: the heading, the inquiry, the explanation, and the conclusion. The first [section] is readily understood. Second, "What are the ten? is the inquiry regarding their number.

Each dharma-phrase employs the ten types of skillful means mentioned previously, and each skillful means unfolds into ten phrases, as in the first [example].
[This is] a phrase. Regarding the appearance of the Buddhas and the formation and destruction of the lands (*kṣetra*), ten [categories] are employed.

Their appearance necessarily accords with the minds, karma, inclinations, understandings, and the maturation of the faculties of sentient beings."
Because they manifest as reflections, these five phrases complete the ten. Thus, it is known that each of the ten phrases employs ten kinds of skillful means (*upāya*).

What is opened by the ten phrases is precisely what was previously manifested; furthermore, within the "Recollection and Entreaty" (*smaraṇa-adhyeṣaṇā*), the fruition likewise employs the ten phrases.

The phrasing contains few openings and closings, and the sequence lacks much forward or backward movement; yet, in meaning, nothing is omitted. This is an answer given by means of indirect expression (*parokṣa-vāda*) to the request made in the preceding thought-moment.
"One" refers to the formation and destruction of all lands within the ocean of pure Buddha-fields, and the Buddhas who arise therein—this is the Buddha-field.
Previously, the assembly collectively desired to know the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s pure land; now it is clarified that within every atom of all lands there exists a Buddha-field.
All are purified by the Buddha; thus, the lands are boundless. This applies to all subsequent phrases as well. Second, it constitutes the supreme field of merit for all sentient beings;
therefore, the text says: "Praising the Tathāgata’s preeminent merits. Third, it is the clarity of attaining perfect enlightenment; the text is extremely clear on this point.
Fourth, it is the skillful means for taming sentient beings, manifesting instantaneously throughout a single kṣetra while seated.
The various buddha-fields serve as skillful means; fifth, they manifest various images for all sentient beings;
sixth, they enter the dwelling places of all sentient beings and show the path to them. As the verse says: "Because they abide in peerless conduct."
Seventh, it is because it reveals the city of the Dharma of omniscience; as the verse says, "By hearing the true Dharma and practicing it fully.

Eighth, it is because it explains the merit of giving to all sentient beings; since giving is the foremost of the ten thousand practices and truly encompasses them all, the subsequent verse says, "Cultivating various kinds of practices. Ninth, it is because it expounds the teachings for all sentient beings.
The admonition and the recording [of the teachings] are for the purpose of knowing the various mental activities and mental karma. Tenth is the ocean of the freely turning wheel of Dharma.
However, the text contains omissions by ellipsis; this is to manifest that the Dharma is boundless and that all dharmas have a source, and thus it is summarized here.
Regarding the four "Buddha-sons," the concluding text following these ten phrases of the Dharma is clear. Second, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... onwards, within the verses...
This is divided into two parts. First, the meaning of the verse’s formal structure is explained. The text contains ten lines. The first line generally clarifies the intent of the discourse.

The next two lines, beginning with “receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power,” distinguish the formal mode of the discourse. The subsequent section, beginning with “contemplating the Tathāgata,” extensively explains the intent of the discourse.

Because there is a desire to speak again, it is necessary to contemplate once more. That which is contemplated is precisely the previously mentioned fruit-virtue (phala-guṇa), which is inconceivable, and...

● Section Eight: From "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards is the section on the manifestation of benefits through the light from the *ūrṇā*.

This causes [the assembly] to seek the light of wisdom so as to be able to realize and accord with the True Dharma-realm previously realized. Within this section, there are two parts: first, the universal manifestation of the light from the *ūrṇā*;
second, the manifestation of the benefits received by the assembly at that time.

Now, the first part is divided into five sections. First, the intention for manifesting light. Second, from between the eyebrows downward, the source of the light is identified to demonstrate that wisdom is first awakened within the Great White Dharma-realm of the Middle Way.
Third, from "emitting great rays of light" downward, the name of the principal light is revealed; this name is established according to its function.
Because it exhausts the limits of phenomena and penetrates the true source of principle, it is called "Universally Illuminating the Times of the Three Worlds. [Dharma-realm]...

This penetrates both principle and phenomena. As for the term "gate" (môn), when the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) serves as the gate, one enters the equality of a single flavor throughout the three periods of time.
Thus, the aforementioned scripture states: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time, all of which are entirely equal; by means of the gate of the three periods of time, one enters the dharma-realm."

Thus, the phenomena of cause and effect, defilement and purity, are clearly distinct; therefore, they serve as mutual gateways. If taken collectively as a gateway, one enters the essence and function of the *Bimbiṣāra* (頻申) Samādhi.
If one takes the gateway itself as the gateway, it is not the true gateway. In the *Dharmadhātu* Samādhi, there is neither duality nor distinction;
subject and object, as well as entry, are extinguished—this constitutes true entry. Fourth, from "that which cannot be spoken" (*avaktavya*) onwards, the inclusion of its retinue is clarified.

The gates of wisdom are immeasurable; all belong to the fundamental [wisdom] and together enter the Dharma-realm. From "The five universally illuminate" downward, it clarifies the scope of the radiant light.
Because wisdom is merged with principle, there is nothing to which it does not pervade.

The second period took place at the Jetavana Grove, where the assembly attained spiritual benefit. This section consists of four parts: first, clarifying the benefit of seeing the Dharma by relying on light;
second, revealing the causes and conditions for realizing that vision; third, clarifying the attainment of the benefits of realization; and fourth, expressing gratitude through making offerings.

△ Now, the first section is divided into two parts: first, clarifying that this assembly sees universally; second, showing that these two types [of beings] pervade the ten directions. Within the former, there are also two parts:

Second, the phrase "or one may see [them] situated in celestial palaces" and so forth, which specifically clarifies the locations where they pervade—namely, the locations within the lands inside the atoms.

this is because the events previously requested in the mind manifest as signs in response. The second section, "In this assembly as described above," etc., shows that these types of phenomena are universally seen by the assemblies throughout the ten directions.

This also has two parts: first, citing this instance to reveal those others; second, from "In this way, throughout the entire dharma-realm," etc., using those to illustrate this. Within this, there is further...
Two [points]: first, the extent of what can be seen; second, the characteristics of what is seen. Within the former, there are again two:

first, a general explanation of the directions; second, the overlapping and subtle [transformations]. Now, for the first: regarding the transformation of directions, within any single world-system, looking west constitutes the east, and looking east constitutes the west;
likewise, the eastern direction appears as the southwest and so forth. This is the method of the directional gates, according to the conventions of each direction.

Regarding "the abiding of directions": the directional characteristics (such as east and west) abide according to their respective objects. Regarding "the arising of directions": from a single *kṣetra* (world-system), many *kṣetras* arise;

all these many *kṣetras* possess directions. Regarding "the delimitation of directions": from the smallest to the largest, all possess the ten directions. Regarding "the arising of the understanding of directions":
the Sanskrit original says "directions follow the course of movement" (*dig-anugama-gati*), meaning it refers to the paths and locations traversed by the directions.

The phrase "the directions of the ocean" generally reveals their depth and vastness. Following the section "relying on sentient beings," there is a further, layered, and subtle analysis of the directions.
Within this, first, the preceding is concluded and the subsequent is introduced; that is, because both the coarse and the subtle are maintained through mental visualization (*saṃjñā*).

Starting from the three phrases below, the subtle basis is analyzed: the first phrase extends vertically to the beginningless past; the next two phrases encompass horizontally both the environment and its inhabitants (*bhājanaloka* and *sattvaloka*); and the following one...

Below every pore, one correctly distinguishes the subtle. Regarding the pores as the primary [locus] and the atoms as the basis, and the realm of space as neither basis nor primary, yet taking the capacity to contain hairs, there are many lands that form a continuous, uninterrupted vertical expanse.

All the sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) are transversely joined at the aforementioned location. Second, from "Because they have attained the vision of the Buddha’s supernatural powers" (*prabhāva*) onwards, the characteristics of what is seen are clarified.
However, the first twelve characters are absent from both sūtras and are thus added for the sake of the meaning. "Enabling them to see" and below constitutes the benefit of seeing;
this benefit appears in the subsequent text and is not yet mentioned here. If one were to change "attained" (*prāpta*) to the word "so-called" (*yad-ucyate*), then—
Or is it what is seen? However, compared to what was previously seen, the text here is abbreviated.

△ Second, from "Those who see this... onwards, it clarifies the causes and conditions for the realization and vision. This establishes the cause for the preceding vision and gives rise to the cause for the subsequent realization.

That is to say, the sudden realization and vision do not occur without prior causes; they all result from the power of the Tathāgata’s transformative influence (*adhiṣṭhāna*). △ Third, "Therefore, all are able to enter into the Tathāgata," and so forth, clarifies the benefit of attaining realization. Within this, there are two parts. First:

This is due to the causes of previous lives. Alternatively, eleven gates are listed separately below to manifest their inexhaustibility;

If it were present, it would restrict the scope to vision alone and fail to encompass hearing and so forth. By taking one as an example for the rest, the meaning can likewise be applied. Following this, the section beginning with "Thus" concludes the discourse.
[Section on] Number. Second, those bodhisattvas, by means of various forms of faith, clarify their ability to enter. This section has two parts: first, a detailed explanation of the ability to enter;
second, a summary of both the subject and object of entry. Within the first part, there were originally ten categories, to which six are now added:

namely, location, land, world, supernatural transformations, faculties, opening the door of faith, and diverse understandings. However, the first three categories do not constitute the [ability to enter].

The "entrance" (*praveśa*) refers to the ability to enter by means of perceiving the realm and so forth; it may also function as a "gate. Among the three types of supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi*), this pertains to both that which is entered and the means of entry;
here, we take the means of entry. Faith (*śraddhā*) is the purification of the mind, while understanding (*adhimukti*) belongs to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).

As for the reason why various understandings are opened up according to their meanings: it is because they penetrate with clarity and because they maintain a seal of certainty regarding the object. These various differences are as explained in the aforementioned sūtra.

"Path" (*mārga*) refers to the one path, the two paths, and so forth, up to the immeasurable right paths and auxiliary paths. "Gate" (*mukha*) refers to the gate of impermanence, the gate of dream-visions, and so on.

"Entry" (*praveśa*) refers to the specific realization through correct certification. "Teaching" (*upadeśa*) refers to the purport of the gates of instruction. The remainder may be understood accordingly.
Second, with the phrase "by such as these," etc., he concludes both the agent and the object. These ten matters and others are numerous, and all are capable of entry.

Under the second section, "How the Bodhisattva’s various samādhis... and below, the attainment of these dharmas is extensively explained. This consists of two parts: first, the extensive explanation of that which is able to enter;
second, the extensive explanation of that which is entered. Within the former, only the single gate of samādhi is extensively explained, by way of analogy for the remaining nine gates.

All these should be explained in detail; they are either not yet fully exhausted, or the middle and superior grades are inherently complete. Within the text, there are three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the specific enumeration;

All are named according to their functional activity (*karmayoga*), and all take the *dharmatā-tathatā* (the suchness of the nature of phenomena) as the foundation of samādhi. Accordingly, with respect to each individual matter, they are all capable of—

It is thus: when correct meditative absorption (*samādhi*) manifests, the initial phrase "universally adorning the dharma-realm" means that by entering this samādhi, one is able to cause the dharma-realm to be universally and wondrously adorned;
this is one sense of the "frequently stretching" pure land, and other concentrations follow this same principle.
Among the hundred gates, the first ninety-nine are individual functional applications; by means of many distinct concentrations, one enters the totality of the Buddha, just as...

The hundred rivers all enter the great ocean, where they finally reach a state of certainty; this is also called *bimśana*. In their totality, they share the same fruit, for they enter the whole by means of the whole, like the ocean entering the ocean.
Were they not to merge into a single identity, how could they exhaustively fathom the great function of the Buddha’s realm?

The specific meanings of the various gates are explained according to the needs of the occasion; fearing prolixity, I shall not elaborate on them here. All refer to them as "Bodhisattvas" to distinguish them from those who have reached the fixed state of fruition.
Third, these bodhisattvas, by means of such [practices] as those described below, summarize the examples given above regarding the relationship between the agent and the object;

only after a period equal to the number of atoms in many buddha-fields can they enter the great ocean of the Buddha’s supernormal transformations. Since this is the case for samādhi, the same applies to the nine gates beginning with liberation;
all are likewise profound and vast, though the text is abbreviated and does not provide a formal conclusion.
Second, regarding the various bodhisattvas dwelling in Jeta Grove: this expands upon what was previously entered. This section has three parts: first, a general clarification;
second, a specific exposition; and third, a concluding summary. Now, for the first: this expands the previous general statement.
However, since the subsequent specific statements all fulfill the general statement, the general statement is not explained in its entirety here.
Below the section "Second, having already abided in tranquility," there is a separate exposition consisting of eleven gates that expand upon the preceding [text] in sequence.

Among these, the meanings of the eleven distinct phrases are as follows: 1. The virtue of the perfection of the stage of wisdom; 2. The virtue of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) manifesting in accordance with circumstances; 3. The virtue of the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) comprehending all phenomena;

4. The virtue of long-standing accomplishment through vows and practices; 5. The virtue of reaching the ultimate further shore; 6. The virtue of the fulfillment of the two benefits; 7. [The virtue of...]

1. The virtue of entering the various stages (*bhūmi*); 2. The virtue of the perfection of the wisdom of the eightfold perfect enlightenment; 3. The virtue of mastery over samādhis; 4. The virtue of the fearlessnesses of intellectual power; 5.

The virtue of benefiting others through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Now, regarding the first [point], up to "having no basis," refers to the virtue of the perfection of the stage of wisdom.
This expands upon the previously mentioned *dharmakāya*. This constitutes the severance of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the purification of the *dharmakāya*. Within the text:
Two [sections]. First, the clarification of the *dharmakāya* at the stage of the cause; second, the differentiation of the *dharmakāya* at the stage of the fruit. Now, for the first:

that which is accomplished at the stage of the cause refers to the accomplishment of the ten *dharmakāyas* within the ten stages (*bhūmis*). Therefore, the first phrase states: "Those bodhisattvas who already dwell in the peaceful stages. This serves as the general statement.
At first glance, this phrase seems to elaborate upon the various stages previously realized in the preceding text. Regarding those stages, in the subsequent text...

Furthermore, there is another distinction. The next two phrases distinguish between sharp wisdom, which is fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*), and universal wisdom-activity, which is subsequently attained gnosis (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
This is because the *dharmakāya* of the ten stages is established based upon these. "Born from the lineage of the Buddha’s wisdom" refers to this.
This reveals that [the dharmakāya] is not separate from its fruit. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "The ten stages of the bodhisattva exist as distinctions based upon the Buddha-wisdom.

Second, regarding the phrase "having already realized and manifested," this refers to the dharmakāya at the stage of fruition, wherein the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is perfected and the dharmakāya is fully manifest because the wisdom is utterly pure;

it is also the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Regarding the phrase "skillfully taming and guiding," this refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) at the stage of fruition, which also accomplishes its objective.
The wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) abides in the state of equality and correctly realizes the *dharmakāya*; it is also the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*).

Having already been able to observe [all things] below, this is the function of the *dharmakāya*, and it is also the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). When these four wisdoms are perfected and the *dharmakāya* is purified, this is the convergence of suchness and wisdom, which constitutes the *dharmakāya*.
Second, from "Universally reaching the ten directions" onwards, is the virtue of the form body (*rūpakāya*) responding according to circumstances.

Because all are the function of the very essence itself, such as "approaching without attachment" and "contemplating without dwelling," and so forth, the process of teaching and transforming beings to bring them to maturity is the function of the form body (*rūpakāya*).
From the third section, "Constantly by means of the wisdom body" (*jñānakāya*) onwards, the wisdom body realizes the qualities of the Dharma; the first phrase serves as the general heading.

The meaning encompasses both ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*) and conventional wisdom (*upāya*). Transcending the lower distinctions, the latter is mostly conventional wisdom. Its power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is firm and stable, serving as the basis for these two types of wisdom.

For the sake of all sentient beings, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) gives rise to its activity; this is the wisdom of dual practice. Therefore, it is like an illusion and so forth—neither existent nor non-existent.
Regarding the fourth point, "skillfully able to accumulate," it refers to the virtues long perfected through vows and practices. Thus, the preceding text says: "Entering into..."
The ocean of pure conduct cultivated by the Tathāgata in the past—the accumulation thereof is the perfection of purity in his past practices;
this text is very clear. Skillfully entering the *dhāraṇīs* means to comprehensively subsume all practices. Possessing the power of fearlessness refers to practices for the benefit of others.
Valiant diligence means to universally urge forth all practices. Cultivating all practices exhaustively means to bring the cultivation of all practices to completion without remainder.

Below the fifth dwelling, "The Limit of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-paryanta*), comes the virtue of reaching the ultimate further shore. It is by dwelling in the dharma-realm that one reaches the further shore;

because the dharma-realm is itself without boundaries, it is called a "limit" (*paryanta*). This phrase also signifies the further shore of realizing the principle (*tattva*), as well as the further shore of all practices (*caryā*) following the stage of cultivation.
Below "Attaining Prajñā," it refers to being able to lead the myriad practices to the further shore and to deliver sentient beings through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
This is the ultimate perfection of great activity. This is the ultimate perfection of the basis, which is mastery in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
This is the ultimate perfection of the realization of the true realm of all Buddhas. The sixth [perfection], through skillful wisdom, fulfills the virtue of the two benefits for oneself and others.

Therefore, the preceding text states: "It is called a 'wheel' because it adorns the wheel of practice and crushes obstacles to fulfillment. First is the practice of benefiting others, which is constant...

Delighting in contemplation, one clarifies the practice for self-benefit; seeing reality arise, the practice for benefiting others is fulfilled. Merit and wisdom become firm, and the practice for self-benefit is perfected.
Below the seventh stage, "Increasing All Roots of Wisdom," one realizes and enters the virtues of the various stages.
The first phrase comprehensively clarifies that the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are already complete. From "valiant" (*vīryavat*) onwards, it generally clarifies the great function.

From "attaining the non-grasping wisdom regarding all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma-anupalambha-jñāna*) onwards, it reveals the realization of suchness (*tathatā*) through wisdom and the skillful perfection of all bodhisattva practices, thereby accomplishing conduct through subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
Because one degree is fulfilled within a single stage (*bhūmi*). Although this section lacks the explicit name "stage," the meaning of "stage" is not deficient.

Regarding the eighth [verse], from "Because there is no duality" onwards, it concerns the perfected virtue of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi-jñāna*). The first phrase is a general statement, meaning that one awakens to the *dharmadhātu* by means of bodhi-wisdom.
Next, "knowing all sentient beings" indicates that awakening others has been fulfilled. "Attaining perfection" refers to [fulfillment] by means of wisdom.
Severing obstructions; because both awakening (*bodhi*) and the severance of awakening are termed "awakening. "Universally emitting the light of the Dharma" below:
the light of wisdom pervades everywhere. "For all the worlds" below: worthy of being an object of offerings (*arhat*). "Vast vows" below: the supreme causes are already perfected.
"Merit surpasses" below: the fruits of clarity are already fulfilled. "The ninth [ground], having attained the sovereign power of all Buddhas" below: samādhi is self-...

Regarding the quality of virtue (*guṇa*): the textual characteristics can be understood [as follows]. Under the tenth section, "The Profound Principle of the Buddha-ground Fully Determined," there are the qualities of the power of knowledge (*jñānabala*) and fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).

The first phrase refers to the power of knowledge through realization (*adhigama-jñānabala*). The passage beginning with "Knowing the letters of all worlds" refers to the power of knowledge through teaching (*deśanā-jñānabala*).
Because one expounds all dharmas within a single phrase, one is fearless. One maintains total retention (*dhāraṇī*) throughout many eons.

There is no forgetfulness; what, then, is there to fear? Regarding the eleventh [point], "the ability to comprehend in a single thought-moment the minds of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time," which follows the section on the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) that benefit others: herein, first is the knowledge of their faculties (*indriya*), followed by "bestowing upon all sentient beings... and so forth.
This clearly explains the bestowal of the Dharma, intended to cause all sentient beings to give rise to great wisdom;

this is the purpose of the teaching. From the passage "Entering the Buddha-realm" onwards, it manifests his four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). "Possessing all-knowledge" refers to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).

"Discriminating the phrases of the Dharma" refers to the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). "Being unattached to the Dharma" refers to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*). From the passage "The most supreme wisdom plays with sovereign ease" onwards...

The wisdom of unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-jñāna*). "Observing all that is below" refers to the body of the Dharma-preacher. "Knowing the oceans of lands below" clarifies the locations where the Dharma is preached.
"Manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment below" constitutes the ultimate preaching of the Dharma for the benefit of others. This is a brief summary according to the sequence of the text.
These correlations have been fully set forth; they appear systematic and comprehensive in both text and meaning, such that it is difficult to exhaustively detail them all.
From the third section, "Those bodhisattvas who are endowed with these [qualities]" onwards, the summary can be understood.
△ Fourth, from "At that time, those bodhisattvas... onwards, [the section on] "Receiving Grace and Offering Worship" consists of three parts: first, the general [statement];

second, the specific [details] beginning with "That is to say..."; and third, the conclusion beginning with "These bodhisattvas...", which summarizes the causes [of their offerings], namely, because they have attained the ten kinds of virtues listed previously.
● Great Section Nine. From the passage "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva... onwards is the section on Mañjuśrī’s Description of Virtue.
Because Mañjuśrī presides over wisdom (*jñāna*), his description of virtue follows the emission of light. The original purpose of emitting light was to cause [the audience] to realize samādhi;

the original purpose of wisdom is to manifest the virtues of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Since one seeks the principle through wisdom, he praises it within the grove. Furthermore, previously, Samantabhadra manifested the principle through practice (*caryā*).
In this passage, Mañjuśrī reveals the principle through understanding; for it is only when understanding and practice are non-dual that one enters into realization.
To speak in general terms, one uses Mañjuśrī’s wisdom of the non-duality of the provisional and the real to understand the principle of the non-duality of Samantabhadra’s essence and function.

By practicing these two as non-dual, one then manifests the essence and function of the Tathāgata’s *viśvasta-samādhi* (the samādhi of the lion’s stretch) as its resultant virtue. This section has two parts; first:

Explanation of the Intent. Following this, the verses are presented; there are thirteen verses in total. They collectively praise the sovereign functions of the three kinds of worlds within this single assembly.
The text is divided into six sections. The first two sections generally extol the groves and gardens, encompassing all three worlds; the former of these is universal.

The latter [section] consists of four parts: first, a broad description; second, a single verse separately praising the world of sentient beings, which encompasses the aforementioned offerings made by the arriving bodhisattvas and those who have already attained benefit;

third, two verses praising the mutual presence of the environment and its inhabitants within the groves, where the former verse describes the inhabitants within the environment and the latter verse describes the inhabitants within the inhabitants; fourth, three verses describing...

"Upper Forest Empty" (Shànglín kōng). Section Five: Three verses describing the inexhaustibility of the primary and secondary aspects of the Perfect Enlightenment (Zhèngjué). Section Six: Two verses collectively manifesting universal inclusion.
● Great Text, Part Ten: From "At that time, those bodhisattvas... onwards, the section on the boundless great function, opening the certainty of accomplishment.

Benefit. Benefit necessarily brings profit to sentient beings. This section has two parts. First, a general manifestation of the causal function: that is, because the Buddha’s samādhi accomplishes the gateway of compassion.

Second, from "having attained such [a state]" onwards, the arising of function based on the essence. This also has two parts: first, clarifying exclusively the functions of the Bodhisattvas and World Rulers emerging from the pores;
second, universally manifesting the various types of functions of the emanated bodies.
The preceding section has three parts: first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition; and third, a concluding summary. Regarding the first [of these], there are five points: 1.
The basis for the manifestation, namely, the gateway of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); 2. The place from which the manifestation issues, namely, each and every pore (*romakūpa*); 3.

The manifested body, namely, many rays of light appearing from the pores, and within those rays, further manifestations; 4. The scope of the manifestation, namely, for the sake of all sentient beings; 5. The manner of the manifestation, according to—

The "Categorization of Subduing" (*anuvartana-vinaya*). Second, regarding the section beginning with "Alternatively, manifesting the unspeakable lower [realms]," there are four distinct clarifications:

first, the transformed teaching (*nirmāṇa-dharma*); second, the place of transformation; third, the mind of transformation; and fourth, the benefit of transformation. Now, for the first [the transformed teaching], there are twenty-two sections, divided into two parts.

The first six clarify the teachings through various gates such as delight and revulsion. The old translation contains eight [sections]; following the sixth gate, it adds a section on the differentiation of worlds.

The "gate of manifesting in the world" does not appear in the Sanskrit original; therefore, it is not included in the sutra. The final sixteen gates clarify only the cultivation of the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*).

Within these, there are two for skillful means (*upāya*), six for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and one gate for each of the remaining perfections. Regarding the term *samādhi* (equipoise) used within the section on dhyāna:
This means that by abandoning all sinking (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), one holds the mind with equanimity and proceeds toward a single object. This is the preparatory means (*upāya*);

while it involves a distracted mind, it is restricted to states where the mind is present (*sacittaka*). As for "equipoise" (*samāpatti*), it refers to holding the mind with equanimity and reaching a single object;

this refers exclusively to the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) found in all stages, and it encompasses both concentrations with and without mind. Supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) are precisely these two types of concentration.
The merits thus induced—these three categories are all subsumed within the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Alternatively, it would be no contradiction in principle to explain various gateways following the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) without assigning them specifically to the ten perfections. Second, from "By means of such as these" onwards, the locus of transformation is clarified.

Third, from "With impartial great compassion" onwards, the mind of transformation is clarified. Fourth, from "Those sentient beings, some of whom, having seen [him]" onwards, [the result of transformation is clarified].
The benefits of these transformations can all be understood. Third, from "according to the various assemblies" onwards is the general conclusion.
Second, from "in this grove, all bodhisattvas" onwards, it universally reveals the manifold types of manifestations of the divided bodies;

herein there are three parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, specifically clarifying the manifold types; third, summarizing their sovereign mastery. Now, for the first: that is to say—
Whether manifesting before or manifesting after, all do so without departing from the original assembly, yet they are universally present. Thus, an ancient said:
"Though his manifested form roams throughout the Dharma-realm, he has not moved a single step from Jetavana. This is precisely movement within stillness, and departure while remaining.
Because phenomena and principle, as well as their beginning and end, are neither identical nor separate. Second, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, this bodhisattva, desiring to...

correctly clarifies the manifestation of various types of bodies for the purpose of transformation. This section has two parts: first, the diversity of the manifested bodies; within this, the first three phrases are general, while the phrase "namely" introduces the specific details.
There are thirteen types of bodies, most of which correspond to those seen by Sudhana, clarifying that what Sudhana saw is precisely this.
Because this Bodhisattva pervades everywhere without departing from his original assembly, he clearly understands that the beginning and the end, cause and effect, mutually penetrate one another.
Those called śramaṇas include such as Meghaśrī; those called brāhmaṇas include such as Paramaśānti; those who have left home for heterodox paths include such as Samantagāmin;
those who practice asceticism include such as Jvalanāgra; those who are flourishing include such as Acalā; and the King of Physicians is Megha.
The caravan leader refers to Anuttarajayā and others; the courtesan refers to Vasumitrā and others.

Regarding the two—Vaiśravaṇa and the musician—their relationship as lord and friend appears to be absent, yet they do possess the friendship of companions, such as when various musical performances were held for the wise householder (Mati-mān-gṛhapati).
In the abode of the *bhiṣaṇī* goddesses, one sees Vaiśravaṇa coming to listen to the Dharma and so forth. The Lord of the World is King Mahāprabha;
he is served by night deities, earth deities, and others. The various devas are Mahādeva and the rest; the masters of crafts and technical skills are Maheśvara and the rest.
Following the second section, "Manifesting such various transformation bodies," the text clarifies the differences in the methods of transformation.
Following the third section, "Although such bodhisattvas pervade everywhere," the text provides a general conclusion regarding their mastery; both passages are intelligible upon reading.
The preceding ten sections clarify the conclusion of the primary assembly (the fourth scripture below).
[○@●] Second Major Section: At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta descended from the Pavilion of Good Abiding. This clarifies the subsequent assembly, which first opens with ten sections:
1. A general revelation of the intent of the assembly; 2. Determining the name and meaning of the assembly; 3. The three characteristics...
1. Analysis; 2. The fourfold perfect inclusion from beginning to end; 3. The categories of persons within the dharma-realm; 4. The characteristics and meanings of the dharma-realm;

5. The objective meanings of the dharma-realm; 6. The comprehensive subsumption of the two stages; 7. The opening and closing of the number of assemblies; 8. The number of presiding deities in each assembly. First, [the analysis].
This refers to the flow from the Buddha’s assembly, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It expounds the *Avataṃsaka* extensively, causing all beings to attain universal awakening.
Every person is a Dharma Master; every category of thing is the Dharma. The sounds of the ten thousand natural resonances are all the sound of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*);

even the atoms within the lands are all places for seeking the Dharma. Only then can one realize and enter the true source of the Dharma-realm; therefore, this assembly follows next. ▲ Second, defining the name and meaning of the Assembly.
Regarding the term "final assembly" (*mòhuì*): it is so called because it flows forth from the Buddha’s original assembly; it does not mean "trivial" or "insignificant.

This clarifies that the end is not different from the beginning—though it is rolled up, it is eternally extended. This clarifies that the beginning is not different from the end—though it is extended, it is eternally rolled up.

Since there is no attainment of distinction between the beginning and the end, they enter identically into the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It may be termed "gradual realization," and the meaning is likewise so. [This is] entrusted to persons.
Because one passes through the successive stages, it is called "gradual. This does not mean that there is a distinction between gradual and sudden within the realization itself.
Thus, we know that what was previously clarified as the "sudden" that is not different from the gradual involves many gates so that the multitude may collectively accord with it.

What is clarified here as the "gradual" that is not different from the sudden involves a single person who practices the stages in a perfect and complete manner. When the gradual and the sudden are non-dual, this is true realization. For this reason, O friends—
This is explained in detail. By taking the root to govern the branches, it is universally entitled a "Sūtra. It is not only Mañjuśrī who originates this assembly;

in truth, Samantabhadra is the one who returns to the source at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). This is because the various assemblies at the Bodhi-maṇḍa are its fundamental basis, and because [the teaching] does not depart from the tree of enlightenment while pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
The rest is as previously stated. Regarding the third point, the fivefold classification: there are also ancient masters who have followed the text.

Explanation: Now, following the structural analysis (*ko-p'an*), there are five sections: first, the characteristics of practice based on stages; second, the characteristics of integrating conditions to enter reality;
third, the characteristics of gathering virtues to form causes; fourth, the characteristics of wisdom illuminating non-duality; fifth, the characteristics of manifesting the vastness of the cause.

The meaning of these may be seen in the preceding text. These five are also called the five practices of a bodhisattva: first, the sublime practice; second, the great practice; third, the... [text continues]
1. Superior practice; 2. Profound practice; 3. Extensive practice. Regarding the fourth [section], the "Complete Encompassment from Beginning to End":

although these are arranged sequentially by relying on the phenomena to manifest their distinctions, in reality, a single stage and a single practice encompass all. Thus, practices and stages are inexhaustible.
Regarding the distinctions: it is precisely the many within the one; there is no obstruction between the one and the many, nor between the deep and the shallow.
Fifth, as for the categories of human beings in the Dharma-realm, there are twenty types: first, bodhisattvas; second, bhikṣus; third, bhikṣuṇīs;
fourth, upāsakas; fifth, upāsikās; sixth, boys; seventh, girls; eighth, devaputras; ninth, devakanyās; tenth...

These twenty categories—first, non-Buddhists; second, śrāvakas; third, pratyekabuddhas; fourth, bodhisattvas; fifth, lay followers; sixth, kings; seventh, ministers; eighth, queens; ninth, princes; tenth, nuns; eleventh, brahmins; twelfth, elders; thirteenth, elders of long standing;
fourteenth, physicians; fifteenth, ship captains; sixteenth, kings; seventeenth, rishis; eighteenth, the mothers of Buddhas; nineteenth, the consorts of crown princes;
and twentieth, various classes of divine beings—encompass the fifty-five types of spiritual friends as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field.

▲ Regarding the sixth meaning of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there are four distinct aspects: First, in terms of the fruition that encompasses and transforms, all are manifestations of the Tathāgata’s ocean-seal (*sāgaramudrā*).
Second, in terms of the causal accomplishment of practice, all are forms manifested by Bodhisattvas according to their respective capacities.

Third, in terms of the principles that manifest the Dharma, all are persons and dharmas of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent origination) within the dharma-realm. Fourth, in terms of distinguishing characteristics, they do not transcend the Bodhisattva.
There are five types of births: first, birth that exhausts suffering, such as that of a skilled physician; second, birth according to one’s kind, such as that of non-Buddhists;
third, superior birth, such as that of the bhikṣu Sudarśana; fourth, exalted birth, such as that of King Mahāprabha; and fifth, final birth, such as that of Maitreya.
Generally, each of the preceding four types of births possesses these five modes. Among them, for the bodhisattva, there are three...
Regarding the manifestation of bodies in various stages: first, at the initial stage, Mañjuśrī alone appears; because those in the stage of faith are inferior, only one person is manifested.

Second, during the intermediate stage of gradual progress, two persons appear, namely, Great Compassion and Right Nature, which are not different from Practice. Finally, in the perfected stage, three persons are manifested.
This refers to the Bodhisattvas Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra. Regarding the seventh point, the meaning of the phenomena of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there are ten general categories:
first, the dharma-realm of primary retribution; second, the dharma-realm of environmental retribution; third, manifested signs; fourth, symbolic meanings; fifth, verbal expression.
Sixth, the meaning and principle; seventh, the functional activity; eighth, the explanation of past causes; ninth, the summary of one's own stage; tenth, the inference of superior progress.
These ten gates constitute a single dependent origination, mutually interfusing without obstruction. Regarding the eighth section, which summarizes the two stages:
among these five aspects, why is Mañjuśrī at the beginning and Samantabhadra at the end? Why does Mañjuśrī appear in two places?
Because that which they represent is different. That is to say, these two sages are the masters of the Dharma-gates. Regarding what they represent, there are briefly three levels.

First, the correspondence between the object of faith and the subject of faith: Samantabhadra represents the Dharma-realm that is the object of faith, as it is the Tathāgatagarbha within the state of bondage.
The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* states: "All sentient beings are the Tathāgatagarbha; Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is its very essence."
Because it is all-pervasive, in the first assembly he immediately enters the Tathāgatagarbha-body Samādhi. Mañjuśrī represents the pure mind capable of faith;
the *Buddhanāmasūtra* states that all Buddhas give rise to the resolve for enlightenment because of Mañjuśrī, thereby representing faith.
This is because Sudhana first beholds him upon the initial arousal of the Great Resolve. Later, Mañjuśrī says: "If one is separated from the root of faith, even with meritorious practice..."
"Not possessing [the marks], etc. clarifies the manifestation of faith. One must have something to believe in order for faith to be established;

if there were no object of belief, one would remain adrift in the long flow of birth and death. Only when the subject (the believer) and the object (that which is believed) are in accord does it constitute right faith. Second, regarding the correspondence between understanding and practice:

Samantabhadra represents the myriad practices that are initiated, because this teaching is expounded everywhere throughout other sutras as the "Practices of Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī represents understanding.

Because one must first comprehend both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) before practice can arise. As Maitreya says below: "That you see virtuous friends and enter the gates of liberation is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī.
Thus, understanding leads to the arising of practice; practice accords with what has been taught. Here, vision and feet mutually assist one another.

This is because it constitutes the true understanding and practice. Third, there is the correspondence between principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*). Samantabhadra represents the principle that is realized;

this is indicated by Sudhana’s entry into his body, as it signifies what has been realized. Furthermore, it says, "I have attained the ultimate body of equality throughout the three periods of time," and "The physical marks of Samantabhadra’s body are like empty space.
Mañjuśrī represents the great wisdom that realizes [this principle]. The Buddha whom he originally served is named... [text fragment ends]

Immovable Wisdom (Acalajñāna). Upon seeing Mañjuśrī as described in the subsequent text, one immediately sees Samantabhadra. This clarity signifies that when wisdom is perfected, one realizes the principle (li).

If the principle were divided into essence and function, then there would be provisional and ultimate [truths]. However, when essence and function are non-dual, the provisional and ultimate proceed together.

When wisdom merges with the principle, mind and object become of a single flavor; this constitutes true realization. Nevertheless, it is through the realization of the principle that wisdom is formed, and it is through wisdom that the principle is manifested.

Therefore, although both subject and object are simultaneously extinguished, they remain distinct and clear. This is why the subsequent passage fully elucidates the two sages: at the initial stage, one has faith in the principle, yet the principle remains hidden and unmanifest;
thus, in the first stage, Mañjuśrī appears without a counterpart of Samantabhadra. In the intermediate stages of understanding and practice, neither of the two is manifest.

This is because it is revealed that all stages are Samantabhadra, and that contact with objects and illuminating understanding are both Mañjuśrī. According to the gate of Mañjuśrī, faith arises from understanding;

faith is free from ignorance, and through faith, understanding is perfected. This understanding is not false view; when faith and understanding constitute true and correct wondrous wisdom, they become perfect.
These three become one mind, whereby one enters the ocean of Buddha-wisdom and attains the ultimate. According to the gate of Samantabhadra:
Entrusting oneself to principle to accomplish practice means that practice is not sought externally; by means of practice one perceives principle, for practice is not outside of principle.
From beginning to end, the *dharmadhātu* is of one suchness (*tathatā*); there is not even the slightest portion that is not the essence of Buddha-wisdom.

This clearly demonstrates that the One Vehicle is not without cause. It fundamentally belongs to Mañjuśrī, not to Śāriputra; therefore, the virtues praised here are all based upon [him].

To cause them to awaken and enter [the truth]. The preceding section has four parts: first, showing the supreme object; second, attaining the supreme benefit; third, approaching the supreme person;

Practice. Now, there is only the vow for samādhi; thus, one’s aspirations are always identical [to those of the Buddhas]. The sixth is the vow to serve [the Buddhas];

Second, by attaining this samādhi, there are internal qualities: first, one generates a great resolve; because this resolve is generated within meditative concentration, it is called "true."
The meaning is the same as "realization and arousal. Second, many samādhis: this refers to the difficult-to-practice concentration wherein the one is many.

Third, many gates of liberation; fourth, many illuminations of wisdom; fifth, many supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Regarding supernormal powers, they mostly pertain to the internal body’s sustaining power.

From "By attaining such [powers]... onwards, it universally harmonizes body and mind, summarizing the attainment of benefit. The Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) gathers those with capacity who have newly aroused the Great Mind, [attaining] sudden...

Each of these consists of ten thousand [subdivisions], all of which are integrated through the Dharma, without distinction between beginning and end. This is not achieved through the power of gradual cultivation; its characteristics are explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Bodhicitta."
Third, from the passage "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva fully and securely dwells" onwards, the text summarizes what has been accomplished and further demonstrates his progressive advancement.
This section consists of three parts: first, it clarifies his own abiding; second, from "He exhorts the bhikṣus" onwards, it reveals the methods of his transformation.

The preceding section clarified the arousal of the mind; the present section exhorts one to abide in and practice it. From the subsequent section on "Abiding in Superior Practices" onwards, there are eight successive layers that progressively bring about benefit;
together with the preceding, these constitute ten stages to manifest their inexhaustibility. The assembly of six thousand bhikṣus concludes above.

first, a summary of what was previously done; second, arriving at the place of conversion; third, revealing the Dharma taught; and fourth, clarifying the assembly benefited. Of these, the first is easily understood.
From "Gradually traveling southward" onwards is the section on arriving at the place of conversion; it concerns the city where [the Buddha] resided.

People generate much merit; therefore, it is called "The Arising of Merit" (*Puṣpabhadrā*). A city represents the defense against what is non-true; it is the true *dharmadhātu*, for all sentient beings emerge from it.
The east is the beginning of the directions and the dawn of illumination; it symbolizes following merit and goodness as one enters the path for the first time.

Furthermore, it symbolizes the fundamental basis for entering the stage of merit and wisdom. As for the *Pāṭalī* grove, this is translated as "High and Remote," because its trees rise up in dense profusion.
Therefore, one should give rise to the myriad practices to adorn the *dharmakāya*. Because it can crush obstacles and veils, it is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*).
As for the "great stūpa," its full name is *stūpa*; this is translated as "lofty and manifest. Formerly it was called *tapa*, which in meaning refers to the place where one returns to the source.
"Temple" (*miao*) means "likeness" (*mao*). Because it manifests the likeness of the World-Honored One, Master Jñānayaśas said: "This city is located in South India.
To the east of the city is a great stūpa, which is the stūpa of an ancient Buddha. This stūpa already existed during the Buddha’s lifetime; it is exceedingly large."
When music is played on the eastern side, it cannot be heard on the western side. Even now, the inhabitants frequently sing the lyrics of Sudhana.
The people within this city all possess the roots of goodness conducive to liberation and are fit vessels for the Way.

This represents that the fundamental awakening of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is the true nature upon which all Buddhas equally rely, is the basis of their practice; therefore, it is further said that this was where past Buddhas once dwelt. (3)
At that time, Mañjuśrī descended [from his seat]. This reveals that the wisdom-function of the Dharma he expounded is vast and expansive;

hence it is called "Universal Illumination. That which is illuminated is profound and extensive, namely the true *dharmadhātu*. This is the formal exposition of the *Dharmadhātupraveśa-sūtra*. Regarding the phrase "at the time of the fourfold exposition of this sūtra":

Regarding those benefited by the teaching, there are briefly two categories. First, it clarifies that the various nāgas, having attained the intent of the primary teaching, seek the Buddha-way and thus abide within the ocean waters, becoming capable of receiving and hearing [the Dharma].
Subsequently, the passage beginning with "furthermore, there are immeasurable" below encompasses the capacities of the three vehicles, whereby they receive the teaching for their retinue;
