"O Householder (the sixth liberation, O Householder).

△ From here below, the third section, beginning with "At that time, the people of Puṇḍravardhana," summarizes the *Sudhana-saṃyukta-parivarta*. First, ten gates are opened: 1. A general exposition of the overall significance; 2.
The distinctions among those who enter through cultivation; 3. The differences in the directions shown; 4. The variations in the pursuit of the goal; 5. The [differences in] seeing...

1. Differences in location. 2. Differences in the six teachings used to dispel [delusions]. 3. Differences between praising and not praising. 4. Differences between inferring and not inferring. 5. Differences between concluding and not concluding.

6. Differences between departing and remaining. First, regarding the initial point: When the Tathāgata manifests his traces, he encounters those whose past karmic conditions are exhausted, gathering in an ocean-like assembly of great vessels as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It is not that the good Sudhana alone is singled out; what is the reason for this? There are several interpretations.
I cite this one example to serve as a warning for those who have not yet awakened. When the Buddha was a youth, he possessed the maturity of an elder;
he exhorted practitioners until his own hair turned white with regret. Since he was capable of such things, how can I deceive myself? Therefore, the following verse says:

"With the power of firm resolve, faith, and joy, Sudhana accomplished this practice; if you possess a heart of reverence and admiration, you too should train in this way. Furthermore, it says: "Train as he did..."

The "fish-egg" (the potential for Buddhahood) becomes like a fish once it is realized; this serves to encourage practitioners, for they must have both a beginning and an end. As the subsequent scripture says:

"Once the mind has been resolved, one can further act in this way, as if putting out a fire on one's own head. The sun and moon emit their brilliance, while fireflies and candles possess no such luster;
when the Great Being manifests his traces, his Way eclipses all other vehicles. Thus the scripture says: "Other bodhisattvas [must practice] for immeasurable kalpas before they can..."

The bodhisattva practices and vows are purified through cultivation; now, this youth has accomplished them all in a single lifetime. Transformation does not require many [lifetimes], for it is completed in one;

practice does not require long duration, for the realization of the meaning is attained through sudden transcendence. How much more so for one who has long accumulated pure causes—why would they not swiftly realize [enlightenment]?

Whether ordinary person or sage is irrelevant; the intent lies in the relinquishing and cultivation. Second, regarding the distinctions in entering the assembly: there are only three assemblies within the stage of Initial Faith.
Regarding the fourfold assembly: [the text] intends for them to have universal faith, thereby manifesting that [the stages] from "dwelling" (*vihāra*) onwards are universally encompassed.

The singular figure of Sudhana manifests that the practice (*caryā*) has already been completed, as entering the [final] stage (*avasthā*) is rare. ▲ Third, regarding the differences in the directions indicated: there are three major positions.

Before the first stage (*bhūmi*), spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are mostly in the south. On the stages themselves, there is no fixed direction. After the stages, both [directions] are combined. However, the reason they are specified as being in the south is that, according to ancient tradition...
There are five meanings. First, taking one case as an example for all: since the spiritual friends in a single direction are already immeasurable, how much more so in the other nine directions?

This first point refers to the actual entities; the remaining four refer to their symbolic significance. Second is the meaning of illumination: it symbolizes abandoning darkness and turning toward wisdom, just as the south represents light.
All things behold one another; the Sage faces south—this is likely derived from these meanings. Third is the meaning of "centering": it signifies the departure from deviance and partiality.
The two sides of east and west accord with the single reality of the central and correct Way. Fourth is the meaning of "generation": the south presides over the Yang.
It gives rise to all things, manifesting the growth of practice as exemplified by Sudhana. The north presides over its yin aspect, revealing the meaning of cessation (*nirodha*);

it turns away from the pursuit of quiescence to extinguish delusions. Thus, when the World-Honored One entered *nirvāṇa*, his golden coffin was placed with the head to the north, precisely signifying the attainment of ultimate extinction.

Fifth is the meaning of "conformity. Turning the left away and facing toward the right constitutes conformity. According to the local customs of the Western Regions, cities, gardens, and residences all face east;
proceeding from the east toward the south follows the movement of the sun and moon, thereby manifesting Sudhana’s conformity with the principles of the teaching.

The correct realization on the ground is free from the characteristics of realization and cannot be indicated by the south. Regarding the karmic function subsequent to the ground, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
That Mañjuśrī has a manifestation yet no fixed direction symbolizes *prajñā*. While there is cultivation in the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), in correct realization there is non-duality.

Samantabhadra is without fixed direction, nor is there anyone who points him out, for he manifests the virtue of the true dharma-realm as universally pervasive. Some people take only the meaning of "conformity" (anuvartana) alone;
this is not among the previous explanations, because the definitive meaning is revealed from this very region. How could one know that the Western Regions are not the locus of such clarity?
Moreover, the teachings that encompass all directions contain manifold implications; what is valued is seeking with an open mind—why must one be dogmatic?
▲ Regarding the differences in the four types of seekers (*catur-yoni*), there are briefly three distinctions.

First, Mañjuśrī went to the City of Blessings (*Puṇyavatī*) himself because [Mañjuśrī’s] faculties were still subtle, he had not yet resolved his mind for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), and his great compassion was profound.

Second, when Meghaśrī descended, Sudhana went to seek him out because his faculties had gradually become superior, he had already resolved his mind for enlightenment, and it served to manifest the gravity of the Dharma. Third, Samantabhadra did not go to Sudhana’s location.
Wealth does not go there, for in the stage of the fulfillment of the Dharma-realm, there is neither coming nor going. ▲ Fifth, regarding the distinctions of the loci of views:

those of the three stages of worthiness have not yet realized [the truth] and are scattered in various places; those on the grounds (bhūmi) have realized the reality and are born into the family of the Buddha, mostly residing in the assemblies of Buddhas;

after the grounds, when they give rise to their function, they are also scattered according to conditions; when Samantabhadra’s causes are perfected, he will surely attain the full fruit and return to the abode of the Buddha. ▲ Sixth.
Regarding "sent or not sent": if the initial Mañjuśrī is explained in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), there was no prior companion;

if explained in terms of manifestation (*vijñapti*), this manifestation arises from internal perfuming by faith (*śraddhā*) based upon the principle (*tattva*), and thus there was nothing further to be sent before. Upon seeing the subsequent Mañjuśrī, the Prajñā reaches its ultimate illumination.

Because one personally perceives the single true dharma-realm of Samantabhadra, there is likewise nothing to be discarded. As for the various companions in the interim, they manifest the great dependent origination;

since the myriad practices must mutually support one another to achieve perfection, they all instruct [the practitioner] to discard them. The meaning of this instruction to discard shall be explained extensively below.
▲ Regarding the seven instances where there is no praise (*an-utthāpana*): in the first section concerning Mañjuśrī, he was not praised prior to his initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*);

it was only after he was taught to generate the mind that he was subsequently praised. As for the lack of praise in the latter two sections, this indicates that his stage (*bhūmi*) is fulfilled and that he has transcended the characteristics of the mind (*citta-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the fact that the various friends in the middle sections all fail to offer praise, there are briefly two conditions: first, they are currently in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as in the case of Sāgara.
Regarding the banners and so forth: second, there is conversion through opposition, as in the case of Jvalanāmukha and others; this is called conversion through contrariety.
It also serves as a warning to beginners not to mistake eccentricity for the true path. Beyond these two conditions, other instances are omitted. ▲ Eighth, regarding "pushing" and "not pushing":

All these friends are humble regarding themselves and recognize their own deficiency, while they defer to the superior and recognize their own abundance. The first [of the four] and the last three lack these two qualities;
yet, because they manifest that the person’s dignity and virtues are already complete, those who are sent away do so to cause them to cultivate further without weariness or satiety.

This also indicates that the dharma-gates presided over by each are distinct. As for not attributing [the praise] to the Buddha: it reveals that the ocean of fruition is free from the marks of cultivation.

Furthermore, the Buddha belongs to the original assembly, whereas Samantabhadra’s extolling of virtues is logically appropriate to be attributed [to him]. Regarding the ninth point, "binding and non-binding": only Samantabhadra is bound;

his binding extends throughout the ten directions, bringing benefit to every atom and land. This manifests that his rank is already perfected and the principle of the *dharmadhātu* is all-pervasive. The others...
All others act contrary to this. ▲ Tenth, regarding those who do not depart: the final two positions involve no departure.

Mañjuśrī is bodiless, manifesting his freedom from marks; Samantabhadra’s stage is ultimate, as he pervades the dharma-realm. All others depart, for they learn from no fixed teacher and seek ever-greater progress.

Next is the formal explanation of the text, which is divided into four distinct sections: first, the clouds of the four assemblies rushing forth; second, the harmonious transformation through the three karmas;
third, those of superior faculties following after; and fourth, the Great Sage’s repeated instruction.

△ Now, the first section is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation; second, from "There are upāsakas... onwards, a detailed exposition of the four assemblies, which constitutes four distinct sections.

Within the [explanation of] the two assemblies, each passage contains three elements: first, the designation of the principal members and their affiliation; second, the enumeration of specific names as follows...; and third, the concluding summary.
The following section concludes the exposition on the abiding in dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). First:

(1) *Upāsaka*, here translated as "male lay follower" (*upāsaka*), so called because he draws near to the bhikṣus and attends to their needs. (2) *Upāsikā*, here translated as "female lay follower" (*upāsikā*), so called because she draws near to the bhikṣuṇīs and attends to their needs.
Both of these receive the name "lay follower" (*upāsaka*) because they have received the five precepts. (3) ...
The "five youths" and the "four youths"—the specific names for these categories each have their own underlying narratives that may be inferred through reflection.
They are all "five hundred" because they represent the five stages of realization, which encompass the fourfold assembly; together, they constitute the two thousand practices of Samantabhadra.
△ Second, at that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, knowing that the three karmas of those below Puṇyavatī City were ready for transformation, acted therein in two ways:

first, he adjusted their faculties through body and mind; second, he bestowed the Dharma according to their individual capacities. Within the first, there are also two parts: first, he generally adjusted the great assembly;
second, he specifically observed Sudhana. Now, for the first: his body manifested majestic light, his mind flowed with compassionate wisdom, and he spoke of skillful means.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "He gave rise to the thought of preaching the Dharma. Second, from "At that time" onwards, there is a separate observation of Sudhana, recognizing his extraordinary nature and specifically turning the Sage’s compassionate regard toward him;
it is for this reason that the name of the assembly, "Sudhana," was established. Although there were five hundred [disciples], it was not because they were singled out.
This section is divided into two parts: first, the heading which introduces the inquiry; second, from "Knowing this youth" onwards, the specific observation of the cause.

Regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*), there are also two aspects therein: first, observing external conditions; second, observing internal causes. Within the former, there are again two parts: first, a detailed explanation;

second, a summary beginning with "By means of this matter... and so forth. Wealth primarily belongs to the environment (*āśraya*). Goodness (*kuśala*) encompasses both the environment and the body (*sambhoga*).

To be born while wealth is manifest is the mark of goodness; thus he is called Sudhana (Good Wealth). Lesser sages revere emptiness; thus they are born in empty rooms. Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) value virtue; thus they are born...
Abundant Dharma-wealth. Second, it is further known that this youth, as described below, observes his internal causes; this observation of causes is by no means trivial.
However, as he has not yet entered the [Bodhisattva] stages, though supported by merit and wisdom, he resembles one in commoner’s attire who deeply harbors virtuous conduct.

Furthermore, this is called "good" (*śubha*); in contrast to the aforementioned "wealth," it is explained that the mind following principle is called "good," while the inexhaustible accumulation of virtue is called "wealth. Thus says the text.
There are ten phrases. The first two concern past causes; from "faith and understanding" onwards, they pertain to both the past and the present. The final phrase of the old translation states:
"Dedicate toward Bodhi so that there are no obstacles. This current translation omits it briefly.

Second, from the passage "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva observed in this way" onwards, he imparts the Dharma according to their faculties. Within this, there are three parts: first, connecting the preceding with the subsequent; second, the Dharma...

There is something to be entrusted. For this reason, he is joyful and causes [the recipient] to personally treasure and uphold it; thus, it is necessary to provide consolation. Second, "extensively for those below" refers to the formal bestowal of the Dharma-gate.

First is the general overview; "that which is called" below is the specific detail. The specific section contains ten phrases: the first is the Dharma of the cause, referring to the accumulation of the myriad practices; the next eight are the Dharmas of the result;
and the last one is that which penetrates both cause and result, as well as both principle and phenomenon. Third, at that time, the text...

In the section on "Exhortation to Practice" within the *Sudhana-ālankāra*, Mañjuśrī acts as the teacher for Sudhana. This section concludes by summarizing what has been previously taught: that [the teaching] is universal and impartial;

it points back to the causal dharmas mentioned earlier to exhort him toward cultivation and progress, to cause him to generate the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) and seek the fruit of Buddhahood attained by previous Buddhas, and to cause him to recollect his past roots of goodness.
This prevents them from disparaging themselves; others who do not possess this capacity will be further instructed according to their suitability.
△ Third, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, those of superior faculties follow along, partaking together in the sublime essence, standing alone as the preeminent peak amidst the gathered stream.
Revering the Dharma and following his teacher, he spoke in verse to seek ordination. This section consists of two parts: first, the introductory narrative of the causes;
second, the formal presentation of the verses. Regarding the first: since he has already resolved his mind [for enlightenment], at what stage does this Bodhicitta reside?

Is the youth Sudhana a saint (*ārya*) or an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)? There have been many ancient explanations. One school asserts that he is a Bodhisattva on the stages (*bhūmi*), claiming that "resolving the mind" refers to the realization of that resolve.

It is the mind. One interpretation states that these are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) of actual retribution prior to the stages [of the Bodhisattva], who possess past roots of goodness and whose faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) has now matured.
Another says that this [previous] view is insufficient as a basis; he himself cites the passage concerning the Earth-Ruling Goddess (*Dharaṇīndrarājā Devī*), which states:

"This person has already been born into the lineage of the Dharma-King. This text can definitively establish [the meaning]. He himself provides two interpretations: first, that their wisdom accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and thus they are born into the family of the Buddha.

They are called those of the lineage of the Dharma King; they have already entered the [bodhisattva] stages. Second, there are those who, based on the excellence of their cultivation through extensive hearing (*bahuśruta-vāsanā*) and their accomplishment of the true nature of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-tathatā*), are born into the lineage of the Dharma King; these are the bodhisattvas of the spiritual lineage within the three stages of the ordinary person (*tri-śaikṣa*).

However, this master’s interpretation, when relying on the former meaning, does not differ from that of the first master; when relying on the latter meaning, it is no different from the subsequent explanation. Why should it be considered distinct?

Furthermore, regarding the statement that one who has realized the lineage of the Dharma King is established in meditative certainty (*niyāma*), how is the text of the *Maitreya-sūtra* to be reconciled? It says:

"While other bodhisattvas require immeasurable eons, this youth purifies the bodhisattva practices within a single lifetime. Moreover, when we see that Samantabhadra and others attained the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*) under various Buddhas, at what stage were they?
One cannot hold to a single passage [in isolation]. [Note: The final phrase "無執一文自" appears to be a fragmentary conclusion or a transition to another argument.]
Regarding the phrase "holding spears and shields," the Venerable Master Xianshou explains that these must be those among the practitioners of faith who are destined for the happy realms (*sugati*).
According to the school of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are three stages. First is the stage of seeing and hearing;

this refers to Sudhana, whose body in his previous life saw and heard such teachings of Samantabhadra, thereby accomplishing the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), as was analyzed in the preceding section on the praise of virtues. Second is the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
To practice the dharmas of these five stages all at once is precisely as when Sudhana, in this very life, attained the stage of Samantabhadra.

Third is the stage of realization and entry (*praveśa*), which is the ultimate consummation of the causal stage, where one merges into the ocean of the fruition. Sudhana’s next birth refers to this stage.

If one asks what specific stage this definitely is: if it is within the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), it is the stage of faith; if it is within the stage of abiding (*vihāra*), it is the stage of abiding.
A single body traverses the five stages; wherever it resides, it is subsumed therein, because it pervades all things, just like the stage of Samantabhadra.

This interpretation is highly consistent with the core tenet of the sutra. Its meaning is as follows: the subsequent reliance on the five stages refers to that which is realized. Furthermore, there is another principle:

by traversing the stages through cultivation, one attains the vision of Samantabhadra, realizing it instantaneously and all at once. Even the celestial sons of hell [attain this] within a single lifetime.
The three levels are suddenly perfected. Why, then, does Sudhana definitively establish himself at the first stage? This can surely be inferred; for ordinary beings and sages are difficult to fathom.
Second, the actual presentation of the verses: formerly they were five-character lines, now they are seven-character lines.

The old scripture had thirty-four verses, while the present version has thirty-seven, including the first verse and the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth. These are divided into three major sections; the first verse serves as the heading.
Praise for seeking deliverance. Next, thirty-two verses specifically praise seeking deliverance. Finally, four verses conclude with praise and a request for exposition.
First, the first half praises Mañjuśrī’s virtues: the upper line concerns self-benefit, and the lower line concerns benefiting others. The second half seeks deliverance:
the upper line indicates the presence of the great resolve (*mahācitta*), and the lower line requests that what follows be heard. Second, the thirty-two verses.

In the second section of the *Pṛthag-stotra* (The Separate Praise) for seeking liberation, there are four preceding verses. These lament one’s own immersion [in suffering] and express self-exhortation regarding one’s inability [to escape]. The remaining verses look up to virtue and rely upon others, entreating them to grant deliverance.
Within the former, it is clearly explained that one is deluded regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), and has lost sight of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).

One creates causes and pursues results, sinking long into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). This involves the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), consisting of karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and suffering. For now, this shall be divided into two parts; first—
The two verses clarify that because one is deluded regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*) act as the cause, whereby one undergoes the fruit of suffering.

The latter two verses clarify that because one has lost the path to cessation (*nirodhamārga*), karma acts as the cause, whereby one undergoes the retribution of suffering. Now, for the first eight lines: the first two lines refer to the afflictions that moisten karma;
the fifth and sixth lines refer to the afflictions that initiate karma. This corresponds to what is said in the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*: "Enveloped by ignorance (*avidyā*), one experiences..."

Water provides moisture; the *asmimāna* (conceit of "I") irrigates it. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Enveloped by ignorance (*avidyā*), one erects the high banner of arrogance and enters the net of craving.
Furthermore, these three categories, having passed away into the past, are collectively termed ignorance. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* calls this the "fundamental ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*).
Regarding the fault of being deluded about the meaning of phenomena (*dharma-artha*), that which is constantly shrouded by the darkness of folly is precisely this delusion.

The Dharma transcends [conventional categories]. "Dharma" here refers to the essence of the mind (*cittatattva*). Because one is deluded regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of the essence of the mind, one creates various karmas.

To distinguish this from other factors that incite karma, it is collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Therefore, the text specifically mentions "the darkness of delusion, ignorance. The *Ṣaṣṭhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"Because one does not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is called ignorance. Nevertheless, all afflictions (*kleśa*) incite karma; hence, the subsequent line says:
The blazing fires of greed and anger constantly burn those who possess the three poisons. However, at the stage of initiating karma, the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) increases;
therefore, various sūtras and śāstras frequently state that it is ignorance which is able to initiate karma. Of these, the first two phrases concern the fault of delusion.

The second phrase refers to delusion regarding the internal lack of self (*anātman*); being stained by this, one insults others and gives rise to pride and arrogance, flowing on through the long currents of birth and death, loftily—
It is difficult to surmount; therefore, it is likened to a wall and moat. The *Ṣaḍbhūmika-sūtra* states: "Birth within the three realms arises entirely from attachment to a self.
The first line refers to the error of delusion regarding external objects: one falsely claims "this is mine" and clings to external spheres, thereby giving rise to craving and defilement.

Without craving, there is no birth; through attachment and craving, one does not escape. Thus, it is compared to a moat. The second, third, and fourth lines refer to the fruits of suffering. Once [craving] has arisen...
"Moistening. Because the accumulated causes have already been established, one enters and exits without rest within the gates of the six destinies;
one remains attached and does not depart from within the city of the three realms. The seventh phrase refers to the conditions that give rise to delusion and the master of bitter fruits;

thus, it is called the "Demon King. The eighth phrase refers to those who give rise to delusion—the persons who undergo suffering. Due to these aforementioned causes and conditions, they sink long into bitter fruits; are they not indeed foolish children?

The final two verses clarify the loss and extinction of the Path. One undergoes the fruit of suffering with karma as its cause; this is precisely because of the arising of *saṃskāras* from the preceding ignorance (*avidyā*).
Among these, the last three lines concern the fruit of suffering that arises, while the first five lines concern the performance of karma through afflictions (*kleśa*).
Within those, the phrases "the delusive play" and "constantly traversing dangerous paths," leading toward various false paths, specifically clarify the engagement in the production of karma.

The remainder refers specifically to the afflictions concurrent with karma. Due to the aforementioned deluded attachment to "self" and "what belongs to the self," three faults arise in relation to the self and its objects:
first, flattery and deception arise toward that which has not yet been obtained; second, envy and jealousy arise toward that which cannot be obtained;
and third, stinginess arises toward that which has already been obtained. Because one creates karma through hatred, anger and resentment arise.
To harbor resentment in the mind is the beginning of thought; its delusive agitation is the end of thought. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
"The wind of anger and hatred blows upon the fire of consciousness; the consciousness burns without ceasing. This unceasing, blazing intensity is itself delusive agitation."
Karma arises from afflictions; being neither fixed nor real, it is called "confused play. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "It is like a performer who manifests transformations with ease;
this is the fire of the mind-consciousness that is blown [into flame]. Being entangled by craving is like being bound by a snare.
One creates karma through greed; because one creates karma for the sake of existence, how could there ever be an end? One who is obscured by doubt is like one born blind.
One creates karma through delusion (*moha*). The *Ṣaḍbhūmi-sūtra* states: "Improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) gives rise to false conduct.
Doubt is precisely improper mental attention. Improper mental attention is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*), and because it is also subsumed under ignorance. If...
Those born blind, deluded regarding karmic maturation (*vipāka*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), see nothing at all;

they constantly travel through perilous realms along various false paths. This clearly explains the fault of losing the path and creating karma. "Constantly traveling through perilous realms" points out the fault with respect to persons; "various false paths" points out the fault with respect to phenomena.
The "path" refers to the causes of karma, namely the three types beginning with merit (*puṇya*). "Various" (*nānā*) means that they are accumulated perversely; they are constantly accumulated.
It is constant. Even wholesome karma that is unmoving is accompanied by delusion, let alone the ten unwholesome paths of action and the heterodox practices of non-Buddhists.
Thus, the First Ground states: "Whatever actions one performs are all associated with inversion.

Regarding the results produced by the final three phrases, the first phrase refers to unwholesome results, while the second phrase encompasses both wholesome and unwholesome results. Since the failure to perceive [reality] is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), there is the subsequent phrase.
Because they constantly suffer these faults, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings are born because of ignorance, and they die because of it.

This implies that if one possesses wisdom, there is no birth-and-death. Since the four preceding verses generally describe sentient beings, the subsequent [verses] on saving myself will thereby constitute saving others as well.
Second, regarding the twenty-eight verses on the Great Compassion that extinguishes delusions, [the author] looks up to its virtues and relies upon its person to request [its teaching].

He extends his saving grace. Within this section, there are two parts: the first thirteen verses praise the person seeking the Dharma, and the latter fifteen verses praise the Dharma for seeking the vehicle (*yāna*).
Within the former, the first three lines in each verse praise Mañjuśrī’s virtues, while the final line in each correctly expresses the request for deliverance.

Within this, there are also two parts. First, there are six verses; it can be understood that these address delusion regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), and express the hope for deliverance.

Second, there are seven verses; these address the loss of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), and aspire to the accomplishment of practice and its fruit. Among these, four [verses] follow, of which the first verse generally seeks the true path.

This refers to the fruits of suffering and the causes of the accumulation of afflictions within the three realms, the nine stages, and the six destinies—all of which you, O Benevolent One, have already extinguished.

There must indeed be a cause for this extinction, which constitutes the True Path. There are two pairs of verses. The first pair seeks the path to Nirvāṇa: the former verse extinguishes the ten unwholesome actions, seeking the path of antidotes;
the latter verse extinguishes the causes of the four inversions, seeking the path of wisdom-illumination. The third pair of two verses seeks Bodhi.

The Path. The preceding verse seeks fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) by perceiving the source of all phenomena. The subsequent verse seeks subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) to accomplish all merits.
These two verses seek the conditions for the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). In contrast to the aforementioned demonic conditions, one vows to rely upon the Buddhas.

With great compassion as the hub of the wheel, one praises the Dharma and seeks the vehicle. Speaking with metaphors, it is said that those who previously lost the right path constantly practice what is deviant.
The Path is like the steps [of a carriage]. Now, by cultivating the myriad practices and constantly walking the Right Path, one is like that secure carriage.

These fifteen verses collectively explain the essence, function, and adornments of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna). Each verse contains a concluding summary, revealing that according to any single practice, all are the Single Vehicle.
Whether phenomenon or principle, cause or fruit, they are all integrated into this single, inconceivable vehicle, which carries all beings forward as one.
Thus, one is able to transport all beings. This text is divided into three sections: first, four verses seeking the vehicle that universally rescues others through the practice of the myriad deeds;
second, three verses seeking the vehicle that perfects self-benefit through the ten perfections; third, eight verses seeking the vast vehicle that extinguishes obstacles through the two benefits.
According to the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), these three sections correspond respectively to the stage prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*) and the first ground itself.
Above. Following the final stage, all positions are mutually integrated and unified as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). One practices perfectly without attainment.
Just as there is no separate vehicle apart from the hub, spokes, and rim of a wheel, there is no separate essence of a vehicle apart from the myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*).

Cause and effect penetrate one another; phenomena and principle are universally fused. This differs from other schools where the essence and its adornments are distinct. Now, first, regarding the four aspects within benefiting others:
The verses consist of thirteen points. The first verse has five parts: First, all Buddha-dharmas rely upon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), just as all spokes converge at a single hub.
Second, practice and vows support one another to carry one to enlightenment (*bodhi*), just as two wheels are required to travel a long distance.
Third, profound faith enters the Dharma, like an axle-pin that secures everything. Fourth, firm endurance is immovable, like the axle-shaft situated within.
The mind-wheel and so forth revolve in dependence [upon it]. The five pure virtues stand at the forefront, like a shaft that leads the way. Based on these five meanings, one may realize *bodhi*.

Therefore, it is concluded as the "Vehicle of *Bodhi*. The subsequent conclusions follow this same pattern; all names are established by taking the fundamental intent from the commentary. Next, the verse has three meanings:
first, the *dhāraṇī* encompasses all phenomena, like a chest holding its contents; second, the compassionate shade provides coolness.
It is like spreading out a canopy; the eloquent exposition of the three or four [truths] is like the chiming of carriage bells. One who possesses these three practices is most excellent.
Regarding the three meanings of the subsequent verse: first, pure precepts are as immaculate as a clean mat; second, samādhi brings comfort to the spirit, like a waiting maiden;
third, the sound of the Dharma awakens beings, like the beating of a drum. Possessing these three dharmas is called the Mahāyāna.

The latter verse has two meanings. First, the virtues of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*): they contain treasures within them like a treasury; they gladden beings by spreading around like a hanging necklace.
Second, just as an ox equipped with a yoke and traces can pull a cart, so too must a person possess shame (*hrī*) and embarrassment (*apatrāpya*) to be able to guide their conduct.

Shame is not committing evil oneself; embarrassment is not causing others to do so; hence it is called "shame and embarrassment toward oneself and others. Furthermore, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:

To rely upon and respect one’s own Dharma while honoring what is noble and good is called *hrī* (self-respect). To rely upon the world while rejecting what is violent and evil is called *apatrāpya* (shame before others). Thus it is said: "others.
Adorned with these aforementioned qualities of *hrī* and *apatrāpya*, one constitutes the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).

Briefly stated, thirteen [points] are presented as its essential framework; by analogy, this demonstrates that all practices (*sarvacaryā*) are capable of benefiting others. [This concludes] two [sections], three verses, and ten [items].

Regarding the "Vehicles for the Fulfillment of Self-Benefit and the Deliverance [of Others]": since the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) are all accomplished herein, there are three fulfillments in the first verse.
First, because the vehicle is composed of jewels, it possesses light and so forth; thus, the fulfillment of the three types of giving (*tri-dāna*) gladdens sentient beings like light.

Second, it covers the stains of broken precepts, rendering the *dharmakāya* pure, like the application of fragrant ointment (*vilepana*). Third, by internally enduring greed and anger, external adversities and conformities cannot disturb one.
Injury. To eliminate sores and blemishes; this, on the chariot, has the meaning of "unbroken" and the meaning of "undamaged.

Thus, the Sanskrit text says: "The sores and blemishes are already extinguished like a vajra. These three instances constitute the path of higher rebirth (*abhyudaya-mārga*), which results in a body of great wealth and numerous retinues;
therefore, they are supreme. Next, the four instances in the following verse [constitute] the perfection of the three karmas through the destruction of obstacles.

"Wheel" (*cakra*) refers to non-retrogression; it is like a chariot moving swiftly. "Leather thong" (*nemi*) refers to the two [virtues] of guarding the gates of the sense faculties and keeping the six sense bases constantly tranquil;
it is like a box holding objects. However, in the preceding section, *dhāraṇī* was already described as the box; why is it mentioned again here? This follows the old translation.
If the Sanskrit original says, "The supreme samādhi within capable dhyāna," the intention is to take up that dhyāna can empty the mind, just as there is emptiness within a chariot.
There is the utility of a carriage. The three, four, *prajñā*, and *upāya* are explained together with the two *pāramitās*.

This means that the upper yoke represents merit (*guṇa*). Now, the yoke-ring is at the tip of the yoke; this clarifies that wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) are the foremost of all virtues. Skillful means accomplish the task, while wisdom accomplishes the crossing [to the other shore].
Task and principle correspond to one another like the two ends of a yoke. Expedient means and reality interpenetrate like a single yoke. The ox is able to...

Citing this: what practice would not precede it? For through diligence one subdues the afflictions, through concentration one matures sentient beings, and through wisdom one accomplishes the Buddha-dharma.

These three are already called the definitive path to victory; how much more so when wisdom possesses both the provisional and the ultimate, and is thus the sublime Dharma. The subsequent verse [explains] these three degrees.

1. If an ox has a driver, it can reach its destination according to his will; if practice has a vow, there is no task that cannot be accomplished, for it can lead sentient beings toward the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of Bodhi.
2. A carriage can carry a load precisely because of firm persistence; if the Dharma does not disperse, it resides within the power of *dhāraṇī*.
3. A driver possesses wisdom and can follow the bends of the water; if vows and practice possess wisdom, they revolve universally and pervasively, being fully endowed [with all qualities].

Regarding these latter three [verses], perfect enlightenment is swiftly fulfilled. The eight verses following the "Universal Interlacing of Samantabhadra" concern the cessation of obstacles through the two benefits within the vast Mahāyāna;
this refers to the stages subsequent to the [ten] bhūmis, with the meaning encompassing both the causal and resultant vehicles. The first verse contains three meanings:

first, the practice of Samantabhadra is the general heading, as it constitutes the station of Samantabhadra. Just as a net interlaces throughout a single chariot, so too is one encompassed by the practice of Samantabhadra.
1. The essence of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). 2. Because of compassion, it carries [beings] far and wide; being without conditions (*anālambana*), it is called "leisurely" (*krama*). 3.

Because it is swift though not hurried, its movement is fearless (*abhaya*). It is not afraid that sentient beings are difficult to transform. In the old translations and the Sanskrit manuscripts, the term "leisurely" (*āśvasta*) does not appear.

In Sanskrit, it is said: "Amidst tranquil conduct, one practices with valor. The old translation states: "That which is directed toward has no inherent nature," clarifying that this is the capacity for speed through non-conditionality (*anālambana*).
Advancing to the meaning. The second verse has three meanings: first, stainless wisdom is like the sturdy and pure wheels of a chariot;

second, illusory wisdom (*māyājñāna*)—which in Sanskrit is called *māyājñāna-sukṛta-susiddhi* (wondrously acting and wondrously accomplished)—is like the skillful construction of the chariot; third, having already severed the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) is like the chariot being free of impediments.
The old translation says "all things are without impediments," which contains both the dharma and the metaphor. Because it possesses these three meanings, it is [the wheel].
Swift. The third verse lacks a simile in the scriptural text; there is only the application of the dharma (*dharmopasaṃhāra*).
The first line takes up the meaning of purity; the second, bliss; the third, vastness like space. The Sanskrit term *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) signifies vastness that can universally illuminate.

Based on the above dharmas and metaphors, there is no virtue that is not complete; one should practice in reliance upon this.

This means teaching one to go and draw near to a friend, giving rise to a mind of insatiable devotion. How does one draw near to a friend? This is the primary cause for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding this "primary" [cause], there are two meanings. First, it has the sense of being supreme. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 20, states: "Unsurpassed Bodhi..."

Regarding the proximate causes and conditions, nothing precedes the virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). This is the second fundamental principle. Although the Dharma exists, if no one explains it, even the wise cannot know it.

Yet, as the saying goes, "all things have a beginning, but few reach their end. Since one must attend to these matters over a long period of time, one ought not to be lax.

This is the initial section, consisting of thirteen phrases. In comparison to the preceding verses, the text exhibits two structural tendencies: first, the former was specific while this is general;

Second, the former was horizontal while this is vertical; the former [treated] compassion, wisdom, and so forth...

Each stage is practiced in common. This training and study, from beginning to end, possesses a sequence of prior and subsequent stages. Within the text, the first two [lines] serve as the general summary, while the remaining phrases provide the specific details.
The "general" refers to the study of understanding and the study of practice; both the initial cultivation and the final cultivation are termed "training and study."

Only when the causes are perfected and the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is fulfilled is there no further cultivation. Furthermore, "learning" (*śikṣā*) subsumes understanding (*adhimukti*), while "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) subsumes practice (*pratipatti*);
thus, these two phrases already encompass [the entire process], as understanding and practice are thereby exhausted. Among the subsequent categories of friends, most consist of only these two.

Regarding the distinct meanings of the remaining phrases: first, the initial arousal of the aspiration; second, the actual performance of cultivation regarding specific matters; third, causing the mind to be all-pervasive. Therefore, the Sanskrit original asks: "What is bodhi... [and so forth].

This is the intended meaning of this question. Second, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī... onwards, the answer is divided into two parts:

Now, the first ten verses are divided into five parts. First, there are two verses praising the generation of the bodhicitta. Second, there is one verse briefly teaching non-satiety.
Third, there is one verse praising the merit of generating the bodhicitta. Fourth, there are five verses providing a comprehensive answer to the extensive teaching.

Fifth, there is one verse concluding with the resulting benefits. Now, for the first part: the first two lines offer a general praise of "Welcome," while the remaining six lines provide specific praise.
This is because of the arousal of the bodhicitta: the first phrase refers to great compassion that transforms beings below; the second phrase refers to great wisdom that seeks enlightenment above;
the next two phrases explain the initial great compassion; and the final two phrases take the great vows as primary. Furthermore, this also constitutes the Four Great Vows.

The second section consists of one verse, which briefly teaches those who are never weary [of practice]: it means that by realizing the nature of things is without grasping, one gives rise to compassion from within stillness;

thus, all Māras become attendants, for since one does not sink into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), even minor Māras cannot destroy one. The third section consists of one verse praising the virtue of generating the resolve for awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Because the merit of generating the aspiration for the sake of all beings is immeasurable, its blessings are praised preeminently. This merit of the wise outshines all other merits as the majestic radiance of its blessings;
it pervades the emptiness of the nature of phenomena like a constellation of stars, and its capacity to produce all manner of blessings is as profound and vast as the ocean.

There are five verses in the fourth [section], which provide a comprehensive response to the extensive teaching and address the aforementioned questions. To speak generally, these are: first, hearing the Dharma in the presence of the Buddha;
second, establishing vows to purify obscurations; third, entering the ocean of skillful means; fourth, pervading all buddha-fields; and fifth, enduring through all time.
When one is untiring in these five, the conduct of Samantabhadra is fulfilled, and one attains the stage of the Tathāgata as a Great Sage. This constitutes the general instruction herein.

"All dharmas" refers to the general faith within the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). The subsequent sections on "good friends" each demonstrate specific practices, signifying the distinct cultivation and realization after entering the stages.
The fifth verse, which concludes the benefits, is easily understood. Regarding the second section in prose, which instructs on approaching a friend, there are two parts:
first, the praise; second, the instruction beginning with "Good son, you now... This means that one should seek a friend who is free from faults.
Thus, the previous questions are all resolved. Within this section, there are two parts: first, the definitive determination; second, the admonition and exhortation. Now, for the first part:

since the Master above commanded that one must seek a friend, this decision cannot be avoided. Regarding the term "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*): it is not yet known how the good Dharma can cause one to know, nor how the evil Dharma can cause one to recognize. Alternatively, both may apply.
"Recognizing" (*śes pa*) refers to clear understanding, while "knowing" (*shes pa*) refers to decisive realization. (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Chapter 4)
14. One who has accomplished eight qualities possesses the characteristics of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). First, ethical discipline; second, learning; third, realization;

fourth, compassion; fifth, fearlessness; sixth, forbearance; seventh, tirelessness; eighth, the possession of skillful speech. Here, the term "genuine" (*bhūta*) is used to distinguish them from those who merely resemble such friends.
Possessing the eight aforementioned meanings, one may be called "true. Furthermore, there are five types of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*):

first, those who understand the causes and effects of good and evil in the world and cause others to cultivate what is wholesome and abandon what is unwholesome; second, those who weary of worldly pleasures and seek *nirvāṇa*;

third, those who possess a compassionate heart and practice the means of deliverance for others; fourth, those who, through the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*), lead beings to practice; and fifth, those who cultivate the attainment of non-obstruction.
One fulfills the practices of Samantabhadra. Regarding these five [stages], each preceding one, in comparison with each succeeding one, is not the ultimate truth;

the truth exists only in the fifth. If a person can practice this, that person is a virtuous friend; the ultimate virtuous friend is none other than the Tathāgata. This is based directly upon the five dharmas.
They are called the "Dharma-Good Friends" (*dharmakalyāṇamitra*). Taken collectively, they encompass all things; thus, the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit are all good friends.

The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (the "Chapter on the Path") constitute the good friends who act as spiritual guides (*kalyāṇamitra*). Furthermore, in the *Lokottara-parivarta*, there are ten types of good friends; fearing prolixity, I shall not cite them here.
Below the passage "Afterward, the good man seeks a spiritual friend," there are exhortations and instructions; following these are the exhortations, while all the rest are instructions.
Even if one has actual faults, one should still forget them and adopt the Dharma. Even the sagely Yao and Shun were still plagued by such matters;

who, other than the Tathāgata, could be entirely without fault? To reject the Way because of a person is to deceive oneself. How much more so when expedient and ultimate teachings are manifold, and it is difficult to distinguish between those who are spiritually mature and those who are not.
