Third, regarding the "Good Son" below here in the south, he points out his subsequent companion. This section has two parts: first, presenting the companion’s environment and its inhabitants;

second, exhorting him to go and instructing him on what to ask. Now, for the first part: as for the "Land of Supreme Bliss," the following knowledge-person (jñāna-puruṣa) serves as the initial [guide].

Abiding, it surpasses the preceding stages because one has faith in what is cherished. As for the mountain named "Wondrous Peak" (Gṛdhrakūṭa), there are two meanings to the term "mountain": first, being tranquil and immovable;

second, being loftily elevated so as to provide a comprehensive view. These serve as metaphors for the First Abode (*prathamā bhūmi*), where the mind of understanding is newly established, and wisdom is brought forth based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Tranquil and unmoving, his wisdom reflects all things without omission. Penetrating to the source of all fruits, he surveys the myriad classes of beings below.
Mounting this summit of the mind, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment; thus it is called "Wondrous Peak" (*Miaofeng*). His companion's name is "Auspicious Cloud" (*Jixiangyun*).

The cloud has four meanings: first, the meaning of universal pervasion; second, the meaning of moistening and nourishing; third, the meaning of providing shade and shelter; fourth, the meaning of pouring down rain. Therefore, these follow next.

"Virtue" refers to concentration (*samādhi*), merit (*puṇya*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). One who possesses these four meanings is called "Auspicious" (*śrī*). Furthermore, because one has newly entered the stage of abiding, it is auspicious;

and because one has newly emerged from the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), he relies upon a bhikṣu to pose the inquiry. As for the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*), this was a simplification by the translator and not an abbreviation made at the time [of the original teaching];
the Sanskrit manuscript fully records the preceding section of the inquiry.
In the fourth period, Sudhana departs; he reflects on the kindness [of his teacher] as he takes his leave.

He is filled with joy and leaps for gladness because he is about to meet his next spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), yet he weeps and sheds tears as he sorrowfully parts from the virtuous voice [of his current teacher]. All subsequent spiritual friends should be understood according to this pattern. This concludes the second section.

Although the meaning belongs to what follows, the text is located here in this assembly because it is spoken within this assembly. Question: The Great Sage possesses the wisdom to expound [the Dharma], and Sudhana possesses the capacity to receive it;
why does he not reveal it all at once, but instead points to others and directs him to serve various spiritual friends?

This question arises as a doubt based on the examples of the subsequent spiritual friends. Answer: There are ten reasons. First, to clarify it in terms of its general characteristics, so as to provide a model for future learners.

First, because of the model [set by the Buddha]. This means that Sudhana sought the Dharma without weariness, and his spiritual friends taught the Dharma without stinginess. Second, to manifest the excellence of the conditions for practice.

This means that a true spiritual friend constitutes the entirety of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), as seen in King Udayana’s meeting with Jīvaka, or the transformation of Viśuddhamati by Viśvantara, and so forth.
Third, to destroy ignorant attachments, thereby preventing one from taking an ignorant mind as a teacher; instead, one empties oneself and seeks everywhere. Fourth, to destroy [wrong] views.

1. To counteract pride: that is to say, it prevents one from failing to examine [the teacher's] lineage and caste, or from feeling no shame in asking humble questions; rather, one must universally show respect and serve them. 2. To break the attachment to biased emptiness:
that is to say, it is not merely a matter of seeking nothing; within the state of seeking nothing, I therefore seek it. 3. To cause one to realize the identity of phenomena and practice:
it is better to have heard little yet be able to realize and enter [the truth], than to possess much learning without practicing or realizing it. 4. To break... [text fragment]
1. Because the teacher of the Dharma is included within the mind, the notions of "my followers" and "my resources" are eliminated.

2. Eighth, it is to reveal that one enters through gradual cultivation by relying on successive stages; for if one does not defer to those who follow, there will be no further progress while remaining in each stage.

3. Ninth, it is to reveal the profound and vast nature of the Buddha-dharma; even when serving all spiritual friends, one does not exhaustively investigate their origins, yet even true spiritual friends are still deferred to.
It is supreme. How could the inferior wisdom of ordinary beings ever know it exhaustively? Tenth, this reveals how Sudhana and his spiritual friends form a dependent origination:
Sudhana has the power to elicit the teachings of the friends, while the spiritual friends have the power to cause Sudhana to realize them; they penetrate one another completely.
Subject and object are not two. When there is no Sudhana outside of the spiritual friends, then the one is all.
When it is clarified that Sudhana traverses the stages, there is no spiritual friend outside of Sudhana; thus, all is the one. The accomplishment of the many stages is entirely Sudhana.

Therefore, there is sovereign freedom in rolling up and unfolding [the teachings], with nothing to be attained. Regarding the ten meanings above, the first applies generally to both teacher and disciple; the next...
The first five [stages] are explained primarily in terms of the provisions (*sambhāra*); the seventh is explained in terms of the teacher;

and the final three are explained in terms of the teaching. The second major section: "At that time, the youth Sudhana gradually traveled southward," and so forth. Herein, there are ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
These are metaphorically assigned to the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*). This means that upon first entering the realm of emptiness, one’s wisdom dwells in the nature of emptiness;
because one attains this stage without falling back, it is called "abiding. Although there are many meanings of "abiding," ten are taught here by way of a complete enumeration.

With the bodhicitta as its essence, the predominance of the "straight mind" is termed "entering the realm of emptiness. As for its characteristics, it is equal to the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space. These are the ten abidings.
The same. This constitutes ten sections. However, regarding the subsequent passages, the ancient masters have categorized the text from one to ten;

here, I shall briefly describe one or two. Master Bianpu divides it into three parts: first, hearing the name and seeking it out, which is the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*); second, receiving what has been taught.

This is the stage of direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). The subsequent "looking up and inferring superior progress" constitutes the stage of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This can be divided into five parts: first, exhorting practice by citing the Dharma;

second, entering according to the teaching; third, requesting respect upon having seen [the truth]; fourth, correctly demonstrating the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); and fifth, looking up and inferring superior progress.
However, although the former two meanings are both explained in terms of the stages and are excellent in their significance, they are inconvenient in terms of the textual structure, because...
Although the definition of "friend" (*mitra*) belongs to the latter section, it was explained previously;

therefore, following Master Yi and the *Wutai Lun*, I have now categorized it by combining the relevant sections into six parts, though the terminology differs slightly. First: Seeking according to the teachings. Second: Seeing, honoring, and inquiring.
Third, praising and receiving the Dharma; fourth, humbling oneself and deferring to the superior; fifth, pointing out a future companion; sixth, expressing regret for departing and taking leave.
Since most texts contain all these elements, they are categorized collectively here; minor variations in their presence or absence will be clarified in the relevant passages.
Furthermore, there are many other sections, which are merely specific details within these six categories, and as many of them are incomplete, they are not explicitly set forth here.

● Now, this Bhikṣu Śrīmegha abides in the stage of the Initial Aspiration (prathamacittotpāda-vihāra). This means that, taking the ten powers of the Buddha as his object, he generates the resolve for enlightenment, gives rise to great compassion, and descends to transform sentient beings.
With compassion and wisdom guiding one another and corresponding to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), it is called the stage of the Initial Aspiration.
The full text contains six sections.

Now, regarding the first section, "Seeking according to the instructions," which follows the subsequent descriptions of the various friends, it is generally divided into two parts: first, recollecting the instructions of the preceding friend;
second, proceeding to seek the subsequent friend. Here, the first meaning is omitted for brevity, or perhaps it was not mentioned because he had not yet entered that stage.

Only the act of seeking is described, and the repeated mention of "gradually traveling south" serves as a general indication of his preparatory application (*prayoga*), signifying that his mind has ascended to a higher level. Thus it is said:
Ascending the mountain, one uses wisdom (*jñāna*) to examine all conduct and positions as a thorough observation. When the mind grasps the essential meaning, it is called "seeking.

Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path, the *Saptasūrya-prādurbhāva-sūtra* states: "The non-attainment of dharmas is 'not seeing. One must forget the mind to sever all conceptualizations.
To remain tranquil without losing illumination is 'correct observation. One hopes to leave behind the light feathers [of distraction], so that the mind is unmoving and at peace. However, first..."

Regarding the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, there are generally four interpretive models: first, interpreting the text according to its specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); second, distinguishing through the teachings (*śāsana*); third, harmonizing the original and the trace (*honjaku*);

and fourth, seeking through the contemplation of the mind (*citta*). Not a single word or meaning fails to be treated in this way. Now, these shall be applied generally, with selection and rejection as appropriate.
The first model is used for broad textual applications; the second is used when the meaning is implicit; the third is used for cases of confusion; and the fourth is the fundamental intent.

Usage. The fourth [category] and the first category share a single meaning; this appears to be a conflation with the Master’s own thought. Having attained this one gate, one does not merely count another’s jewels.

Entrusting matters to reveal the Dharma is a subject found extensively throughout the scriptures; to slight this one gate is to distance oneself further from liberation. Therefore, in the subsequent explanation of the "Friend," the "Support" (the environment), and other phenomena, this gate is frequently employed.
If one relies on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), these characteristics are numerous and easy to understand.
The section beginning with "After the second seven days" is divided into three parts: seeing, paying respect, and inquiring. This pattern occurs frequently below. Here is the first:
having been separated from the characteristics of the seven factors of enlightenment for seven days, he forgot his current state and only then attained the essential meaning;

thus, it is called "seeing. He saw [the Buddha] on a separate mountain, which signifies the simultaneous flow of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*), as he walked slowly in meditation-walking (*caṅkrama*).

"Stillness" (*sthiti*) refers to cessation (*śamatha*); it is not dwelling in distracted thoughts. "Practice" (*caryā*) refers to insight (*vipaśyanā*); it is not dwelling in a state of mental quiescence.

If explained according to the formal characteristics of the practice, this refers to the proper cultivation of the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*. Second, "then he went forward" and so forth clarifies the performance of respectful etiquette, as he honors both the person and the Dharma.
Third, "he addressed the Noble One" and so forth concerns his inquiry into the essentials of the Dharma, which is his primary purpose. Within this section, there are three parts; first:

He first declares his own resolve, clarifying that he is a fit vessel for the Dharma. Next, from "but I do not yet know" onwards, he formally presents his questions to demonstrate that he has come for the sake of the Dharma.

As for the omissions within these questions, they are merely due to the abridgment of the translation; were it not so, how could Sudhana have known [the answers] if the friends had not been fully enumerated?
Following this, from "I have heard, O Noble One," onwards, he praises their virtues and requests them to speak, imploring them to grant him deliverance. That is to say:

One who possesses wisdom is well able to possess compassion and be free from stinginess; therefore, one should explain [the Dharma] to them. "Inducing" (*yòu*) refers to inducing through parables, which is instruction (*śikṣā*) that establishes prior understanding.
"Admonishing" (*huì*) refers to admonishing and demonstrating, which is exhortation (*avavāda*) that establishes prior practice. The following cases should all be understood accordingly.

Although there was extensive questioning previously, it only reached the point of the perfection of the causes; here, the request is concluded with the expectation of the fulfillment of the fruit. Thus, both the arousal of the mind and the intent of the practice are summarized.
In the third section, "The Auspicious Cloud Descends," there is the praise and the bestowal of the Dharma, which constitutes the actual entry into the *dharmadhātu*.

Within this, first the vessel for the Dharma is praised, and subsequently the *dharmadhātu* itself is correctly revealed. Regarding the first [section]: the reason for the praise is to cause the precious vessel to become firm and to take joy in hearing the supreme Dharma.
This passage has two parts: first, the presentation of two difficulties; second, the specific citation of the preceding questions, which serves as the explanation.

The subsequent objection consists of ten phrases, with slight variations in their grouping. Following the sequence, these are restated based on the preceding text. The first phrase restates two phrases from the preceding general section:
that both "learning" (*śikṣā*) and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) constitute the bodhisattva path. The remaining nine phrases restate the specific details.

First, "diligently seeking the domain of the bodhisattva" refers to the preceding text’s mention of initiating bodhisattva practice and setting out toward the bodhisattva domain. Second, diligence... [text continues].
The "seeking of the bodhisattva’s vast and pure practice" subsumes the preceding three phrases. That is to say: "practice" subsumes the preceding "practicing" bodhisattva practice;
"vast" subsumes the preceding "pervasive" bodhisattva practice; and "pure" subsumes the preceding "pure" bodhisattva practice. The old translation contains all three:
first, the path of renunciation, which is the preceding "practice," because practice is itself renunciation; second, the path of purification... [text continues].

The first is purity; the third is the vast mind of triple purity, which is the aforementioned pervasiveness—only this phrase is joined [to the preceding], while the others each constitute a single sentence, as they respond to a single question.
The fourth is the aforementioned transformation, because the bodhisattva’s practice also undergoes transformation. The fifth is profound entry.
1. Because of entering deeply into the vast gates of liberation; 2. Because of being born forth, for it is only through various activities that one can be brought to birth;

3. Because of observing, for one observes that the mental activities of sentient beings are diverse; 4. Because of increasing and expanding, for only by practicing the path of non-abiding does one increase and expand;
The old translation says: "Seeking the gates of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa" means that by not abiding in nirvāṇa, one is born [into saṃsāra].
The gate of death. Not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa is the gate of [liberation]. Not abiding in either is the meaning of "exiting.
Because one does not abide in either, one is able to abide in both; this is the meaning of "entering. Abiding while not abiding is therefore called "manifestation.

When the eighth stage is accomplished, the mind has no attachment to either the conditioned or the unconditioned. What practice could then not be perfected? Therefore, the World-Honored One said: "Exhaustion is non-existence..."
The exhaustion of phenomena does not mean the exhaustion of the conditioned, nor does it abide in the unconditioned. Within the realm of the conditioned, it demonstrates the unconditioned;

within the realm of the unconditioned, it demonstrates the conditioned. What, then, could there be to which one might cling? Ninth is "perfection," for it is only through this that one can eliminate the subtle transgressions of sentient beings and thereby achieve true perfection.
△ Second, "Good son, I have attained... correctly demonstrates the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is precisely the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
Within the context of extolling its excellence, its name is now specifically cited. Here, in this correct demonstration, only its essence and function are manifested.

The text consists of two parts: first, the clarification of its essential characteristics; second, the discernment of its superior functions. This is the first part. The text contains five phrases that fully encompass both name and meaning. Below, the name is concluded with: "I..."
This is solely because of attaining this dharma-gate of the wisdom of non-grasping that universally perceives the equal realm of all Buddhas through mindfulness.
In the text, the first phrase serves as the general summary, referring to the power of sovereign and decisive understanding. There are two meanings of "sovereignty":

first, sovereignty over the object of observation; whether one observes or does not observe, whether it be a single [object] or many, one possesses mastery over them all. Second, sovereignty over function.
Whether one wishes to go or wishes to stay, it is accomplished according to the mind. "Certainty" (*niścaya*) also has two meanings: first, because of the decisive judgment of wisdom;

second, because of faith that is free from doubt. "Resolution" (*adhimokṣa*) is synonymous with "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*); it also has two meanings: first, as the cause of faith, because of the acceptance of an object.
The second is the cause of function. It confirms and maintains the object; it perceives the distant as near, and the large as small, because it transforms according to the mind.

Faith and wisdom support one another so that external objects cannot disturb it; therefore, it is called "power" (*bala*), which is the meaning of *samādhi*. The remaining four phrases provide separate explanations for the preceding general statement.
First, "the eye of faith is pure" explains the meaning of the preceding "certainty of faith," which refers to the desire to cultivate mindfulness.
Regarding the Buddha-samādhi: one must first possess correct faith. Because faith and understanding arise together, it is called the "eye," whereby one perceives with clarity and distinction.

By virtue of possessing faith and wisdom, one develops profound patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) and aspiration toward the true qualities and powers [of the Buddha], causing the mind to become thoroughly pure; therefore, it is called "purified."
The illumination of the light of the two wisdoms explains the meaning of the superior wisdom of decisive discernment. The *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra* states:
"If one wishes to enter the Samādhi of Single Practice (*ekavyūha-samādhi*), one must first hear the Prajñāpāramitā and practice according to its teachings; only then can one enter it.

As for the term "single practice," it refers to the practice of the single Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is itself without even oneness. Thus that sūtra says: "The Dharma-realm has a single characteristic. One should fix the conditions of mindfulness upon the Dharma-realm. This means...
This refers to the meaning of "resolute understanding" (*niścita-adhimukti*) herein. Furthermore, it reveals that all Buddhas are equal and non-dual.

If we consider the stage of manifestation, this is precisely the essence of the "Abiding in the Production of the Thought of Enlightenment" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), because it causes [the nature] to be developed through the power of hearing the熏 (*vāsanā*) based on the original nature of understanding; thus, it is called "resolute understanding.
Third, "the universal eye is clear and penetrating" explains the meaning of mastery over the objects of contemplation; for there is no object that is not contemplated.
It is said that the Universal Eye takes suchness as the Buddha. Since there is no phenomenon that is not suchness, there is nothing that is not the Buddha.

It takes awakening as the Buddha. Since there is no mind that is not awakening, all minds are the Buddha. When one accords with the realm of sole suchness through the awakening of the empty mind, one does not stir from the dharma-realm.
Reaching the source of tranquil illumination, both mind and objects are the Buddha; subject and object are simultaneously extinguished. Is this not so?
How universal! Such a true eye is only then clearly penetrating. Regarding the four types of pure conduct, this explains the meaning of the aforementioned power.
It is not merely pure faith; rather, whether sinking or uplifting, all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), all grasping (*upādāna*), and all obstacles to samādhi fail to arise.
Therefore, it is called "pure. Because the mind creates the true realm, it is termed "conduct" (*caryā*); this is precisely the single practice. Second is the wisdom-eye, which is pervasive.
Observing what follows, we shall distinguish its superior functions. Previously, the essence of function was clarified through the *ekavyūha-samādhi*;

now, the function of that very essence is clarified. This function is inexhaustible and, in brief, possesses two types: first, internal function; second, external function. Now, within the first two phrases, there are three functions.
The wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) universally observes all realms; this is the function of the universal eye (*samanta-cakṣus*). It is skillful...
Skillful means is the function of the illumination of the light of wisdom. Being free from all obscurations is the function of pure conduct.
With the phrase "by means of a purified body" and below, its external functions are clarified. First, through the seal of resolute belief (*adhimukti*), one goes and stays according to the mind;

herein there are three parts: first, clarifying going while remaining unmoved; second, with the phrase "by the power of faith and understanding" and below, maintaining without mental effort; third, with the phrase "by the eye of wisdom" and below.

One sees them without having to go there. Within this, there are three parts: first, the general heading; second, the section beginning with "That is to say," which specifically reveals the great number [of Buddhas];
and third, the section beginning with "In each and every direction according to what is seen," which clarifies the distinct phenomena seen therein. All of these are clearly intelligible.
Fourth, "Good Son," I have only attained the lower [level]. This is a modesty regarding oneself and a recommendation of others as superior. Within this, there are two parts:

first, modesty regarding oneself and knowing one thing, which concludes the stage of self-benefit; second, recommending the superiority of others and knowing their manifoldness, which constitutes the increase of superior progress.

△ Now, for the first part: it concludes by indicating its name. "The equal realm of all Buddhas" refers to that which is observed; it encompasses the ten directions horizontally and extends through the three periods vertically.

It exhausts the three periods of time and its meaning penetrates the ten bodies; therefore, it is called "all. This refers to the aforementioned single practice of the Samādhi of Universal Contemplation (*samantaprasāda-samādhi*).

One contemplates their Dharma-body, and by extension, the ten bodies of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions. The true and the responsive are non-dual, and the ten bodies are perfectly interfused—all of these are the objects of mindfulness.
There are two kinds of equality: first, equality regarding phenomena, wherein one receives the intention to benefit and bring joy to all Buddhas.
First, they are equal in terms of transformation, because all their activities are entirely identical.

Second, they are equal in terms of principle, because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body, and the Buddhas of the three periods of time possess no dual essence. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "If even a single Buddha appears in the world..."
All emerge together; when one Buddha enters *nirvāṇa*, all enter *nirvāṇa*. Why is this? Because the *dharmatā* of all Buddhas is without dual characteristics.
To know otherwise is not true mindfulness of the Buddha. Therefore, the aforementioned sutra says: "If one gives rise to such a conception..."
"This Buddha, this most supreme one"—this is an inverted view and not the true meaning. Those who cannot see the Perfectly Awakened One lack the wisdom of attainment.

To bind oneself to the ability to observe is for the light of superior wisdom to shine upon; yet to see the Buddha by grasping at signs is to stagnate in expedient means. To know the Buddha as empty and quiescent is to sink into true wisdom.
For those who contemplate non-contemplation, they do not grasp at phenomena and are ever true; for those who contemplate non-contemplation, there is no such thing.

"Remaining unmoving while truly functioning; movement and stillness are without attainment. This refers to contemplating the true Buddha and universally perceiving the Dharma-gate, which collectively summarizes the preceding two points to conclude their designation.
This is precisely the aforementioned "universal eye of clear penetration. Thus, this latter phrase may serve as the general title. Question: The Dharma-gates are infinite;
why does the initial friend immediately instruct one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha? Answer: Briefly, there are ten reasons.
Regarding the meaning: first, because the *nien-fo samādhi* (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) precedes all other practices. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The bodhisattva takes the *prajñāpāramitā* as mother and the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* as father. Second, because one can only accomplish supreme practice by relying upon the Buddha.

Third, because its merit is great and it is easy to accomplish, it serves to encourage all beings. Fourth, because its contemplation penetrates both the profound and the shallow, it is able to universally encompass all.
Fifth, because it eliminates heavy obstacles, it acts as a supreme condition. Sixth, because it simultaneously encompasses both persons and dharmas, it is easy to apply its protection.

Seventh, because Bodhisattvas of the ten stages all practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Eighth, because it is taught at the beginning of the *Ratnaśrī-sūtra*. First, this mindfulness of the Buddha [is like] the ocean-cloud.
The teaching of the Dharma is based on the Sangha as its excellent abode for the sake of sequential order. Ninth, "the mind itself is the Buddha" is for the purpose of unifying the object of focus.
Tenth, it is to manifest that those in the first stage (bhūmi) resolve their minds toward the Buddha and delight in making offerings.
△ Second, from "Just as the various Bodhisattvas... onwards, [the section] on inferring excellence to know their multiplicity. This contains three parts: first, a general heading;
second, a detailed exposition; third, a concluding summary. ▲ Now, for the first: Generally, there are two intentions in all such inferences of excellence.

First, a general reference to the practices of all Bodhisattvas, meaning that while the excellent practices of Bodhisattvas are immeasurable and boundless, I know only one. This is what is indicated in the heading by the word "but" (而).
"Various Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with immeasurable wisdom," and so forth. Second, regarding a single practice, one knows only a small portion.
For example, in the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), there are many gateways; I know only one, while others cannot know them.

As shown below in the twenty-one gateways within the distinct sections, all are based on the recollection of the Buddha. The subsequent comparisons of excellence may be understood by analogy with this. And it says:
Regarding the "gates": they are so called because they accord with the two entries into the Buddha-realm and because they accord with the traversing of each respective realm and wisdom.
Below the phrase "the second" (referring to the section on the gates), there are twenty-one distinct gates; each first presents its name and subsequently explains its characteristics and functions.
All are named according to their specific activities and functions. According to the Jin translation, each gate contains the term "samādhi," which is now omitted here for brevity.

The ancient masters divided [the ten recollections] into two groups: the first ten concern the Buddha’s excellence in the perfection of his sublime qualities; the latter ten concern the Buddha’s mastery in the wondrous application of his powers.

My current explanation differs slightly, being organized into three sections: first, clarifying the distinctions among the objects of recollection; second, harmonizing and explaining the scriptural text.
Third, regarding the method of gathering through mindfulness:

first, concerning the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) and three bodies (*trikāya*), the contemplations differ. Briefly stated, there are ten types. The first eight consist of the three bodies; the latter two consolidate the former to form the ten bodies.
That is to say, when one contemplates the Buddha of the three bodies, this constitutes three contemplations, each of which is further divided into the primary [body] and its retinue (*niṣyanda*).
This constitutes six gates. Within the categories of retribution and transformation, one further distinguishes between the internal and external to form eight.
The ninth refers to the non-attainment of nature and characteristics; the tenth refers to their profound, interpenetrating integration. Regarding these ten types:

first, if one contemplates thus—that the Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, which is pure like space and devoid of a thinker of thoughts—then such mindfulness is of True Suchness; this is mindfulness of the Dharma-body. Second...
The Flower Treasury World-Ocean is non-different from the Dharma-realm; it abides by virtue of the Truth (tathatā) and does not depend on a physical land.

This is the nature-land of mindfulness, possessing thirty marks as numerous as the atoms within a lotus-treasury world. All of these are the marks of the retribution-body (saṃbhogakāya) of mindfulness.

Fourth, there are inexhaustible virtues, each of which is inconceivable; these are the internal virtues of the retribution-body of mindfulness. Therefore, the aforementioned sutra says: "All modes of deportment..."
In the interim, one should constantly contemplate the merits of the Buddha, day and night without even a moment’s interruption; such is the practice that should be performed.

Fifth, one contemplates the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), adorned with immeasurable jewels and extending throughout the Dharma-realm; this is the contemplation of the Land of Retribution (*vipākakṣetra*).

Sixth, one may contemplate the marks of the Buddha, complete with the thirty-two characteristics, whether in their entirety or individually, whether in reverse or in forward order, or as being sixteen feet or a thousand cubits tall—all of these are contemplations of the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
1. The physical marks, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—these are all the virtues of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) to be recollected.
2. The pure lands of other directions, with their water-birds and forest trees—these are all the environments of the transformation body to be recollected.

3. The first two [categories] are the essence (*svabhāva*); the latter six are the attributes (*lakṣaṇa*). There is no essence apart from the attributes, and no attributes apart from the essence. Essence and attributes penetrate one another; this is the true Buddha, the true reality.
The Earth. This is the ninth contemplation: the non-attainment of the nature and characteristics [of phenomena]. Tenth, by means of the nature, one dissolves the characteristics;

as the characteristics dissolve in accordance with the nature, the preceding nine gates are unified into a single principle. Thus, every virtue is inexhaustible and every characteristic is infinite. Every atom and every world-realm is filled, like the net of Indra.
This is the tenth contemplation: the profound, layered integration and subsumption. Having attained these latter two gates, all that precedes is revealed as truly real. Thus it is said in the Sutra:
While the explanations are given according to specific distinctions, their meaning must necessarily be integrated and harmonized.
Regarding the second part, the commentary on the scriptural text: the current recollection of the ten bodies constitutes the latter two gates; thus, there are twenty-one gates in total.
In the preceding twenty gates, each consists of two sub-gates that bring to mind a single Buddha, thereby forming ten bodies as the ten visions of the Buddha.
The final gate integrates these all into a single totality to form the tenth gate; this means that the first two gates are the Buddha of Vow, also called the Body of Vow (praṇidhāna-kāya).

The commentary explains that the "body of aspiration" (praṇidhāna-kāya) aspires to be born in Tuṣita; the first gate refers to the palace, which is the celestial abode and so forth, while the latter gate refers to the mental disposition (*āśaya*), which is the actual essence of the aspiration.
Therefore, it is called the "Gate of Ascent" in the Sanskrit original. In truth, the Tathāgata’s aspirations pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
To cause [beings] to see according to their inclinations is the meaning of "arising. Therefore, the ten ways of seeing the Buddha are called the "arising of vision.
The third and fourth gates are the Buddha of Original Nature; he is named the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*), because the Buddha takes wisdom as his fundamental nature.

The former gate is the wisdom of the ten powers, while the latter gate is non-apprehending wisdom (*anupalambhajñāna*); since wisdom is lucid and penetrating, it constitutes "vision. The fifth and sixth gates are the Buddha of the Dharma Realm (*dharmadhātu*).
It is named the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). In the former gate, there is no differentiation among all realms;

in the latter gate, one enters that which is invisible, subtle, and difficult to know—both of which are characteristics of the Dharma-body for the sake of universal manifestation. The seventh and eighth gates are the Buddha as Sustainer (*sthiti-dhāraka*).

It is called the "body sustained by the power of name. The former gate refers to many kalpas; the latter gate refers to many periods of time. Both are sustained by one's own power, constantly causing beings to see it as a manifestation that accords with their perceptions.
These ninety-two gates are the Buddha according to the inclinations [of beings], called the "mind-made body" (manomaya-kāya), which accords with the inclinations of sentient beings.
Because it arises according to one's wishes (*yathābhiprāya*): the former section, by pervading all lands, reveals the multiplicity of the birth-body (*janmakāya*);

the latter section, by pervading all worlds, explains that according to the mind’s inclination, one sees [the Buddha] everywhere, so as to be universally perceived. The eleventh and twelfth are the Buddhas of Nirvāṇa.

This is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). The former gate refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*, while the latter gate refers to *nirvāṇa*. Since the emanation itself is subject to cessation, it is described as *nirvāṇa*.

One must understand that the quiescence of its nature constitutes profound insight. The thirteenth and fourteenth [bodies] are the *samādhi-buddhas*, termed the *vaśitā-kāya* (body of sovereign power).
Emerging from one's dwelling through the front gate is the function of this samādhi. Sitting cross-legged in full lotus posture is the characteristic of this samādhi.
Seeing all Buddhas within a single day is the meaning of "immeasurability. Proceeding from there to transform sentient beings is the meaning of "non-reliance."
Therefore, it is called the Samādhi Buddha. It is seen as immeasurable and without dependence. Having sat cross-legged, its body fills the Dharma-realm;

how could this not be majestic power? The fifteenth and sixteenth [buddhas] are the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, named the Bodhi-body. In the former gate, they are manifested instantaneously within a single pore.
This point is subtle. The latter gate abides at the limit of the moment (*kṣaṇa*), revealing the profundity of time.

Attaining buddhahood in this manner is non-attachment to all things; it is the vision of non-attachment. The seventeenth and eighteenth [stages] are precisely the mind-buddha, termed the "body of merit" (*puṇyakāya*).

The former gate concerns the dharmas in which the mind abides, while the latter gate indicates the sovereign mind. Therefore, the Sūtra causes the mind-buddha to abide in this vision, following the mind.

The turning of the Dharma constitutes the body of merit. The nineteenth and twentieth [categories] are the Buddha of karmic retribution, whose name refers to the body adorned with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

In the former gate, this is the manifested karmic retribution; in the latter gate, it is the true karmic retribution. Seated within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), he is adorned by an ocean of marks.
Whether true or manifested, both cause sentient beings to have faith, so that they may see with deep conviction. The final gate encompasses all ten [categories].
Because the body [is thus], it is said that the "clouds of bodies" are equal to the realm of empty space. Thus, the ten Buddhas and their ten bodies are all equal to empty space;

they are both identical to the true nature (*dharmatā*), serving as the adornment of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space. This is a distinction made according to different gates of teaching, yet when one is raised, all are encompassed within the perfect whole.

Only in this way does it constitute the *Avataṃsaka* recollection of the Buddha. The above has been a brief analysis. According to the differences in what is recollected, these many [aspects] are established.
Section on the Gates. If one were to address each of the ten contemplations individually, I fear it would be too prolix to set them forth all here.

Third, regarding the gate of the "Able-to-Recall" (nengnian) which gathers and binds [the mind], there are briefly five types. First is the gate of contemplating the Buddha by means of right mindfulness directed toward the object.

Whether true (dharmakāya) or manifested (nirmāṇakāya), whether the support (āśraya) or the supported (ālambana), these are all objects. To recite the name belongs to the mouth; it is not yet true mindfulness, and thus it is omitted here.
[The text] does not speak [of these]. Second is the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha as the mind-only encompassing of objects: "This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha.
The ocean of the Tathāgatas' right and universal knowledge arises from the thoughts of the mind. How much more so, since there is no difference between the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.

Third is the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha wherein both mind and object are extinguished: "The mind is the Buddha, yet the mind is not-mind. The Buddha is the mind, yet the Buddha is also not-Buddha."

The Buddha is neither mind nor Buddha; being far removed from all things, there is nothing to be thought of—only then is this true mindfulness. This is the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha wherein the four mental objects are ungraspable.

It simultaneously illuminates both phenomena and principle, such that existence and non-existence are ungraspable. In the profound stillness of the gate of equality with reality, what Buddha is there and what mind?

In the brilliant clarity of discerning phenomena and principle, the mind is ever-present and the Buddha is ever-present. When both are simultaneously absent, one enters correctly; stillness and illumination are unified.

Flowing: The fifth is the gate of the fivefold, layered, and inexhaustible mindfulness of the Buddha. Since principle (*li*) is inexhaustible, phenomena (*shi*) are fused with that principle and are likewise inexhaustible.
Therefore, each single gate encompasses all gates; these five gates are fused into a single unity.

This is precisely the point where the mind that is mindful herein merges with the previously mentioned ten Buddhas as its object—neither merging nor dispersing, yet entering into one another in layers.
This is profound and an inconceivable realm. Among these initial "good friends" who promote excellence, all the various gates are fully present.

While subsequent good friends may have specific functions—such as the Householder Vimukta employing the gate of "Mind-Only," or Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabha contemplating the marks and signs—all of these are distinct meanings derived from the gates within this [initial section].
By correlating these five gates with the scriptural text, one can understand them through the power of reflection.

It is attained. This single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is praised with joy in all the teachings; its principles are profound and far-reaching, and it is widely practiced by the world.
Therefore, I have again briefly described it, without wearying of detailed exposition. Regarding the section "Thus, etc. below, the summary can be understood accordingly.

Fifth, "Good Son, in the country of Nalika... and so forth. This indicates the subsequent spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Within this section, there are two parts: first, the actual presentation of the good friend;
second, the praise of how the friend brings about benefit. Now, for the first part: this refers to the good friend of the stage of "Preparation" (*caryā-pratipatti*).

As for the "Country of Sāgaramukha," because that country is situated precisely at the mouth of the Southern Sea, it symbolizes that the ocean of the contemplative mind (*citta-bhāvanā*) serves as the profound and vast gateway for preparing the ground of the mind. This is the comparison.
Regarding "Cloud over the Ocean": the ocean represents a dharma-gate, for it is like a universal-eye dharma-cloud that deeply and extensively covers and moistens all sentient beings.
This symbolizes the arising of ten kinds of deep and extensive compassion while observing sentient beings within the stage of purifying the grounds (*bhūmi*).

The subsequent passage, beginning with "The bhikṣu Cloud over the Ocean was well able to discern," praises the friend's accomplishment of benefit; the text contains ten phrases, the first being general and the remaining nine being specific, each phrase [expressing a distinct quality].
The first point refers in advance to the benefits accomplished by the latter friend. The second is the benefit obtained upon seeing [the Buddha].

The third is hearing of the past causes of the Flower. The fourth is the praise for generating the Great Mind. The fifth and sixth, as well as the seventh, are all explained by the Universal Eye (Samantabhadra).
The eighth is hearing of the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants. The ninth is the characteristics of generating the mind. These should be understood from the text itself.
At the sixth stage, Sudhana departs, expressing his longing for the Master’s virtue and bidding him farewell, as has already been explained above (in the fifth scripture).

Second is the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, who represents the stage of "Cultivating the Ground" (*bhūmi-karman*). This means that he constantly accords with the mind of emptiness, purifying eighty-four thousand dharma-gates until they are clear, pure, and white;
because he thus refines and cultivates the ground of the mind, it is called "Cultivating the Ground. The full text contains six sections.

Regarding the first [section], "Seeking by Relying on the Teaching," there are two parts. First is "Correct Contemplation by Relying on the Teaching," which clarifies the rehearsing of what has been learned.

Second is "Seeking Subsequent Friends," with the intention of desiring to know what is new. Furthermore, the former involves being able to reflect upon what has been studied, while the latter involves being able to study through reflection.

Nevertheless, reflecting on the former still pertains to the preceding stage; that is to say, one has previously approached virtuous friends and subsequently heard the True Dharma, and now one maintains right mindfulness.
Contemplation and practicing according to the teaching are the four proximate causes and conditions among the twenty-five [factors] of *nirvāṇa*.

Now, the former meaning is subsumed under the subsequent "progression," while the latter meaning is subsumed under the preceding "friend" (the guide); they mutually function as hooks and locks, with the primary and the attendant intermingling.

Therefore, according to this comprehensive judgment, they are assigned to the latter category. The following sections should all be understood accordingly. Now, regarding the first [section], within the contemplation of the former:
There are eleven phrases. The first phrase serves as the general heading, meaning: having heard the instruction of a virtuous friend, one maintains single-minded right mindfulness.

The subsequent ten phrases, which follow in accordance with that, constitute the specific details. In the old translation, all ten phrases state "right mindfulness and observation," meaning that the mind neither sinks nor becomes agitated, such that tranquility and insight flow together.
Now, this [state] is contained within the general heading, while the specific phrases within it follow accordingly.

Thus, "penetrating" (*prativedha*) applies to "contemplation" (*manasikāra*) and so forth; according to the specific context within each phrase, the appropriate term varies. That is to say, for "light of wisdom" (*jñānāloka*), "contemplation" is appropriate;

for "gate of liberation" (*vimokṣamukha*), "penetration" (*prativedha*) is required. Regarding the term "conformity" (*anuloma*): it means that there is no contradiction between the phenomena and their underlying principles.
First, it refers to mastery over the objects of observation as previously contemplated; second, it refers to the liberation through the functions as previously realized; third—
1. That is, to uphold the aforementioned *ekavyūha-samādhi*. 2. Furthermore, to extol the various gates of *samādhi* within the superior [practices]. 3.

Fourth, to revere the aforementioned hearing of the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma. 4. Fifth, to contemplate the aforementioned Buddhas who were seen. 5. Sixth, to delight in the aforementioned abodes in the ten directions. 6.

Seventh, to comprehend the aforementioned lifespans, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth. 7. Eighth, to behold the aforementioned Buddhas attaining perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). 9. Ninth, to enter the aforementioned...

The dharma-realm that is expounded is the Samādhi of One Practice. Because the Buddha who is the object of contemplation is identical to the dharma-realm, this constitutes the realm of the Buddhas prior to the ten stages of abiding.
It should be understood that one subsequently descends through the stages in succession to seek the later spiritual friends.
Second, approaching Samudramegha (Sea-Cloud), he beheld him, paid his respects, and inquired. This section has two parts: first, the act of beholding and paying respect;

second, the inquiry beginning with "He addressed him. Within this, there are two further parts: first, the personal account of his resolve for enlightenment; second, the formal inquiry into the essentials of the Dharma beginning with "Yet I do not yet know...
Among these, the term "wheel of birth and death" refers to its revolving without end, like a water-drawing wheel (*ārā*). As for the "wheel of great vows," it is [the wheel that] exhausts...
Because the realm of sentient beings is boundless, the Great Vow only reaches its conclusion when that realm is exhausted; thus, in contrast to birth and death, it is designated by the term "wheel.

The meaning of other points you have asked about can be understood from their characteristics. Although they contain profound principles, the scriptural texts are so vast that they cannot be explained in detail here.

In the third period, following the section on "Sāgaramegha," there is the "Praise and Bestowal of the Dharma. This passage is divided into two parts: first, the praise of those who are vessels for the Dharma;

second, the bestowal of the essential teachings. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the inquiry by Vajragarbha, because it is difficult to find those who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment], and if one does not so resolve, one is not a vessel for the Dharma;
next, the response by Sudhana, stating that [the teaching] is not false; and finally, the words spoken by Sāgaramegha.

This is the formal praise of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*). It consists of two parts: first, the presentation of the praise; second, the explanation of the praise, beginning with the words, "Good son, if among all beings... This section also has two parts:

first, that because the necessary causes and conditions are difficult to assemble, those who arouse [the mind] are rare; second, that because the characteristics of the aroused mind are superior, those who arouse it are difficult to find.
Regarding the first of these, there are also two parts: first, the negative formulation; second, the positive formulation, beginning with the words, "Therefore, a bodhisattva must obtain..."

This is explained in sequence. There are eleven phrases. Taking the cultivation of spiritual friends as the condition (*pratyaya*), all others are the causes (*hetu*). The first phrase serves as the general summary:

it refers to having planted the *samantabhadra* dharma-gate of non-attainment in past lives, thereby establishing the spiritual lineage (*gotra*). The second point concerns attaining the true reality; this is the specific explanation.
First, one attains the wisdom-light of *tathatā-samādhi* and realizes the true nature of the mind. Not dwelling upon appearances is called "knowing the mind through skillful means."
Because it contains and preserves all merits, it is called a "treasury" (*kośa*). This constitutes the straightforward mind; therefore, it is termed the "right path.
Having attained this radiance, one is able to truly resolve the mind for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); other cases may be inferred accordingly. Second, regarding the generation of the bodhicitta:

because the characteristics of the inferior [levels of] generating the mind are superior [to those previously discussed], this section specifically reveals the characteristics of the bodhicitta and likewise instructs on how to generate that bodhicitta.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the individual explanations; second, the conclusion. Now, for the first part, there are eleven phrases, which also constitute three minds and four great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*).
The first five are vows to deliver sentient beings. The next one is the vow to sever afflictions (*kleśa*), meaning to abandon attachment. The next two are vows to study the Dharma gates.
The final three are vows to achieve the Buddha-way: first, to perfect the form body (*rūpakāya*); second, to pacify all obstacles; third, to achieve [the ultimate state].

The Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). In this context, all phrases follow the Sanskrit original; if they were to conform to the conventions of this land [China], it would be appropriate to say, "One generates the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇācitta*) in order to rescue and deliver all suffering sentient beings.
The ten phrases are to be understood accordingly. Furthermore, these ten minds are for the most part identical to those of the Stage of Practice (*caryābhūmi*).
Fearing that it would be too prolix for those who do not understand, the following section, beginning with "Furthermore, good sons, when I first resided...

and so forth, serves as a summary. △ Second, from "Good sons, when I first resided... onwards, is the formal transmission of the essential Dharma. This refers to contemplating the ocean of Dharma, beholding the Buddhas, and hearing the Dharma.

A verse says: "Even if one were to carry [the scriptures] upon one's head for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, and offer one's body as a seat filling the three thousandfold world-system, if one does not transmit the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, there is ultimately no way to repay [their kindness].
