1. The precept of the path to awakening (*bodhimārga-śīla*): this is the eighteen unshakable brahma-conducts (*aṣṭādaśāvikopita-brahmacarya*), because one does not waver from the two benefits [of self and others].

2. The precept of non-attachment to all phenomena (*sarvadharma-asakti-śīla*): this is the thirteen unattached brahma-conducts (*trayodaśāsaṅga-brahmacarya*), because by perceiving suchness (*tathatā*), one accomplishes the noble path (*āryamārga*).

3. The precept of not abandoning the bodhicitta (*bodhicittāparityāga-śīla*): this is the sixteen abiding brahma-conducts (*ṣoḍaśasthiti-brahmacarya*), because the mind reaches the principle (*tattva*). 4. The precept of not falling into the two vehicles (*yānadvaya-apāta-śīla*)...
The precept of the ground (*bhūmi-śīla*) refers to the fifteen *brahmacarya* of non-extinction. When one acts in accordance with principle, it is never extinguished;

this differs from the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*), whose intentional observance of precepts is subject to extinction. The eighth is the precept that constantly takes the Buddha-dharma as its object (*ālambana*). This refers to the fourteen *brahmacarya* of non-contention (*araṇa*).
Since both phenomena and principle are fully present and nothing is outside the Buddha-dharma, what is there to contend with? Thus, it is always an object of focus.

Ninth, the precept of constantly recollecting omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) with the mind: this is the seventh, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) praised by all Buddhas. It is the upholding of the precepts in accordance with principle;
its movement accords with the noble mind and takes the Buddha’s wisdom as its object. Why would the Buddha not praise it? Tenth, the precept of the aspiration and delight that is equal to space:
this is the ninth, the holy life of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Because one does not apprehend subject or object, it is maintained with mastery.
Eleventh is the precept of being without dependence on anything in all worlds; this is the eighth [category], the non-dependent holy life (*brahmacarya*).
It does not rely on fame or gain in the present life, nor does it seek the fruits of human or celestial rebirth in future lives. Twelfth is the precept that is without deficiency or leakage.
This is the second, the flawless holy life (*brahmacarya*), because it is not violated by the thirteen [types of offenses] that involve forfeiture and so forth, and thus remains without deficiency.

The thirteenth is the unclouded precept, which is the nineteenth, the undisturbed holy life, because it is associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The fourteenth is the precept without omission.
15. The precept of being untainted by defilement (*asaṃkliṣṭa-śīla*). This is the third aspect of the untainted holy life (*brahmacarya*):
because one does not dwell upon various causes and conditions for breaking the precepts, one remains undefiled even when hearing the sound of bracelets or anklets.
16. The precept of non-regret (*an-anutāpa-śīla*). This is the twelfth aspect of the faultless holy life (*avadya-brahmacarya*): because one does not commit an offense.
Because remorse is an obstacle to attainment. Seventeenth is the precept of non-weariness: it is the sixth [precept] that prevents the obscuration of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
One should maintain non-weariness toward its objects so that they cannot obscure it; for it is like the swan and the pearl, or the grass-tie, which remain unbroken through being maintained.
Eighteenth is the precept of purity: it is the tenth [precept] that increases the Bodhisattva’s pure conduct, as it differs from the Lesser Vehicle, which concerns only mundane purity.

Nineteenth is the precept of being free from dust (*viraja-śīla*). This is the fourth, the stainless Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*); because one does not commit offenses leading to downfall (*pāyattika*), one is free from the dust and stains [of transgression].
Twentieth is the precept of being without defilement (*vimala-śīla*). This is the first, the unbroken Brahma-conduct;

for if one commits the four or ten grave offenses, it is like a broken vessel that can no longer be used, as these are the most defiled and heavy [offenses]. This brief explanation appears to have a basis and is also consistent [with the scriptures].
Regarding the ten kinds of precepts in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, I fear that [a detailed explanation] would be too prolix and difficult to comprehend.

From the fifth section, "Good Son," and below, there is an indication of future spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). This refers to the "Stage of Noble Birth" (*janmaja-vihāra*), which concerns virtuous friends.
As for the land named Daratipata—translated into Chinese as "Possessing Abundance"—it is called "noble" because it is born from the holy teachings and so forth.
As for the city named Vajra-koṭi (Vajra-layer), it is so called because the vajra-phrases of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are accumulated therein, rising in successive tiers.
The Great Being named Megha—alternatively transcribed as Miga—is translated as "cloud" in both versions. He expounds the gateway of the wheel of syllables.
Because it contains the moisture of the rain of Dharma; because one cultivates and studies the clouds of the Buddha-teachings of the three periods of time to rain upon all beings.
Regarding the sixth stage, when Sudhana departs, his prostrations and departure may be understood as before.
● Fourth, the Elder Maitreya. He was born into a noble dwelling and into a family of the Buddha-dharma; because his lineage was most honorable, the text likewise possesses six [sections].

Regarding the first [section], "Seeking in Accordance with the Teaching," there are two parts. First, recollecting the instructions of his former friend, which consist of fifteen phrases: the first is general, and the remainder...
[This section is] distinct. From "After observing thus" below, he seeks the subsequent stage.
Second, from "He then saw him" below, [he sees and] pays respect and inquires. This has three parts: first, seeing; next, from "Sudhana" below, paying respect;

and finally, from "He said" below, inquiring. Within this, there are two: first, his own account of generating the resolve for enlightenment; second, from "But as yet" below, questioning regarding the Dharma. There is...

There are thirteen phrases. The first two are general; the next ten are specific; and the final one is a concluding request. Within the specific section, both the horizontal and vertical dimensions are explained.
The horizontal explanation is readily understood. The vertical explanation pertains to the ten stages (*bhūmi*): (1) because the mind of realization has been generated, it is never forgotten;
(2) because there is no transgression, one resolutely seeks the Buddha-dharma; (3) because the perfection of patience increases, one is pure and humble; (4) the perfection of vigor...
Because [his resolve] increases, he does not shrink from toil. Fifth, because he enters the secular world to transform sentient beings, he possesses the universal gate of dhāraṇī.

Sixth, because prajñā is manifest before him, the light of his wisdom is free from obscuration. Seventh, because skillful means are predominant, he attains wondrous eloquence; thus, the provisional and the real are practiced in tandem.
He discerns the profound meaning. Eighth, through the power of right mindfulness, he acts in a single thought-moment; because this surpasses all else by many multiples, he retains the Buddha-dharma.
Ninth, occupying the rank of a Dharma Master, he expounds all dharmas. Tenth, because his perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is fulfilled.
This is named "Universal Wisdom. The characteristics of these ten stages are also clearly evident in the text.

I only pray that you will provide the concluding summary for the third section, beginning with "At that time, Megha... This section consists of two parts: first, praising the vessel of the Dharma; second, bestowing the Dharma-gate.
Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the inquiry; second, Sudhana’s respectful response; and third, Megha’s immediate [response].
Next is the respectful praise, which consists of two parts: first, respect; second, praise. Regarding the first:

the disciple prostrates to the teacher because the bodhicitta is the cause of Buddhahood and is capable of extensively producing all virtues. As stated in the "Chapter on the Merits of Generating the Mind":
"The merits of generating the mind are immeasurable; even if all wisdoms were to speak together, they could not exhaust them. This is as extensively praised by Maitreya below.

Regarding virtue, the *Dharmadhātunirviśeṣa-śāstra* states: "One who pays homage to the bodhicitta is like a person who pays homage to the first day of the waxing moon rather than the full moon, because the former is rare to behold;
yet it is by means of this [first day] that the full moon comes to be. Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 38, says:

The initial resolve and the ultimate attainment are not two distinct things; of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult. To seek to deliver others before one has delivered oneself—therefore, I pay homage to the first arising of the bodhicitta.
How much more so for one who has not yet preached the Dharma, nor fixed the relationship of teacher and disciple, yet subsequently bestows the Dharma upon themselves.

Just as one ascends to their formal seat, they do not violate the gravity of the Dharma. The first three [sections] all concern the Sangha; to show respect to laypeople in such a manner would be improper, and therefore it is not done so.
Second, he then joins his palms and offers praise. This section has two parts: first, the general; second, the specific, beginning with "Good son. Within this, there are three parts:

first, praising the excellence of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); second, praising the rarity of those who produce such a resolve; third, concluding the praise by establishing its benefits. Regarding the first of these:
Three. First, it clarifies the virtue of the profound and vast nature of cause and effect. This virtue is ultimately accomplished, yet its merit returns to the initial aspiration.

Since you have been able to give rise to this aspiration, you will certainly achieve success; moreover, because the beginning and the end are perfectly interfused, this mind is instantaneously complete.
Thus, the aforementioned sutra states: "All merits abide within the very first bodhicitta. Next, [this applies] to all Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
"Below. The virtue of being respectfully protected by the Ten Kings: because there are superior virtues within, it subsequently causes all realms of sentient beings to descend [to safety].
The virtue of externally benefiting sentient beings is likewise manifest and can be understood. Second, 'Good son, thus the Bodhisattva... below:

this praises the difficulty of encountering those who initiate [this practice], for such persons are difficult to meet because they are able to possess these virtues. Within this, there are two parts: first, a general praise; second, 'What...'"
For this reason, the following section provides an inquiry and an explanation. First, the intent of the inquiry is: "In what way is he difficult to encounter? The explanation states:
"Because a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind can bring about supreme benefit for all sentient beings. The analogies used to correspond with the Dharma are clear from the text.

Third, from "At that time, Megha extensively [taught] below" onwards, it is a summary of praise establishing the benefits, as it benefits those present in the assembly. This section is not found in the older translations of the sutra.
△ Second: At that time, Megha returned to his original seat and presented his own Dharma-gate. This section has two parts:

first, manifesting supernatural powers to benefit sentient beings so that they may witness it with their own eyes; second, formally transmitting the essential points of the Dharma so that they may hear them.

Now, regarding the first part, ascending the seat: both sutras are present here. Following the manifestation of supernatural powers, he transmits his own Dharma; "the initial face-gate" refers to the mouth, which reveals the path of the explicit teaching (*nītārtha*).
[The text] circulates. It also indicates that *dhāraṇī* must be maintained through the secret of speech (*vāg-guhyaka*).

Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Adornment of the Wheel-Syllable and Phrases, ancient masters cite three interpretations by the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman: first, concerning the characteristics of the syllables; as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, "the circle of syllables is complete like the footprint of an elephant.
Second, concerning that which is expressed; because it exhausts all principles and is perfectly complete, it is like a wheel that is full. Third, concerning excellence...
As for "use," it refers to the *Sūkṣmasvara-dhāraṇī*. It possesses the sense of being transmitted and the sense of extinguishing delusions, just like the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) and so forth.
This is an adornment expressed through the teaching of the syllable "wheel" (*cakra*); this explanation has already been provided. Now, I shall further rely on the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*.
To elaborate upon its characteristics: the fifth chapter of that sutra is titled "The Chapter on the Wheel of Syllables" (*Akṣaracakraparivarta*). The sutra states:

"This is a dharma-gate that pervades all places. That is to say, if a bodhisattva abides in this dharma-gate of the wheel of syllables, then from the initial generation of the sublime mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) until the attainment of Buddhahood, all various activities for one's own benefit and the benefit of others performed during that interval [are encompassed]."
One attains accomplishment, just like the initial vowel *a* (ā). This is the bodhicitta.
If one contemplates this syllable and becomes in resonance with it, one is identical to the essence of the Dharmakāya of Vairocana; that is to say, this *a*-syllable wheel is like a peacock’s tail.
A wheel-mark radiance encircles the practitioner, who abides within it; this is precisely abiding in the state of Buddhahood.
As a verse says: "The eight-petaled white lotus opens all at once, brilliantly manifesting the letter A in the color of pure light.

Furthermore, the three syllables Ā (long-drawn), VA, and VA encompass the three families: the letter Ā belongs to the Tathāgata family, the letter VA to the Lotus family, and the letter VA to the [Vajra] family.
In the Vajra Family, each individual family contains five syllables. Regarding what is called the "wheel of syllables" (*akṣaracakra*), it is from this wheel’s rotation that all syllables arise;
"wheel" here carries the meaning of "production. For example, from the syllable *a* (in the rising tone), four syllables are produced:
first, the long-drawn *ā* is the wheel of practice (*caryācakra*). Having already resolved upon enlightenment, one must necessarily cultivate various practices. Second is the syllable *aṃ*.
It forms the wheel of Bodhi; having practiced it, one will certainly realize Bodhi. Third, the syllable *Aḥ* is the wheel of Great Quiescent Nirvāṇa, which is the destination of Bodhi.
Fourth, the long-drawn *Ā* is the wheel of skillful means, meaning the great function of Nirvāṇa.
The syllable *A* is in the center, with the four syllables surrounding it. From the bottom upward, they revolve to the right like a wheel. Taking one as the starting point...

Example: other characters are to be understood by analogy. If a practitioner realizes and penetrates this, they will be able to enter the gateway of *dhāraṇī*, wherein the various arrays of the wheel of names—revolving and without attainment—are perfectly established in their respective positions; therefore, it is called "Adornment.
Furthermore, the five syllables beginning with "A" (upper tone)—the first four of which correspond respectively to the [opening of the Dharma Flower Sūtra] within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...
"Showing, awakening, and entering. The fifth single character is not present in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; it is subsumed within "entering" (*praveśa*).

The rest is as explained in the "Chapter on the Wheel of Characters" (*Akṣaracakrakrama-parivarta*). The profound meaning underlying these characters shall be analyzed in detail in the section concerning the various arts (*kalā*).

The reason for explaining this immediately prior [to that section] is that, in order to enter secular society and transform sentient beings, one must maintain both existence and non-existence, using characters to express meaning. Thus it is stated in the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*.
It is said: "The profound characteristic of signlessness is beyond the capacity of those with inferior wisdom. To transform them, existence and non-existence are taught together.
For instance, the initial letter 'A' signifies non-arising, thereby revealing the emptiness of intrinsic nature;

yet, by arranging the forms of the letters, it does not lose its quality of existence, and thus they are said to exist together. Furthermore, this is for the sake of dhāraṇī so that nothing may be lost. Since one is a physician, one likewise employs the letters."
The Wheel. Because it subdues and overcomes obstacles, and because the syllable *dhṛ* (to hold) is appropriate for use within the Noble Teachings.

Regarding the section beginning with "the second, that which is to be performed," this is the actual transmission of the essential Dharma, intended for the listener to hear. Within this, there are two parts: first, the designation of its name and essence; second, the analysis of its function. Now, for the first:
as for the "Dhāraṇī of Sublime Sound and the Dharma-Gate of Radiance," this is precisely the aforementioned Dharma-gate of the Syllable-Wheel (*akṣara-cakra*). However, regarding the syllables...
The "letter-aspect" refers to the forty-two letters; "sound" refers to the fourteen vowels, namely *a*, *ā*, and so forth.
Through sounds, one enters into syllables; from these syllables, there is an inexhaustible emergence. Beneath each and every syllable, many meanings emerge.

Because he has mastered the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*) through his excellent and wondrous voice, he understands the languages of the ten thousand species. Thus, sound and syllable are raised together, intending to mutually complete one another.
Since wisdom is their essence, they are called "light. The section beginning with "In a single thought-moment" distinguishes their functional activity; this expands upon the older sūtra.
It is not merely that he knows their words; he also understands the secret dharmas of their mental intentions and so forth. "Fourth, good son, I only... and below:
this is a humble acknowledgment of one's own limitations while deferring to the excellence of others. First, by saying "I only," he humbles himself regarding his knowledge of one [aspect];

then, with "as for those various... and below, he defers to the excellence of others regarding their knowledge of many. There are fifteen phrases, all of which are the sublime signs of the distinctions in Mañjughoṣa’s mastery. Among these, there are two [points].

First, there are four phrases that follow conventional speech and sound: (1) because one takes up mental images through conceptualization based on words as the cause, giving rise to vitarka and vicāra which act as causes, the simultaneous mental factors are called "retinue"; (2) the application of designations according to region differs;
(3) names; and (4) speech and sound. Subsequently, all [beings] are able to universally enter into all [phenomena], as explained by the following eleven phrases.
The Dharma-words of all Buddhas differ according to what they expound. First, some expound the principle of wisdom (*prajñā*), which is true within phenomena;
it is profound and esoteric, like the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Furthermore, the three mysteries (*triguhya*) of the intentional meaning are also called "secret.

Second, those that expound bodhi and nirvāṇa and below all manifest the multiplicity within the one, collectively revealing their extreme profundity. Within this, there are four types: first, the extensive; second, the supreme.
1. The five unsurpassed; 2. The six distinctions; 3. The realm of discipline; 4. Mantras and dhāraṇīs; 5. The specific elucidation of wondrous sounds; 6. The perfection of the wheel of syllables;

7. The production of the wheel of syllables. Because these [first seven] are profound and vast, they are all termed "oceans. The final three concern the ultimate exhaustion of phenomena and principles;
therefore, they are all termed "boundaries" (*koṭi*).

The fifth section, beginning with "Good son," indicates the subsequent friend. The village is named Dwelling in the Forest because he dwells in the perfection of skillful means and has established his virtuous conduct.
Because he is advanced in years and mature in virtue, he is called an Elder (*sthavira*). Within his own body, he manifests the realms of many Buddhas;

because his mastery over meditative concentration is sovereign, he is named Liberation (*vimukti*). This signifies that all the roots of goodness cultivated at this stage of dwelling are for the sake of...
Because he seeks to deliver all sentient beings and lead them even to the realization of Great Nirvana, his goodness in the sixth period is inferior;
longing for [the Buddha’s] virtue, he bows and takes his leave. (End of the Sixth Sutra).

● The fifth liberation concerns the elder who dwells in the perfection of skillful means. He maintains the truth while conforming to worldly conventions, practicing immeasurable expertise to transform beings without abiding [in extremes].
The text likewise possesses the six aspects.

Regarding the first section, "Seeking by Relying on the Teachings," there are two parts: first, the cultivation and realization of the preceding dharmas; second, seeking the subsequent spiritual friend.

Within the former, there are also two parts: first, clarifying reflection and cultivation; second, manifesting the benefits of cultivation. Now, for the first [of these], there are eleven phrases: the first is general, and the remainder are specific.
The "subtle eloquence" within the general [section] refers to the aforementioned *Sughoṣa-dhāraṇī*. Both versions contain the term *dhāraṇī*.

The "ornamented dharma-gate" refers to the *Akṣara-cakra-dharmamukha*. Regarding these two gates, because the mind follows their principles and meanings without any divergent conditions, it is called "single-mindedly.
In the remaining phrases of the specific section, the general encompasses the particular; all are focused on single-minded recollection.
These words do not appear in either of the two sutras. However, within each of the ten phrases, there is a characteristic of cultivation (*bhāvanā-lakṣaṇa*), namely:

first, deep entry into language; second, the skillful means of mindfulness; third, observation and liberation; fourth, the accomplishment of roots of goodness; and fifth, the purification of skillfulness.

Sixth, the wisdom that gathers through clarity and sharpness; seventh, the great power that makes those [qualities] firm; eighth, the non-retrogressive aspiration and joy; ninth, the expansion of those merits.

The final phrase, "without attainment," serves as a concluding summary of the meaning. From the passage "contemplating thus" onwards, it demonstrates the benefits of cultivation, because it strengthens the various dharma-gates such as vows and so forth.
Second, from "gradually" onwards, it concerns seeking the subsequent spiritual friend. Regarding the "twelve years": [text continues].

Regarding "Great Sameness" (Dàtóng) and "Ocean Cloud" (Hǎiyún): Former masters interpreted these as representing the Dharma. Because one distinguishes between self-benefit and further progress, practicing each of the six perfections, they speak of "twelve.

Now, there is another interpretation: within the twelve bases (*āyatana*) where the six sense organs encounter their objects, one must be free from attachment both internally and externally to achieve liberation.

Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings. (From the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader," *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*).
It is said: "One enters right concentration within the eye-faculty and arises from samādhi within the object of form.
By means of this, one attains mastery over the dhāraṇī of the eye and so forth; it is only after twelve years that liberation is fully realized."

Regarding the section beginning with "Having seen him for the second time," there are two parts: seeing and paying respect, and the inquiry. Within this, first is the act of seeing and paying respect, which includes expressing one's own joy because of long-standing aspiration.
Second is the inquiry, beginning with "O Noble One, I... and so forth, which contains two sub-sections: first, declaring one’s own resolve for enlightenment;

second, inquiring about the essential points of the Dharma. Regarding the first of these (the declaration), there are three parts: first, the general; second, the specific; and third, the concluding request. Now, the first [is as follows]:

[He] knows. Second, regarding the desire to specifically describe the characteristics of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*), there are three aspects in total: first, the desire to exhaustively reach the realm of the Buddhas;

second, the desire to hear [the teachings] below, which is the desire to fully exhaust the source of the Dharma; and third, the desire to be equal with all Bodhisattvas below, which is the desire to align with the practices of the Bodhisattvas.
Third, "O Holy One, I now... and so forth is the conclusion of the request, meaning it concludes the aforementioned generation of the resolve.
The [physical] marks serve as the opening for the inquiry; thus it says, "With such a mind, he went to the presence of the Sage.
Second, from "I have heard" down to "the Sage," is the consultation on the essentials of the Dharma. This section has two parts:

first, praising the one capable of providing instruction, which also serves as the opening for the inquiry—as when it says, "capable of opening the Buddha-realm," this constitutes a request for that opening. Other instances should be understood by analogy. Following this is: "I only pray that, out of compassion..."
"Alas! [The text] below requests that he explain what is doubted.
"The third period: Liberation, Elder... below correctly demonstrates the *dharmadhātu*. Within this, there are two parts: first, entering meditative absorption to demonstrate through silence.

The answer is given after emerging from meditative concentration. △ Regarding the reason for demonstrating [the practice] within concentration in the preceding section: it is taught in reliance upon the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). In this stage, concentration increases;

that is, the function arising from concentration begins to be fully equipped with skillful means (*upāya*), and one cultivates intensively in this stage so as to subsequently attain a state where the mind is stable and immovable.

The text consists of three parts: first, the causes and conditions for entering concentration. "Past roots of goodness" serve as the cause, indicating that it is through one's own cultivation. [The subsequent part follows...]
There are three conditions: first, the sovereign power of the Buddha, which manifests original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*);

second, the power of Mañjuśrī’s mindfulness, which possesses both faith and wisdom—this is already evident from the fact that Sudhana encountered Mañjuśrī as his cause; and third, the power of the principal and attendant bodhisattvas.

Regarding the second point, "immediately entering" and below, this cites the name and essence of the meditative concentration: it refers to the universal gathering of all lands within one's own body, through the mind-only wisdom that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

*Dhāraṇī*. It is so named because it causes the essence and its functions to revolve without obstruction. From "Having entered the three samādhis" onwards, the text clarifies the functional application of meditative concentration (*samādhi-karmopayoga*).
This section has three parts: first, a general clarification of universal inclusion; second, a detailed manifestation of manifold aspects;

third, causing sentient beings with corresponding capacities to see and hear. Within the first part, there are two divisions: first, clarifying the distinctions in the dimensions of what is manifested; second, from "In this way... onwards...
The phrase "the signs of mastery over the manifest and the manifested are clearly and distinctly revealed" means that the body appears like a bright mirror reflecting forms and images.

"There is no obstruction" is the general statement; it briefly contains four meanings: first, regarding what is manifested within the body, whether the basis (*āśraya*) or the supported (*adhiṣṭhita*), they do not obstruct one another;
thus it is said that each is distinct and does not become confused with the other. Second, the body and...
In that land there is no obstruction. With a body that contains the lands, one enters the lands within the body, such that there is nowhere it does not pervade.

This is what is meant by the non-obstruction of the internal and external, the one and the many. Therefore, it is said that the body and the Buddha-lands interpenetrate one another without mutual obstruction.
From this very point, the principle of "multiple layers" (repetition) arises; namely, a body containing lands enters the lands within the body.
The body within a land can also contain a land, and the land contained therein likewise contains a body that contains it.
Thus, bodies and lands are infinite and inexhaustible. It is like an image formed from bronze in a mirror: when facing a bright mirror, the mirror enters into the image.
Just as a land resides within a body, so the image enters the bright mirror; just as the body pervades the land, they thus manifest one another in infinite layers.

This is clearly visible. The three—beginning, middle, and end—are ungraspable. Whether one contracts a great *kṣetra* (world-system) to enter into a single body, or expands the body to be vast enough to contain all *kṣetras*, this is not yet inconceivable.
It is only when they mutually penetrate one another in infinite layers (*anava-sthāna*), while their original characteristics remain as they were, that it is called "inconceivable.
Therefore, it is said that there are various forms and images, yet no coming or going. The *Huāzhǎng pin* (Chapter on the Array of Flowers) says: "By means of a single *kṣetra*-seed..."
Entering into all; all enter into one without remainder. Their essence and characteristics are as they were originally, without distinction.
Being equalless and immeasurable, they are entirely pervasive. The four elders maintain clear and lucid wisdom without attainment, as described below.

Because it extensively explains the function of attaining inconceivable liberation, it is called "liberation. Second, from the passage beginning with "various Buddha-fields" onwards, it specifically demonstrates the multiplicity.
The Characteristics. Third, "The Dharma taught by those Tathāgatas" and below, causes those with the capacity to see and hear it.
△ Second, from "At that time, Liberation... and below, the words spoken upon emerging from samādhi. This section has four parts:

first, clarifying the emergence from samādhi, because the task to be performed has been accomplished and the time for teaching the Dharma has arrived; second, from "Addressing Sudhana... and below, indicating the name and essence of the samādhi, which is non-attainment.

As before, there are two kinds of adornment: first, the adornment wherein both the environment and its inhabitants (*bhājanasattva*) are fully adorned; second, the adornment consisting of the mastery of manifestation.
Third, "Good son, I abide below" and so forth explains the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is the meaning of universal inclusion.
Fourth, "Good son, I see thus... and so forth reveals the essential characteristic of concentration, namely that there is no coming or going, because it is the contemplation of mind-only.

The reason this meditative concentration (*samādhi*) was explained immediately preceding [the present section] is as follows: Previously, the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) were presented in general; now, the essentials of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) are being clarified.
