first, clarifying how he transforms those traveling on land so that they may know the existence of the ocean; second, "Good son... [and so forth].
I know all the jewel-islands beneath the ocean; I manifest within the ocean to cause beings to cross it. Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying thorough knowledge;
second, clarifying transformative benefit. Regarding the former, such jewel-islands exist within all oceans—those of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), the Buddha-dharma, and so forth;
for now, I shall explain them solely in reference to the ocean of birth-and-death. In the text, five kinds of matters to be known are briefly cited.
First, knowing the treasure; second, knowing the difficulty; third, knowing the water; fourth, knowing the time; fifth, knowing the ship.

Now, regarding the first: "treasure" refers to the treasure of wisdom. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If one does not enter the great ocean of birth and death, one cannot produce the treasure of all-knowledge.

There are twelve phrases [regarding this]. First, within the ocean of birth and death, that which is profound, tranquil, and unmoving is called the "Treasure Isle"; this is the *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity).

1. This wisdom is the essential nature (*svabhāva*). 2. The two bodies and minds, along with the myriad objects, are all sites of jewels. 3. The absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is the nature of the jewels.
4. Non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*) is the root of the jewels. 5. Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) is the seed of the jewels;

because it is unchanging, and because "seed" refers to its category, the term "Buddha-seed" also encompasses Buddha-nature. 6. The ocean-like sands of inherent qualities are the varieties of the jewels. All of the above are originally present.

Jewel. The next four constitute the jewels of cultivation and accomplishment: first, taking *dhūta* practices, the observance of precepts, and the cultivation of meditative concentration and tranquil reflection as the Jewel of Purity;
second, taking the wisdom of dependent origination as the Stringing Together; third, taking the manifestation of the original name as the Emergence;

and fourth, taking hearing and the cultivation of arising as the Making. The final four constitute the uses of the jewels: first, the formation of the faculties for the three vehicles and the possession of the bodhicitta. Tenth...

1. Precious vessel. 2. Illuminating principle and severing delusions as the precious function. 3. The three truths as the precious object. 4. Shattering ignorance and manifesting clarity as the precious light.
Because there are various names for these, it is said "all. Second, "I am also able to know all the dragons... and below refers to knowing what is difficult;
that is, all afflictions and karma within birth and death. "Dragon" refers to the poison of anger. Yakṣas and rākṣasas... [text continues].
The nature of the *kṣetra* (field) is predominantly greed; the *bhūta* is delusion. *Bhūta* here is translated as "self-born" (*svayambhū*);

because they belong to the class of *yakṣas* and do not arise from parents, they are called "self-born. Furthermore, their nature is predominantly deluded. In this way, all subsequent cases illustrate the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Violating the object and losing mindfulness" refers to the dwelling place of hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth. One should also know that the great ocean bestows its depths and shallows.

Below, one knows the water; that is, one immediately knows the distinctions among the characteristics, seeds, and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the mental consciousness (*vijñāna*), which revolves in birth and death, deep and bottomless.

That which is easily transformable is termed "shallow. The waves of the seven consciousnesses involve the nearness or distance of defiled habits; those habits that are proximate are easily awakened to and understood.
As for the quality of the water’s color—whether good or bad—it corresponds to the conditions of goodness or evil, resulting in black or white retribution. This is evident in actual phenomena.

[He] knows. Furthermore, he skillfully distinguishes and knows that which is below the sun and moon; this is called clearly knowing the seasons—namely, the ripening of the faculties and the movement of the cycles of the Dharma.
Within such times, it is appropriate to cultivate tranquility; within such times, it is appropriate to cultivate generosity, up to and including wisdom.

Because of good and evil, there arise changes of suffering and pleasure, calamity and auspiciousness. Nirvāṇa is the time of day; saṃsāra is the time of night. [The ignorant] are deluded regarding saṃsāra.

Long is wisdom, while birth and death are brief—spanning three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, a hundred *kalpas*, three births, or a single birth. Yet, upon awakening, it is but a moment; in delusion, it becomes vast and remote. Thus, they speak of "prolongation and brevity.

Even down to the subtle fusion of a thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*) and an eon (*kalpa*), there is nothing not clearly understood. When the worldly boat loses its timing, calamities arrive one after another;
when one deviates from the Dharma for a single moment, one sinks into samsara for many eons. The fifth [chapter] also knows this: below, it understands the boat.
The boat: one immediately understands that the myriad practices are not the same. Having skillful means makes it firm; lacking skillful means makes it brittle.
Having practiced in the past makes it smooth; not having practiced makes it rough. Having a limit to birth and death makes it small; having no limit to birth and death makes it great.

Regarding the eight winds of the world—four adversities and four favors—the adverse course is non-path, while the favorable course for attaining bodhi is the wind of skillful means. The favorable course for nirvana...
Turning to the right is *parivarta* (circumambulation); turning against *nirvāṇa* is a leftward rotation. To accord with principle is security; to deviate from principle is peril.
That which is good may be practiced; that which is evil may be ceased. These two [principles] encompass all Buddha-dharma. Second, "I, by means of such...

and below concerns the benefit of transforming others. Within this, there are four parts: first, concluding the previous section and introducing the subsequent one; second, "Good son, by means of my excellent ship... and below.
This demonstrates the aspect of benefit. Third, "Good sons, I shall launch the great ship," which clarifies that there will be no harm.

Fourth, "If there are sentient beings who obtain the sight of my launching," which concludes the ultimate benefit. Since these ten oceans have been enumerated, one should know that the preceding oceans are to be explained according to this model;

it is not a mere speculative assertion. The first four [oceans] concern self-benefit, while the latter six concern the benefit of others. The meaning of the final three sections of the text is explicit.
(Below is the fifteenth sutra. ● Third, the Most Excellent Householder:
dedicating equally to all Buddhas. This means that he is equal to the path of dedication of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time regarding the virtues to be dedicated.
He is called "most excellent" because he has attained supreme supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Because it is able to transcend [all worlds], it is equal to all Buddhas; because there is nothing superior to it, it is called the city "Joyful Garland.
Because it is equal to all Buddhas, one perceives neither beauty nor ugliness; all attain pure contemplation and the joy of delight for the sake of adornment.
The first [section], "Seeking according to the Teaching," can be understood. Regarding the second, "Seeing and Paying Homage in the City East":
this consists of two parts—first, the act of seeing, and second, the respectful inquiry. As for the first, "seeing in the city east" is because it signifies the dawning of the Buddha-sun.
Those who dwell in the Forest of No-Sorrow dedicate their merit in the same manner as the Buddha, because they are free from love and hatred. Regarding the "innumerable merchants" and so forth:
the Buddha acts as the caravan leader while the Bodhisattvas act as the merchants; although the external benefit of the wealth of the Dharma accrues to others, the merit returns to oneself.

Subsequently, when Sudhana approaches and respectfully inquires, he mentions his own name so that his reputation, long established, may be known, thereby manifesting his status as a vessel for the Dharma and hoping that [the teacher] will hear of him.
In the third section, following "That elder... and below, there is the praise and the bestowal of the Dharma. First is the praise; then, from "Good son, I have already...

and below, is the bestowal of the Dharma. Within this, there are two parts: first, the designation of its name and essence; second, the explanation of its functional activity. Now, for the first part:

"The Bodhisattva practice that reaches all places" clarifies the pervasiveness of its function. From "It has no essence" and below, it reveals the excellence of its essence. Because it has no essence...
There is nothing that cannot be accomplished. Because its function does not rely on a substantial essence, its preparatory application is non-active, and its wisdom has no fixed abode;

therefore, there is nothing it does not pervade. "Second, 'Good sons, how... and so forth" clarifies its functional activity. This section is divided into two parts: first, a self-inquiry; second, "Good sons, as for me... and so forth, which provides a detailed explanation.
Within this explanation, it clarifies that [the Buddha] reaches all places and extensively expounds the Dharma. In the text:
Second: First, the three thousandfold world systems are cited; later, the ten directions are illustrated by analogy. Within the former section, there are two parts: first, the teaching of the Dharma;

second, the instruction to abandon what is not the Dharma (the latter clarifies the intent of the teaching). Later, regarding the passage "As it is with these three thousandfold worlds," the illustration of the ten directions is also divided into two parts:

first, the teaching of the Dharma. Regarding the fact that within the six realms of existence there are all three phrases: the first phrase provides a general analysis; the second phrase clarifies the fruit; the third phrase... [text continues].
Regarding the cause: from "Afterwards, son of good family, I speak thus" below, the intention is explained.

From "Fourthly, son of good family, I only... below, there is the humbling of oneself and the deferring to excellence. Within this humbling of oneself, the words of adornment are added, because pervasive arrival at pure conduct is itself an adornment.
The latter two [points] may be understood accordingly.
● Fourth, the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā [dedicates] by means of the dedication that reaches all places.
This means that through the power of her great vows, she causes the offerings produced by her roots of goodness to pervade all things.

"Siṃhavijṛmbhitā" (Lion’s Stretch) refers to her expansive and sovereign mastery, reaching everywhere without exception. "Bhikṣuṇī" (Female Mendicant) refers to her pure compassion, which causes goodness to be universal. [This is the] land.
It is called the "River of Boundless Limits" because it flows everywhere throughout all streams of virtue.
*Kaliṅga* was formerly translated according to its literal meaning as "established through combat," referring to the founding of a city based on victory in battle;

here, it symbolizes this dedication of merit, which—through the vast power of faith and understanding and unimpeded wisdom—ensures that the virtues one has cultivated reach everywhere without exception.
The meaning is the same as during wartime.
First, one should seek it by relying on the teachings. Regarding the statement that King Prasenajit donated the Jeta Grove (Sunlight Garden):

because the nuns’ dhūta practitioners mostly resided in the king’s garden, they relied upon external protection; this symbolizes that through the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they give rise to supreme radiance, causing goodness to pervade everywhere.
The Dharma-realm and its gardens are all, without exception, identical with wisdom;

therefore, there is a light named [the second]. From "After Śrīmati heard this... onwards, it consists of seeing, paying respect, and inquiring. Within this, there are three parts: first, seeing; second, paying respect; and third, inquiring.

△ In the first [section on seeing], there are two parts: first, seeing the support (the environment), and second, seeing the supported (the Buddha). In the former, there are six parts: first, the forest trees of untainted merit. No...
Because they are established as dharmas that lead to outflows (*āsrava*), each has its own signification; one may appropriately investigate these matters.

Furthermore, beneath the various ponds and pools within the two groves flow springs of the eight liberations. As for the water of eight virtues: it is light, cool, soft, delicious, pure and odorless, temperate, and free from affliction.
Beneath the various trees exquisitely adorned with celestial jewels, seats of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnya*) are spread.
Furthermore, the adornments differ according to the variations in the dharmas. Within this passage there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the enumeration;

and third, the conclusion; all of which are clearly evident. Fourth, from the phrase "In this great garden... onwards, it describes the manifold adornments of the myriad practices, for the matters of adornment are not singular.
Fifth, from the phrase "At that time, the youth Sudhana saw this... onwards, it sets forth their causes; because these causes are supreme, the matters of adornment are inconceivable. Sixth...
"Three thousand great thousand [world systems]" and below clarifies the sovereign function of the fruit (*phala*).

Because it extensively accommodates all things without destroying their original characteristics, from "At that time, Sudhana saw the bhikṣuṇī" and below, he beholds the primary retribution (*vipāka*). Within this, there are four parts:

first, a general clarification of the manifestation of the supreme virtues of her universal seating; second, a specific clarification of the distinctness of the dharmas she expounds throughout those realms; third, a summary of the various types of teachings heard; [and fourth, the conclusion].
The Dharma-Arousing Mind. Fourth, manifesting the causes and explaining the accomplishment of mastery. First: there are fourteen similes that illustrate its supreme virtues;
in each case, the Dharma is presented first, followed by the simile. Regarding Varuṇa: he is the Lord of Water (*Varuṇa*).
Because this deity can fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings, the others may be understood accordingly. Second: "Or seeing him seated" specifically clarifies that which pervades.

The manifestations of the Dharma differ, comprising thirty locations in total. These are broadly divided into three groups: the first sixteen locations are for the eight classes of celestial beings, including devas and nāgas;
the next two are for those of the Two Vehicles; and the final twelve are for all Bodhisattvas. Within the first group, there are two divisions:

the first seven are for the devas, while the remainder are for miscellaneous classes of beings. Within the former, there are again two: the first two are for the form-realm devas (*rūpāvacara-deva*), and the remaining five are for the desire-realm devas (*kāmadhātu-deva*). This is the first [of the latter].
First, for the Śuddhāvāsa devas, he taught the "Dharma-characteristic of Inexhaustible Liberation," in order to remedy the Arhats' seeking to exhaust their physical and cognitive faculties.
Second, for the Brahmā King, he taught the "Universal Gate of Differentiated Pure Sound-Wheel";

while the Brahmā King's universal response reaches only his own assembly, this teaching extends broadly to the three thousandfold world system, such that there is nothing it does not respond to. This was in the First Dhyāna.
Brahmā King, the Brahma-sound is pure and subtle, yet it pertains only to the mundane world. From the second dhyāna upward, light replaces sound; these are not the pure wheels [of speech].
Now, for the sake of explaining the words and sounds of the supreme flow of the Dharma-realm, they are truly pure and subtle, being perfectly complete in every respect.

Second, there are the five heavens, clarifying the heavens of the desire realm. First is the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, which brings forth supramundane pure minds that transcend the world.
1. Abiding in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), they are adorned with the sublime Dharma, surpassing the implements of emanation for the sake of adornment.

2. Seeing the Tathāgata-garbha, they possess complete mastery over its revolutions, surpassing worldly satisfaction. 3. Universally adorning the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without being restricted by temporal divisions.

4. The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*) are addicted to desire; therefore, they feel a particular sense of weary detachment. The final nine clarify the various classes of beings; the Four Great Kings are included within the first.

Third: Because the intention is directed toward the eight classes of beings, the southern direction is omitted. First, because the *nāgas* are able to undergo transformations, raising clouds, flashing lightning, and raining down adornments;
second, because the *yakṣas* delight in flying through the air and harming sentient beings; third, because the *gandharvas* can perform music to produce joy and pleasure;
fourth, because the *asuras* are skilled in illusory arts as adornments; fifth, the *garuḍas*... [text fragment ends]
1. *Nāgas*: Because they cause terror to the great ocean by beating their drums. 2. *Kinnaras*: Because they constantly perform the music of the Dharma with Śakra. 3. *Mahoragas*:
Because they harbor much poisonous anger and give rise to suffering and affliction. 4. *Humans*: Although they are vessels of goodness, they mostly practice what is unwholesome;
even if they practice benevolence and righteousness, it is not superior [to the others]. 5. *Rākṣasas*: Because they mostly commit acts of slaughter and harm. (Rākṣasa)
Regarding those who follow behind: because one wishes to combine the latter two as "human and non-human," the subsequent three [categories] mostly concern antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
The remainder mostly concern humans, so as to cause them to produce wholesome states; according to what is expedient for the world, they are led toward the supramundane.

Seeing the principle of the supramundane is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). There are two dharmas of the two [types of] existence that constitute the two vehicles: first, the śrāvaka, whose wisdom is inferior and whose power is weak.

Because they are weak. Second, the Pratyekabuddhas cultivate merit for only a full hundred kalpas, because the light of their wisdom regarding dependent origination has not yet extinguished its conditions.
Third, there are twelve dharma-gates for Bodhisattvas; the text is divided into three parts: first, the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*); second, the ten grounds;

and third, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Now, for the first part: in relation to what precedes it, this refers to the Three Vehicles; in relation to what follows it, it applies generally to the stages prior to the grounds. It is pervasive.

This is because it causes one to universally accord with and train in quiescent illumination. If categorized by faith and aspiration (*śraddhā-adhimukti*), it belongs to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

The ten stages (*bhūmi*) mentioned below subsume the three preliminary stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti-pūrva-vidyā*); this is because the latter subsumes the former, unlike the case of Sāgaradhvaja, in which the former subsumes the latter.

If faith and aspiration are taken as the stage of practice through faith (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), then they pertain generally to the stages prior to the [ten] grounds; therefore, the positions of the three preliminary worthies are called the "stage of practice through resolute belief" (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and are also termed the "stage of faith" (*śraddhā-bhūmi*). [This is] not yet...

Because they realize suchness (*tathatā*). Second, there are the ten stages (*bhūmi*), which are divided into ten distinct levels. First, the Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) makes ten great vows;
because these are superior when compared [to others], the ten vows are placed at the head. Because they fulfill one million *asaṃkhyeya* vows, it is called a "collection" (*caya*).

The second stage is so called because it is free from the defilement of transgressions. The third stage is designated as "worldly cultivation" because one cultivates the eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

The fourth stage is initially designated as "transcending the world" because one attains the light of wisdom consisting of non-activity and the activity of non-arising. The fifth stage involves ten kinds of equality which serve as the seven purities of mind;

they purify the flower of the mind. Thus, the Jin translation says "the treasury of the pure mind-flower. As for "treasury," it refers to the mutual interpenetration of the ultimate and the conventional.

It is contrary [to the worldly]. It is difficult to harmonize yet capable of harmonizing, for it encompasses all mundane and supramundane truths and wisdoms. In the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*), *prajñā* manifests before one;

its radiance shines everywhere upon dependent origination and so forth. In the seventh stage (*saptamī-bhūmi*), one possesses the skillful means within meditative concentration and the superior practice within existence, wherein the provisional and the real are practiced together as an adornment for all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). In the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
He attains mastery over all three worlds, responding universally like the moon, for he is able to cause the ten bodies to act as one another.

In the ninth stage, taking non-apprehension as his skillful means, his power of the perfections increases preeminently; endowed with non-acquisitive wisdom, he is well able to preach the Dharma for the sake of adornment.
In the tenth stage, he has severed the ten obstacles, perfected the ten perfections, and completed the three great eons.

Because they all share the meaning of being "wheels" (*cakra*). Finally, there is one dharma for those who have attained equal enlightenment (*sambodhi*): though it lacks the name "equal enlightenment," it possesses the reality of equal enlightenment.

First, it occurs after the tenth stage; second, it is the attainment of vajra-wisdom, which refers to the so-called "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*) that shatters and disperses the habitual tendencies of the afflictions.
One attains the vajra-body for the sake of adornment. Having attained equal enlightenment, one clearly perceives that this spiritual friend is not of an inferior station;
therefore, the dharma obtained is called "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*). As for the term "dedication," it refers merely to the provisional stages of the superior and inferior spiritual friends.
One may understand this by following the same pattern. ▲ Third, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana saw such as these...
onwards, it is understood as a summary of how he heard the Dharma in various ways and resolved his mind [on enlightenment]. ▲ Fourth, from "For what reason? Because this bhikṣuṇī...

onwards, it generally reveals the underlying cause and explains the attainment of mastery. This section has two parts: first, because the transformer (the bhikṣuṇī) is endowed with *prajñā*, a brief enumeration is provided.

There are ten gates to manifest inexhaustibility; each is designated by a specific name according to its particular function and power, yet all are governed by non-attainment and non-abiding, and are collectively termed Prajñāpāramitā.
The "Universal Eye," "Renunciation and Attainment," and so forth, are precisely the gates of Prajñā.
Second, below this "Garden of Sunlight," because the faculties of those to be transformed have already matured. △ Second, the time of Sudhana.
The youth saw the Lion-Stretch [the Buddha] and prostrated in homage. Within this, first he beheld the Victor and resolved his mind; next, light was emitted to receive him;
finally, he formally performed the rites of respect. △ Third, from "He addressed [him]" onwards, he inquired about the Dharma.

Following the third bhikṣuṇī’s speech, she bestows upon them her own dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This section has two parts: first, the definition of its name and essence; second, the manifestation of its functional activity.

Within the first part, there are three sub-sections. First, the designation of the name: because the mind discriminates all phenomena as being erroneous, the essence of *prajñā* resides in non-discrimination (*avikalpa*).
If one were to abandon discrimination and grasp at non-discrimination, that would itself be called subtle discrimination (*sūkṣma-vikalpa*); this mind is likewise [not the true essence].

Because it is quiescent, it is called "extinguished. This also refers to the initial arising of the awakened mind; the mind has no initial characteristic because it is far removed from subtle conceptualization. Next, the words "The Holy One...
by Sudhana serve as the inquiry, while the subsequent words "The Bhikṣuṇī... provide the explanation.

The nature of wisdom in a single thought-moment universally illuminates the three periods of time without omission. Because it illuminates through the nature of wisdom, there is no discrimination; this is non-discriminative wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
It illuminates all things instantaneously; it is not entirely devoid of cognition. Therefore, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is free from five characteristics:

first, it is free from the absence of mental attention (*amanasikāra*); second, it is free from the stages characterized by vitarka and vicāra; third, it is free from the tranquility of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*);

fourth, it is free from the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*); and fifth, it is free from conceptual construction regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha*). Because it is free from these two sets of five, it is "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*).
Distinct. Excluding the first three and the fourth, it illuminates all phenomena; therefore, "universal illumination" explains "non-conceptuality.

The two characters "manifesting" (*xiǎnshì*) do not exist in the Sanskrit original; rather, the light of the wisdom of its own nature (*prakṛti-jñāna-prabhā*) is that which is capable of illuminating.

Therefore, in the older translations, the name of the dharma-gate attained is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*). This name is also retained in the subsequent section on "inferior excellence. Because it is profound and subtle, it is able to...

This causes the Perfectly Awakened One to personally receive the sound of the Dharma. Second, Sudhana said: "Noble One, what is the sphere of this light of wisdom? and so forth; this section distinguishes its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*).

Within this, there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer beginning with the words "The bhikṣuṇī said. Within the answer, there are two parts: first, clarifying its universal function;
second, clarifying its cognitive function. Within the former, there are also two parts: first, distinguishing the basis upon which the function relies; second, the actual [function].
This reveals the functional activity. First: because the light of supreme wisdom enters the King Samādhi, it is called "King" (*rāja*).
As the *Jñāna-sūtra* (Treatise on Wisdom), fascicle 8, states: "All samādhis enter into this; therefore, it is named 'King. Its essence is suchness (*tathatā*)."
As the essence is fundamentally quiescent, true wisdom accords with this; therefore, it is called "subtle" (*mèi*).
Through the preceding dharma-gates, one knows all phenomena and thereby manifests fundamental wisdom, wherein the provisional and the real are non-dual.

Now, because this wisdom of reality that is identical to the provisional accords with the principle that is identical to phenomena, all samādhis enter therein—such as the fourteen and twenty-five samādhis of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It is called the King of Samādhis. Because of this, he is able to ascend and preach the Dharma, extensively destroying all forms of existence (*bhava*).
It should be understood that because he subsequently attains such a king of samādhis, he descends to correctly discern the functions of karma.

Second, "Good son, I see all sentient beings without discriminating the marks of sentient beings" and so forth clarifies the function of his wisdom; therefore, within the aforementioned title, the subtle distinctions are set aside.

This is distinct. It is also the same as the previously mentioned "universal" [function]. It causes non-discrimination to serve as the attainment of non-obstruction, wherein the function of wisdom is sovereign.

In all cases, the principle is first indicated and then explained, clarifying that while contacting objects, one penetrates them without discrimination. The fourth point regarding humility and deference, etc., can likewise be understood.

● Fifth, the woman Vāsukī. She is associated with the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit, because by the power of this dedication, one is able to accomplish an inexhaustible treasury of merit.
Vāsukī means "Friend of Heaven" (Devamitra) or "Friend of the World" (Lokamitra).

He is also named Ratnamitra (Jewel Friend), because he transforms beings through skillful means according to the world of humans and devas, and because he is highly esteemed as a treasure by the world.

As for the name of the country, "Perilous and Difficult" (Khaṇḍaka), it is so called because it follows perverse, non-Dharmic paths that those of inferior status—the ordinary and the small—cannot traverse. The phrase "upper, middle, and lower" refers to what follows.

The term "village" (grāma) is according to the Sanskrit original; "country" (deśa) follows the older Chinese translations. As for the name of the city, "Jewel Adornment" (Ratnavyūha), it is so called because it follows the perverse [paths] while conforming to the ways of the world, and is able to...
Because it gives rise to an inexhaustible treasury of merit.

Within the first section, "Seeking by Relying on the Teachings," there are two parts: first, the benefits achieved by relying on the teachings; this is presented first in general terms and then in detail. The detailed explanation establishes two kinds of benefit.

The first phrase concerns the benefit of seeing the true Dharma, which arises from having previously heard of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). All subsequent points concern the benefit of attaining expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Due to the wisdom that distinguishes the three periods of time, one subsequently descends gradually to seek the subsequent stage. Within this, there are four parts: first, seeking with single-minded intent to see;

second, the arising of doubt due to shallow understanding; third, the praise of the teaching by those of deep wisdom; and fourth, approaching according to the teaching. The first is easily understood.

Regarding the second, "In the city there was a person who did not know [the descent] below": this refers to the arising of doubt due to shallow understanding, because [the process of] descending is difficult to comprehend.
That he knew Sudhana’s mind was merely because he observed his external appearance; it also demonstrates that Sudhana’s stage of seeking the Dharma was still shallow.

Third, as for the passage beginning "Among them, there was one who first knew of this woman," this refers to the profound wisdom of praising and instructing: first praising, and then instructing. Regarding the phrase "to the north of the marketplace":

a market is a place of clamor and confusion, whereas the north presides over cessation; thus, it signifies the cessation of clamor and confusion. As for "dwelling in her own home," this means she had reached the ultimate [stage].

Ultimately empty and quiescent. This means that while practicing dhyāna within the realm of desire, he possesses great compassion; while dwelling amidst defilement for the benefit of others, he possesses great wisdom.

Quiescence is his own home, whereas benefiting others is his guest-house; thus, he employs both compassion and wisdom. At this time, Sudhana descended and, following the instructions, went to visit him.
Second, seeing beneath his residence; this consists of two parts: first, beholding it, and second, respectfully inquiring about it. Within the first part there are also two:

first, beholding the *pariṇāmanavibhūti* (the environment), which reveals its majesty by extensively manifesting that within ultimate emptiness (*atyantaśūnyatā*) there is no excellence that is not fully present.

1. Subsequently, at that time, Sudhana saw this woman; below [this], he sees her primary retribution (*vipāka*). Within this, she possesses the virtues and functions of both the principal and her retinue.
2. At that time, Sudhana went before her and paid respectful greetings.

Third, regarding the passage beginning with "He then spoke," [the Buddha] bestows his own *dharmadhātu*. This section has four parts: first, the designation of the name; second, its functional activity; third, the excellence of the dharma-gate;
and fourth, the causes and conditions for attaining this dharma. Now, for the first: "The limit of detachment from desire.

Ordinary beings are defiled by desire and remain within it without weariness; those of the Two Vehicles perceive desire and seek to leave it through skillful means; whereas Bodhisattvas understand the nature of desire...
There is nothing to be abandoned; this is itself the true path. Therefore, one does not sever desire, nor does one dwell with it, yet attains liberation.
To be stained yet unstained is called the limit of freedom from desire (*vairāgya-koṭi*). Because there is no separation from that which is already separated, [the text continues].

Regarding the second point, "I am able to follow," and so forth, this reveals the functional activity (*karmaprayoga*). Within this, there are two parts: first, manifesting in a form identical to their own bodies; second, "Good son, if... and so forth.
There are sentient beings who, being bound by the desires of their minds, are benefited by the Dharma through thirteen samādhis;

all of these accord with whatever is appropriate for those experiencing desire, whereby they attain this profound and inconceivable samādhi. Third, at that time, the youth Sudhana addressed Vāsantī...
[the passage continues] ...to clarify the excellence of the dharma-gate. This section of the sūtra consists of twelve and a half lines; it is found in the old translation.

There has not yet been [a response]. This passage is divided into two parts: first, the question; second, the answer beginning with "At that time, the woman said. The intent of the preceding question is as follows:
Since worldly defiled desires turbidly disturb the pure truth, how can the sutras state that by entering into all-knowledge one attains the most supreme stage?

The intent of the present explanation is as follows: Desire is the root of evil and the primary source of birth and death. It even obstructs rebirth in the heavens, let alone the Great Enlightenment. Therefore...

The *Anuvyañjana-parivarta* states: "For example, just as the fire at the end of an eon burns Mount Sumeru until nothing remains, so too, when the mind is entangled by greed and desire, one can never give rise to the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha. Now, wishing to sever it, one must first allow it full rein;

first one lures it with the hook of desire, and afterwards one slays the mad elephant of desire. Using poison as medicine—how could this not be superior? This passage consists of four parts, the first of which clarifies...
Desire can obstruct the Path. [This section consists of: first, the general principle; second, citing scriptural evidence for its establishment; third, that desire is the root of faults;

and fourth, the benefit of abandoning it. Now, for the first: from gross attachment down to the subtlest, it obstructs the Three Vehicles; this refers to subtle desire. As for coarse and heavy desire, it obstructs all superior matters.

Thus, the *Upper Scripture* says it obstructs the attainment of rebirth in the heavens, while the *Lower Scripture* states it is the root of great faults. Second, regarding the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the sages...
Regarding those of inferior status, I shall cite examples to establish this point, briefly mentioning three matters.

First, the rishi possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā), who was the original cause for the World-Honored One’s [existence], suffered the humiliation of being mounted upon his neck; likewise, Udraka Rāmaputra also lost his five supernatural powers, yet it is not said that he bore such a burden.
Second, as for the gods and asuras who constantly engage in warfare: the asuras covet the nectar of immortality (amṛta), while Śakra covets their celestial maidens.

This is the origin of war and conquest; the details are as commonly explained. As for the ten-headed *rākṣasa* who burned the great city of Laṅkā in the South Sea—this is not seen in the sūtras or śāstras.
The Tripiṭaka Master says it is from non-Buddhist texts (*bāhyaka-śāstra*).

According to the Sanskrit original, it concerns the place on the shore burned for the sake of a woman’s beauty, namely the great city of Laṅkā belonging to the ten-headed *rākṣasa*. Thirdly, there are various kings below [this], which clarifies...

Desire is the root of transgression. King Zhou of the Zhou dynasty was resplendent [in power] until Baoxiang extinguished it; King Wuding of the Yin dynasty was brilliant and prosperous until Daji cut him off.
In nine cases out of ten, states were lost and families ruined. Nothing arises except through craving; thus one revolves in the cycle of birth and death.
For these four reasons, the Bodhisattva [speaks] below to conclude the benefits of detachment. From "The fourth, Sudhana said, 'O Noble One'" below, he distinguishes the attainment.
Regarding the causal conditions of the Dharma, first there is the question, followed by the answer. As for the gift of a single *māṣaka* coin, there are briefly three points:

first, because one is able to relinquish even a single *māṣaka*, one attains freedom from greed; second, although a single coin is extremely minute, through the bodhicitta, it becomes a source of such sovereignty;

third, because giving to the Buddha constitutes the most supreme field (*kṣetra*), it results in a superior retribution. Thus, since the triad of agent, object, and field are all supreme, how much more so [the merit]?
Supreme and empty-quiescent—what fruit would it not summon? The remaining three sections may be understood [as follows] (the sixteenth sutra).
● The sixth, the householder Viśuddhila, entrusts all roots of goodness into universal equality and dedicates them;

thus, phenomenon and principle do not conflict, for all enter into the principle of equality. Regarding Viśuddhila: formerly translated as "enveloping," the new translation renders it as "closely joined."
Furthermore, the meaning should be understood as inclusive. This means that within the stūpa, all Buddhas are included; it encompasses all roots of goodness and enters into the principle of equality.
In the Jin translation, it is named *Śubhapāla*, which means "Exquisite Goodness," because the merit of making offerings to a Buddha stūpa is the most excellent and sublime of all good deeds.
As for the city being named "Pure Reaching the Other Shore," it signifies that there is not a single root of goodness that does not purify obstructions and attain them, reaching the ultimate limit.
Those who constantly make offerings at Buddha-stūpas do so because it is the most excellent among all roots of goodness. It is not yet clear for what reason they specifically offer to this stūpa;
some say that within the stūpa there is a sandalwood throne, and that this is done with the desire to universally make offerings to infinite Buddhas—this is indeed reasonable.
However, the subsequent sūtra states: "When I opened the Tathāgata’s sandalwood throne stūpa," from which we know that it must certainly refer to the Buddha.
This is the title.

Regarding the second part of the first section, "Seeking by Relying on the Teachings," there are two parts: first, recollecting the instructions of the former friend; second, seeking out the latter friend. Now, for the first:
previously, this twelve-line passage was missing. Within the text, the initial sentence is general, while the subsequent section beginning with "Observing that Bodhisattva" is specific.
There are another thirteen samādhis, which are those previously mentioned by the friend; they correspond in sequence as follows: first, the samādhi of coming to my presence;
second, the samādhi of a brief sight; third, the samādhi of conversing; fourth, the samādhi of grasping the hand; fifth, the samādhi of ascending the seat;
sixth, the samādhi of a brief observation; seventh, the samādhi of seeing him stretch his limbs; eighth, the samādhi of seeing him blink his eyes; ninth...
He maintains the *samādhi* of Embracing. He performs the *samādhi* of Ten Kissing. He contemplates all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). This concludes the preceding section;

the subsequent gradual descent into the lower realms may be understood from what follows. Second, having gone to the house of the lay devotee (*gṛhapati*), he sees him, pays him respect, and inquires after his well-being.
Following the words "The third householder said," he bestows his own *dharmadhātu*. This section contains four parts: first, the designation of the name; second, the manifestation of its essence;
third, the resolution of doubts; and fourth, its functional activity. Regarding the first, "the limit of non-parinirvāṇa": *pari* means "to enter.

It refers to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) into which all Tathāgatas do not enter as parinirvāṇa. Thus, the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "As with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), so with parinirvāṇa."
The nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is also like this. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "There is no nirvāṇa at all; there is no Buddha who has entered nirvāṇa, nor is there a nirvāṇa belonging to a Buddha.
It is far removed from both the subject that awakens and the object awakened to. Whether as existent or as non-existent, it is entirely free from all such [dualistic] states."
This is also its meaning. Second, "Good sons, I do not give rise to a thought" below clarifies the essence.

If one has a mind directed toward *nirvāṇa*, then there is the perceiver and the perceived; however, at the moment of peacefully conforming to *nirvāṇa*, one is without a mind regarding entering or exiting it.

Thus, the mind conforms to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), knowing that the Buddha is eternally constant. Third, "except for... below explains away a doubt. The doubt is as follows: [If] all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time...
"He has entered *nirvāṇa*. How can you say he does not exist? The commentary explains: "He merely manifests this in order to subdue sentient beings.

Now, regarding the statement that he does not enter *nirvāṇa*, there are briefly three meanings. First, it is because his subtle existence persists even as he manifests extinction. The *Prādurbhāva-sūtra* states:
"For example, just as the element of fire performs the function of fire throughout all worlds, yet at times its flames may be extinguished in a single location—how could [the fire]..."
Is fire extinguished in all places? The *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata is likewise.
While performing Buddha-works in all worlds, he may manifest entry into *nirvāṇa* in one world once his tasks there are complete; yet, how could he enter extinction in all worlds?
For the True Body (*dharmakāya*) is eternally quiescent. Thus, the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "The Tathāgata does not [act] for the sake of the various bodhisattvas..."
The Bodhisattva says: "Although all Tathāgatas have attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*, he does not manifest that state to them. Why is this?
It is because he desires to cause all bodhisattvas to see all Tathāgatas as eternally abiding before them, just as if they were presently present."
Because the Great Nirvana is endowed with the three perfected virtues—the Mahāprajñā, Liberation, and Dharma-body—when it is said that the body is eternal, it follows that Nirvana is eternal.
The three [virtues] profoundly accord with Prajñā because they are free from conceptual attachment and grasping. Therefore, this sutra says:

"I do not give rise to a mind," and the "Chapter on Manifestation" says: "Nor does one give rise to the thought of duality or non-duality. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva is forever detached from...
Because all conceptualizations and attachments have ceased, this is the distancing from both the perceiver and the perceived. When the one is lost, the two concepts vanish;
when duality is lost, the profound becomes even more profound. "Good sons, I have opened that sandalwood seat below to reveal its functional activity."
Within this, there are two parts: first, a general clarification of essence and function; second, a discussion of the object through question and answer. Now, for the first:
"The essence is samādhi, called the inexhaustible Buddha-lineage. Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) refers to the spiritual potential (*gotra*), because it takes non-nature as its nature.

As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, know that dharmas are eternally without nature. The Buddha-lineage arises from conditions; therefore, they speak of the One Vehicle. This is the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
The seeds [of Buddhahood] attain Buddhahood according to conditions; the Dharma-nature is inexhaustible, so how could the Buddhas ever come to an end?
Therefore, it is like striking water to form patterns: as soon as one strikes, a pattern arises, yet the patterns never cease. How much more so for the substance of the water itself!

If the myriad dharmas rely upon space, then even if heaven and earth were to overturn, empty space remains serene and unmoving. Thus, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is itself the eternal body, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Ten.
The body is perfectly integrated; how could it ever be exhausted? Following the passage where Sudhana says, "I ask," there is a sequence of questions and answers regarding the realm of experience.

First the question, then the answer. Within the answer, there are two parts: first, the clarification of the past; second, from "In this way, the future... onwards, which serves as an analogy for the present and future—both of which can be understood.
Fourth, from "Good son, I only... onwards, he humbles himself and defers to the superior. Within this deferral to the superior, although the Elder knows the three...
The world is not extinguished. One has not yet been able to know [it] in a single thought-moment, nor has one attained the equality of the subject and the object.
Fifth, the good son goes down from here to the south to visit the Friend Who Shows the Way. This section has two parts: first, the prose exposition.
The subsequent verse is a hymn of praise added because of his great compassion and venerability. "A mountain upon the sea" refers to the southern region of South India;

it symbolizes that Great Compassion follows along [into the world], entering the ocean of birth and death while dwelling upon the mountain of nirvāṇa, and remaining within the ocean of great compassion without being drowned by craving or views. At this sixth stage, Sudhana bows down and takes his leave.
Commentary on the Newly Translated Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Zhenyuan Era, Scroll Six.
Engraved by imperial decree at Daexingwang Temple in the Kingdom of Goryeo during the year Yihai of the Shouchang era.
*Commentary on the Newly Translated Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Zhenyuan Era*, Scroll Seven (From the second page and a half of the sixteenth sūtra to the first half of the twenty-fourth sūtra).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Dachongfu Monastery in Taiyuan Prefecture, by Imperial Command.
(There are eleven spiritual friends: 1. Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; 2. Bodhisattva Samantaguṇaviśuddhacāritra; 3. Mahādevī; 4. Bhūmidevatā Akṣayamatī; 5. Rātridevatā Vasanti; 6. Samantagandhavati...)
1. The Night Goddess Śrīmatī; 2. The Night Goddess Viśvālokanarati; 3. The Night Goddess Sarvasattvatrāṇojaḥśrī; 4. The Night Goddess Praśāntarutasāgaravatī; 5.
The Night Goddess Sarvapuranirvyūhavyūhaśrī; 6. The Night Goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasandarśanā.
● The seventh is the Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā Avalokiteśvara, who is entrusted with the dedication that accords equally with all sentient beings.
This means that by means of roots of goodness, he benefits all sentient beings with an impartial mind. As for the term "Avalokiteśvara," his three karmas serve as a refuge;

through the ten supernatural powers, he responds appropriately, perceiving without omission and benefiting without exception. It is for this reason that he is able to accord with others through an impartial mind.
"Anurūpa" (順). Regarding "on Mount Potalaka": this [name] translates as the "White Small Flower Tree. This mountain abounds in such trees;

their fragrance is perceived from afar, and those who hear or see it are inevitably filled with joy. Thus, it carries the meaning of "conformity" (*anurūpa*). Now, regarding Avalokiteśvara, he is sometimes called Guanshiyin.
In Sanskrit, he is called *Vairocani*, which means "one who observes the world. Master Hu erroneously wrote *Vairocana* and translated it as "light. [The character] *shi*...
*Vara* means "sovereign" (*svatantra*) in this language; *cārvāta* means "sound. Because there are two forms in the Sanskrit original, the translators have rendered them with two different names.
Thus, the "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "By contemplating his voice, all attain liberation"—this refers to Avalokiteśvara.
However, in that same sutra, the initial section concerning vocal action describes how invoking his name eliminates the seven calamities.
The two bodily acts of prostration can fulfill two vows; the three mental acts of mindfulness can purify the three poisons, which is the meaning of "sovereignty" (*svayambhū*).
However, because the verbal act of frequently reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara involves much effort yet yields results easily, we now adopt the complete sense of the term:

"Avalokiteśvara. Here, "contemplation" (*avalokita*) refers to the subject that contemplates, which encompasses all modes of contemplation; thus it is called "True Contemplation" (*bhūtadarśana*). It is pure...
One should constantly aspire to and gaze upon the contemplation of purity, the contemplation of vast wisdom, the contemplation of compassion, and the contemplation of loving-kindness.
The "world" (*loka*) is that which is contemplated; it pervades all worlds, meaning there is nothing—whether mountains or oceans, Buddhas or sentient beings—that is not contemplated.
If one speaks of "sound," this too is that which is contemplated; it refers to all those with the capacities who are to be saved. If one speaks merely of "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*), then...
This belongs to the function of transformative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*). To speak fully, one should say "Avalokiteśvara," which encompasses both the subject and the object.

Since the subject must necessarily have an object, the latter is omitted here. When both subject and object are transcended, there is no longer a need for observation; their mutual integration and inclusion constitutes true sovereignty (*īśvara*).

Regarding the first section, "Seeking by Relying on the Teachings," there are fifteen phrases in the preceding portion. The first is the general contemplation of cultivation; the subsequent section, beginning with "Entering that Bodhisattva...
and so forth, specifically clarifies what is cultivated. First is the "profoundly deep faith and understanding of the *garbha* (matrix)," which refers to that very samādhi.

This means not giving rise to thoughts or words such as "the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa. "Garbha" here signifies inclusion and encompassment; the rest may be understood accordingly. Hereafter...

Gradually descending toward the lower realms, secondly, one sees its western face descend; there, one beholds it with reverence and inquires. This section has two parts: first, the act of beholding, and second, the respectful inquiry.

The preceding section has three parts: first, seeing the superior environment and inhabitants; second, manifesting the benefits accomplished by the vision; third, the friend’s bestowal of praise and inclusion. Now, for the first:

"He saw [him] on the western side" means that it is the Buddha whom he originally serves, intended to cause sentient beings to take refuge; it is because the sun of wisdom is about to set, prompting him to observe;

and it is because he enters the night of birth-and-death to compassionately rescue those in suffering. The rest of the text can be understood accordingly. Second, from "After Sudhana had seen... onwards, it manifests...

The benefit of seeing [the spiritual friend] is that, by cultivating one’s body and mind through the熏習 (vāsanā) of great compassion, one immediately attains superior mindfulness upon seeing their person.

There are briefly four meanings regarding the statement that "a good spiritual friend is none other than the Tathāgata": first, because they lead one to the ultimate state, making one identical to the Buddha;

second, because their essence comes as it is, being devoid of the characteristic of coming; third, because this [spiritual friend] is the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), which is itself the Buddha; fourth...
1. Because he attained perfect enlightenment from time immemorial. 2. From the passage "At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara saw from afar...

onwards, it should be understood as the section on sympathetic praise and gathering, because his profound great compassion gathers [beings] through accordance with them. 3. From the passage "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, the gate of reverence may be understood.
Third, at that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara emits light down to Jambudvīpa to praise and bestow the Dharma.
This section has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. Within the prose, there are also two parts: first, the praise; second, the bestowal. Now, the first [the praise]:

First, he touches [the crown of] his head to receive him, because his honorable status is so prominent. This sign of reception differs from that in the preceding sutra, and furthermore, it does not mention the location where the light is emitted.

According to the meaning of the Sanskrit original, the "golden jewel-flames" and so forth are all the light from his hand, similar to how, in the first assembly, the Buddhas of the ten directions touch Samantabhadra’s head.
From the second section, "Good son, I have already accomplished... and below, he bestows [the teaching] upon himself.

The Dharma-realm. Within this, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the name and characteristics; second, the extensive explanation of its functional activity. Regarding the first, there are also two sections: first, the presentation of its name;
second, the manifestation of its essential nature and characteristics. Now, for the first: compassion is not based on attachment or biased views, but is identical to the compassion of the Tathāgata;
therefore, it is called "Great. Because it responds universally in a single thought-moment, it is called "Swift. Thus, responding through compassion constitutes the gateway of practice. Hereafter...
"Good son, from this point downward, I shall briefly reveal the essence and characteristics [of the teaching], which also serves as an explanation of its name.
'Impartially teaching and transforming' refers to great compassion; because it is of the same substance and without conditions, it is called 'impartial.

'Gathering in and subduing' refers to the gates of practice. 'Continuing without interruption' conveys the meaning of 'swift': being swift means responding instantaneously, while continuing means remaining ever-present. Furthermore, 'gate' refers to the Universal Gate."

Because he manifests through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*), he is called "Universal" (*pu*) for his impartial salvation of all without exception; because his realization penetrates the divine, it is termed a "Gate" (*mukha*). [Section] Two:

"Good sons, I constantly dwell here," etc., extensively reveals his functional activity (*karmaprayoga*). This section has two parts: first, revealing his functional activity by way of the Universal Gate;
second, revealing his functional activity by way of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Within the former, there are also two parts: first, the brief exposition.
The latter part is extensive. Now, for the first [section]: Because he is identical to the Tathāgata’s wondrously enlightened true mind, he is constantly present before all Tathāgatas;
because his essence is identical to the great compassion of sentient beings, he manifests universally before all sentient beings.

This "universal manifestation" is precisely the manifestation through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*). According to the *Sahasranetra-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā attained perfect enlightenment long ago and is titled...

The Tathāgata Saddharmaprabhāsa manifests as a bodhisattva; in meaning, this is equivalent to a Buddha. However, his gathering through the gate of compassion is vast, and the conditions for this land are profound;

there is not one who has not been granted compassionate salvation by turning their heart toward him. One should constantly recite his name and contemplate his dharma-gate. Hereafter, it is explained separately starting from "generosity" (*dāna*).
This is the meaning of "universal manifestation," which consists of eleven phrases; the first four are the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*).
[The first] is subsumed [by the mind]. The next six are subsumed by the three karmas. The final one is subsumed by the myriad categories.

Yet these eleven [manifestations], when compared to the thirty-five responses in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, may at first glance appear few; however, in terms of their underlying meaning, they are actually many.

This is because those thirty-five responses are merely instances within this [text] of manifesting a form-body or preaching the Dharma. Furthermore, the number thirty-five is a brief enumeration of the general outline; the myriad [responses]...
Their categories differ in form; how could they be fixed by a single locus? Regarding the passage "I, a son of good family, practice...

and below, this explains the functional activity (*karmavipāka*) by way of the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because it rescues those from all fears. However, the two meanings of "Universal Gate" (*samantamukha*) and "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) are mutually pervasive; they are merely manifested according to their predominant aspect.

Within this, there are three parts: first, causing them to be free from fear; second, manifesting the cause of such freedom; third, causing them to reach the ultimate. Now, for the first part, [it is] complete.

Regarding the five fears: while the old translation [of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*] had eighteen, the current version has twenty-two, as it adds those from kings, officials, illness, indolence, and the failure to obtain what is sought.

In the Sanskrit manuscript of the old translation, the five fears beginning with "lack of livelihood" were grouped together in one place; however, in the current version, the two fears of "the great assembly" and "evil destinies" are placed at the end.
According to the *Bhūmi-sūtra* and its commentary, there are only five fears; all others, such as being beaten or bound, are subsumed within these five.
Therefore, regarding the so-called "five fears": first, the fear of being unable to subsist; second, the fear of ill repute; third, the fear of death; fourth, the fear of the evil realms;

and fifth, the fear of the majesty and power of the great assembly. These five characteristics refer to the dread of lacking the means of livelihood and being unable to sustain oneself from day to day.

This is called the fear of not being sustained. If one acquires an evil reputation, no one will respect or support them. The first two [fears] pertain to all three types of karma. Regarding the fear of death:
when the causes for existence are exhausted and one is about to relinquish the retribution of this life, there is nothing more extremely terrifying than death.

As for the fear of the miserable realms (*durgati*), it is a loathing of those realms and a dread of being born there. Therefore, the fear of death is the dread of losing this body, whereas the fear of the miserable realms is the dread of acquiring that [other] body.

Because they pertain to the body, both are bodily actions (*kāyakarman*). The majestic power of the Great Assembly also extends to all three types of action. The five fears generally have two factors as their causes:
first, because of false wisdom, which involves grasping through conceptualization, views, and attachment; these are the aforementioned first three causes.

Second, because one's roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are meager; this refers to the latter two causes. False wisdom is precisely the discrimination of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); by means of this, one falsely grasps at a self.
Because of the notion of "mine" (*mama-kāra*) and because of attachment to what is "mine," there is the fear of death; seeing a self-body (*ātma-bhāva*), one fears the relinquishing of life.
Because of attachment to what is "mine," there are the first two fears. Attachment solely to wealth and profit constitutes the fear of not being able to sustain oneself (*a-jīvikā-bhaya*).

Attachment to profit along with reputation constitutes the fear of ill repute (*a-śloka-bhaya*). As for the latter two causes: having few merits, one fears falling into the evil realms (*durgati*); having little wisdom, one fears...
Regarding the great assembly, how can one be free from them? By abandoning "self" and "what belongs to self," one abandons the first three [fears].
By increasing merit and wisdom, one is free from the latter two. Therefore, the sutra below says: "Right mindfulness manifests before one.

How do these five encompass the other fears? However, the five fears are mostly explained in terms of their results; these twenty, however, apply to both cause and result. As for the perilous paths, there are two types. If...

The world’s perils and obstacles are subsumed under the fear of non-sustenance (*ajīvikā-bhaya*) and the fear of death (*maraṇa-bhaya*). If they are causes for rebirth in the evil destinies (*apāya*), they constitute wrong knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).

There are three kinds of feverish distress (*paridāha*): the distress of losing wealth is subsumed under the fear of non-sustenance; the distress of being in a crowd is equivalent to ill-repute (*ayaśas*);

and the distress of the three poisons (*triviṣa*) is the cause of fear. Regarding delusion (*moha*), there are two types: delusion regarding directions and so forth is subsumed under the fear of non-sustenance.

If the mind is deluded by the cause of fear regarding the masses, this bondage is also subsumed under the fear of non-sustenance (*anājīvikā-bhaya*). Killing and harming are subsumed under death (*maraṇa-bhaya*).
Kings, officials, poverty, and illness are all subsumed under the fear of non-sustenance. Regarding the transition into darkness, there are two meanings: the transition into manifest darkness.

It is also included within the fear of non-sustenance (*ajīva-bhaya*). The dark realms of evil destinies and the transmigrations through the three miserable states are all subsumed under the path of evil.
Why fear indolence? If one fears indolence, one is indeed a person of wisdom. In the older Sanskrit versions of the sutras, this fear does not appear at all.

The fear of separation from the beloved is strictly the fear of death, though it also includes the fear of non-sustenance. The fear of encountering the hated is strictly the fear of the evil paths, though it likewise includes [the fear of non-sustenance].
Fear for one's livelihood is the terror regarding the body; fear for death and for not having a livelihood is the terror regarding the mind.

These are comprised within the [fears of] "massive power" (*saṃbhāra*) and "ill repute. Sorrow, lamentation, grief, and despair are the characteristics of the two fears of death and not having a livelihood, though they also extend to the other three.

The fear of not obtaining what one seeks is also comprised within the fear of not having a livelihood. Other details may be inferred by analogy. From the phrase "Furthermore, he makes this vow" onwards, [the text] reveals...
The cause for detachment is the taking of refuge through the three karmas. My three karmas can bring about liberation and enable one to abide in right mindfulness;

that is, to be free from self, what belongs to self, and false wisdom. "O sons of good family, by means of these various [teachings] below," and so forth, he causes them to reach ultimate realization.
If they give rise to the great mind, they shall attain the stage of non-retrogression, and all fears will be forever eliminated.

△ Second, the verses from "At that time, Avalokiteśvara... and below. These verses, as well as the subsequent verses on Sudhana’s reception and explanation, are entirely absent from the old translations.
This section is divided into two parts: first, the statement of the intent; second, the verse text. Although these are *geya* (verses following prose), they also contain *gāthā* (stanzas).
There are thirty-nine and a half verses, which are further divided into five parts. The first part consists of three verses praising him and describing himself.
The second section consists of one and a half verses, praising his respectful inquiry. The third section consists of thirty-two verses, eulogizing the bestowal of the Dharma.

The fourth section consists of one verse, clarifying self-effacement and the recommendation of excellence. The fifth section consists of two verses, indicating subsequent exhortations for practice. Now, the first [section].

The first verse, which resembles the preceding prose and depicts the encounter with the friend and his environment (the *sāśraya-sāśrita*), is a summary (*uddāna*) compiled by the redactors who have taken the purport of this sūtra and strung together its textual passages.

The second section, consisting of one and a half verses, praises the respectful inquiry; it is also in *gāthā* meter. It should not be considered a verse recited by the Bodhisattva in response to Sudhana’s words.

If it is intended as praise, it serves as an abbreviated counterpart (*pratibimba*) to what precedes it and may thus be classified as *geya*. The third section begins with "I am the Brave... [and so forth].
The following thirty-two verses are a hymn of praise for the bestowal of the Dharma. This section consists of two parts;
the first two verses were compiled by the redactor to describe the previous act of touching the crown of the head in acceptance. The Sanskrit text states:

"The Pure Being of Great Compassion stroked the crown of the youth Sudhana’s head," which is similar to how the Honored One of Perfect and Wondrous Marks replied to Akṣayamati in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Below this is the section concerning Maitreya.

The section praising Sudhana’s dwelling also has its own compilation, which forms a continuous sequence of verses. If one changes the character "I" (吾) to the character for "at that time" (是時), the principle [of the text] will be correct.
The remaining thirty verses are a formal versification of the preceding prose concerning the bestowal of the Dharma-realm upon oneself; within this, there are two parts.
The first two verses previously set forth the names and characteristics; the remaining verses extensively distinguish their functions.

Taken together, these verses summarize the aforementioned Universal Gate of Great Compassion, as this gate accords with various types of beings to extract them from suffering. The text consists of three parts: the first provides a general explanation;

the next twenty-four stanzas specifically manifest [the details]; and the final three stanzas conclude by showing the benefits. Both the general explanation and the conclusion summarize the abandonment of causes. Now, for the first part, there are three [sections].
When karma is turned away from, one is immediately freed from the cause of fear; when liberation is attained, one is immediately freed from the fruit of fear.

Within the second section, which specifically elucidates these points, twenty fears are presented in twenty verses, though they do not follow the original sequence. Of the first fifteen fears, each is addressed by a single verse:
the first verse treats the fear of bondage; the second, the fear of being killed; the third, the fear of kings and officials; and the fourth, the fear of attachment.
1. Fear of separation; 2. Fear of being separated from darkness—meaning deep forests and remote valleys that obscure the light of the sun; 3.
Fear of being separated from dangerous paths—meaning precipices and steep cliffs are themselves dangerous paths; 4. Fear of meeting those one hates; 5. Fear of bodily oppression;
6. Fear of ill repute; 7. Fear of confusion; 8. Fear of mental oppression; 9. Fear of illness. Thus, O Brahmā...

The original intent states: "Whether one is deaf, blind, or mute; or has impaired faculties, or is entangled by the signs of disease—may they obtain a body endowed with the marks and signs of humans and devas.
Those who call upon my name shall all have their wishes fulfilled. (13) One is freed from the fear of lacking a livelihood;

(14) one is freed from the fear of poverty, because of the estrangement of kinsmen in a state of indigence; (15) one is freed from the fear of the evil realms. The above [sections] each consist of one verse in the Sanskrit original.
Following this, there is one line which concludes by saying: "Such a person who recites my name shall have all their wishes fulfilled.
(16) There are two verses praising the absence of fear regarding the majesty of the great assembly, because as a great bodhisattva, one constantly hears the Dharma.
(17) There are two verses praising the absence of fear regarding relocation; for being exiled to a foreign land constitutes a perilous calamity. Thus.
18. Constantly contemplating day and night that there shall be no relocation, one causes rebirth in the Pure Land;

how could there be any further migration or change? This single verse praises the freedom from the fear of not obtaining what is sought. Being constantly worthy of offerings, what is there that cannot be obtained? 19.

Two verses praise the freedom from the fear of burning affliction (*paritāpa*). When the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) mutually scorch and karmic delusions blaze intensely, this constitutes burning affliction. Twenty verses [follow] to praise...
One is freed from the fear of death. Since sorrow and grief are both manifestations of fear, they are not treated separately in the verse.

If one wishes to include them, they are subsumed within the fear of death. Laziness is not a form of fear, and therefore it is not mentioned in the verse. By correlating the topical outline with the verses, the meaning of the text becomes clear;

what appeared difficult has now been explained, and there should be no further doubt. The three verses on the three realms summarize the benefits achieved. Within this, they recapitulate the previously mentioned abandonment of causes. Among these:

The first verse accomplishes [the practice] through the vehicle of vows; the latter two verses distinguish the benefits for sentient beings through the three types of action (*trikarma*). The prose section clarifies that which can evoke [the response] through the three types of action;

now, this verse clarifies that which can respond through the three wheels (*tricakra*). Just as the moon appears when the water is clear—where the evocation reaches its limit and the response arrives—the two meanings mutually complete one another, while the two texts are abbreviated by way of mutual implication.

Furthermore, while the prose clarifies that which can evoke [the response] through the three types of action by means of respectful invocation, the verse clarifies it through the sincere recitation of the Name.
This refers to speech and mind. ▲ Fourth, the single verse beginning with "I have attained great compassion" expresses self-humbling and the deferring of excellence to others;

the first half humbles oneself, while the second half defers excellence to others. ▲ Fifth, the two verses demonstrate subsequent exhortation to practice, although they do not specifically point [to the object].
Since he has already ordered a universal search, the latter two sections do not recapitulate what preceded them.

From the fourth section, "At that time, Avalokiteśvara... onwards, he humbles himself and defers to the superior; having long since attained perfect enlightenment, he still does not lose his humility.

Within this section, there are two parts: first, the formal expression of humility and deference; second, Sudhana’s reception and understanding. This segment should also include the bestowal of the Dharma;

however, it was previously separated to conform to the six-part structure, and is therefore analyzed here. Within this, first is the description of the ritual for teaching, followed by the actual recitation of the verses.

There are thirty verses, which are broadly divided into three sections: first, one verse that serves as a general praise; second, twenty-six verses that provide specific praises; third, [the remaining verses...]
The three verses constitute the concluding praise. First: because the virtues of the Bodhisattva are profound, the multitude’s praises cannot exhaust them.

Second, within the specific praises, there are four parts. The first praises the Dharma-gate attained: namely, leading with wisdom that has transcended objective conditions through unconditional compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*).

The second consists of one verse praising supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because the universal gate manifestations are all wondrous applications without obstruction. The third consists of three verses.

I shall now express my intention for this praise. It is said that the Sage’s virtue is vast and profound, difficult for inferior intellects to fathom; yet, having heard of it, I have given rise to eloquence and respectfully praise his virtuous renown.
Just as one sees the sun by means of its light, [this work] consists of twenty-one verses in four sections, extensively praising his supreme virtues.

Within these, there are two parts: first, ten verses praising the adornment of his physical marks, though one or two lines therein clarify his mental vows and the nature of his mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).

The body and ear [are mentioned]. The final eleven verses praise the profundity and vastness of his karmic activity. Among these, there are three sections: first, the initial two verses generally praise the all-pervasive and impartial nature of his compassionate salvation;
second, three verses praise how his reliance (the environment) and what is relied upon (the inhabitants) are wondrously adorned, fulfilling the vows of sentient beings;

third, six verses show his compassion following the myriad classes of beings to extract them from suffering and provide consolation. The third section consists of three concluding verses of praise. The first verse therein concerns the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).

The first [verse] is fulfilled; the next verse shows the perfection of both self-benefit and benefit for others; the subsequent verse shows the fulfillment of awakening for oneself and others. The three lines concern awakening oneself and awakening others, while the final line expresses the aspiration to be born together and realize the same realization.
Fifth: At that time, there was a bodhisattva who descended and pointed out his later companion. This section has two parts: first, the entry of the earlier and later companions into the assembly;
second, the pointing out by the Great Sage. Herein is the first. The companion’s name is *Samyaktva-ananyacārin* (正性無異行). Regarding the character for "conduct" (*cārin*), it has two meanings:

when referring to traveling through lands, it is pronounced with a level tone; when referring to making offerings to Buddhas and benefiting sentient beings, it is pronounced with a departing tone, meaning he is able to pervade [all realms].
Because it acts yet lacks the nature of action, it is called "Right Nature" (*samyaktva*). Its former name was "Right Direction" (*samyag-gati*); "direction" here carries the meaning of "action.
It travels universally through all lands to teach and transform sentient beings, yet it is devoid of the characteristics of coming and going; thus it is identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Pervading all places while lacking any form or appearance, it constitutes the "Dedication of Accordance with Suchness. Regarding those who come from the East: the East is the foremost among the various directions, and Suchness is the [foremost] of the ten thousand...

The beginning of the Dharma: "Coming from space" refers to the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Reaching the summit of the Cakravāḍa mountains" refers to its being all-encompassing and unsurpassed.
"The feet moving the earth" means that True Suchness is like the earth; for it is not manifested without the feet of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

"Assembling as before" means that by conforming to sentient beings, one attains the characteristic of Suchness. From "At a later time, Avalokiteśvara... onwards, the Great Sage provides the instruction.
Sixth: At that time, Sudhana descended [from the tower], longing for [the Master’s] virtue and bidding him farewell.
