According to the Sanskrit original, these first two lines should have been placed after the act of taking leave; they are now moved to the front so that the journey toward the ultimate goal proceeds without looking back and without a beginning.

● The eighth is the Bodhisattva of Rightness and Non-differentiated Practice. This is based on the dedication through the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*), meaning that the roots of goodness are dedicated in union with Suchness. The meaning is as previously explained.
First, seeking by relying on the teachings; second, prostrating at his feet, showing reverence, and inquiring;
third, from "The Bodhisattva said" onwards, he bestows the Dharma-gate upon him. Within this, there are two parts: first, indicating the name and essence; second, manifesting the functional activity.
Now, because a single thought-moment transcends many [eons], it is called "swift"; yet because there is no coming or going, it is called "immovable. Ten.
Mañjuśrī then departs, calling himself "Universal Gate" (*Samantamukha*). Following these words, the activity and function of the gate are revealed, which consists of four parts:
first, the presentation of the inquiry; although there are three questions, the intent is to proceed with rapidity. Second, from the Bodhisattva’s reply, its profound depth is revealed.
Third, from Sudhana’s address, he receives the power [of the gate] and requests an explanation. Fourth, from the Bodhisattva’s reply, the previous [questions] are directly answered.
Question: Among these five [sections], the first answers the place where the Dharma is attained. That is to say, True Suchness (tathatā) is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
it possesses virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and is fully endowed with auspiciousness. By virtue of this majestic power, there is nothing that is not produced.

It is named "Universal Production" (Pūrvotpāda); therefore, it is able to remain unmoving while reaching everywhere. Second, from "From that, it issues forth" onwards, it answers the duration of time. Third, one by one...

4. Regarding "within each thought-moment," the answer concerns the proximity or distance of the location. That is to say, within each thought-moment, how many great strides are taken, and after passing through many eons, is this distant or swift?
5. Regarding "one world after another," this reveals its accomplishment and benefit.
Regarding "likewise from the east," this illustrates the ten directions by analogy. As for the phrase "it is also thus," there are two meanings: first, [coming] from the eastern direction; also...
They come from nine directions, beginning with the southwest. Second, they come here from the world-system called Endowed with Auspicious Treasures (Śrīgarbhasampanna) in the east;
it is the same for the other nine directions as well, starting from the east. As mentioned above regarding Mañjuśrī, he comes from the Golden World (Suvarṇabhūmi);
this is because the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is omnipresent, and since one world-realm is all world-realms, his body and so forth are likewise so. Therefore, he is considered supreme.
It says: "He skillfully arrays his body so that it pervades the entire dharma-realm. The remaining sections on humility, deference, and so forth may be understood through these three parts.
(This concludes the seventeenth sūtra.)
● The Ninth Mahādeva. This is entrusted to the dedication of liberation that is unbound and unattached.

It is called "liberation" because one is not bound by signs (*nimitta*) and does not become attached to views (*dṛṣṭi*), thereby possessing mastery over activity. He is called "Mahādeva" (Great God) because he manifests a great body;
because his pure wisdom is sovereign, being neither bound nor attached, he is called a "God" (*deva*); and because he universally responds in accordance with principle, he is called "Great. Sublime.
Because its function is difficult to fathom, it is called "divine" (*shen*). That which "resides in the gate and presides over the city" corresponds to the rank of the Dharma Master;
for he acts as the master of the gateway of the wondrous Dharma. It is also called "endowed with gates," because all manifold dedications are fully complete therein.

Regarding the first section, "Seeking by Relying on the Teachings," there are two parts: first, recollecting what has preceded; second, proceeding toward what follows. Within the former, there are also two parts.

First, regarding the recollection of the vast practice of the preceding dharmas: this refers to the aforementioned dharma-gates; they are not unknown because of a lack of wisdom, nor are they unaccomplished because of a lack of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
These constitute supreme merits. Second, "the Bodhisattva dons the firm armor of progress" refers to the virtues accomplished through cultivation as a cause. This concludes the gradual progression.
[The section on] "Proceeding Further. Second, from "After Sudhana had questioned him" onwards, [the text describes] seeing, honoring, and inquiring.

Third, at that time, under the Great Heaven, he was granted the Dharma-realm; herein there are two parts: first, the granting of the skillful means of the Dharma, and second, the formal granting of what is attained.
△ Now, for the first part: manifesting signs and praising the friend to cause him to joyfully enter. "He fully extended his four arms," and so forth.
Regarding this: from the perspective of the actual event (*vastu*), those who give rise to the bodhicitta are rare; they gaze with pure eyes and offer scattered flowers as an act of worship.

If we consider the symbolic meaning (*saṃketa*), it refers to unfolding the four *apramāṇas* (immeasurables) and grasping their expressed referent—the dharma-gate corresponding to the *tathatā* of the supreme lineage.

One should first purify oneself to cleanse the body and mind, and subsequently benefit others; thus it is called "scattering flowers. It also symbolizes the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), which extensively gather [beings].
[The assembly] causes the body and mind to be purified so that nothing is not seen. △ Second, from "Good son, I have already accomplished... onwards, the actual bestowal of the Dharma-realm.
This section has two parts: first, the name and essence; second, the activity and function. Now, for the first: namely, the six perfections and great compassion.

[These] are like clouds that cover and moisten, and like a net that gathers and encompasses. Following this, from "Then Sudhana said... onwards, there is the question-and-answer regarding the activity and function. First, the question; then...

Answer: The answer is that one gathers sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Within this, there are two parts: first, manifesting jewels to induce giving, thereby teaching them through the means of attraction of generosity (*dāna*);

second, from the passage "Good son, as I have done for you... onwards, it serves as an analogy to teach the remaining [means]. Within this latter part, there are three sections: first, the fulfillment of the aforementioned perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), which corresponds to the means of attraction of generosity;

second, the extensive explanation of ethical discipline (*śīla*), which corresponds to the means of attraction of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*); and third, the analogical explanation of the remaining perfections and...

Regarding the other summaries: first, concerning the statement "causing the cessation of those obstacles to superior practice that prevent the desire to give," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, identifies four obstacles to giving: first, lack of prior habituation; second, scarcity of objects to be given;
third, attachment to excellent and pleasing material wealth; and fourth, deeply longing for the fruit of abundant wealth in the future.
Now, causing that to be perfumed removes the first hindrance; providing material gifts for the present removes the second hindrance.

By honoring the supreme cause, one is free from further attachment and gives rise to the bodhicitta without seeking future results. [End of section. Second, furthermore, "Good son, if there is... and so forth, extensively explains *śīla* (ethical discipline);
this constitutes the inclusion of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). This entire passage, consisting of both prose and verse, is found in the old translation.
[This is] non-existent. *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 43: All beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) is briefly of three kinds.

Regarding the characteristic [of arising], it is explained that there is no characteristic of arising because it is the function of the very essence (*tattva*).

Since the essence itself has no arising, how could its function have cessation? This is the third pair. Regarding the power of the essence, it is able to cause the characteristic to be non-substantial;

this is explained as being "like an illusion. Regarding the power of the function, it is extensively able to benefit; this is explained as being "not empty. This is the fourth pair. Regarding the essential nature...
How is it that it is profoundly still and unchanging? How does it transcend birth and death? As for its essence (*svabhāva*), how can it follow the flow while its nature remains eternally constant?

Thus, it is not subject to transformation or decay. This is the fifth pair. What virtues does its substance possess? It is inherently beyond words and enables one to transcend speech. What virtues does its function possess?

It skillfully contemplates the characteristics of essence and appearance, yet these are inherently empty. These ten are also called the "Ten Bodies Without Attainment. However, there are five stages...
The essence (*tī*) is but a single essence; the fivefold function (*yòng*) is but a single function. Outside of essence there is no function; function is itself essence.
Outside of function there is no essence; essence is itself function. Essence is the *dharmatā*; function is the response of wisdom (*jñāna*).

Since these two are not two, principle and wisdom are perfectly interfused, constituting the body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) which is solely non-attainable. Following appearances, ten aspects are manifested to represent it.

It is inexhaustible. Observing in this way, what is there to be attached to or grasped? This is called the inconceivable realm of the wisdom of self-awakening that accords with reality through objective conditions (*ālambana*).
Is this not the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata? If one explains it by means of five pairs, they unfold and clarify one another in succession.
This is also termed "essence and function. However, each subsequent term explains the preceding one. The first four are negations (*pratiṣedha*), while the last one is an affirmation (*vidhi*).
The first [negation] means that the essence of function is realized as cessation; it does not mean that the essence of function is a response that comes from nowhere. The second [negation] states:

"If that were so, it would be subject to arising and ceasing, because the Buddha-body arises within the worldly realms. Therefore, the function of responding must not come from elsewhere, lest it perish.
Because it is extinguished. Therefore, the subsequent explanation states: "The nature of the Dharmakāya is such that there is no distinction between its being accomplished or unaccomplished;

how, then, could there be arising? As the function of the very essence, it is fundamentally without arising; what, then, could be extinguished? Third, it asks: "If this is so, is it real or is it empty?

What is real? The equality of the Dharmakāya is real. What is empty? Its functional application is not true [in the sense of being substantial], and thus it is empty. Therefore, the explanation says: "Illusion."

If that which is manifested by wisdom is real, how can it fail to provide benefit? How then could it be called illusory? Fourth, [the opponent] says: "If this were so, there would be transition and destruction.
That which is manifested by illusory wisdom moves from defilement to purity—is this not transition? Adapting to objects and according to capacities, its essence may well be subject to destruction.
Therefore, he explains again: "Having already transcended birth and death, how could there be any transition? This is precisely the eternal body; how [could it change]?"
It can destroy [all conceptualization]. Fifth, it is said: "If this is so, and since the hundred negations have been severed, how does one awaken and enter?

Therefore, it is indicated that the Buddha-body is non-dual, being sealed and sustained by the single Dharma of true reality (*dharmatā*); thus, speech and thought are utterly severed in order to eliminate all numerical categories."
Therefore, it is said that there is "one mark. This one is not [inherently] one; the mark is also not a mark.

Not only is the mark of phenomenal characteristics non-existent, but even the substantial mark—the true mark—is likewise non-existent. Thus, it is said: "The nature and marks are fundamentally empty. Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* says:
The Buddha abides in the profound and true *dharmatā*, which is quiescent, devoid of marks, and identical to empty space.
Yet, within the context of the supreme ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he manifests various activities. All deeds performed for the benefit of sentient beings exist by virtue of this *dharmatā*.
There is no distinction between that which possesses marks and that which is markless; they all enter into the ultimate state of being without marks—this is precisely what is meant.

If we speak of these in terms of their essential nature (*tattva*), they largely accord with the meaning of the "Eight Negations" in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. However, all of them are both characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and nature (*dharmatā*).
According to the commentary on that treatise, each is explained by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): namely, that all phenomena (*dharma*) are not self-arisen, nor do they arise from another.
It is neither co-existent nor causeless; therefore, one knows there is no arising. This applies to all ten phrases. This is the identity of phenomena with reality (*tathatā*).

If analyzed according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), that [previous explanation] refers to the lack of nature in the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is why it is said to be "non-arising" and so forth.

The present explanation refers to the fact that the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally non-arising and so forth. Since function is identical to essence, there is no distinction between nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). There is yet another approach to this, the meaning of which is explained elsewhere.
[○@△] Second, "Good sons, when I thus know all Tathāgatas," and so forth, correctly elucidates the three types of *dhyāna* and specifically reveals their functional applications (*karmaprayoga*).

This section has three parts: first, the *dhyāna* of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), which is the functional application of the bliss of tranquil meditative concentration;

second, the *dhyāna* that draws forth and generates merit; and third, the *dhyāna* that benefits sentient beings. The former two constitute the functional application of universal progression (*samantagati*).

Application. ▲ First, this is the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) that is identical with cessation (*śamatha*), which was previously explained; now, it explains the cessation that is identical with contemplation.
This section has two parts: first, restating the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, from "contemplative observation" (*cintā-vipaśyanā*) onwards, the four dhyānas are formally revealed.

Thus, the Tathāgata-dhyāna guides the four dhyānas, differing from those of ordinary beings and the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Although the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ, the four dhyānas themselves constitute four distinct stages.

The forest of the four dhyāna factors is largely identical in meaning. That is to say, the first dhyāna possesses five factors: vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and samādhi (concentration).

The second possesses four factors: adhyātmasaṃprasāda (internal clarity), prīti, sukha, and samādhi. The third possesses five factors: upekṣā (equanimity), smṛti (mindfulness), prajñā (wisdom), sukha, and samādhi. The fourth possesses four factors:
upekṣā, smṛti, aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā (neutral feeling), and samādhi. As for their designations: the first is called "with vitarka and with vicāra" (savitarka-savicāra-śamatha).

[The four dhyānas are: first, dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra; second, dhyāna without vitarka and with vicāra; third, dhyāna without vitarka or vicāra; fourth, dhyāna free from joy; and fifth, dhyāna free from bliss.

Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The first possesses vicāra, joy, and bliss; the subsequent ones gradually abandon the preceding factors. This is its meaning. According to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
The forest of the four dhyāna factors is summarized into four categories: first, the obstacles abandoned; second, the factors of counteraction; third, the factors of benefit;
and fourth, the samādhi that serves as the basis for those two. Among these four, the latter three are factors, while the first is not a factor.

Although each subsequent obstacle abandoned is a factor for each preceding stage, with respect to their own respective levels, none of them are considered factors. Now, regarding the first: within the first dhyāna...
First, the contemplative observation that reaches various objects is precisely vitarka (initial inquiry) and vicāra (sustained examination), which serve as the factors of counteraction.

"Contemplation" is vitarka, and "observation" is vicāra. "Firmly adorned" refers to the characteristics of vitarka and vicāra, which universally illuminate various objects and distinguish the spheres of vitarka and vicāra;
it is not merely observing the faults of the five desires, hence the term "various. Second, perfection.
"Fullness below" refers to joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*), which serve as the limb of benefit. This is because they are perfectly complete, vast, profound, and conformable;
because the joy of the Dharma pervades the state of the limit of equality (*samatā-koṭi*); and because of pliancy and delight. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Joy and bliss mean that one has already attained the desired goal; having attained great pliancy, body and mind are harmonized and supple. (3)

"Not giving rise to any conceptualization or discrimination" refers to that which is free from obstacles. The meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle merely abandons desire, evil, and unwholesome states;
however, the profound and wondrous One Vehicle abandons all delusions, and only then constitutes the realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening, identical to the *tathāgata-dhyāna*.
Next, it provides great compassion to rescue and protect all sentient beings, thereby distinguishing itself from the ordinary and the Lesser Vehicle. Ordinary...

Having previously attained joy and happiness through the minor departure from sorrow, one is now personally free from sorrow. One takes on the sorrows of sentient beings; this does not hinder one’s ability to rescue and deliver them.
Fourth, the single-mindedness of immovability is the samādhi that serves as the basis for those two [joy and happiness]; it is called the "limb of support.

This refers to the nature of one-pointedness of mind that arises from the careful and correct observation of the object of focus, serving as the basis for the limbs of antidote and benefit. It relies upon—

The power of concentration (*samādhi*) functions through the transformation of applied thought (*vitarka*) and so forth. As for the obstacles abandoned [by it], because they lack the substance of active application (*abhisamskāra*), they are not constituent factors (*aṅga*);

thus, it does not serve as their basis. However, when it is said that those two [applied thought and sustained thought] cultivate the first dhyāna, this summarizes the first dhyāna and likewise belongs to its basis.
The basis for the four dhyānas is essentially no different in its general principle. Regarding the phrase "the second [dhyāna] stills all mental karma" and below, this clarifies the second dhyāna.

This phrase refers to the cessation of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), which are the obstacles to be abandoned. Vitarka and vicāra are coarse and agitated; they give rise to the three consciousnesses and disturb the second dhyāna.
Just as one sees nothing when pure water is disturbed by waves, the first dhyāna serves as the remedy for them, and thus they are the objects to be remedied. Therefore—
When the illness is exhausted, the medicine perishes. Second, the power of wisdom that gathers all sentient beings is courageous and fierce;

this is internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), which constitutes the factor of the practice of counteraction (*pratipakṣabhāvanāṅga*). In the Hīnayāna, internal purity consists merely of faith that can purify the mental states and cause concentration and other factors to flow inwardly.

In the Mahāyāna, internal purity is constituted by encompassing the three factors of the third dhyāna: equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*). By means of these three dharmas, [it is established].

It is still covered by joy (*prīti*), and its functional power has not yet prevailed; it can only abandon external *vitarka* and *vicāra*, and is therefore combined as "inner serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).

Now, "gathering all sentient beings" refers to [focusing on] sentient beings in every moment of thought; thus, the power of wisdom is courageous and fierce, which is equivalent to right knowledge (*saṃprajanya*).

Since the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*) has not yet manifested, it is contained within these two [factors] and is therefore combined as one branch. Third, the mind is delighted and gladdened by joy (*prīti*). This is...

The factors of joy and bliss are the benefits of practice. Regarding the cultivation of the second dhyāna: that very samādhi which serves as the basis for those two [factors] exists only in the first dhyāna;
it is absent in the remaining three. Thus, when cultivating the second dhyāna, there must be the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).

"Third, contemplating the self-nature of all sentient beings" and below clarifies the third dhyāna. This phrase consists of the three factors of equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*).

These constitute the counteractive practices (*pratipakṣa*) of cultivation. Contemplating sentient beings alone is the factor of mindfulness; because this contemplation includes their nature, it is clear comprehension;
and contemplating only the self-nature is the factor of equanimity. [In the second dhyāna, these two] were combined into one and the term "self-nature" was not mentioned.

This is the nature [of equanimity]. However, this is the "equanimity of formation" (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), not the "feeling of equanimity" (*vedanā-upekṣā*). This means that the mind’s formations are brought into balance by abandoning the fault of joy.
Second, there is the wearying detachment from birth and death, which is the obstacle to be abandoned. The joy of the second dhyāna is the obstacle to the third dhyāna;

it is like a poor man who rejoices upon finding treasure but falls into deep sorrow when losing it. It is better not to have it at all, so as to be free from both sorrow and joy. Joy is [the root of] birth and death.

Therefore, it is now said that one "becomes weary" [of the lower realms] and dwells in the bliss of nirvāṇa; this is the factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*), which constitutes the benefit of spiritual practice.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Free from joy (*prīti*) and characterized by tranquility, there arises a mental feeling (*citta-vedanā*) that is utterly serene and contrary to joy.

At that time, one experiences within both the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*) and the mental body (*manas-kāya*) the sensation of bliss (*sukha-vedanā*) as well as the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*). For this reason, it is designated in various places as 'bodily sensation' (*kāyika-vedanā*)."

Because it is blissful, it is said that the bliss of the third dhyāna is the most profound and subtle. Now, one transcends this further and dwells securely in the eternal bliss of the tranquility of nirvāṇa.
However, the bliss of the first dhyāna is like water atop a mountain of earth and stone; the bliss of the second dhyāna is like a pool of water atop a mountain of pure earth;
and the bliss of the third dhyāna is like a mountain of pure earth situated within a great lake—the bliss pervading everywhere.

Beyond the body; the body abides within bliss. This is the cultivation of the third dhyāna. Immediately following the samādhi of the second support, one is able to descend through all four to clarify the fourth dhyāna.
Although the text contains only two [points], they encompass all four. That is to say, the various sufferings, afflictions, and fevers of all sentient beings are the obstacles to be abandoned.
However, suffering, pleasure, grief, and joy are all obstacles to the fourth dhyāna. If one attains the fourth...

In the fourth dhyāna, the four feelings are all extinguished, and there remains only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*); this is the factor of benefit. The purity of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi*) serves as its antidote.

In the third dhyāna, equanimity and mindfulness coexist with the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), and thus they are not yet called "pure. Now, because the feeling of pleasure is absent, it is called "pure.
That which is now extinguished—the heat and affliction—is the obstacle to be abandoned; that which is able to extinguish it is equanimity and mindfulness, serving as the antidote.
The branch of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the distancing from all agitation of the two extremes, accompanied by self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana*).

However, this equanimity of worldly benefit is, from the perspective of the supramundane, also suffering. Because one erroneously conceives of pleasure within lower forms of suffering, it is now entirely relinquished;
for it is contained within all burning afflictions (*paridāha*). This single phrase contains three sections. Second, the cultivation.
The Fourth Dhyāna. This is explained by relying on the two bases of samādhi and consulting the sūtras and śāstras to interpret the scriptural text;

it is not based on this [current] interpretation. Why are the characteristics of the four dhyānas distinguished? Below the section "Increasing and Perfecting," the dhyāna that produces merit is introduced.
There are three merits: first, it can induce wisdom and vows, unlike ordinary beings who relish the flavor of dhyāna. It does not...
Together with the Śrāvakas, one enters into the wishless (*apraṇihita*). Therefore, one is able to draw forth the vow for omniscience (*sarvajñatā-praṇidhāna*).
From within the two or one samādhis, many samādhis and the spheres of liberation emerge. Third, one accomplishes transformations such that there is nothing that is not produced.
These three are the characteristics of difficult practices; they constitute universal wandering. [The passage] beginning with "Good son, I have practiced" below clarifies abundance.
The meditation for benefiting sentient beings involves every kind of skillful means that brings benefit; it also carries the meaning of "universal wandering. The text is divided into three parts.

First, causing one to leave desire and enter the homeless life, there are fourteen perceptions (*saṃjñā*), which are largely identical to the ten perceptions found in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Next, the section beginning with "If there are sentient beings dwelling in seclusion" establishes the conditions that assist the path. Finally...
"Good son, when I practiced in this way," and so forth, means that by causing the abandonment of evil and the advancement of good, one practices the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Second: "Good son, I only... and so forth, means to humble oneself and defer to the superior. Third: "Good son, not far from here... and so forth, indicates the subsequent friend.
This subsequent stage is the "Radiant" (*Arciṣmatī*); because it is presented as being similar to the mundane world, it is said to be "not far. It relies upon...
The Radiance of Principle (Ratnaprabhāsa) is called the Bodhimanda because it accords with principle; thus, it is said to be "right. Regarding "Observing with Joyful Eyes":

the patience of the Dharma-eye regarding principle and the compassionate eye observing all things both carry the sense of joy. Furthermore, through superior meditative concentration and the power of retention, one observes all things excellently.
Within these three verses, there are thirteen stanzas divided into three sections. The first section consists of ten stanzas, which versify the preceding "bestowal of the Dharma.
The next two stanzas express self-effacement and the recommendation of others who are superior. The final stanza describes approaching to show the subsequent friend. Now, for the first section:

it only versifies the general response regarding the ten dharmas asked about, with slight deviations from their original order. The first four correspond in sequence to the first four dharmas; the fifth skips ahead to versify the fifth dharma.

Verse seven is a restatement of the sixth; verse eight is a restatement of the fifth; verse nine is a restatement of the tenth; verse ten is a restatement of the eighth; and verse eleven is a restatement of the ninth.
These conclude with the Master’s humility and his indication of what follows; the text is clear and may be understood accordingly. At this fourth stage, Sudhana bows down and takes his leave.
● Third is the night goddess Sarvasattvālokanayanapramuditā, a spiritual friend on the stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).

This is because she has attained supreme meditative concentration and the great dharma-dhāraṇī, and is able to radiate the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom. As for the correspondence between name and meaning, it has already been explained as before.
Although there are six textual passages, their meaning differs slightly from what preceded.
Regarding the first [section], "Seeking according to the Teaching," there are two parts. First, reflecting on the benefits already attained;
second, from "Having made this reflection" onwards, seeking the subsequent friend. Within this, there are four parts: 1) the desire to seek the subsequent friend;

2) from "At that time, the goddess Priyadarśanā" onwards, the empowerment of the virtuous friend, which consists of eleven phrases—the first being general and the remainder specific; 3) from "At that time, the youth Sudhana suddenly gave rise to this thought" onwards...

Regarding the benefits conferred by the empowerment: the previous empowerment was to make known the benefit of associating with a spiritual friend; the present ability to give rise to mindfulness is itself the conferred benefit.

This consists of ten phrases, which correspond respectively to the ten distinct phrases mentioned previously. From "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, it correctly clarifies the progression toward the subsequent stage.
Second, seeing that night goddess descend, he pays homage, inquires, and consults her. This section has three parts: first, observing her activity to enter through realization;
second, offering praise with verses; third, inquiring about the essentials of the Dharma. Within the first part, there are four sections. The first is seeing her environment and its inhabitants.
Second, beholding the entrance into the Dharma-gate; third, seeing the great function; fourth, clarifying the realization and entry.

The latter three are the same as before in bestowing the Dharma-realm upon oneself. [○@△] Now, the first can be understood. [○@△] Second, regarding the "Gate of Liberation of the Stainless Banner of Universal Joy and Great Swift Entry":
this refers to beholding the entrance into the Dharma. "Swift" means that in a single thought-moment, one subdues [all things]; the old translation says "great power," which reveals this.

Its function is able to universally accord with the capacities of all sentient beings; thus it is called "Universal Joy" (*Samantamukha*). It crushes and subdues what is high and prominent; therefore, it is named a "Banner" (*dhvaja*).

[○@△] Third, regarding the upper and lower parts of its body, one clearly perceives its great function. This section has three parts: first, emanating transformation bodies from all pores to preach all dharmas;
second, manifesting past deeds (*pūrvayoga*) within the pores; third, manifesting [various realms] within the pores.

The body that accords with [the beings'] types. This explains their fundamental practices. The first section also has three parts: first, a general explanation of the characteristics; second, a specific exposition of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*);

and third, an analogical explanation of the remaining practices. The first part is readily understood. Regarding the second part, "That which is called... and so forth, it specifically expounds the ten perfections, which are divided into ten sections.
Each section contains internal sub-sections for differentiation. Within each section, there are both general and specific conclusions at the textual junctures.

This may be understood. First, regarding generosity (*dāna*): there is nothing among objects that is not relinquished, no field of merit (*kṣetra*) to which one does not give, and no mind that is not impartial.

Because these three wheels are equalized, the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is accomplished. Second, within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), first it causes one to cultivate the cause; next, [the passage] beginning with "In all worldly... [explains the result].

One does not seek immediate results. Later, after the section on causing all sentient beings [to attain] below, it explains the benefits of the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-vinaya*). Within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), first one is led to cultivate the causes of the three patiences;
next, after the section on the bodhicitta below, one is led to perform dedication (*pariṇāmana*); and next, after the section on all sentient beings below...

The section beginning with "Showing the fruit of non-forbearance" and continuing with "Later, praising all Tathāgatas" shows the fruit of forbearance. Within the four perfections of vigor, there is a general exposition of the three types of diligence that universally governs all practices.

Within the five dhyānas of meditative concentration, the initial stage causes one to leave desire behind, while the subsequent stage, beginning with "Abiding in the garden of the Dharma," [leads to further realization].

He causes beings to cultivate dhyāna. Within this, first he causes them to attain the dhyāna of dwelling in happiness in the present life; next, from "he further expounds for them" onwards, he brings forth the dhyāna that generates merit;
and finally, from "he causes the assembly of beings" onwards, he brings forth the dhyāna that benefits sentient beings. Among the six perfections:

The first clarifies the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*); the latter, for the sake of those below, simultaneously distinguishes both the fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) wisdoms.

Although these constitute the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), from the perspective of what is primary and secondary, each of the six also possesses all three types of wisdom. Within the seventh, the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), the first is precisely the skillful means of the union of existence and non-existence.
Because he contemplates emptiness while engaging with existence, next, for some he expounds the skillful means of neither abiding in saṃsāra nor abandoning [nirvāṇa];
subsequently, for others he expounds the skillful means of progressing toward the fruit by dwelling in celestial palaces. Within the eight great vows, there are ten vows in the text:
the first two clarify them collectively; the next five are vows of seeking the higher goal; the next two are vows of supernatural powers; and the last...

1. Regarding the two types of benefit, they correspond to the vows for downward transformation. Within the nine powers (*bala*), the accumulation of the factors conducive to enlightenment corresponds to the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*);
the others correspond to the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*). 2. Within the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), the first clarifies the knowledge of maturing sentient beings;

subsequently, it explains the knowledge of enjoying the dharma-bliss through the mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in every thought-moment. 3. As stated regarding the bodhisattva’s various *pāramitās*, the following cases are to be applied by analogy.
It speaks of other practices, namely the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), the means of conversion (*saṃgrahavastu*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and so forth.
Second, "furthermore, within each and every pore, she manifests those night goddesses" refers to manifesting her past deeds (*pūrvayoga*) within the pores.

Of these two preceding sections, the former involves the inexhaustible arising from within a single hair, while this present section involves the inexhaustible inclusion within a single hair. Within this, [the text continues].

It also manifests the characteristics of the ten perfections of the past. The text is divided into three parts: first, the general; second, the specific; and third, the conclusion. The first part is readily understood.

The second part, beginning with "practicing the perfection of giving" (*dānapāramitā*), is the specific section. Within this specific section, each item begins with the word "practice. The first two of these are readily understood.
Within the three types of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*): first is the patience of enduring suffering;

second is the ability to endure all harmful actions and malicious speech directed at one’s own body and mind, which is the patience of enduring enmity and injury—wherein harmful action pertains to the body and malicious speech pertains to speech;

and last is the patience of thoroughly examining phenomena (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*), which endures all karmic consequences. Within the four types of diligence (*vīrya*): the first three phrases correspond to the three forms of diligence. First...

The first phrase refers to donning the armor; the second phrase refers to gathering what is wholesome; and the final phrase refers to benefit and happiness. Within the five dhyānas, there are eight phrases:

first, the requisite conditions; second, skillful means; third, cultivation; fourth, attainment; fifth, the remedying of hindrances; sixth, fulfillment; seventh, the arising of function; and eighth, mutual inclusion.

The first six constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), while the latter two constitute the drawing forth of meritorious qualities. The subsequent five perfections follow the same pattern of phrases.

Although there are variations in quantity, the general principle is the same for all. Within the six *prajñās*, the explanation based on both the auxiliary and the primary applies to all three types of wisdom (*jñāna*).

First, the "provisions" (*sambhāra*) refer to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). "Purification" (*viśuddhi*) refers to the counteracting of obstacles; this is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). "The sun" refers to the dispelling of darkness; this is the fundamental wisdom. "Clouds" refer to compassionate coverage;

the flowing moisture and the expounding of the Dharma constitute the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). "Treasury" (*kośa*) refers to inclusion, and "ocean" (*samudra*) refers to depth and breadth. As for "practice" (*caryā*)...
"Cultivation" refers to the gateway for entering into principle. The first four [perfections] all encompass both the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms.

They enter [the path] with everything fully complete, without any deficiency or omission; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

Fourth, when a son of good family, a bodhisattva, achieves the lower stage of the summary, first they shall obtain the vision of people, next they shall obtain the Dharma, and finally they shall encounter virtuous friends everywhere.
Regarding "encountering [them] everywhere," there are briefly two meanings. First, true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) constantly pervade the world;

because they accord with the Dharma, one always encounters them. Thus, Maitreya said: "A person who is not a vessel for the Dharma, even if dwelling together with a son of the Buddha for immeasurable eons, will not know his realm.
By contrast, this implies that those who are vessels will certainly encounter them constantly. Second, since...
When concentration and wisdom proceed together, there is no object that they do not accord with; both serve as vessels for the Way and are both virtuous friends.
Thus, the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance" states: "The wondrous Wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata—all of it consists of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
If one can awaken to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) upon hearing it, such a person constantly beholds the Buddha. To be able to practice in this way is to protect the True Dharma."
[This is] the Hall. ▲ Regarding the section "When these words were spoken": Sudhana looked up and asked, "Since you have already clearly instructed me, why should I ask further?

In what place should I seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)? The previous [passage] provided a general instruction; now he specifically asks about Māyā. ▲ Regarding the section "The Rākṣasī replied":
This is a repeated answer concerning the search for Māyā. It is not different from the previous general [instruction]. Since he was able to ask again, it returns [to the specific].
He answered again, responding with four points. First, because the friend is omnipresent; second, because the friend has the Dharma as its essence—these two together constitute the first phrase.
Third, because the body is identical to the friend and is all-pervasive; fourth, because wisdom merges with its object, like a shadow or a dream.
Thus, the swift mind immediately travels throughout the ten directions, and the compliant mind is present in all four phrases.

Furthermore, the first three [stages] are free from the characteristics of objective realms, while the last one is free from the characteristics of mental objects; thus, there is nothing sought at all, and one truly enters into the principle.
This is the seeking of non-seeking, which is the seeking of no-attainment.

Second, at that time, Sudhana [descends]. He sees, pays respect, and inquires. Within this, there are three parts: first, seeing; second, paying respect; and third, inquiring. Regarding the first [seeing], there are two parts:
first, clarifying the cause for seeing, which is because he receives and practices the teaching. However, this receiving and practicing actually extends through all three stages.
The old translation merely says "receiving and practicing its teaching. Furthermore, since the rākṣasī is nearby and she instructs him to seek a spiritual friend, it is emphasized here.

This is the summary statement. Second, from "At that very moment" onwards, the text correctly clarifies the act of beholding. Within this, there are two parts: first, beholding the support; second, beholding the supported.
[○@、] Regarding the first, there are three sections: first, beholding the lotus flower; second, beholding the pavilion; third, beholding the precious throne. Now, for the first:

because the self-nature of the dharmadhātu realized therein is undefiled, it is called a "lotus flower. Since ignorance has been opened, it does not depart from within the mind, as if emerging from the earth.
The leaping upward also symbolizes that the causes of the myriad practices of intrinsic purity emerge from the ground of the Dharma-nature.

This is the flower of Samantabhadra at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). It is called "Great" because the *Daśadharma-sthiti-parivarta* states that its measure pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

As for the towers and pavilions atop the platform being named "Containing the Ten Directions," how much more so would the lotus flowers not pervade the Dharma-realm? The mention of the "ten pillars" and so forth refers to symbolic representation.
The Dharma-ear. Second, regarding the pavilions above and below the terrace: it clearly reveals the towers and galleries, signifying the ability to realize the two wisdoms;

because these manifest repeatedly based upon what has been realized, wisdom encompasses all without exception, which is why it is said to "admit the ten directions. The comprehensive integration of the five stages, both in their own nature and in their superior progress, is termed the "thousand pillars.
Each individual feature possesses symbolic significance for the Dharma; fearing that excessive detail would weary the reader, I shall not elaborate further. Third, as for those towers...

Within the pavilion, below the "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel," one clearly perceives the precious throne; this represents the essence of wisdom as the emptiness of phenomena (dharmas), and thus it is situated within the tower.

It is fully endowed with the qualities of its nature and extensively manifests adornments. This section has two parts: first, the clarification of the primary throne; second, from "At that time" onwards, the clarification of the inclusion of the retinue.

[○@、] Second, Queen Māyā was seated upon that throne, clearly manifesting her primary retribution (*vipāka*). This passage is placed at the beginning to indicate that at that time, Sudhana saw such a throne.
Within this section there are also two parts: first, a general clarification of the manifestation of the body;

second, from "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, a specific revelation of the clouds of bodies. Within this latter part there are also two: first, the physical marks of the body; second, the activities of the body. [△@、] Regarding the former, there is furthermore...

Second. First, the inconceivable bodies of the myriad classes are clarified; second, the preeminent body of the single class is clarified. Within the first, there are two parts: first, the clarification of specific characteristics;
second, the manifestation of the universal essence. Now, for the first [part], there are forty-six bodies. In the Sanskrit original and the old Chinese translation, there are only forty;
that is to say, the "body of vast power" corresponds to the "universally pervasive body" in the Sanskrit original, and the "body dwelling in peace and bliss" corresponds to... [text continues].

In the Sanskrit original, there is the body that extinguishes inverted views, the body of non-interruption and non-exhaustion; this is the body that constantly manifests in the Sanskrit original, the body of great majestic power.
Furthermore, it reiterates the previously mentioned body that extinguishes inverted views, the body of form without dependence, which is non-abiding and free from delusion.
In the Sanskrit original, this explains non-discrimination. Excluding these six bodies, there remain only forty. At this point—

In the middle [section], there are cases that refer solely to phenomena (*vastu*), such as "universally pervasive" (*paryanta*) and "universally manifest" (*pratyupasthita*); and there are cases that refer solely to principle (*nyāya*), such as in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, fascicle 13, which states:
"The body of form is unborn, because it has no origination; the body of form is unceasing, because it is eternally quiescent."
Alternatively, phenomena and principle are mutually penetrating: for example, the thirty-two types of non-arising form-bodies (rūpakāya), because they are accomplished through illusory vows;
the thirty-five types of non-arising form-bodies, because they manifest according to the karma of sentient beings; and the thirty-two [types], which accord with one's own vows.

The thirty-five [points] correspond to the karma of sentient beings; all of them manifest the principle through phenomena. The remainder may be inferred accordingly, as they are identical to the ten bodies (*daśakāya*).
Fearing prolixity, I shall not provide a detailed correlation. Second, regarding Sudhana’s vision of Māyā, below, we shall distinguish its pervasive essence.

This refers to being free from the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), hence it is called "non-form" (*arūpa*) and so forth. There is no truly permanent form and so on. The text contains eight phrases.
The first five [categories] specifically clarify the five aggregates (*skandha*). Their definitions, however, differ through a process of mutual abbreviation and inclusion:

1. Form (*rūpa*) manifests from conditions. 2. Feeling (*vedanā*) extinguishes the mundane; as for the term "transformative extinction," it means that impermanent feeling is extinguished and transformed into permanent feeling.

3. Perception (*saṃjñā*) perceives objects according to their appearance. 4. Mental formations (*saṃskāra*) depend on illusory karmic activity; since they are not [substantial] activity, they are called "non-activity. 5. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*).
Because wisdom is also empty of intrinsic nature. The sixth phrase generally reveals that which is beyond words. The seventh phrase refers to the impermanence that has already ceased.

The eighth phrase refers to the eternal quiescence that has already been realized. Second, "At that time, Sudhana again saw... and so forth clarifies a class of bodies that are transcendentally superior.
The old translation contains only "transcendental superiority" and lacks "form like [the Buddhas]"; the present translation possesses both. Within this, there are two parts; first—
This is the general heading, which simultaneously indicates both "similarity" (*sadr̥śa*) and "excellence" (*atiśaya*). What follows below is the specific exposition;

second, specifically revealing it through the phrase "acting in equanimity. Within the first part, there are also two sub-sections, the first of which clarifies the ten [powers]. (Note: The Sanskrit original simply states:

"manifesting immeasurable form-bodies such as these," which encompasses both types of bodies, as both possess this activity. The subsequent section, beginning with "acting in equanimity," provides the specific exposition.)

The Practice of Deliverance. This subsequently clarifies the practices of merit and wisdom. Herein is the first [section]. First is *dāna* (generosity), which is mentioned first; therefore, it is described as "great compassion.

Second, from "giving birth to the Tathāgata" onwards is *śīla* (ethical discipline). This is because ethical discipline can increase the factors of awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and because it encompasses the virtues of the Buddha.
1. "Observing and contemplating below" refers to the patience of thoroughly examining the Dharma (*dharmapravicaya-kṣānti*). 2. "Diligently applying effort below" refers to vigor (*vīrya*). 3.

8. Accomplishing great vows corresponds to the perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*). 9. Sporting in the various sovereign powers of the Tathāgatas corresponds to the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).

10. Attaining the light of the Buddha’s wisdom corresponds to the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*). Regarding the second [section], "the cultivation of the fulfillment of all the various merits of the Tathāgatas," this clarifies the practices of the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*).
The eleventh sentence is divided into three parts: the first two sentences provide the heading, and the subsequent six sentences set forth its essence.
The latter three lines form the conclusion. Now, for the first: the preceding line indicates merit (*puṇya*), while the subsequent line indicates wisdom (*jñāna*).

In the "Chapter on Transcending the World," there are ten lines for each to manifest their inexhaustibility. Next, the six lines beginning with "constantly and joyfully observing" specifically set forth the essence of merit and wisdom.
The four bodhisattva practices do not transcend merit and wisdom; the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*) is explained according to the six paramitas.

The first three are merit (*puṇya*); the last one is wisdom (*jñāna*). The middle two pertain to both merit and wisdom. If based on the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), skillful means (*upāya*) assists the first three;

aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) assists diligence (*vīrya*); power (*bala*) assists meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and wisdom (*jñāna*) assists transcendent wisdom (*prajñā*). Merit and wisdom can thus be understood.
Second, "giving birth to all bodhisattva stages" clarifies the positions of merit and wisdom. Third, "accumulating" and below clarify merit and wisdom comprehensively.
It also includes supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). 4. From "valiantly" (*vīryavat*) downward: the practice of advancing and applying merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna*).

5. From "universally accomplishing" (*samantataḥ pariniṣpatti*) downward: the practice of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). 6. From "constantly and diligently guarding" (*nityam ārakṣaṇa*) downward: the practice of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

The final three lines, beginning with "always delighting in praising," conclude the [cultivation of] merit and wisdom: the first line concludes merit; the second line concludes both; and the third line [concludes] by virtue of possessing the aforementioned two.
"May you become the Mother of Buddhas.
[○@△] Second, from the passage "At that time, the youth Sudhana saw Māyā... onwards, he pays homage and realizes entry.
His own path is already profound, and he manifests his body as equal to hers. Above, among the myriad diverse manifestations and distinct forms of Māyā, there were many; now, this Sudhana—
The body of Sudhana is a single entity that manifests universally in response to those seeking the Dharma; thus, within the identity of his essence, there is multiplicity.
If Māyā and Sudhana both manifest universally without being divided, then both are cases of abiding in the essence while responding universally. Māyā is also of the same essence:

the one is the many, because although she appears differently according to those to whom she responds, she possesses no dual essence. Sudhana is also of the same essence: the many are the one, for all... [the various manifestations are non-dual with the singular reality].

Regarding the location of Sudhana: it is because he is the Sudhana before a single [form of] the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, when these two are viewed in relation to one another, they both encompass the identity of essence and the difference of essence;
for a single Māyā responds to many Sudhanas, and many Sudhanas face a single Māyā.
[○@△] Third, from "The Great Sage below" onwards, he inquires about the essentials of the Dharma. As for the reason for describing Mañjuśrī and his various spiritual friends:
if considered in terms of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), because it is the ultimate stage of the causal position (*hetu-bhūmi*), all are subsumed within this.

If considered in terms of meeting conditions (*pratyaya*), then from the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) onwards, every single virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and the Dharma obtained from them are all included among those met.

Third, from the passage where Lady Māyā addresses Sudhana, she reveals her own *dharmadhātu*. This section has three parts: first, the name and essence; second, the functional activity; and third, the fundamental source.
Regarding the first, the name contains six characters with specific meanings. Second, regarding the essence of great wisdom (*jñāna*), it is because its nature is all-pervasive.
Regarding the two aspects of the vow (*praṇidhāna*): first, the specific vow, which is the vow to become the Mother of the Buddha; second, the general [vow].

Because one vows to universally encompass the vast vows of Samantabhadra. Regarding the three wisdoms and two meanings: first, because expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) can give rise to great vows and can accomplish illusory phenomena;
second, because ultimate wisdom (*prajñā*), which is *prajñāpāramitā*, can give birth to the true body (*dharmakāya*) of the Buddha. Regarding the four illusions and two meanings:
first, because the substance of vow-wisdom is empty and its own characteristic is called "illusion. As the aforementioned sutra says: "Illusory wisdom is itself bodhi..."

Sa. The Bodhisattva is precisely illusory wisdom (*māyājñāna*). These two are non-apprehendable (*anupalabdha*), yet they can accomplish all that is not done. The second is that which is produced by wisdom;
it takes birth as a Buddha as an illusion, meaning that while not destroying the small body, it is able to contain all extensively, because it arises from the non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Regarding the two meanings of the five adornments (*pañcavyūha*): first, one adorns the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the spheres of all Buddhas with the illusion of great vow-wisdom; second, [one adorns]...

Because one can achieve Buddhahood by taking the illusory wisdom of great vows as one's own adornment, and because the non-apprehension of the ten meanings constitutes the Great Dependent Origination, it is the mother of all Buddhas.

[○@△] Second, "Therefore, she is constantly the mother of all bodhisattvas," and so forth, clarifies the functional activity (*karmaprayoga*). This section has two parts: first, this sentence provides a general clarification;

second, from "Good son, as I... onwards, it provides a specific exposition. Within this latter part, there are four sections: first, she is the mother of the present Vairocana Buddha; second, she is the mother of the past Buddhas;
third, she is the mother of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa—this meaning extends through the three periods of time; fourth, the conclusion.
The Infinite Mother of Buddhas, penetrating both horizontally and vertically. [This section] has two parts: first, a general explanation of her being the mother of Vairocana of the ocean of lands.
Regarding the term *Siddha*: in full it is *Siddhārtha*; in the new translation it is *Vasiddhārtha*;

in the Tang language it means "one who accomplishes all things" or "one who accomplishes all meanings. The rest of the text is understandable. Furthermore, later [it says]: "O son of good family, I..."

second, the explicit clarification of his sovereign entry into the womb; third, the inconceivable multitude of oceans contained within his abdomen;

and fourth, citing this as an example for the ten billion worlds. Regarding the first part, there are four sections: first, the light entering the body; second, "Furthermore, within that light... and so forth, concerning the light.
1. Manifesting the eight phases [of a Buddha’s life]. 2. Furthermore, from the passage "He also saw the Tathāgata in the past... downwards, it manifests the causes and effects of Buddhahood. 3.

1. From [the phrase] "The two bodhisattvas at that time by means of their supernormal powers descended. This refers to the manifestation of the Bodhisattva’s supernormal powers. 2.

Furthermore, from [the phrase] "Again, by means of his spiritual power, he emitted a great light. When this light shone, it pacified suffering. 3. Furthermore, from [the phrase] "In order to provide protection and refuge...

This refers to the manifestation of the transformation of entering the womb. 4. "Those various bodhisattvas within my womb... Having entered, they walked about. 5. Thirdly, from [the phrase] "Furthermore, in every thought-moment... [This describes how] the womb enveloped them.
"The oceans of beings are inconceivable. From "Fourth, son of good family, in this way" below, he takes this world-system as a model for the ten billion [worlds].

Within this, there are two parts: first, the actual comparison; second, from "Furthermore, I... below, the manifestation of the inconceivable character. Within the first, there is the actual clarification followed by an interrogation and explanation.
Regarding the preceding section, the text consists of four phrases: first, "originally non-dual," because it refers to the nature of oneness;
second, "nor again is it one"—this phrase does not appear in the old translations, while the Sanskrit text reads "nor is it non-dual.

This has two meanings: first, the initial phrase negates duality, and the subsequent phrase negates unity. It does not abide in a single place, which establishes the negation of duality mentioned above; nor does it abide in many places.
Abiding. To establish the above, one is sent away; even this "one" is not truly one, for it has attained only a single portion thereof.
Second, the two preceding lines distinguish the essence: it is called "non-dual" because its nature is one, yet it is also not non-dual because it does not maintain a state of non-duality.
This is thus a negation upon negation, and an abstraction beyond abstraction. Therefore, an ancient said: "When I speak of 'non-duality'..."
It merely states that there are not two; it does not mean that existence and non-existence are two. Therefore, only when both are extinguished can the subtlety of the essence be revealed.
Thus, the aforementioned scripture says: "Always regarding all phenomena as neither dual nor non-dual;
whether phenomena are dual or non-dual, one ultimately has no attachment therein. The following two lines represent the function of the essence. In a single locus, there are many...
Because all locations are [the manifestation of] function. Thus, the aforementioned scripture says: "The one body becomes immeasurable; the immeasurable returns to being one.
Fully understanding all worlds, it manifests forms pervading everything. This is because it is the function of the very essence itself: the one is not one, and the many are not many.
Furthermore, it does not abide in a single location, for it does not destroy the many; nor does it abide in multiple locations, for it does not destroy the one. Moreover...
It does not abide in a single location, because its substance is all-pervasive. It does not abide in multiple locations, because that would contradict its nature.
Furthermore, it does not abide in a single location, because the one is itself the many. It does not abide in multiple locations, because the many are themselves the one.

Moreover, it does not abide in a single location, because within the many there is no singular nature. It does not abide in multiple locations, because within the one there is likewise no multiplicity. Thus, both [possibilities] are abandoned.
“Universally entering the merits of the Buddhas” refers to the meaning of the "wisdom-illusion" (*jñāna-māyā*) explained therein.

and so forth, she acts as the mother of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa; this meaning extends through the three periods of time. The three Buddhas of the past are Vairocana.

Whether horizontal or vertical, they are all her mothers without end. If this were so, then Māyā alone would be the mother of all Buddhas, while others would be excluded from that status.

Māyā being one is all; others being like Māyā, all are one. This is thus...

men who possess this vow also become their mothers. Thus, Māyā, upon attaining Buddhahood, is likewise the mother from whom [the Buddha] is born.
Vairocana, being endowed with the vow, is also able to give birth. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time are likewise so. This is precisely the case.
The meaning of the Flower Adornment (Avataṃsaka) giving birth to the Buddha.

First the question, then the answer. Within the answer, there are two parts: first, clarifying the original events; second, concluding by linking the past with the present. Within the first part, there are six sections. First: The Cakravartin King’s remote antiquity.
The statement that "this is not an object known by Bodhisattvas in their final birth" reveals that it is known only by the Buddha;

it shows that this is not merely a matter of great antiquity, but also that time possesses no characteristic of time, because the Buddha’s wisdom accords with reality. 2. To the lower left of that king’s city, there was a Buddha about to attain enlightenment.

"Good son, 'past' refers to the mother of all [Buddhas] throughout the entirety [of time and space]. This means that across the three periods of time and throughout the ten directions, she is the mother of the Buddhas of the present and future;

first, it refers to the past, present, and so forth in relation to the period after the arousal of the mind; second, at the very beginning of the arousal of the mind, even one's final body does not know [it], nor is there..."

Regarding the beginning of meditative concentration: thirdly, while vows have a beginning, being a mother has no beginning. Just as initial awakening (ādikṣānti) is identical to fundamental awakening (mūlajñāna), the initial and the fundamental are non-dual;
since the initial has no beginning, how much more so when kalpas and thoughts are perfectly interfused, such that raising one encompasses all?
That light is emitted from the center of the navel is because those of the same vital breath are born and grow from this very source; every Buddha thus proceeds from the principle of non-duality.
First, "Birth": because that which gives birth and that which is born are of one and the same flavor.

● Second: From "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, the second section specifically clarifies the convergence of conditions (*saṃnipāta*). There are ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), which are divided into nine sections for the purpose of their collective exposition.
First is Indraketudhvajarāja (Lord of the Banner of Indra’s Crest). He is a spiritual friend characterized by the power of mindfulness of illusory wisdom. As for "Indraketudhvajarāja":

his compassionate wisdom possesses supreme function, and its light is pure and sovereign; thus he is named "Lord" (*indra*). It is called "light" (*ketu*) because it destroys darkness. This arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*); hence [he is the son of] his father.
This is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). The dharma-gate attained is named "attainment-free pure mindfulness. The text contains six sections:
first, seeking according to the teachings; second, from "seeing those celestial maidens" downward, seeing, honoring, and inquiring.

On the third day, the goddesses announced below and bestowed upon her the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). This section has two parts: first, the designation of its name and essence; second, the inquiry and response regarding its sphere.

Now, for the first part: by means of non-apprehending wisdom (*anupalambha-jñāna*), she universally contemplates the three periods of time and the ten directions in a single thought-moment, such that there is nothing not clearly perceived.

There is no past, future, or present; it is called "pure" because it is free from discursive thought and unmixed with divergent thoughts. By means of this right mindfulness, one contemplates the merits of the Buddha, which are beneficial for compassion and wisdom;
therefore, it is called "adorned. Following the passage where Sudhana says, "He then spoke," there is a dialogue concerning the realm [of practice].

Within this, first comes the question and then the answer. In the question, there are two parts: first, the question regarding the realm, and second, the question regarding its cultivation and attainment.

Regarding the Dharma, the subsequent answers are also twofold: the first answer concerns practice, and the second answer concerns the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Within the former [the answer on practice], there are three parts:

its essential nature is quiescent and devoid of all marks (*nimitta*). Next, the three gates are categorized by time to clarify the characteristics of the "past.
That which has ceased is called the past; that which has not yet arisen is called the future; and that which has already arisen but not yet ceased is provisionally designated as the present.
They are named "present," yet their names differ; all are established based on phenomena (*dharma*). Since time has no separate substantial entity, it is said to be equal.
If one takes up the phenomena existing within time, the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide;
since none of these can be apprehended, they are all equal. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The past mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind..."
Because they are equally unapprehendable (*anupalabdha*). According to the distinctions among phenomena, even phenomena lack intrinsic nature; how then could time possess differentiation?

Next is the gate of the purity of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala-pariśuddhi*). However, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that each practice, such as the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), possesses its own three wheels, which are largely the same with minor differences.

In this context, there are two intentions. First, to establish that the three times are unattainable, which constitutes the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*). Second, to specifically clarify how this encompasses all preceding categories:
the object of knowledge is the first sphere; the mind and mental factors that know it are the second sphere; and their union is the third sphere.
Because it is far removed from the duality of the perceiver and the perceived and their combined characteristics, it is the third:

purity. The final section clarifies the gate of non-abiding. The mind’s abode does not transcend these three. If it were to abide within, it could not depend upon objects; if it were to abide without, it could not arise from the mind.

It cannot be obtained. Second, you should diligently cultivate and guard the six gates beginning with "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*); this is the provisional aspect that concerns only phenomena, which is the characteristic of skillful means (*upāya*).

"Those" refers to the fact that it also pervades the ten stages (*bhūmi*). "Characteristics" refers to the characteristics of the various obstacles present within each stage and their respective remedies;

these are the characteristics of the subject and object of observation, as they are distinguished according to the ten stages. "Attainment" refers to the correct realization of supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*).

"Fruit" refers to the attainment of mundane and supramundane wisdom through the power of having realized that wisdom. "Characteristics" here refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). Attainment...

The fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is the cause, while the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is the fruit. Because the subsequently attained wisdom takes conventional reality as its object, it is called "worldly" (*laukika*);
yet because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), it is also called "supramundane" (*lokottara*). Regarding the statement "all are realized," generally all three are termed "realization";

specifically, however, realization refers only to the fundamental wisdom, whereas "knowing" applies to both types of wisdom. As for the phrase "the wisdom of enlightenment at the stage of fruition in one gate," it is like the various natures (*dharmatā*).

Regarding "characteristics": because it awakens to all phenomena, it penetrates both the fundamental [wisdom] and the subsequently attained [wisdom], as well as the objects of knowledge to be abandoned. Furthermore, it simultaneously abandons the afflictions.
As for the "various essences and functions," the mental states associated with the four wisdoms of enlightenment and the single true *dharmadhātu* are all the essence of *bodhi*.
The enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and its land, which teach and transform sentient beings, are what are termed "function. These pervade the three realms through a single gateway.

One awakens to the inconceivable realm of the Three Vehicles because the *dharmakāya* is identical [in all]. Furthermore, the profound and inconceivable realm of the Two Vehicles is the domain of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
it is secret and difficult to fathom. Through the gate of "Four-in-One," one does not grasp at any marks, which immediately manifests *prajñā*.

This comprehensively encompasses the preceding three gates, wherein one realizes the mark of non-realization; how much more so regarding the others? Through the gate of "One-in-Five," this is the mark of *vimukti* (liberation). It is serene...
Stilled and pure, it is true liberation; it is the Vajra-samādhi, and also Vajra-wisdom. Its sharpness destroys all that cannot be crushed;
it can shatter the habitual tendencies of the dust [of afflictions]. Because it is firm and indestructible, deluded thoughts do not stir—this is precisely samādhi.

Regarding the yellow city of Kapilavastu: it serves as a model for all things through its central path. That one does not "attain" the Dharma involves, in brief, four meanings:
first, because it is identical to the dharma-gates of worldly arts; second, because the Dharma has been entrusted [to others] so that its circulation may be universal;
third, because it signifies that the essence of all dharma-gates is non-dual; and fourth, because it reveals that non-attainment is the true attainment.

the meaning is that the syllables themselves are the gateways, for by means of the syllables one enters the wisdom that is beyond syllables (*anakṣara-jñāna*). Thus, Vairocana...

Furthermore, the Mañjuśrī Five-Syllable Sūtra says: "By upholding this dhāraṇī, one enters the equality of all phenomena and swiftly achieves Mahāprajñā.
Reciting it even once is equivalent to upholding all eighty-four thousand practices."
The *Tārā-piṭaka*. However, the first five syllables are the mantra of Mañjuśrī; here they shall be explained according to the *Pañcākṣara-sūtra*.
First, "A" signifies the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). By means of the gate of non-arising, one enters Prajñā. Yet, there are two interpretations. First, non-arising itself is Prajñā.

"De" (德) is fully explained as "the power of majestic virtue" (*tejo-bala*). Because a bodhisattva attains this gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*), they are able to penetrate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and sever all obstacles.
The second syllable, "ra" (囉), signifies purity, being unstained and free from the defilement of dust.

What is now called "manifesting infinite subtle understanding" means that there is nowhere that is not understood; thus, there are no subtle defilements as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Third...

that is to say, while the higher [truth] is non-arising and free from defilements, thereby transcending the conventional to reveal the real, this very reality itself is ultimately unattainable. When both the real and the conventional are simultaneously absent, this is the true *dharmadhātu*.

All phenomena are equal, which is precisely what is meant by "universal illumination. Fourth, regarding the phrase "all phenomena have no conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra*): it means that since all conditioned formations are empty...

name-and-form is the very substance of the twelve links of existence and of saṃsāra. The four aggregates are called "name" (nāma), while the kalala and subsequent stages are "form" (rūpa).
Consciousness conditions name-and-form, and name-and-form conditions form; these two phenomena thus depend upon one another in turn, like two bundles of reeds.
The reeds turn together; therefore, the essence of birth and death does not transcend name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Name-and-form is the very locus upon which sentient beings depend.
Departing from this name-and-form, one enters Prajñā. The seventh is the syllable *Na*, through which one awakens to all phenomena as being tamed and tranquil.

This is the meaning of "universally crushing. The wheel (*cakra*) is that which crushes and subdues; the two syllables *maṇḍa* are also the wheel, and they carry the meaning of "coolness.

The eleventh syllable, *va*, is the realization that all phenomena transcend the path of speech; this refers to the perfection of principle beyond words.
It is partial. If one follows words, when one is spoken, the other two cannot be attained. By entering the wordless, there is nothing that is not spoken;
thus it universally gives birth to all things while abiding nowhere. The twelve *ḍa* syllables awaken to all dharmas because the true mind is unmoving.
When the true mind is unmoving, there is nothing it does not illumine, like the full moon and stars suspended in the sky, unmoving and serene.
The flowing light shines everywhere. The thirteenth syllable, *ca*, is because one realizes that all phenomena (*dharma*) are as they truly are—unborn;

therefore, the meaning of this universally shining radiance is precisely the capacity for subduing and sustaining. Thus, it is able to subdue.

All afflictions are eliminated. If there were something that suppressed them, one would not be able to bring them to rest and eradicate them. By realizing that the nature of delusion is empty, one can illuminate the quiescence of its essence;
only then can afflictions be ultimately extinguished. Regarding the fifteenth letter, *ka*: one awakens to all phenomena because an agent cannot be found.

yet the karma of good and evil does not perish. The sixteenth syllable, *pa*, is the awakening to the fact that the nature of all phenomena is such that time cannot be apprehended.

"Formations" (*saṃskāra*). Formations are the aggregate of grasping (*upādānaskandha*), for they are capable of grasping at birth and death. "Accumulation" (*cita*) is the very meaning of "aggregate. Regarding the term "Universal Wheel" (*samantacakra*), there are two meanings:

That which can maintain the elements is the true *dharmadhātu*. The *dharmadhātu* can sustain the entire collection of phenomena, for when one examines them with subtle discernment, not a single phenomenon exists outside of the *dharmadhātu*.
