now, it is explained that through cultivation, one attains the Dharmakāya. This text is divided into four parts, the first of which is the general [introduction].

I. Heading. II. What are the ten? This is the inquiry regarding the number. III. First, the following is the detailed explanation. IV. "If a bodhisattva... and so forth is the summary. The text is readily intelligible.
Regarding the phrase "the adamantine indestructible body": both the *dharmakāya* and the *jñānakāya* are termed the "adamantine indestructible body.
Because the essence of *dharmatā* is firm, it is indestructible; because wisdom accords with principle, it likewise is [indestructible].
It is indestructible. Because principle and wisdom are one and the same, it differs from the cognition of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇajñāna*), which is impermanent.

When essence subsumes function, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); all are indestructible. If the Dharma-body were defined solely in terms of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), then the meaning of the "waxing moon" would be inconsistent.
Thus, we know that the Dharma-body is precisely the non-obtaining body of the ten bodies. The remaining text may be understood accordingly.
[This] is understood.
△ Second, regarding the passage "Furthermore, there are ten kinds of skillful right paths" and below, it clarifies that there is no error in preaching the Dharma;

that is, the fourth intention, which is to benefit others without falsehood, while simultaneously manifesting the third [intention]: that this necessarily depends on one's own practice being non-false and non-delusory.

All the teachings expounded therein are skillfully composed; they accord with the capacities of beings and are not in vain. Within the text, there are likewise four sections—namely, the heading, the inquiry, the explanation, and the conclusion—which are all clearly evident.

Fourth, "Good son, I [only] know a little," and so forth. This is a humble acknowledgment of one's own inferiority while deferring to the excellence of others. Within this, there are two parts: first, humbly acknowledging one’s own knowledge of one thing;

second, as in the following sections, deferring to the excellence of others by acknowledging that they know much. Within this latter part, there are three sections: first, a general explanation of superior practice; second, a specific explanation of the seven purities;
and third, the conclusion establishing that [the teaching] is not in vain and that one is unable to fully describe it. Of these, the first is easily understood. Next is "abiding."
[The section on] the past concludes. Below, the seven purities (*saptaviśuddhi*) are explained individually. In the Hīnayāna, there are only seven: first, purity of precepts (*śīlaviśuddhi*);

second, purity of mind (*cittaviśuddhi*); third, purity of view (*dṛṣṭiviśuddhi*); fourth, purity by overcoming doubt (*tīrṇavicikitsāviśuddhi*); fifth, purity regarding what is and is not the path (*mārgāmārgajñānaviśuddhi*); sixth, purity of practice (*pratipadviśuddhi*); and seventh, purity through the abandonment of practice (*pratipadājñānakṣayaviśuddhi*). In the present sutra, these are expanded into ten purities;
that is, the addition of the three aspects of the Buddha-dharma across the three times constitutes the general meaning, while the following seven are the specific details.
"Purity" refers to the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time. Within the latter seven [categories], there is both opening and closing.

That is to say, "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) are combined into a single purity. Clinging exclusively to a single principle is called "view"; being stalled between two paths is termed "doubt.

Since their meanings largely overlap, they are further combined with "purity of practice" (*caryā-viśuddhi*) and "abandonment of practice" (*caryā-prahāṇa*), because those of the Hīnayāna seek only the extinction of cessation (*nirodha*). Thus, they are opened [as distinct categories].

The purity of the abandonment of conduct (*caryā-prahāṇa-viśuddhi*) exists [in the Śrāvaka vehicle], but it is not so in the Mahāyāna; therefore, these two are combined. Because there is no weariness in the cultivation of progress, the purity of the excellence of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma-adhipati-viśuddhi*) is added.

Because benefiting sentient beings is the fundamental purpose, the purity of subduing sentient beings (*sattva-vinaya-viśuddhi*) is added. Since two are combined and two are added, there are specifically seven.
At the beginning of the Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*), these ten purities exist; they correspond exactly with the current Sanskrit manuscript. Now...

The [first] seven are established as eleven when including the stage of seeing (*darśana*) and the stage of doubt (*vicikitsā*). If categorized by their stages: the first two among the seven belong to the period prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Since one has just turned away from the faults of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is appropriate to guard against them with ethical discipline (*śīla*). Furthermore, because one desires to give rise to true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*), it is logically necessary to practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*); however, at this point, one has not yet attained accord with the principle.

They are judged to belong to the mundane. The next three [fetters] exist in the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), because within the Path of Seeing one abandons the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Attachment to precepts and rituals is precisely that which is not the Path; one knows that untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) is the true Path. At the time of the Path of Seeing, all ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are absent.

The reason for mentioning specifically these three is that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of these three as being heavy. Furthermore, among the ten underlying tendencies, there are the five views (*dṛṣṭi*).
And doubt. These only obstruct the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); the remaining four [afflictions] pertain to both the Paths of Seeing and Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and thus are omitted here.

Among these six, there are three roots and three derivatives. To speak specifically of their roots, the three derivatives are as follows: the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) follows from the view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) follow from doubt (*vicikitsā*);

and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) follows from the grasping at precepts and vows (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*). Therefore, when the three roots are severed, the three derivatives are also severed; yet, only the three purities are established above.

The five purities are identical in both the Great and Small Vehicles. In the Small Vehicle, the purity of practice (*caryā-viśuddhi*) pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), because it initiates the practice of abandonment.

The purity of the abandonment of practice (*caryā-prahāṇa-viśuddhi*) pertains to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), because one relies on this practice to realize abandonment. In the Mahāyāna, the latter two are both situated in the path of cultivation;

since they involve abandoning obstacles and accomplishing virtues, these two exist there. In reality, their practice is simultaneous. However, if distinguished by stages, from the seventh stage downward, [the former] is...
The purity of the abandonment of conduct arises because one severs the fetters by cultivating the Path. From the eighth stage upward, one enters the stream of the Dharma and accords with Bodhi;

therefore, it is called the purity of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Now, these are cultivated simultaneously and horizontally, each being perfectly interfused; this is intended to demonstrate their excellence.
The subsequent statement, "one must certainly [proceed] with sincerity," concludes the section and reveals that [the author] is unable to say more.
Fifth, "Good Son" and below indicate the subsequent friend. *Sumanā* is the flower of wondrous intention (*miao-yi*), also called "pleasing intention" (*yue-yi*);
because there are many of these by the side of the city gate, it is also located in South India. One shall obtain this friend through seeking.

The "supreme and wondrous mind" refers to the various supreme and enduring qualities. The youth represents pure wisdom; since wisdom consists of all virtues, the birth of the young girl represents pure compassion.
Compassion is the root of all virtues, and as wisdom and compassion guide one another, they are thus gathered in a single assembly.

At the conclusion of the assembly of conditions, he shall behold Maitreya, for he is to succeed to the rank of Buddha. Sixth, at the section beginning "Then Sudhana," he departs after paying homage out of longing for [the Bodhisattva’s] virtue.
Ninth, at the section beginning "At that time, the youth Sudhana, in the most tranquil [place]," there appear the youths Devasena and Śrīsaṃbhava.
The maiden, through illusory wisdom, returns to an illusory spiritual friend. The text also possesses six parts:
first, seeking according to the instructions; second, from "seeing the virtues" [of the youth] downward, seeing, revering, and inquiring.
Third, regarding the section on the boys and girls below, after they have received the dharma they have attained, there are two parts: first, the designation of its name and essence;

second, the discernment of its functional activity. Now, for the first: it means that all dharmas—whether subject or object, cognition or wisdom, defiled or pure—are entirely dependent on conditions because they lack a fixed nature and abide like an illusion.
As the Treatise says: "The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty, for they arise dependently like illusions."

Following this, below the section on "attaining this liberation," the functional activity (*karmayoga*) is distinguished. This consists of three parts: first, a general explanation; second, a specific exposition; and third, a concluding eulogy.
Regarding these, the first [the general explanation] may be understood as it stands.

△ Second, "so-called below": there are ten distinct sections. In each, the upper phrase provides the heading, while the lower phrase explains the meaning of illusion through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

According to the Sanskrit original and the Jin translation, the first section concerns the world as being like an illusion; thus, among these ten statements, the first is general and the remaining nine are specific.

Since the general statement applies to all three worlds, its explanation simply states: "arising from causes and conditions. This is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and it is called [the general definition].

It is the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition), not the *hetu-pratyaya* among the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*). Following the original scripture, it is thus called the "world. Regarding the distinction of the nine phrases:
the first five refer to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) as being like an illusion; the next one refers to the container world (*bhājana-loka*) as being like an illusion;

and the final three refer to the world of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*jñāna-samyak-saṃbodhi-loka*) as being like an illusion. Within the initial world of sentient beings, the first is explained in terms of the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*). Sentient beings...
Because suffering arises from the afflictions and karma that produce its fruit. Second, it is explained in terms of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*);

for the world is like an illusion, as the world is precisely what is encountered when one contemplates the twelve links in their forward order. If one follows the Sanskrit original, the Jin translation states, "The three realms are like an illusion," which differs from the general statement.
The three realms all depend upon the twelve links of dependent origination. To explain: if someone were to ask, "Since the fruit arises from conditions, it is said to be like an illusion;

however, the cause does not arise from conditions, so it should not be like an illusion," [the answer is that] with respect to the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), both the five causes and the seven fruits are equally like illusions.
Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "For example, as a magically conjured person might further conjure another conjured person, the latter is just like the original conjured person."
This is what is called "karma. That which is created by a conjured person is called the "fruit of karma. Thus, both karma and its fruit are like illusions and transformations.
Regarding the statement "ignorance and so forth": ignorance initiates karma, and sensation (*vedanā*) is able to moisten it.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The fundamental limit of birth and death consists of two kinds: first, ignorance; second, craving for existence (*bhavarāga*). Between these two..."
Regarding birth, old age, death, and so forth, the term "successive" (展轉) briefly has two meanings. First, from afflictions and karma, one summons the five [aggregates] beginning with consciousness;

furthermore, depending upon consciousness and the others, craving, grasping, and becoming arise. This is the arising of causes based on effects, which constitutes dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);

all these lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Second, as for the twelve [links], their mutual generation in sequence—viewed from the perspective of that which is produced—is likewise devoid of self-nature.

Third, all things are like an illusion. If it were asked, "Are the two aforementioned categories of external objects also like an illusion? this is why it is stated generally that "all are like an illusion.

If one were to rely on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and exclude the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), taking only four out of the five categories of phenomena, then this would refer only to a partial "all.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed nirvāṇa, I [would likewise declare it to be like an illusion]."
It is said that all phenomena are like dreams and illusions; they arise through conditions, and nirvāṇa is manifested through conditions.

Furthermore, in order to refute the arbitrary conceptualizations of the minds of sentient beings, it is explained that "the view of self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth refers to the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) and others, which, due to beginningless evil habits, internally grasp at a self.
This is associated with the four delusions (*kleśa*). Moreover, within the six consciousnesses, one externally grasps at what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), being deluded by various false objects.
Because the mind and so forth are equal [in nature], they are said to be like an illusion. This means that if someone were to ask: "The present is like an illusion; what about the past and future?

it is therefore stated here that all three times are illusory. If even the present, which is directly before one's eyes, is entirely like an illusion, how much more so the past, which has already ceased, and the future, which has not yet arisen—how could these not be like an illusion?
Thus, they are treated as identical to the present. Furthermore, they likewise arise from the distortions of the view of self and so forth.

Regarding the first two lines, which all mention "the view of self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth: this means that with the view of self as the primary factor, it subsumes the remaining afflictions; thus, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is employed.
The fifth [line] clarifies that mental factors dissociated from thought (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), such as arising, are like illusions. This is because there might be someone who asks:

"If the substance of the characterized phenomena (*lakṣya-dharma*) arises from conditions like an illusion, then the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as arising should not be like illusions. Therefore, it is explained that arising and the others are all entirely like illusions.

This means that based on the initial arising, temporary functioning, transformation, and destruction of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth are established.

Furthermore, dharmas such as birth, aging, sickness, and death are conventionally designated upon form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Therefore, the four characteristics and the rest are all false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*);

from false conceptualization they arise, and their abiding is not unlike an illusion. According to the old sūtras, there are sentient beings who undergo birth, cessation, the birth of birth, the cessation of birth, and birth, aging, sickness, and death.

All are abodes of illusion (*māyā-vihāra*). The two terms "arising" and "ceasing" are precisely the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*); this [text] omits them here. Second, regarding the view that all lands (*kṣetra*) are abodes of illusion:
this refers to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) being like an illusion, encompassing both the defiled and the pure.

The defiled lands of sentient beings arise from the three inversions (*viparyāsa*), because they fail to realize that [all is] mind-only (*cittamātra*) and falsely grasp at objective realms. As the aforementioned Sūtra says: "All lands..."

As for the land, one merely contemplates that which is sustained by it. Since there is deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the perceptions of the mind are all inverted; these are manifestations of ignorance (*avidyā*) and thus apply even to pure lands (*śuddhakṣetra*).

For those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, ignorance is not yet exhausted, and thus the lands they perceive vary in various ways. Since it is called "ignorance," this distinguishes them from the Buddha-lands.
Regarding the latter three types of wisdom, the world of correct awakening is like an illusion, arising from the conditions of the pure portion (*śubhāṃśa*).
Because they arise from conditions, the Bodhisattva understands them to be like illusions and gives rise to great compassion. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "All phenomena are like illusions;
they are far removed from mind and consciousness. Since wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion."
△ Third, "Good son, the self-nature of illusory manifestations is inconceivable" is the concluding praise.
Regarding the term "self-nature," it encompasses both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Why is it inconceivable? First, briefly; later, extensively.

Briefly stated, it is inconceivable in its breadth with respect to phenomena (*vastu*), inconceivable in its depth with respect to principle (*tattva*), and inconceivable as being both deep and broad when considering both phenomenon and principle together.
Illusory phenomena do not exist, for their substance is unreal. Illusory phenomena are not non-existent, for their characteristics are not obliterated.

If one views illusory phenomena as being without illusion through the gate of emptiness, only then does one fully understand illusion. If one views them through the gate of existence, illusory transformations are not non-existent, for their nature and characteristics are not lost.

Thus, illusory phenomena are not identical, because their nature and characteristics differ; yet they are not distinct, because they lack two separate substances. This is the mutual interpenetration of emptiness and existence.
Thus, while both identity and difference are established, having already departed from the two extremes, one also forgets the middle way.

Because of this mutual penetration, the many can manifest within the one, and the one can manifest within the many; this layering of phenomena without obstruction is called the inconceivable. Therefore, it is said in the *Zhongjing Pusheng*: [Text omitted as per instructions]
The virtuous skillfully enter the illusory net of boundless phenomena. Regarding the detailed exposition, there are further three gateways:

first, a general clarification of illusory phenomena; second, the manifestation of existence and non-existence; third, neither identity nor difference. [○@△] Now, for the first: a single piece of cloth as an illusion forms a single person.
Briefly, there are five meanings. First, the cloth upon which [the illusion] depends, which serves as a metaphor for the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).

Second, the magician’s artifice, which serves as a metaphor for the causes that give rise [to phenomena], namely karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). Third, the illusory person manifested, which illustrates the phenomena produced by those causes.

Fourth, the fact that when a person is born they are simultaneously dead, which illustrates how the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Fifth, the ignorant and childish, who mistakenly grasp at these metaphors as being real.

Regarding the dharmas of persons: now, taking the second as the cause, one causes the realization of the third, the accomplishment of the fourth, and the elimination of the fifth affliction, thereby returning to the principle of the first.
[○@△] Second, the manifestation of existence and non-existence: among the five aforementioned meanings, each possesses both existence and non-existence.

That is to say, regarding the headcloth, its nature exists while its appearance does not, because it is concealed by the illusory person. Regarding the two arts, their function exists while their substance does not.
Because the cloth lacks intrinsic substance, the three persons (the weaver, the wearer, and the observer) exist as appearances while lacking reality;

since there is no real person, yet they appear to exist, birth is non-existence and death is existence, because there is nothing to be attained. The five sense objects exist conventionally but do not exist ultimately, being merely false perceptions.

Furthermore, within each of these five, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). The six propositions are as explained regarding the cloth. The first is "existence" in terms of conventional designation.

1. Because it is taught in terms of nature (*dharmatā*). 2. Because it is non-existent when considered in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). 3. Because it is both existent and non-existent, as both nature and characteristics are explained together. 4.

Because it is neither existent nor non-existent, as nature and characteristics mutually negate one another. Furthermore, because that which possesses the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) is the object of understanding (*jñeya-viṣaya*).

Moreover, because that which transcends the preceding five [alternatives] is the object of practice (*caryā-viṣaya*). The rest may be understood by analogy. If these various categories are interwoven with one another, they form...

The various four-line [verses], etc., may all be considered in this manner. Regarding the third point—that they are neither identical nor different—among the five pairs, they are in each case neither identical nor different, and so forth.

To clarify their being neither identical nor different by way of the third characteristic, namely that they exist substantially yet lack intrinsic reality: among the five pairs, they are in each case neither identical nor different, and so forth.
To clarify their being neither identical nor different by way of the third characteristic—that they exist substantially yet lack intrinsic reality—it is as follows: this...

Because there are two yet no duality, they are not different. Because there is also no non-duality, they are not one. Because they are neither identical nor different, they are not "neither-one-nor-different.

Because they are indeed not one, they are not "not-different. If one uses the two meanings regarding the first handkerchief to distinguish the non-identity and non-difference of the two meanings regarding the third illusory person, there are briefly ten propositions. However, as for the nature of existence, it simply abides in itself.

The meaning of "position" (*sthiti*) is as follows: "the non-existence of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇābhāva*) signifies the sense of following conditions; "the existence of characteristics" signifies the sense of differentiation;

and "the non-existence of reality" (*tattvābhāva*) signifies the sense of the emptiness of essence. Regarding the ten phrases: first, the meaning of the illusion produced upon the cloth and the meaning of the differentiation within the illusion are combined into a single limit, which is called "non-differentiation.
This is a case of the fundamental following the derivative; by means of the derivative, non-differentiation is clarified. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Dharmas..."

The body transmigrates through the five destinies; this is called a "sentient being. The Tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure, coexisting with its causes, whether arising or ceasing, and so forth.
Second, by unifying the meaning of the cloth remaining in its own position with the meaning of the illusion being empty in essence, they are made into a single limit, which is called "non-different.
This is the process of returning the derivative to the fundamental, clarifying non-difference from the perspective of the fundamental. As the Sūtra says: "All..."

Sentient beings are themselves suchness; they do not undergo further extinction, and so forth. Third, regarding the subsumption of the branches into the fundamental source from which they derive, and the subsumption of that fundamental source into the branches from which it proceeds—these two are mutually fused and inseparable. This clarifies that the fundamental and the derivative are equal and non-different.
Because the two preceding sūtras are inseparable, (4) the branches that are subsumed within the root and the root that follows along with those branches—these two mutually negate one another;

therefore, they are called "not different. This is the simultaneous dissolution of both root and branch, clarifying their non-difference, because in the equality of the real and the false, difference cannot be found. Next, the four gates below have the meaning of "not one," namely, five...
The meaning of the handkerchief abiding in its own position refers to the principle of the arising of the differentiated characteristics upon the illusion.

These two—the fundamental and the derivative—are contradictory and opposed; therefore, they are called "not one. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgatagarbha does not reside within the ālayavijñāna.
Therefore, while the seven consciousnesses undergo birth and cessation, the Tathāgatagarbha is neither born nor ceases. This is what is meant. [This concludes] the section on the six handkerchiefs.
The meaning of "illusion" and the meaning of "the essence of illusion being empty" are, in these two cases, respectively the root and the branch;

they are diametrically opposed and mutually exclusive, and therefore are not one. The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "The seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate, do not experience suffering or pleasure, and are not the cause of nirvāṇa;

only the Tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering, pleasure, and so forth. Because the former [meaning] opposes the initial [point] and the latter excludes the subsequent, these two meanings are distinct; hence, it is called [a distinction].
They are not one. This means that when they are opposed, each turns its back on the other; they are separated by a vast distance, like two people facing away from each other toward the east and west.
When they harm one another, they devour each other, like two wild beasts mutually grappling and biting.

They are not one because they are proximate, as the preceding scriptural passage does not describe them as being intermingled. Eighthly, because they are extremely contradictory and harmful, both vanish yet do not vanish.
It is utterly contrary [to conventional perception]. Both existing and yet not existing; neither non-existent nor extinguished—the meaning is not singular.
This refers to the non-identity of formation and destruction. Because the seven consciousnesses are empty yet existent; because True Suchness (Tathatā) is hidden yet manifest.
Regarding the nine superior states and the four non-identities, they are neither identical nor different, yet they are also not one, because their meanings do not intermingle. Ten.
However, it is not that different principles apply universally, for phenomena are non-dual. If one takes various aspects through the perspective of non-difference, they are perfectly harmonized;
if one takes various aspects through the perspective of non-identity, they appear extremely contradictory, yet this very contradiction is what constitutes the unobstructed attainment of phenomena.
Just as it is with the mutual relation between a cloth and an illusion, so too do techniques and their counterparts interlace to form a complete expression; this should be understood accordingly.

Contemplate this: all [phenomena] proceed through the gateway of illusion and possess manifold distinctions; thus, they are difficult to conceive. It is not merely that the phenomena are numerous, but also that the principles are profound.
Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom them; therefore, it is said that all Buddhas are great illusionists.
Fourth, "The two of us below" [indicates] humbling oneself and deferring to the superior; this first section on the "virtuous son who has escaped" exists in all three sūtras.
Fifth, "At that time, the youth Guṇākara below" [indicates] pointing out the subsequent friend; herein there are two parts: first, the secret empowerment through power.

Below the passage "Afterwards, he addressed Sudhana," it is revealed through these words. This section has three parts: first, indicating the location; second, pointing out the person; and third, instructing on how to inquire.

Regarding the first [part], there are also three sub-sections: first, citing the result; second, showing the cause; and third, the purpose. Now, for the first [sub-section]: "The country is named Pṛthuṣṭhala (Vast Field).
This is because a Bodhisattva in his final birth is the excellent field of merit for all sentient beings. "Near the gateway to the ocean" means:

Because it is most intimate as one is about to enter the ocean of wisdom, the garden is named "Great Adornment" (*Mahāvyūha*); this is because the causes—the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*)—perfectly adorn the fruit.
Furthermore, it is because the grove of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), with its forest of the myriad practices, adorns one's own fruit.
Regarding the phrase "within which there is a vast multi-storied pavilion," etc.: in terms of phenomena, its interior is expansive, being equal to empty space; thus, it possesses manifold radiances.
It is "luminous" because it can universally illumine all. It is "adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels" because it encompasses both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).

As for the "many-storied pavilions," in terms of the Dharma, the two wisdoms (*jñāna*) are mutually dependent and the conditions of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are interrelated; thus they are called "pavilions. Wisdom itself is the *dharmadhātu*.

This is what is meant by "vast and great," named Vairocana and so forth, which accords with and fulfills the aforementioned meaning. Because the radiance of the two wisdoms universally illuminates both phenomena and principle, wisdom encompasses all virtues;

this is the "Treasury of Adornments. Since the myriad practices of the *Avataṃsaka* do not depart from this, the following section—from "the various roots of goodness of the Bodhisattvas" downward—reveals the cause.
These roots of goodness and their retributive fruits refer to his past causes; they are those very roots of goodness.

Because of the retribution of those [past] fruits, through the power of mindfulness and vows, and with respect to their present conditions— thereafter, when a son of good family abides in non-conceptual cognition,
it is based on what is currently being performed.

first, the touching of the crown to reveal the realm of the universal Dharma (*dharmadhātu*) by consecrating his head; second, the passage beginning with "Sudhana immediately obtained... which clarifies the attainment of the benefit.
Observing outwardly, one attains Prajñāpāramitā (the Perfection of Wisdom). Receiving the touch of the crown of the head as an internal realization, one attains Samādhi.

Within these ten phrases, the first establishes mastery over meditative concentration (samādhi), the second gathers its retinue, and the remainder distinguishes the functions of concentration. At the end, the passage beginning with "In this Sahā world" concludes by generalizing the application [of the teaching].
This is truly because Sudhana and others universally perfected the practice of Samantabhadra;

thus, they benefited at every stage. [○@△] Third, from "At that time, Samantabhadra... onwards, it clarifies that because the cause is profound and vast, the fruit is manifest as supreme. This section has three parts: first, the inquiry and response regarding the vision;
second, the formal manifestation of the characteristics of the cause; third, the conclusion of the cause and the attainment of the fruit. Now, for the first: this refers to the aforementioned fruit.
The causes belonging to the subordinate [section]. Second, from "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" downwards, the characteristics of the cause are correctly revealed.

This is divided into three parts: first, a general explanation of the practice for seeking bodhi; because giving (*dāna*) is the foremost of practices, it is explained in detail. Second, from "Good son, I... downwards.

To be free from faults and to accomplish virtuous conduct refers to the remaining nine perfections (*pāramitās*). Having previously and explicitly taught the first five, the first of these is ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Not giving rise to anger or malice is patience (*kṣānti*). Never for even a single moment departing from the bodhicitta is diligence (*vīrya*). A mind that attains freedom from hindrances is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Not giving rise to delusion is wisdom (*prajñā*).
These alone abide in the lower [stages], and thus the latter four are revealed in accordance with this. "O sons of good family, I..."
Below "Universally Adorned and Purified," there is a general clarification of the practices of compassion and wisdom, briefly citing four types of practice. The text is divided into four parts:

first, the actual citation of the four practices—namely, (1) the practice of adorning the buddha-lands, (2) the practice of gathering in sentient beings, (3) the practice of serving spiritual friends, and (4) the practice of seeking the Dharma;

second, from "Good son, within the ocean of my Dharma" onwards, which serves as a counter-illustration of the profound earnestness with which one seeks the Dharma, showing that not even a single word or phrase is ever abandoned.
How much more so for the whole? For a single phrase is identical to all others, just as a single drop of water from the ocean [is identical to the ocean].

From "O sons of good family, the Dharma I seek... below, this explains the pursuit of the Dharma in accordance with the principle; that is to say, it fulfills the aforementioned adornment of the lands and the gathering of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the former also extensively encompasses skillful means, vows, and wisdom. From "I, in this way... below, the third section concludes the inexhaustibility. Therefore...
"Good son, 'I [attain] such as this' refers to the formation of the fruit through causes. Within this, first are the causes, which consist of eleven phrases;

because there is the efficacy of producing the fruit, they are called 'powers,' and they also manifest the power of mastery (*balapāramitā*). Subsequently, based on these [causes], the following clarifies the attainment of the fruit."

[○@△] Fourth, "Good son, you see this body of mine" and so forth. The application of contemplation here is boundless. This section has three parts: first, citing the benefits to encourage contemplation;
second, observing and seeing its extraordinariness; third, comparing it to manifest its superiority. Within the first part, there are three sub-sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation;
third, the conclusion. The initial heading is clear. Second, from "Good son, this wondrous body of mine" onwards is the explanation, which refers to the profundity of the cause.
Because it is difficult to see. Within this, there are three parts: first, the section on the difficulty of seeing in accordance with illumination;

second, the section beginning with "Good son, if there are sentient beings who have not yet planted [roots]" which reveals the difficulty of seeing; and third, the section beginning with "Good son, if there are sentient beings who hear my name."
This clarifies the benefits of seeing and hearing [the Dharma]. Within this, there are four points: first, the benefit of non-retrogression;

second, the benefit of maturation for some sentient beings within a single day and night. Because faculties may be sharp or dull and hindrances may be shallow or deep, the speed [of progress] differs.
3. "Good sons, by means of such [teachings] as these," and so forth, [the text] concludes with multiple approaches. 4.
Furthermore, from "Good sons" onwards, it reveals the distant fruit, namely, that one can be born in a pure land within a birth-body (*janma-kāya*). How is this body born? There are two meanings:
first, regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), when it serves as the essence of the land, it is called a "pure land"; when it serves as the essence of the body, it is called "purity."

First, regarding the body (*kāya*): although there is a distinction between the supported and the support, their essential substance (*tattva*) is one. To manifest this unity of substance, it is called the "birth-body" (*janmakāya*).
Second, regarding characteristics and functions: "land" (*kṣetra*) refers to the land upon which the body relies; "body" (*kāya*) refers to the land within the body.

This is intended to show that the fundamental nature of the body and the land is mutually integrated. Third, from "Good son, you should observe... onwards is the summary exhortation to observe. Second, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards...
He beholds what is marvelous. Within this, there are three parts: first, he sees the three worlds contained within a single hair;

second, he further sees Samantabhadra Bodhisattva beneath each and every world, seeing the pervasive great activities of Samantabhadra’s body throughout the lands—these lands being precisely the lands within the hair;
third, at the point where Sudhana descends, Sudhana himself sees that his own manifestations are equal to those of Samantabhadra. Third, the excellence [of the teaching].
Below the section on what Sudhana saw, there is a comparative evaluation that reveals his excellence. This consists of three parts: first, a comparison of his roots of goodness;

second, from the beginning down to Sudhana, a comparison of his entry into the lands (*kṣetra*); and third, from Sudhana down to Samantabhadra, a general revelation of the characteristics of his transcendence over all other gateways.
Within this last part, there are two sections: first, a specific clarification of its horizontal and vertical depth and breadth; second, a general manifestation [of these qualities].

Equal and all-pervading. First, there are ten oceans in total. The text is divided into four parts: the first three provide specific explanations, while the latter seven conclude by applying these examples.
First, the explanation of the *kṣetra-samudra* (ocean of lands). 1. "A single step transcends" reveals its horizontal vastness. 2. "Exhausting the kalpas of the future" reveals its vertical length.
3. "Yet one cannot know it" reveals its profound depth. 4. "Treasury" (*kośa*) refers to its capacity for inclusion; "ocean" (*samudra*) refers to its depth and breadth. Second, likewise...

1. They cannot know [the Buddha’s ocean] below; this clarifies the ocean of the Buddhas. 2. Furthermore, they cannot know [the Bodhisattvas’ ocean] below; this clarifies the ocean of the Bodhisattvas. 3.
Furthermore, they cannot know [the entry into] the realm of sentient beings below; this concludes the analogy for the seven oceans: First, the ocean of the realm of sentient beings;

Second, the ocean of the faculties of sentient beings; Third, the ocean of teaching and taming; Fourth, the ocean of the wisdom of awakening and accomplishment; Fifth, the ocean of supernormal powers...

6. The ocean of all stages (*bhūmi*). 7. The ocean of all paths. Thus, below, the summary concludes with the statement that they are "inconceivable," because the qualities of the *dharmadhātu* are unobstructed and inexhaustible.
Second, beneath a pore of Samantabhadra, Sudhana summarizes their equality and pervasiveness.
Regarding "immovability": it means not going from here to there, nor from there to here; it does not emerge.
This is because they do not perish in this realm to emerge in that realm, nor do they perish in that realm to emerge in this realm;

for they are omnipresent while remaining unmoving, and they are still while appearing to move. Their emergence and disappearance are identical in nature; this and that are mutually identical; this and that are mutually contained; this and that are brilliantly complete;
and their secret concealment and manifest appearance are simultaneously accomplished. Thus, the Indra’s Net of infinite interpenetration is everywhere present.
Because it is immovable.
△ Second, from "At that time" onwards, it clarifies the completion of the stage and the attainment of Buddhahood. The text contains ten phrases:

the first is general, the next eight are specific, and the final phrase is the conclusion. This corresponds in meaning to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Because it is Equal Enlightenment, the causal stage having already... [text continues].

It is fulfilled; there is nothing further to be cultivated. Therefore, it is simply called "equality" (*samatā*), for one no longer seeks anything further. This constitutes the sudden perfection of cause and effect within a single lifetime; even the sequential practice (*xingbu*) is sufficient.
It is not merely a contemplation of principle (*li-guan*); from beginning to end, all is perfectly interfused. The above concludes the section on seeing, hearing, and direct realization.

Fourth, from the passage "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" onwards: having heard of the inconceivable supreme virtues of the Buddha, the preceding prose section had merely manifested the perfection of the causes, whereas these verses now set forth the function of the fruition;
they do not, however, serve as a mere verse-by-verse commentary on the preceding text. Nevertheless, there are two intentions [for their inclusion]: first, in relation to Samantabhadra.
The meaning is this: "To see me is difficult to conceive," yet I am still at the stage of cause; now, your fruition is even more profound. Second, in contrast to Sudhana:

while Sudhana and others are equal to the Buddha, they represent only the perfection of the cause; it is the aspect of the fruition that should be revealed. Since the ocean of fruition transcends words, it cannot be described.
Now, as the principle has manifested, the Buddha reveals his fruition in contrast to the cause, thereby manifesting the ultimate aspect of Sudhana’s fruition. Therefore...

The verse and its prose commentary alternate between cause and effect. The text is divided into three parts: first, the verse indicates the virtues, exhorts the audience to listen, and grants permission to speak;

second, from "At that time, all the Bodhisattvas... onwards in the prose, the assembly is shown to be thirsting for and desiring to hear [the teaching]; third, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva...
onwards, the characteristics of virtue are extensively set forth to lead the assembly to seek fulfillment. Within this, there are two further divisions; first, the prose repeats...

The instruction permitting the explanation of the limits [of what can be taught] has two intended meanings. First, that which I have explained is like a single drop, whereas that which remains unexplained is like the great ocean.
Second, that which can be conveyed through words is like a single drop, whereas that which cannot be expressed is like the great ocean.
It is like the great ocean. From the line "The subsequent Buddha-wisdom is vast" (*paścād buddhajñānaṃ vipulaṃ*) onwards, the verses themselves are correctly revealed.

There are ninety-five verses, which are broadly divided into two parts: first, ninety-three verses separately praise the Buddha’s virtues; finally, the last two verses conclude that these virtues are inexhaustible.

Exhort you to have faith and not to doubt. △ Within the preceding section: the first eighty verses explain the Dharma through direct teaching (*dharmadeśanā*), while the final thirteen verses clarify it through parables (*dṛṣṭānta*).
These collectively praise the twenty-one kinds of supreme merits of the ten bodies of Vairocana in their perfection.

Although the *Lokottara-parivarta* (Chapter on Transcending the World) contains only the names [of these merits], their meanings appear in several places throughout the great treatise (*Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*). They are explained extensively in the various *Saṃgraha-śāstras*.
Regarding its characteristics: for now, all are first designated by names based on their transcendence of the world, and subsequently established as titles of merit based on non-attachment.

Dividing the text according to its phrasing, there are two parts: the first verse clarifies the general statement, while the remainder clarifies the specific statements. First, regarding the initial part: this refers to the "wondrous realization being entirely fulfilled."
This refers to the wisdom of all Buddhas. It is because they have perfectly and universally awakened to all conditioned and unconditioned objects that ought to be realized;

it is pure, wondrous, complete, and correctly awakened. In this text, the general characteristics of the Buddha’s wisdom are described: "vast" means its essence is all-pervasive; "identical to space" is a common metaphor.
Space has many meanings, but briefly there are four below. "Pervading the minds of all sentient beings" explains its vastness.

The characteristic [of the Buddha-nature] is that the essence of the minds of sentient beings is free from thought and equal to space; because it is non-dual in essence with all Tathāgatas, it has the meaning of being pervasive as emptiness.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "For example, the great ocean flows secretly beneath the lands of the four continents;
there is no one who digs and does not find water. The Buddha-wisdom is likewise: it enters universally into the hearts of all sentient beings. There is no practitioner who..."

One cannot realize it. For one who has thoroughly understood worldly delusions, that which perceives all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as being entirely non-existent is itself the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is because, in accordance with ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), one awakens to all dharmas; just as space is without attainment or non-attainment, this understanding is thorough. This fourth phrase is the characteristic of awakening:
it does not give rise to discrimination, and being free from both the subject of awakening and the object of awakening, it is called "wondrous awakening" (*miao-jue*). Awakening is...
"Awakening. This phrase reveals the meaning of being like space—mindless and without support. Thus, the aforementioned sutra states: "The Buddha’s wisdom has no place of support;
it is like space, which has nothing upon which to rely. [○@△] The remaining ninety-two verses separately reveal twenty-one virtues, arranged into nineteen sections, as the final three are combined.

The first verse clarifies that the two types of activity are eternally severed; that is, regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), there is the attainment of the merit of unimpeded transformation.
The Buddha’s unobstructed wisdom is characterized by non-attachment and non-obstruction regarding all things, their categories, and their specific distinctions.

This is not like that of the *śrāvakas*, for whom there is said to be obstruction regarding extremely distant times and places—thus it is called "unilaterally unobstructed. This is the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) that is free from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because it is complete. In the text, the first half explains the Dharma; "knowing in a single thought" reveals the excellence of that knowledge. The second half illustrates this through a simile.

There is one verse which clarifies the realization of the signless Dharma: that within existence and non-existence there are no two distinct marks. True Suchness (*tathatā*) is supremely pure, and this refers to the merit of being able to enter [it].
That is to say, one realizes and enters True Suchness, which fundamentally lacks two marks, and furthermore enables others to realize it as well. This is...
The virtue of abandonment is *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvana). In the text, the first three lines indicate non-abiding in nirvana, while the fourth line indicates non-abiding in saṃsāra.
The three verses on the three realms clarify the merit of abiding in the Buddha-abode, wherein the Buddha-activities are performed effortlessly and without cessation.

This means that by abiding in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), one is able to accomplish the Buddha-work without effort. Therefore, the text says:
"Some see [the Buddha] and so forth"; this is precisely his grace and virtue.
Fourth, the fifteen verses beginning with "Or seeing purity" clarify the attainment of the equality of the Buddha;
that is, the merit of non-differentiation regarding the basis, intention, and activity within the dharmakāya. This means that the aforementioned buddha-activities are both common and uncommon.
Next, it is explained that all these Buddhas dwell together in mutual interpenetration. Therefore, the sutra text extensively enumerates the Buddhas, all of whom pervade one another.
The reason they mutually pervade is that there is no distinction among the three aspects of the Buddhas.

What are these three? First, the identity of the supporting wisdom; second, the identity of the altruistic intention (*āśaya*); and third, the identity of the activities of the emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Because of these, they mutually pervade one another.
This is also consistent with the "equal intention" (*samatābhiprāya*) taught in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Relying on this to interpret the sūtras constitutes a correct application.
Furthermore, based on the principles of the text, it is proven that all these Buddhas are the body of Vairocana. That is to say, this passage states: "This trichiliocosm..."
The world: Akṣobhya is therein. Although the Tathāgata Akṣobhya originally resided in the eastern direction, his being said to be "here" now clarifies that he is not different from this [world].
Furthermore, since the Tathāgatas such as Amitāyus and Candrabuddhi pervade the ten directions, how could they be separated by this [world]?

Moreover, since it is said in all cases that "some see him," we know that a single Buddha appears differently according to the perceptions of those who behold him. If one were to say that this passage separately praises other Buddhas, [it would be] simply...
To say that Akṣobhya is in this world-system—what is meant by "praising his virtues"? It is actually praising Śākyamuni that one speaks of "Akṣobhya. How could such wording be considered sequential?
Moreover, the Flower Treasury ocean of lands is entirely the realm of Vairocana; as for Amitāyus Buddha being "one hundred thousand [lands] away," and so forth.

They did not emerge from within the *kṣetra-vyuha* (world-system). Within a single layer [of the world], is it not the case that the Original Teacher (*mūla-śāstṛ*) manifests diverse transformations according to names?

Since both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* speak of the original teachers and their emanations throughout the ten directions, we know that the teaching of the *Dharmakara-pūrva-yoga* regarding the sixteen princes was all taught as a skillful means (*upāya*).
The "trace gate" (*jia-men*) of the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of the sixteen princes, while the "life-span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) chapter speaks of the original [teacher].
The gates have all already been swept clear. Therefore, by reasoning through the principle, one sees that everything is the vivid manifestation of Vairocana’s Ocean Seal.

For what reason do you not say that the Buddhas are those manifested by yourself, rather than saying they are others? Thus we know that Buddhas such as Bhadraśrī and Akṣobhya are all the Original Teacher.
This is the unique, profound meaning of the *Avataṃsaka*; be careful not to treat it with levity. The text has three parts; first, the eight primary figures and their attendants.

The first three [aspects] are identical in terms of purifying the buddha-fields and gathering in sentient beings. Next, the four [aspects] are identical in their subtle inclusion and the turning of the Dharma.

The final three generally manifest many gates, concluding the preceding and generating the subsequent. These three sections are all identical in their performance of deeds; they are all for the sake of sentient beings, which constitutes the identical intention (*āśaya*);
and they all rely upon Buddha-wisdom, which constitutes the identical basis (*āśraya*). If explained from a general perspective, the first is the performance of deeds, while the next...

This is the aspiration; the latter is the basis. This preceding section also reveals the seventeenth merit: the quality of manifesting Buddha-fields according to the differences in their respective resolute convictions (*adhimukti*).

The five verses beginning with "Or seeing Śākyamuni" (the last three verses) clarify reaching the state of non-obstruction, which is the cultivation of all meritorious qualities that serve as antidotes to obstacles.

According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, the first four [verses] are merits for one's own benefit (*svārtha*), while from this point onward they are all merits for the benefit of others (*parārtha*).

Within the benefit of others, the transformation and treatment [of sentient beings] are clarified first; therefore, they are explained next. This refers to having already mastered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through habitual practice.
[The attainment of] the [Buddha-]nature and omniscience serves as the antidote to the afflictive obstructions and the cognitive obstructions.

By means of this, one eternally severs all bases and locations for habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Within the text: the first half-verse, or rather the vision of its long-term accomplishment, indicates that all habitual tendencies have already been eternally severed;
the subsequent half-verse reveals the benefit of others; the next verse cultivates the path that acts as the antidote; and the final verse distinguishes...

One remedies the obscurations by means of the ten perfections. Since it was stated above that one may see [the Buddha] as having already attained perfect enlightenment for a long time, he is certainly not newly enlightened.

Whether appearing newly enlightened or having been enlightened for a long time, these are all transformations according to the needs of sentient beings; the true Buddha cannot be described in terms of being "long-standing" or "newly arisen."
The six [verses] consist of three stanzas that clarify the unshakeable nature of the Dharma; this is the merit of subduing all non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

That is to say, the two paths—teaching and realization—are not turned aside by others, and thus they are able to subdue others. Within the text, the first two [stanzas] refer to these two paths: teaching and realization.
The latter one refers to the body of the same class that is currently being destroyed.
Verses sixteen through twenty-two clarify the non-attachment (*anupalambha*) in practice:
even when born into the world, one is not attached by worldly dharmas; because the mind is without high or low, the eight winds of the world are unable to cause attachment.

The text is divided into six sections. First, three verses [show that the Buddha] does not attain [anything] when manifesting in the world in eight aspects, because even the palace ladies and attendants do not attain [anything].
Second, there is one verse on the non-attainment by both self and others, because Amitābha’s prophecy is that of Śākyamuni himself.

Third, there is one verse on the non-attainment regarding cessation and formation. Fourth, there are three verses on the non-attainment in the celestial palaces. Fifth, there are six verses on conforming to the world.
The skillful transformation of the interim is without attainment. There are two verses in the sixth [section], which summarize that non-attainment wisdom can universally adapt to capacities.

The first phrase indicates that the essence of wisdom is non-dual and without attainment; the second phrase refers to sudden realization. The following two phrases concern the characteristics of the phenomena realized, briefly indicating four contemplations:

first, the contemplation of mind-only; second, the contemplation of causes and conditions; third, the contemplation of impermanence; and fourth, the contemplation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. These are the four contemplations.

The "Linked Verses" (*Lianhuan*) conclude that once worldly phenomena are understood, only the emptiness of the mind-nature remains; how could there be high or low such that anything could be attained?
The subsequent verse briefly illustrates the wondrous nature of universal conformity, for within the single and the many, one enters immediately into the ungraspable transformation.
The eighteen verses following "The Eight Tathāgatas Abide" clarify the establishment of the inconceivable, which is the formal establishment of the merits of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
The twelvefold division of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) is what is established; because it is profound and vast, it is inconceivable. Within the text:
The first fourteen verses explain what has been established; the latter four verses reveal the inconceivable. Within the former [section], there are three parts.
First, the initial three verses establish all phenomena in general. Second, the two subsequent verses demonstrate the established principles.

Third, the nine following verses specifically establish the four bodhisattva practices. Now, regarding the first part: the first one and a half verses establish the Dharma shared with the Two Vehicles, while the final one and a half verses establish...
Regarding the *asādhāraṇa-dharmas* (unshared qualities): the first half of the verse concerns the establishment of merit, namely the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

The latter verse establishes the nature of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), which is the dharma that cannot be grasped. "Selflessness" refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); "signlessness" refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

The non-arising of the nature of karma is due to these two types of emptiness; because it arises from conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature and does not arise. Furthermore, there is no loss, for karma is not destroyed.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "There is no self, no agent, and no experiencer; yet the karma of good and evil does not perish.
The *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states: "Though empty, it is not annihilated; though existent, it is not eternal; the retribution of results is never lost—this is called the teaching of the Buddha.
As for the statement that "all is utterly transcended," this also merges emptiness and existence, such that the traces of the Middle Way are cut off, and thus it is like space.
This mark of quiescence is ineffable; the subsequent line employs the power of skillful means to provisionally express it through speech.

There are two verses that demonstrate the establishment of peaceful virtues, which correspond to the three wheels of the Buddha. The former verse represents the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*).

Regarding the latter two lines, because the speech and mind employ a vast sound without moving from mindfulness, they are called "vast"; this means it pervades the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, Maudgalyāyana—
Investigating its limits, there are nine verses in total. These are separately established as four types of bodhisattva practice, which are thus divided into four parts:

the first verse concerns the practice of the *pāramitās*; the next half-verse concerns the practice of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); the third half-verse clarifies the practice of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

and the final seven verses concern the practice of maturing sentient beings. Within this last section, there are two divisions; the first verse generally manifests how a single voice accords with the various classes of beings.

The latter six sections specifically clarify the differences in what is heard. This is the first [section]. The first half concerns that which is followed, and the second half concerns that which follows.

Regarding the term "one sound" (*ekasvara*), it is also called the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*). As explained at length in the "Chapter on the Manifestation [of the Buddha]" (*Samantamukha-parivarta*), I shall now provide a brief explanation. That is to say, by means of a single Brahma-sound (*brahmasvara*).

Pervading all places, it enables each listener to hear it differently; this is called "one voice" (*ekasvara*). Within a single Brahma-voice, it fully possesses the sounds of all categories of beings;
therefore, it is named the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*). It is like the celestial maiden Sādhu-vaktrā. Thus, the aforementioned sutra says:
"The linguistic dharmas of all sentient beings are completely and exhaustively expounded in a single word. Furthermore, it is the "one sound according to type" (*yathā-jāti-ekasvara*).
To preach a single Dharma that pervades all places, yet for each to hear it according to their own faculties—whether great or small—is called the "Single Sound" (*ekasvara*).
To fully expound everything through the sound of a single category is called the "Perfect Sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*). Thus, the aforementioned sutra says:
"Within a single utterance, the Tathāgata expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras. Furthermore, because all is one, it is called the "Single Sound. One...
Thus, all names are called the "Perfect Sound. As the aforementioned sutra says: "The Buddha, with a single wondrous voice, is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions;
all voices are fully contained within it, and the rain of Dharma pervades everywhere. It encompasses the ocean of all speech and all sounds according to the various classes of beings."

Throughout all lands, one constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel. Furthermore, through various kinds of sounds, it pervades the entire dharma-realm and universally accords with all phenomena, whether material or non-material;
therefore, it is called "the single sound" (*ekasvara*). Because it does not lose its melodic cadence while manifesting various dharma-gates, it is called the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*).

These two aspects are mutually constitutive: if it were pervasive yet lost its cadence, it would be perfect but not sound; if it had cadence but was not pervasive, [it would be sound but not perfect].

This sound is not "round" (perfect). Only when it is pervasive and without omission can it be called the "round sound. It is also called the "single sound" because it causes all to understand according to their respective capacities.
"Capacities" refers to the distinctions of superior and inferior—such as those of the three vehicles, the five vehicles, and the immeasurable vehicles—since each hears differently.

"According with" refers to the myriad classes [of beings], for even those such as nāgas and devas understand according to their respective types. Second, regarding the six verses beginning with "Some have desire," there are differences in what they hear;
therein are three parts: first, in the initial verse, they hear the gate of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*); second, in the subsequent verse, they hear the gate of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
The ten points of training (*śikṣāpada*) refer to the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) and the five grave offenses (*pañcānantarya*).

whether internal or external, all are of one identical true mark. Eighth is the prostration of great compassion: with each individual prostration, one universally takes upon oneself the suffering of all sentient beings.

Practice is of two kinds: first, the phenomenal (dharma), and second, the principle (li). The phenomenal is as described in the Vaipulya *Buddhanāma-sūtra* and other texts, which encompasses the myriad practices.

The principle is as described in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, where one contemplates that the nature of offenses is empty and resides neither within nor without; this is also found in the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-caryā-darśana-sūtra* and the "Anuvyañjana-parivarta."

The two types of repentance are complete. In the *Contemplation Sūtra*, it is clarified that diligently paying homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions day and night constitutes ritual repentance (*śīla-pratikramaṇa*).

To contemplate the mind as being without mind, arising from inverted thoughts, and if one wishes to repent, to sit upright and contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)—this is the repentance of principle (*tattva-pratikramaṇa*).

In the "Chapter on the Marks and Subtle Features" (*Anuvyañjana-parivarta*), it says to equalize the realm of sentient beings and repent for and eliminate all obstacles of body, speech, and mind; this is...

Within the "Chapter on the Secondary Marks" (Anuvyañjana-parivarta), the remedies are fully present; in the current text, they are contained though not explicitly complete. The text is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of what is to be repented;

The arousal of body, speech, and mind constitutes the instruments for creating karma. Regarding the three types of action (trikarma) and ten branches (daśāṅga), those which produce various evils through the three poisons (triviṣa) constitute the essence of karma (karmasvabhāva).

The *zhǐchàn* (Solemn Repentance) means to stand with hands joined and kneel respectfully, verbally reciting the words and phrases. The section beginning with "Pervading the Dharma-realm" clarifies the objects toward which one faces.

Regarding "pervading the Dharma-realm," there are briefly two meanings: first, because the objects and mental states of the sins committed in the past were widespread, the present repentance must likewise be universal;
second, because it accords with the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), what sin would not be eliminated? The section beginning with "All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas" is the proper...
To distinguish what is countered: one should recollect the Buddhas of the ten directions. To "turn away from former evil friends" means to repent with a sincere heart;

this excludes insincere practice, for if one is lax and indulges the mind, transgressions will not be extinguished. "Repenting" includes self-reproach, self-rebuke, and the dread of the evil realms, as well as not concealing one's flaws.
"Not creating them again" refers to severing the continuous stream of the mind and abiding securely in the pure precepts. One.
"All merits" refers to cultivating merit to compensate for transgressions; were it not for this, how could one move mountains or fill up ravines?

This general confession is undertaken because of a clear understanding that cause and effect, as well as good and evil, exert a reciprocal influence. It is also the means by which the True Dharma is protected. From "Third, thus...
