Fifth, next is the clarification of the practice of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). First, regarding the designation of its name:

because one previously did not rejoice in the virtues of others, one now practices sympathetic joy to celebrate and gladden them, thereby removing the obstacle of envy and giving rise to impartial goodness. However, in other contexts, sympathetic joy follows after the request for the turning of the wheel (*adhyeṣaṇā*);
that is, first one purifies the vessel of the body, next one rejoices in the rain of Dharma, and finally one gathers others to be like oneself, dedicating [the merit] toward the three [refuges].

Therefore, this sequence is established. Now, it is clarified that rejoicing (*anumodanā*) is a specific category within the practice of repentance (*pāpadeśanā*). Because their respective scopes and functions differ, it is explained first.
"Equally equal, vast and great, one is fit to hear the Dharma" introduces the subject. The phrase "Second, all that exists throughout the Dharma-realm" and below explains its characteristics;
that is, rejoicing in four categories to encompass all virtues: first, rejoicing in the virtues of the Tathāgatas; second, and those of the ten directions... [text continues].
Below [the stage of] rejoicing in the goodness of the six destinies and four modes of birth throughout the ten directions and three times; below that, rejoicing in the goodness of the two vehicles;

and below that, rejoicing in the goodness of all Bodhisattvas. The Buddha is the most supreme, which is why he is explained first. As for the remaining three categories, they proceed from the inferior toward the superior.
In the *Sūtra of the Great Perfection of Wisdom*, the "Chapter on Rejoicing" explains how the waters of the great trichiliocosm ocean are divided by a single hair split into a hundred [parts].
One might divide the waters of the great ocean into drops and know their number, but the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) cannot be known;

therefore, it is inexhaustible and equal to the realm of empty space. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, even the merit of sympathetic joy extending through successive transmission to the fiftieth person is difficult to calculate, let alone that of the very first.
This is because one rejoices in the provisional and ultimate merits of the Tathāgata; thus, the Buddha is supreme. (3)
Thus, the following concludes the inexhaustible [practice].

The sixth section further clarifies the practice of requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. First, as for the title, it refers to "Exhortation," which removes the obstacle of slandering the Dharma and gives rise to the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion.
While Śrāvakas seek only their own liberation and merely perform repentance, Bodhisattvas take pity on sentient beings; therefore, they must [perform this exhortation].

Exhortation. First, the request that the Buddha may rain down [teachings] universally, so that one will surely be thoroughly moistened. Second, the explanation of the characteristics of what is possessed, which has two parts:
first, citing the object of the request; second, from "And I... onwards, clearly explaining the method of requesting. Third, from "In this way... onwards, summarizing its inexhaustibility.
The seventh section, the practice of requesting the Buddha to remain in the world, consists of three parts: first, the designation of the title, which refers specifically to the act of exhortation;

second, the explanation of its characteristics, where the initial statement—“all those who,” etc.—speaks from the perspective of the most eminent case, namely requesting only the Tathāgata, while the subsequent explanation follows the general sense, wherein all three vehicles (triyāna) are included in the request;
third, the concluding summary of its inexhaustibility, beginning with “in this way,” etc.
Eighth, furthermore, "Constantly Following and Learning from the Buddha. The following three sections are all dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). The first two are specific aspects within dedication;
therefore, at the end of the seventh line of the subsequent verses, "dedication" is explicitly mentioned. This is because these two [sections] are intended to be subsumed under dedication.
If they were explained separately, they would constitute the essential nature of the two types of practice—benefiting oneself and others—which are also explained individually.
The roots of goodness to be dedicated are now designated by this name; in meaning, they are equal to the dedication of all Buddhas and also constitute the practice for one's own benefit.
Second, the explanation of the characteristics, beginning with "In this Sahā world," is divided into two parts: first, learning from the Original Teacher;

second, applying it to all [others]. Within the former, there are also two: first, clarifying that which is learned; second, distinguishing the learner. Within the former, there are again two: first, clarifying the causal practice; second, [clarifying the resultant practice].
First, from "down to the lowest" (*yāvad adhamā*), the function of the practice of the fruit is distinguished.
Second, from "in this way, all [Buddhas] below," all Buddhas are exemplified. Third, from "in this way" (*evam*) onwards, the inexhaustibility is summarized.

The ninth section, "Constantly Accordant with Sentient Beings," first presents the title: this refers to following the various types and faculties of sentient beings to bring them benefit and accomplishment;

that is, the practice of benefiting others (*parārtha-caryā*). Second, from "Throughout the entire dharma-realm" onwards, the characteristics are explained. This section has two parts: first, the formal exposition;

second, the interrogation and explanation. Within the former, there are also two parts. First, the sentient beings to be accorded with: the four modes of birth and the nine categories of beings, the meaning of which is seen [in the source].
Regarding the Night-Goddess Sarvasattvatrāṇī: from the passage beginning "After this, [beings] of such a kind," I shall explain below that she correctly accords with them.

This section is divided into two parts: first, why she accords with them; second, the detailed explanation of that. The first part is further divided into two: first, to cause the Buddhas to rejoice; second, to increase great compassion. Now, for the first: first, the inquiry. The intent of the inquiry is:
"If the Buddhas themselves should accord with [beings], why is it necessary to accord with those born [as sentient beings]? The intent of the explanation is: "If one accords with sentient beings..."
This constitutes compliance with the Buddha; if one does not comply with sentient beings, the Buddha will not be pleased. Why is this? [The text] poses a challenge below, stating:

"Because it increases great compassion. Within this, there are two parts: first, the challenge; second, the explanation. Now, for the first: the intent of the challenge is to ask, "Since the Buddha and sentient beings are vastly separated, why would complying with sentient beings cause all Buddhas to rejoice?
The intent of the subsequent explanation is to state that the Buddha takes great compassion as his essential nature; if [one does not...]

This follows the sequence of arising. It does not accord with the essence of the Buddha. The text consists of three parts: first, the explanation by way of the Dharma; second, clarification by way of analogy; third, the application of the Dharma. Now, for the first part:
"Great Compassion as its essence" indicates that it is the Great Compassion of the same essence (*sāmbhogika-kāya*). As stated in the *Samantabhadra-caryā-prasthāna-parivarta*:

"When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment," and so on, up to "universally perceiving all sentient beings entering [nirvāṇa]."

Nirvāṇa is of one single nature, because it realizes that all sentient beings are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Thus, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) continues uninterrupted to rescue and protect all.
Second, the following analogy from the "Wilderness" section clarifies this: Saṃsāra is called a "wilderness" because it is utterly remote and provides no refuge.
The failure to produce wholesome dharmas is likened to a desert of sand and gravel. The Buddha’s *bodhi* and its teachings are like the king of great trees; wisdom is...
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is like the branches and leaves; the Bodhisattvas rely upon this training, which is likened to the flowers.
The Buddhas realize this and designate it as the fruit. All sentient beings serve as its roots, and great compassion serves as its water.

Just as water nourishes the tree’s roots so that the flowers and fruits flourish, one contemplates all classes of beings with compassion as the cause for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. The textual composition is thus complete. Next, [the stage of] birth.

The section from "In the vast wilderness of death" (*śmaśāna*) downward consists of four parts: first, the actual synthesis, which briefly omits the branches and leaves; second, the re-examination and detailed explanation from "Why is this so?

(*tat kasya hetoḥ*) downward; third, the conclusion from "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) downward; and fourth, the summary and instruction for understanding from "O son of good family, you... (*kulaputra tvaṃ...*) downward.
"Third, the Bodhisattvas... and so forth concludes the inexhaustibility.

The tenth section, "Furthermore," clarifies the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). First, the title is stated: "Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*) means turning back; "direction" (*nāmanā*) means tending toward.

One turns back the wholesome roots one has cultivated and directs them toward three locations: the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), enlightenment (*bodhi*), and sentient beings. This eliminates the obstacle of narrow-mindedness.
It gives rise to vast goodness. Second, from the initial "prostration" downward, there is the explanation of the characteristics. This section has two parts:

first, clarifying the roots of goodness to be dedicated, which refers to the preceding nine gates; second, from "all of them" downward, it correctly clarifies the dedication itself. Within this, the primary clarification is the dedication toward sentient beings so that they may attain Bodhi—this is the dedication toward Bodhi.
It extends throughout the entire Dharma-realm, its meaning being identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Therefore, the essential requirement is...

Regarding these three: every bodhisattva must necessarily transform those below through great compassion and seek that which is above through great wisdom, while remaining free from the conceptual marks of both sentient beings and bodhi.
Furthermore, these three must necessarily support one another; each possesses all three, and only by doing so is any single one truly established.

This means that in order to realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one must turn toward sentient beings; by transforming sentient beings, one accomplishes one’s own benefit, for it is through the severing of hindrances and the realization of truth that this is achieved.
Furthermore, one turns toward *bodhi*; by swiftly realizing *bodhi* and possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), one severs the two hindrances and only then exhaustively reaches reality.

The remaining two [turnings] should be understood by analogy. To summarize, there are briefly ten points to be grasped by extension: namely, because they rely upon the three dharmas, [the first turning] brings about cessation.

Because of the three paths; because of the purification of the three clusters; because they manifest the three Buddha-natures, accomplish the Three Jewels, unify the three bodies, possess the three virtues, attain the three types of enlightenment, realize the three nirvāṇas, and abide securely in the three kinds of secret treasuries—these are called the "three dharmas."

These are the essence, characteristics, and function, which are also the three types of *prajñā*. That is to say: that which is directed toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) relies on the dharma of essence;

that which is directed toward bodhi relies on the dharma of characteristics; and that which is directed toward sentient beings relies on the dharma of function. The remaining nine sets of three dharmas should be understood in the same sequence accordingly.

The text consists of two parts. First is the aspiration to be free from suffering, to accomplish virtue, and even to attain nirvāṇa. Second, from the passage beginning "If there are sentient beings...

onwards, is the generation of the resolve to take their suffering upon oneself. Since suffering arises from karma, how can it be taken away? Briefly, there are seven points. The first is the arousal of the compassionate intention (*karuṇā-āśaya*).

1. Having transcended the mundane realm, one may not necessarily be able to [physically] undergo such matters. 2. By practicing various ascetic austerities, one later becomes a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings;

this is called "substituting for suffering. 3. By retaining delusions to moisten rebirth, one accepts a body subject to existence and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them not to commit evil;
when the cause perishes and the effect is extinguished, this is called "substitution. 4. If one sees sentient beings committing deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), one should...

They undergo great suffering. There is no other expedient means; it is necessary to sacrifice one's own life and fall into hell oneself in order to cause them to be liberated from their suffering—this is precisely what is meant by "substitution.
Fifth, from the moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one constantly dwells in the evil realms, even during times of famine, becoming a great fish for the sake of others.
This is precisely what is meant by "substitution. The six great vows and suffering are both identical to true suchness (*tathatā*).

Now, by means of these great vows that are themselves true suchness, one secretly reaches the suffering that is itself true suchness. Taking the seven dharma-realms as one's own body, there is no distinction between self and others; when sentient beings undergo suffering, they are themselves the Bodhisattva.

Among the seven meanings mentioned above, the first consists solely of the aspirational intention (*āśaya*); the next two serve as conditions; the next two constitute actual substitution; and the final two...

This is the contemplation of principle. However, it is only by means of having an object of focus that one can truly act as a substitute. Third, "In this way, the bodhisattvas cultivate... and below is the summary of their inexhaustibility.
Fourth, "Good son, this is called... and below is the conclusion on the benefits, intended to bring about understanding.

Thus, the twelve verses that follow all praise the superior qualities of the Sūtra and should be divided into four parts; first, five verses praise rebirth in the Pure Land.
The next two verses praise the merit of hearing this sutra. The following four verses generally manifest the five fruits. The final verse praises the ultimate fruit;
therein, the characters "願我" (wàn wǒ) should be changed to "是人" (shì rén), at which point there will be no confusion.

For now, we shall follow the text as it stands, for the meaning can be understood from the text itself. Not being born in the Flower Treasury World (*Huá zàng*) but being born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Jí lè*) involves, in brief, four [points].

First, because he possesses an object of cognition; second, because he desires to lead sentient beings to take refuge in a single source of reliance; third, because he is not separate from the Flower Treasury World;
and fourth, because he is the original teacher himself.

[○@] The second section consists of one verse. It provides a general summary of the ten gates, concluding the inexhaustible [qualities]. It also specifically corresponds to the ten vows and the ten inexhaustible phrases.

The twenty verses on the "directions and locations" (dig-deśa) that follow consist of seven verses. These summarize and manifest the supreme virtues of the sūtra; the text is further divided into two parts.
There are first two verses that praise the previously mentioned benefits of hearing [the teaching]. The subsequent five verses praise and generally manifest the benefits of all practices.
The prose commentary has three parts: first, a general explanation of the five fruits; second, a specific explanation of the fruit of the Pure Land; and third, the fruit of ultimate bodhi.
Regarding birth in the Pure Land, this was already addressed within the previous vows; here, however, we shall summarize only the beginning and the end, dividing them into two parts.

The first four verses praise the five fruits in general, while the final verse praises the ultimate fruit. Now, for the first part: the full text contains all five fruits. The first verse praises the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*); the next verse praises the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*);
the next verse praises the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*); the next half-verse praises the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*); and the latter half [of that verse]...
The first verse concerns the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). The final verse praises the ultimate fruit (*niṣṭhā-phala*), which may be understood accordingly.

The third section consists of three verses praising the conclusion and exhorting the acceptance and upholding [of the teaching]. The first half-verse concludes the various practices mentioned previously;
the next one and a half verses further elucidate the supreme benefits; and the final verse concludes by dedicating [the merit] so that it may reach all sentient beings.
△ Third, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" onwards, the conclusion of the praise is established; this is the arising of the meaning.

This assembly has entered meditative absorption, and no Buddha has yet spoken. The ancient masters collectively established that the Buddha causes [the assembly] to realize [the truth] instantaneously.

◎ The third major section. From “At that time, the World-Honored One” onwards is the section on the dissemination of the teaching (*pariṇāmanā*). This section has two parts: first, pointing to the Dharma taught; second, the assembly receiving and upholding it. Regarding the first:
having already been spoken to Samantabhadra, this constitutes the conclusion of the meaning; now it is said to be “spoken by the Buddha.”
This meaning also arises from the following intent, which seeks to encompass everything in its entirety. There are two aspects to this:

first, within this specific assembly, although the Buddha is the presiding master, because all virtuous friends are subsumed under the general category, they are also considered to be the Buddha’s teaching.

Second, it encompasses all nine assemblies, as [the teachings] do not arise apart from the King of Bodhi Trees, but are taught instantaneously and all at once throughout all places. As previously seen, Samantabhadra is present at the Bodhi...

The Prologue. This section subsumes the derivative into the fundamental and encompasses the derivative within the fundamental; it is spoken by the Buddha. Following the passage on Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, there are two parts:
first, the assembly that receives and upholds [the teaching], and second, the general manifestation of that reception and upholding.

Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the listing of the bodhisattvas; second, the listing of the śrāvakas; and third, the listing of various other classes. Now, for the first [the bodhisattvas]: the text contains...

There are four categories. The first two categories consist mostly of those present at this assembly. The third, Samantabhadra, by his nature is always in attendance and thus pervades all nine assemblies.
The fourth consists of those gathered from various worlds; its scope encompasses two meanings: first, the newly arrived multitude who have come from afar as mentioned previously;
second, those gathered throughout the nine assemblies, both from distant and near locations. However, there is no textual basis for this in the Sanskrit original. Second, the two [great...].

The passage beginning with "The wise Śāriputra" below enumerates the assembly of śrāvakas, who are restricted solely to this particular gathering. The two passages following "All the various beings in the world" enumerate the assembly of miscellaneous classes.
The phrase "Having heard what the Buddha taught, they were all greatly rejoiced, and they believed, accepted, and practiced it" demonstrates their faith and acceptance.

This applies generally to all the preceding assemblies; however, this particular circulation specifically pertains to the ninth assembly. If it were to apply to all nine assemblies, there would be no contradiction in principle.

Why must this necessarily encompass all nine assemblies? Furthermore, according to the previous precedents, even after the teaching of the Dharma, elements such as the manifestation of the scene and the confirmation of realization are still lacking.
Nevertheless, following the Sanskrit text itself, it possesses both a beginning and an end.

In the past, our Buddha, throughout an ocean of great kalpas, Practiced austerities for the sake of sentient beings, Realizing this inconceivable gate of liberation. How fortunate to hear it and be able to praise and expound it!
May these supreme causes all be offered as a dedication, That the precious reign may endure in peace and the imperial way flourish.
The Four Graces, the hundred officials, and all sentient beings together realize the Mysterious Gate and equalize their wisdom with the ocean.
(From the *New Translation of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary* by Zhenyuan, Scroll Ten).
Within these ten scrolls of this commentary, the first five scrolls were obtained through divine inspiration at Kiyomizudera.

Having borrowed the brushwork of various individuals to complete the five volumes of one section of this scripture—which had previously been incomplete—I have dedicated them to be permanently enshrined in the Nyoirin-in.
This year, as the Imperial Palace was newly constructed, I have undertaken the task of carving [the woodblocks] and casting the Buddha images;
thus, I have redoubled my resolve for transcription, hoping that the Buddhist teachings may be perpetuated and the branches of the scholarly grove may flourish within the Buddha-hall.

Though this work may not be imperishable and its fragrant flowers may not endure without decline, it is here that the *Guang jing* (Sutra of Light) is preserved. If one merely relies upon what is hoped for, it is difficult to find fault; thus, I have inscribed this title outside the book.
Although I fear my calligraphy is poor, I do so solely to cultivate karmic connections with those who look up to it.
On the sixteenth day of the ninth month of the Eikyō era,
Kongo Busshi Chōken (born in the tenth year of Shōwa at the age of sixteen),
recorded this colophon.
The aforementioned twenty fascicles of the *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) by Fazang of the Zhengyuan era have been missing from the Tripitaka for many years.
In the Jisi year of the Shaoxing era, the Great Master Yuanzheng Yihé obtained them from Liang Gong, the Imperial Pharmacist Dinglai, at Wujiang.
He then raised funds through collective sponsorship to carve woodblocks, completing twelve fascicles.
The late Lord Prefect Liangzhong, while visiting the Master, discussed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and obtained a commentary to read;
he could not put it down from his hands. Joyfully, he requested the Master to complete the remaining eight fascicles and also sought the essential outline (*kārikā*).
Before long, however, the Lord Prefect passed away, and neither was completed. We, Pu and others, feel heartache and shed tears of blood as we pursue the realization of our predecessor’s will.

I have urgently ordered this to be carved and printed so that, upon encountering the mourning period for my parents, I may provide meals for the Sangha and offer universal alms, thereby propagating the Buddha’s teachings and universally benefiting future generations. May the merit and blessings of this act assist all who take refuge in it to transcend to the Pure Land.
On the eleventh day of the tenth month in the twenty-fifth year of the Shaoxing era, the orphaned and grieving son.
Written with tears of blood by Pu Jun as an offering for irrigation and cleansing.
